- Mechanistic models predict that resistance increases and leakage current rise non-monotonically under bias–temperature–humidity stress due to trap formation and void growth; typical onset occurs within weeks to months and accelerates with cycling, producing measurable efficiency loss in circuits. <cite id="74b7b265-2">Electromigration-void distributions evolve with time, and humidity-driven nucleation accelerates resistance change modeled via analytic distributions leading to performance loss; experimental lifetimes reflect this growth.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-0">Water interactions with dielectrics and metals introduce time-varying traps/leakage paths, causing stepwise or continuous degradation in switching and conduction losses.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-6">Long-term storage data show progressive corrosion and chemical degradation driven by humidity over months to years, with failure modes linked to component materials.</cite>
- Real systems show annualized assembly-level degradation dominated by board-level failures (solder joints, bondlines) and package dielectric breakdown under humidity; replacing hygroscopic underfills with polymer-ceramic or hydrophobic adhesives and applying conformal coatings can reduce the rate-of-change by an order of magnitude. <cite id="fe435fbd-1">Environmental reliability analyses tie humidity and moisture to performance degradation timelines in electronics, underscoring mitigation benefits for shelf-life and field reliability.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-8">Moisture-driven corrosion is a primary cause of yield loss and post-delivery failures, with time scales governed by diffusion-limited reactions and cycling duty cycles.</cite>

2) Photovoltaics
- Baseline degradation in mature PV is typically ~0.5–1% per year; humidity raises this rate via moisture ingress, corrosion, and PID. <cite id="0f3fe608-1">Field-degraded PV modules commonly show 0.6–0.7%/yr power loss under benign climates due to multi-physics mechanisms including moisture effects.</cite> <cite id="aa1e7faa-7">Reviews attribute expected PV lifetime and degradation to humidity/radiation/temperature drivers that accelerate material and interfacial failures in field conditions.</cite>
- Humid microclimates and corrosion-prone materials can show much higher slopes: <cite id="0f3fe608-5">PID may reach 30% loss in extreme cases; mature PV generally shows 0.5–1%/yr, with humid exposure pushing losses to higher percent-per-year under un-mitigated designs.</cite> <cite id="0f3fe608-3">Severe humid environments can exhibit 8–15% annual performance degradation without adequate encapsulation and mitigation, versus ~60–70% cumulative over decades for other failure modes when unchecked (illustrating mechanism specificity).</cite>
- PV materials and interfaces modulate humidity damage: EVA yellowing and hydrolysis reduce transmittance and cohesion, metal grids corrode and crack, and backsheets delaminate—each adding series resistance and recombination losses that accumulate over years under tropical to arid humid cycles. <cite id="aa1e7faa-2">Moisture in EVA drives corrosion, delamination, and discoloration, directly linking environmental humidity to electrical and optical efficiency loss paths.</cite> <cite id="aa1e7faa-3">Accelerated simulations in cool humid climates replicate one-year degradation and highlight formulation- and design-sensitive pathways.</cite>

# Interpreting the Coupling of Humidity and Material Properties

- Diffusion–reaction control. Time constants for moisture ingress scale with RH, water vapor permeability of encapsulation, and diffusion solubility in each layer; reaction rates (hydrolysis, corrosion, trap generation) set activation energies that dominate whether efficiency is stable or drifts. <cite id="74b7b265-5">Moisture-related breakdown and leakage in Cu/oxide layers are included in reliability models that couple diffusion with electromigration- and stress-driven damage.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-0">The water–device interface governs adsorption kinetics and trap formation; materials with low hygroscopicity and robust interfaces reduce these rates.</cite>
- Hygromechanical coupling. Hygroexpansion deltas and adhesion hysteresis under humidity accelerate kink growth, delamination, and corrosion, producing stepwise efficiency drops synchronized with thermal cycles. <cite id="74b7b265-8">Electromigration, mechanical stresses, and humidity are interdependent drivers in interconnect reliability; delamination and resistance increases correlate with hygromechanical fatigue.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-6">Electrostatically shielded assemblies still degrade via moisture-assisted chemical pathways; adhesives and bondlines are particularly vulnerable over extended humidity exposure.</cite>
- Electrochemical pathways. Higher ionic conductivity from water uptake increases leakage and electrochemical dissolution; materials with lower oxygen/water solubility, conformal barrier layers, and corrosion-resistant overplates maintain lower time-dependent losses. <cite id="aa1e7faa-1">PID losses increase over long exposures in humid climates because moisture permeates over time to create leakage routes between biased and grounded contacts.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-1">Moisture condensation during duty cycles drives corrosion and performance loss; encapsulation integrity and desiccation at shipment/settling matter for time to first failure.</cite>

# Mitigation: Materials and Process Levers

- Barrier and surface treatments. Replace hygroscopic underfills with low-k hydrophobic dielectrics; add diffusion barriers (SiN, oxide-nitride-oxide) and moisture-scavenging additives; apply conformal hydrophobic coatings (e.g., acrylic/silicone/parylene) to contacts and bondlines. <cite id="74b7b265-5">Integrating barriers in Cu/low-k interconnect reliability models reduces moisture-driven breakdown and leakage; practical stacks add diffusion blocks and interface oxynitrides.</cite> <cite id="0f3fe608-5">PV encapsulation/bi-potential architectures that suppress PID deliver large energy gains by interrupting moisture-enhanced leakage paths.</cite>
- Design for hygromechanics. Match CTE across layers, provide standoff features to avoid capillary condensation at pads/edges, and use corrosion-resistant metallurgies and plating; simulate hygroexpansion and contact angle changes over RH–temperature windows. <cite id="fe435fbd-6">Design choices that limit hygroscopic absorption and manage adhesion reduce long-term corrosion/chemical degradation rates observed in storage and field use.</cite> <cite id="74b7b265-8">Layout/stack designs that minimize electromigration and hygromechanical coupling improve lifetime under humid operation.</cite>
- Environmental control. Bake-out and conformal coating before sealing; humidity-aware packaging and sealing integrity; dehumidified storage and operation in high-humidity regions; monitoring and conditioning of PV tilt to limit dew formation. <cite id="fe435fbd-0">Controlling water forms (adsorbed, capillary, dissolved) reduces performance degradation and reliability risks across device types.</cite> <cite id="0f3fe608-3">In humid regions (>70% RH), annual degradation without mitigation can reach 8–15%, highlighting the value of controlled environments and improved encapsulation.</cite>

# Modeling and Prediction Horizons

- Microscopic models relate RH, vapor permeance, solubility, and reaction kinetics to time-dependent leakage paths and contact resistivity; macroscopic circuit/IV-circuit models translate to Voc, J0, FF, and PCE or to logic delay/leakage power. <cite id="74b7b265-2">Electromigration-void models with diffusion-informed nucleation capture resistance drift timelines under bias–temperature stress; adding humidity terms for surface reaction improves fit to data.</cite> <cite id="fe435fbd-0">Trap generation and interface resistance evolution with water exposure support physics-based parameterization for life-cycle or reliability simulations.</cite>
- Empirical calibration with field/simulated-accelerated data anchors slopes in climate-specific humidity and material property sets; risk stratification is by permeance (barrier stacks), hygroexpansion (stack design), and ionic conductivity (encapsulant/metal chemistry). <cite id="0f3fe608-1">PV field studies calibrate annual degradation 0.6–0.7% per year and attribute climate differences to humidity-driven mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="aa1e7faa-3">Accelerated-humidity simulations replicate one-year losses, letting material-property levers be tuned to predict multi-year behavior.</cite>

# Practical Implications and Remaining Gaps

- For a given device/package or PV module, tripling humidity from 30% to 70% often increases annual efficiency loss from ~0.5–1% to >2–5% or higher if materials have high permeability or poor corrosion protection, with non-linear jumps when encapsulation breaches or PID paths form. <cite id="0f3fe608-3">Humidity >70% associates with 8–15% annual degradation in severe, un-mitigated cases, consistent with leakage and encapsulant failure mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="0f3fe608-5">PID-induced losses can be an order of magnitude higher (up to 30%) than typical background losses when moisture-assisted leakage dominates.</cite>
- Key uncertainties include the long-term evolution of polymer dielectric constants/leakage with repeated hygrothermal cycles and the latent-time to PID initiation under partial encapsulation; quantitative models that couple hygroexpansion, hygroelectricity, and corrosion kinetics remain an active research area. <cite id="fe435fbd-0">Reviews call for integrating multi-physical water effects into device reliability models to capture efficiency drift and failure initiation accurately over time.</cite>

# Quick Decision Rules (for design/qualification)

- If the system operates above ~60% RH: choose low-permittivity, low-permeability dielectrics with robust interfaces; add barrier stacks; apply conformal coating; verify stack CTE match; avoid hygroscopic underfills; qualify moisture bake and rework procedures. Expect to cut annual efficiency loss from >1–3% down toward ~0.6–0.7% if baseline materials and climate match. <cite id="74b7b265-5">Barrier-integrated Cu/low-k models show significantly reduced moisture-driven leakage and breakdown when stacks are optimized.</cite> <cite id="0f3fe608-1">Baseline PV climates around 0.6–0.7% per year illustrate attainable goals with robust encapsulation.</cite>
- For PV in humid microclimates: add PID-resistant encapsulation and bi-potential architectures, increase humidity-aware operation (tilt, cooling), and inspect/bi-loc voltage taps periodically. <cite id="0f3fe608-5">PID-resistant technologies and humidity management produce sizable energy gains by suppressing moisture-enhanced leakage paths.</cite>
- Monitor signature degradation modes: rising DC leakage/Rds-on, contact bump lift, pad corrosion, EVA yellowing/blisters, and Voc/FF decline under bias/temperature/humidity stress—these indicate moisture-driven aging is active and require materials/process re-tuning. <cite id="fe435fbd-0">Moisture-driven trap creation and interface resistance increase manifest as DC and RF performance losses that accumulate over time.</cite> <cite id="aa1e7faa-1">PID diagnostics (e.g., reduced Voc under contact to ground) reveal moisture-assisted leakage paths consistent with high RH exposure.</cite>

Summary

Changing the gas ratio shifts reaction pathways between CO(H2)-derived and CO2‑only routes, modulates catalyst surface chemistry (adsorbed intermediates like CO, CO2−, H*, and CHx), and adjusts thermodynamic equilibrium, which jointly determine methane production and selectivity. Across relevant systems (DRM, steam reforming, methanation/Sabatier, Fischer–Tropsch), increasing H2 relative to CO or CO2 generally favors CH4 formation from CO hydrogenation, while introducing water suppresses CO2 hydrogenation and methane formation when CO is absent, and tuning CO levels via RWGS balances methane vs CO by-products. <cite id="0cf8a500-3">Dry reforming of methane produces syngas via CO2 + CH4 → 2CO + 2H2 (ΔH = +247 kJ/mol), inherently yielding H2:CO ≈ 1</cite> and <cite id="0cf8a500-8">MDR generates syngas with H2:CO ≈ 1</cite>, whereas <cite id="0cf8a500-2">processes targeting FTS methanol often deliver H2:CO ≈ 2.1–2.3</cite> to favor C‑number growth. <cite id="d11a52ca-0">CO2 methanation via Sabatier uses H2 with CO2 to produce CH4</cite>, but <cite id="99441fa9-3">increasing temperature promotes CO formation via the reverse water–gas shift (RWGS), decreasing methane selectivity</cite> and <cite id="d11a52ca-1">water presence and low-temperature operation raise CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity</cite>.

How gas ratios affect selectivity and yield: mechanism-by-mechanism

Syngas H2/CO ratio (Fischer–Tropsch/dry reforming integration)

- Low H2/CO (≈1) near DRM stoichiometry: Syngas favors CO-rich pathways. In FTS, a 1:1 H2:CO feed promotes water–gas shift–type equilibria and CO- rather than H2‑limited chemistry, reducing formation of longer-chain hydrocarbons and increasing methane via CO hydrogenation. <cite id="0cf8a500-3">DRM yields H2:CO = 1</cite>, and <cite id="0cf8a500-8">co‑production of syngas with H2:CO ≈ 1 is characteristic</cite>. <cite id="0cf8a500-1">Experiments spanning wide H2/CO/CO2 mixtures in low-temperature FTS demonstrate sensitivity of product distribution to syngas composition</cite>.

- High H2/CO (≈2–2.3) for FTS: Excess H2 suppresses CO2 incorporation and channel-selective growth, increasing olefin/paraffin formation and lowering methane, consistent with industrial integration targets for methanol/FT. <cite id="0cf8a500-2">An H2/CO ≈ 2.1–2.3 syngas was reported favorable for methanol and low-temperature FTS</cite>. This aligns with the DRM–FT coupling rationale: <cite id="0cf8a500-8">MDR supplies H2:CO ≈ 1 feedstock that can be upgraded to H2/CO ≈ 2 for FTS via water–gas shift</cite>.

Implication: Raising H2 beyond CO shifts selectivity from CH4 to C2+ in FTS-like conditions; conversely, H2-deficient feeds (H2/CO < 1) tend to increase methane evolution through CO hydrogenation on Ru/Co sites. <cite id="0cf8a500-1">Wide-range H2/CO/CO2 syngas mixtures in FTS alter product distribution</cite> and <cite id="d11a52ca-5">Ni/Co systems catalyze CO2 and H2 partial conversion into CH4 with tunable selectivity</cite>.

Steam-to-carbon (H2O/C) and autothermal regimes

- Steam reforming and DRM balance: Increasing steam (H2O/C) drives CO dissociation and H2 formation, elevating H2 and diluting CO; this suppresses CO disproportionation and methane formation via CO hydrogenation on metallic sites, while favoring syngas formation. <cite id="0cf8a500-5">FA decomposition combined with steam reforming of methane can adjust H2:CO ratio during syngas production</cite> and <cite id="0cf8a500-9">co‑controlled Ni particle size yields high CO2 and CH4 conversions and H2/CO ≈ 0.9 at 850 °C</cite>. In DRM, <cite id="0cf8a500-4">CO2/CH4 > 1 increases CH4 conversion via RWGS but reduces H2 selectivity</cite>.

- Autothermal/partial oxidation trade-off: Adding O2 (partial oxidation) boosts CO2/CO selectivity and heat release, which can raise CO levels (favoring methane via CO hydrogenation if O is limited) but also shifts RWGS equilibrium at higher T, lowering CH4. <cite id="99441fa9-1">Temperatures above ~450 °C increase CO via RWGS and decrease methane yield in CO2 methanation</cite> and <cite id="99441fa9-5">Ru-based methanation over Fe‑Cu/CeO2–Al2O3 converts CO2 deeply but generates ~100% CO selectivity due to RWGS, diminishing CH4</cite>.

Water-to-CO2 ratio (methanation/Sabatier vs CO2 hydrogenation)

- H2/CO2 with limited CO: In CO methanation, methane is produced from CO and H2; without CO or with excess H2 relative to CO2, the thermodynamic drive for CH4 formation from CO2 decreases and CO2 preferentially hydrogenates to methanol/formaldehyde, lowering CH4. <cite id="d11a52ca-0">CO2 methanation is a well-known Sabatier route to CH4 from CO2 + 3 H2 → CH4 + H2O</cite> but <cite id="99441fa9-3">CO formation via RWGS competes and lowers CH4 selectivity; higher temperatures exacerbate this</cite>.

- Water addition on Ru/Co/Ni catalysts: Water suppresses CO2 methanation and shifts hydrogenation toward CO species conversion; on Ru systems, CO methanation is favored over CO2 methanation, so increasing H2O increases CO2 conversion to CO (RWGS) and then to CH4 (on Ru) with high carbon selectivity (>99%). <cite id="d11a52ca-1">Low-temperature Sabatier operation with adequate H2/CO2 and water achieves high CO2 conversion and methane selectivity</cite> and <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru catalysts can maintain high CO2 conversion and >99% carbon selectivity to methane via CO pathways</cite>.

CO presence and suppression (selectivity lever)

- Suppressing CO formation: Lowering temperatures or limiting CO2/CO2* coverage (via H2-rich feeds, excess H2, or Ru preconversion) suppresses RWGS and raises CH4 selectivity from CO methanation. <cite id="99441fa9-1">Raising temperature increases CO via RWGS and decreases methane yield</cite>, while <cite id="99441fa9-3">Ru‑SA catalysts sustain high CO2 conversion and >99% carbon selectivity to methane</cite> by preferentially converting CO.

- Excess CO with limited H2: Selectivity drops toward CO-rich gaseous products; catalysts like Fe–Cu/CeO2 show CO2 conversion ~40% with nearly 100% CO selectivity via RWGS, so CH4 formation is suppressed. <cite id="99441fa9-4">Fe–Cu/CeO2–Al2O3 converts CO2 to ~40% with ~100% CO selectivity, minimizing methane</cite>.

Catalyst-specific notes

- Ru for COx hydrogenation: Ru favors CO hydrogenation to CH4, with very high carbon selectivity on Ru/SA; water and CO content control branching. <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru/SA exhibits high CO2 conversion with >99% carbon selectivity to methane</cite>; <cite id="99441fa9-5">Ru-based systems show pronounced RWGS activity, generating CO from CO2 that then methanates with high carbon selectivity</cite>.

- Ni/Co for CO2 methanation: Ni–Co catalysts exhibit tunable selectivity to methane and CO by adjusting H2/CO2 ratios and water. <cite id="d11a52ca-5">Co is active for CO2 methanation; methane selectivity depends on the H2/CO2 and CO content due to partial conversions of CO2 and H2 to CH4</cite>.

System-level design levers and trade-offs

- Raising H2/CO by coupling DRM + shift: For downstream FTS, first produce H2/CO ≈ 1 syngas via DRM and then run an RWGS/water–gas shift to push H2/CO ≈ 2, reducing methane and favoring C‑chain growth. <cite id="0cf8a500-8">MDR yields H2:CO ≈ 1</cite> and can be upgraded to H2/CO ≈ 2 for low‑T FTS. <cite id="0cf8a500-2">H2/CO ≈ 2.1–2.3 is favorable for FTS/MeOH</cite>.

- Methanation process design: To maximize methane, supply CO with H2 and suppress RWGS by (i) CO-free feed, (ii) Ru-based catalysts to convert CO→CH4, or (iii) operate below RWGS‑activating temperatures and maintain water to maintain H2/CO balance. <cite id="99441fa9-1">Above ~450 °C, RWGS increases CO and decreases CH4 yield</cite>; <cite id="d11a52ca-1">low-temperature, water‑rich Sabatier conditions enhance CO2 conversion and methane selectivity</cite>.

- DRM feed ratio (CO2/CH4): Increasing CO2/CH4 increases CH4 conversion via RWGS but reduces H2 selectivity, raising the H2/CO below unity and shifting away from FTS favorability; lowering CO2/CH4 favors H2 and suppresses RWGS. <cite id="0cf8a500-4">CO2/CH4 > 1 raised CH4 conversion but lowered H2 selectivity via RWGS; CO2/CH4 < 1 favored H2 and suppressed RWGS</cite>. <cite id="0cf8a500-9">At 850 °C, controlled co‑operation yielded H2/CO ≈ 0.9 with >90% CH4 and CO2 conversions</cite>.

Practical guidance and when methane goes up or down

- Methane increases when:
  - H2/CO or H2/CO2 is high and CO is converted (Ru/Co/Ni catalysts), enabling CO + 3 H2 → CH4 or CO2 + 4 H2 → CH4 + 2 H2O at suitable T/P and water. <cite id="d11a52ca-0">Sabatier directly produces CH4 from CO2 + H2</cite>; <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru systems achieve >99% carbon selectivity to CH4 from CO pathways</cite>.
  - CO2/CH4 is high in DRM, driving RWGS to CO then CH4. <cite id="0cf8a500-4">CO2/CH4 > 1 raises CH4 conversion via RWGS</cite>, with <cite id="0cf8a500-9">H2/CO ≈ 0.9 achievable while converting >90% CH4/CO2</cite>.
  - Temperature is low or water is present to suppress RWGS, channeling CO2→CO→CH4 on Ru/Co. <cite id="d11a52ca-1">Low-temperature Sabatier yields high CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity</cite>; <cite id="99441fa9-3">Ru-SA maintains high CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity >99% in presence of CO</cite>.

- Methane decreases when:
  - H2/CO is low or oxygen/partial oxidation raises CO2/CO, favoring CO disproportionation and CO2 hydrogenation to oxygenated intermediates (CO2→COOH/CHO) rather than CH4. <cite id="0cf8a500-3">H2:CO ≈ 1 from DRM is marginally favorable for CO hydrogenation</cite>; lowering H2 via steam-to-carbon dilution suppresses methane formation.
  - Reverse water–gas shift is thermodynamically favored at higher T or CO2-rich conditions, converting CO to CO2 and tying up reducing power in CO2 reduction to CO rather than CH4, or shifting equilibrium away from CH4. <cite id="99441fa9-1">Temperature increase via RWGS reduces methane yield</cite>.
  - Excess CO with insufficient H2 or catalyst preference for CO conversion: CO methanation competes with CO2 hydrogenation to oxygenates; selectivity drops. <cite id="99441fa9-4">Fe–Cu/CeO2–Al2O3 yields ~100% CO selectivity from CO2 conversion, suppressing methane</cite>.

Putting it together: a ratio-based tuning playbook

- To increase methane:
  - Use H2-rich relative to CO/CO2 (for Sabatier or Ru/Co methanation), keep H2/CO2 in a range that favors CO2→CH4 over CO2→CO, maintain water and low-to-moderate temperature to suppress RWGS, and choose Ru/Co catalysts that prefer CO/CO2 hydrogenation. <cite id="d11a52ca-0">Sabatier converts CO2 + H2 to CH4</cite> and <cite id="d11a52ca-1">water-rich, low-temperature operation raises selectivity</cite>; <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru-SA achieves >99% carbon selectivity to methane</cite>.

- To decrease methane (suppress to raise syngas/H2):
  - Lower H2/CO by steam-to-carbon or O2 addition (autothermal), increase CO2/CO ratio in DRM/FTS, or operate hot enough to activate RWGS; favor FT-ready H2/CO ≈ 2. <cite id="0cf8a500-2">FTS favors H2/CO ≈ 2.1–2.3</cite>, as achieved by <cite id="0cf8a500-8">DRM-to-FT coupling via shift</cite> and <cite id="99441fa9-1">RWGS activation at higher temperature</cite>.

Edge cases and catalyst dependence

- Ru vs Ni/Co: Ru systems typically yield >99% carbon selectivity to CH4 on CO methanation, whereas Ni–Co systems show mixed CO2-to-CH4 and CO formation depending on ratio and water. <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru catalysts achieve >99% carbon selectivity to methane</cite> and <cite id="d11a52ca-5">Ni/Co catalysts exhibit tunable methane selectivity with CO2 and H2 partial conversion</cite>.

- Dry reforming strategy: tune CO2/CH4 to target H2/CO; above unity favors CH4 conversion but lowers H2 selectivity; below unity shifts to higher H2 and lower RWGS, improving syngas quality. <cite id="0cf8a500-4">CO2/CH4 > 1 increases CH4 conversion via RWGS but reduces H2 selectivity; CO2/CH4 < 1 favors H2 and suppresses RWGS</cite>.

Microkinetic intuition

- Adsorption competition on metallic sites: Excess H2 lowers CO dissociative chemisorption and promotes CO2 activation to CO then CH4; water promotes CO formation and suppresses CO2 methanation until CO is converted on Ru. <cite id="99441fa9-5">On Ru/Al2O3, CO2 is converted to CO via RWGS (adsorbed bicarbonate) and then CH4 on Ru, explaining high CO selectivity</cite>; <cite id="99441fa9-3">CO accumulates under high T, reducing CH4 selectivity</cite>.

Actionable takeaway

- If your goal is more methane: enrich H2 relative to CO/CO2 and control CO chemistry with Ru/Co catalysts, maintain water and moderate temperatures, and suppress RWGS so CO/CO2 hydrogenates to CH4. <cite id="d11a52ca-0">H2 + CO2 → CH4 (Sabatier)</cite>, <cite id="d11a52ca-1">water-rich, low-temperature operation yields high selectivity</cite>, <cite id="d11a52ca-3">Ru systems show >99% carbon selectivity to methane</cite>.

- If your goal is less methane (more syngas/Fts): lower H2/CO via steam reforming or autothermal oxidation, increase CO2/CH4 in DRM to drive RWGS and raise H2/CO below FT targets (≈1–2), and operate at temperatures where RWGS dominates to reduce methane. <cite id="0cf8a500-2">H2/CO ≈ 2.1–2.3 favors FTS</cite>, <cite id="0cf8a500-8">MDR provides ≈1 H2:CO for shift to FT</cite>, while <cite id="99441fa9-5">RWGS activity at higher T reduces methane yield</cite>.

Summary

- Metal species on catalyst surfaces—defined by their oxidation state, coordination (M–O–M bridges, singly-coordinated M*), dispersion, and the host’s electronic structure—govern how molecular oxygen is split into radicals (•O, O–•, •O2–) and how hydroxyl/other oxidizing species (•OH, RO•) are generated. These radical pools then set the rates and selectivity of oxidation via Eley–Rideal or Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanisms, often with measurable changes in turnover frequency (TOF) and activation energy as sites evolve under reaction conditions. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies are important to improve performance of reducible metal oxide catalysts</cite> <cite id="1773a134-6">The nature of lattice oxygen anions and metal–oxygen bonding underlies heterogeneous partial oxidation catalysis</cite>.

How metal species generate radicals and oxidants

1) Lattice oxygen activation and metal–oxygen redox
- Isolated cationic metal centers and oxygen vacancies activate O2 and split water/peroxides, producing •O, O–•, •O2–, and hydroxyl radicals that oxidize substrates. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies accelerate surface reactions in reducible oxides</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancies can significantly improve NH3-SCR by enhancing adsorption/activation of NO and NH3, consistent with increased formation of reactive oxygen and hydroxyl species at defect sites</cite>. 
- On Mn-based oxides, mixed-valence Mn–O–Mn bridges and Mn2+ sites act as Lewis acidic centers that polarize O2 and assist one-electron transfer; Mn–O–Mn cleavage generates Mn3+–OH/•OOH/Mn4+ species that can release •OH/•O. <cite id="1773a134-5">Mn oxidation state and lattice oxygen in Mn-based TiO2 control low-temperature NH3-SCR, highlighting the role of Mn–O redox in NO and NH3 activation</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-6">Manganese-based oxides are effective for VOC oxidation, with performance linked to their structure and redox properties</cite>.

2) Transition metals bridging O2 and supports (V, Fe, Cu)
- Vanadium pentoxide on TiO2 provides adjacent V5+/V4+ centers that shuttle oxygen atoms to adsorbed NH3/NO, producing •NO, N-containing radicals, and N2O/N2 via recombination; operando DRIFTS resolves NO2−/N2O intermediates and stepwise electron transfer across vanadium oxide motifs. <cite id="80ef33dc-0">In situ DRIFTS over V2O5/TiO2 reveals SCR intermediates and mechanisms including electron transfer on vanadium oxide species</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-5">Over V2O5(WO3)/TiO2, conversion proceeds via two surface vanadium atoms, evidencing M–O–M redox coupling in SCR</cite>.
- Iron oxides and Fe3+ cations catalyze Fenton-like H2O2 decomposition to •OH under aqueous conditions, showing how divalent/trimetallic iron species polarize and split peroxides; heterogeneous analogs on supports show comparable roles for surface Fe(III)-hydroxide/oxo species. <cite id="7fa5b0c2-2">Iron salts (Fe2+) catalyze H2O2 decomposition to generate hydroxyl radicals in aqueous Fenton-like chemistry</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-5">Dual roles of iron oxides in hydroxyl radical generation in presence of different organic functional groups</cite>.
- Copper redox pairs (Cu+/Cu0 on oxides) and cupric centers can also transiently generate •O or •OOH via O2 reduction and subsequent electron transfer to Cu+; while often secondary to Mn/V sites in NOx/CO oxidations, they participate in hydrocarbon oxidation pathways when present as singly-coordinated surface cations. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies act as radical-generating sites in reducible oxides, consistent with Cu+/Cu0 participation in O2 activation</cite>.

3) Ceria and redox-buffered acidic sites (Ce, W)
- Ceria provides mobile oxygen storage and variable valence Ce4+/Ce3+ that stabilize O–• and •OOH intermediates and supply electrons to surface radicals. In Mn–Ce systems, charge-transfer to Mn2+ at Brønsted acidic sites enhances hydroxyl radical initiation. <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Mn-based SCR improves with oxygen vacancies that enhance surface activation, illustrating how redox-active supports tune radical formation</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-4">V2O5/TiO2 mixed with WO3/MoO3 are widely used in SCR; promoters adjust acid/redox properties and pathway coupling</cite>.
- Operando perspectives emphasize coupling between vanadium redox, NO and NH3 adsorption, and radical recombination; mechanisms vary across compositions, but the unifying principle is that metal–oxygen bridge redox and oxygen vacancy density govern radical pools. <cite id="80ef33dc-2">A perspective reviews SCR mechanisms (Langmuir–Hinshelwood vs Eley–Rideal) for NH3-SCR to N2/H2O, highlighting roles of NO and NH3 surface radicals</cite>.

4) Metal–support synergy tuning hydroxyl radical abundance (Au/TiO2-like)
- When metal cations are weakly interacting on acidic oxides, surface hydroxyl pools and •OH yields can be substantial, enabling radical-mediated oxidation without excessive CO coverage poisoning typical of Langmuir–Hinshelwood kinetics. Studies of supported Mn2+ and Cu centers show metal–support charge transfer lowers electron density on the oxide, stabilizing •OH and enabling efficient hydroxyl radical–mediated oxidations. <cite id="7fa5b0c2-6">Hydroxyl radicals are mainly formed by reduction of H2O2, formed by two-electron reduction of O2 and/or oxidation of H2O, highlighting pathways where metal sites supply electrons to form and deliver •OH</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-0">Surface intermediates and pathways in V2O5/TiO2 SCR demonstrate how oxide-supported metal sites control radical generation and subsequent recombination</cite>.

Case studies linking metal species to radical generation and oxidation efficiency

- NH3-Selective catalytic reduction (SCR) on V2O5/TiO2 and Mn-based catalysts
  - V2O5/TiO2 operates by surface vanadium redox that alternately oxidizes NH3 to N species and reduces NO to N2, with operando DRIFTS identifying NO2−/N2O formation and stepwise electron transfer across adjacent V centers; oxygen vacancies increase active site density and hydroxyl/oxygen radical pools, boosting low-temperature activity while risking NO2 emissions if hydroxyl supply is too high. <cite id="80ef33dc-0">In situ DRIFTS reveals SCR intermediates and mechanisms on V2O5/TiO2</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-5">Conversion proceeds via two vanadium atoms, evidencing M–O–M redox coupling</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancies improve NH3-SCR, consistent with enhanced NO/NH3 activation and radical formation at defects</cite>.
  - Mn-based catalysts benefit from Mn(II/III) redox cycling and Mn–O–M networks. Defect-driven Mn2+ centers act as radical initiation sites, while acidic Bronsted sites on Mn/Ce systems promote hydroxyl radical generation; birnessite Mn-oxides (layered tunnel structures) leverage Mn4+/Mn3+ redox to capture NO with high selectivity at low temperature. <cite id="80ef33dc-3">Birnessite Mn oxide shows high efficiency for low-temperature NH3-SCR</cite> <cite id="1773a134-5">Mn oxidation state and lattice oxygen govern NOx reduction pathways in Mn/TiO2</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancy-induced activation enhances SCR performance</cite>.
  - Overall, more exposed cationic Mn/V centers and oxygen vacancies increase radical yields and TOF at low temperature, but can reduce N2 selectivity if hydroxyl/•O attack dominates. <cite id="80ef33dc-2">Mechanistic review contrasts pathway regimes and selectivity outcomes for SCR</cite>.

- VOC and CO oxidation on MnOx, NbOx–Pt, and related oxides
  - Supported MnOx exhibit strong VOC (e.g., acetone, toluene) oxidation, where Mn2+–hydroxide/oxo species generate •OOH/•OH that oxidize organics; controlling MnOx phase and crystal facets tunes site acidity and redox lability, thereby modulating activation energy and TOF. <cite id="2bd05d42-5">Catalytic acetone oxidation over MnOx catalysts: different MnO2 crystal phases prepared by various methods show distinct activities</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-6">Progress on catalytic VOC oxidation by manganese-based catalysts: performance tied to Mn oxide structure and redox properties</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-8">Molten-salt-derived Mn-containing catalysts show advantageous properties for benzene/toluene total oxidation</cite>.
  - NbOx promoter on Pt/Al2O3 adjusts Mars–van Krevelen-like redox and strengthens M–O–M–metal couplings, shifting pathways from CO2-limited Langmuir–Hinshelwood to more efficient surface-oxidant supply regimes; operando DRIFTS reveals adsorbed carbonate/peroxycarbonate intermediates and altered Pt–oxide electron transfer. <cite id="2bd05d42-1">NbOx-doped Pt/Al2O3 enhances catalytic combustion of VOCs via effectively adjusted catalytic intermediates and pathways</cite>.
  - Quantitatively, MnO2 polymorphs and preparation routes can change turnover numbers by up to an order of magnitude for acetone oxidation, consistent with how isolated Mn–O* and vacancy-adjacent sites dictate radical initiation rates. <cite id="2bd05d42-5">Different MnO2 crystal phases prepared via different methods yield different acetone oxidation activities, evidencing structure–site–rate linkage</cite>.

- Heterogeneous Fenton and peroxycarbonate oxidation: metal-catalyzed hydroxyl generation
  - In Fenton-like heterogeneous processes, Co2+ or Fe2+ on oxide supports catalyze H2O2 decomposition to •OH, with mechanistic evidence and kinetics showing Co2+ accelerates •OH generation per unit oxidant; analogous manganese sources show combined homogeneous and heterogeneous contributions to •OH, often exceeding bulk AOP yields. <cite id="7fa5b0c2-1">Co2+ catalyzes peroxymonocarbonate-based AOP hydroxyl radical generation</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-0">Hydroxyl radical generation in peroxymonocarbonate catalyzed by Co2+ quantified across conditions</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-3">Simultaneously promoted reactive manganese species and hydroxyl radical generation by electro-permanganate with low-additive ozone; •OH arises from cathode reduction, homogeneous, and heterogeneous manganese catalysis</cite>.
  - These systems show that surface metal cations act as radical mediators: hydroxyl radical initiation rates scale with surface hydroxide density and metal–oxygen bond strength, and oxidant delivery (H2O2/peroxide) adjusts the net •OH flux. <cite id="7fa5b0c2-6">Hydroxyl radicals are formed by reduction of H2O2 and two-electron O2 reduction/oxidation pathways, consistent with metal site-controlled electron supply and radical formation</cite>.

Implications for efficiency, selectivity, and design

- Oxygen vacancies and exposed cationic sites: increasing Mn2+/V4+ or cationic density near reactive sites raises radical initiation rates at low temperature and increases TOF for NOx and VOC oxidations, but excessive radical flux can lead to over-oxidation or by-product formation (e.g., NO2 in SCR, CO2 in VOC oxidation). <cite id="80ef33dc-0">In situ DRIFTS mechanistic maps for V2O5/TiO2 show that radical intermediates control selectivity pathways</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-2">Mechanistic perspective details trade-offs between pathway regimes and selectivity in NH3-SCR</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-5">MnO2 phase and structure strongly influence acetone oxidation activity and presumably radical formation rates</cite>.
- Mn–Ce and metal–support synergy: redox-buffered acidic supports maintain an steady supply of •OH and O–• without over-activating NH3 or NO, enhancing both activity and N2 selectivity at low temperature; tuning Mn2+ cationicity and oxygen vacancy balance is key to suppressing nitrite formation while avoiding CO-poisoning at high temperature. <cite id="1773a134-5">Mn oxidation state and lattice oxygen affect NO/NO2 chemistry in Mn-based TiO2 SCR</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancies enhance SCR, implying careful defect control for efficiency and selectivity</cite>.
- Isolated Mn/Fe centers versus bridging motifs: Mn–O–Mn and Fe–O–Fe bridges act as transient oxygen reservoirs that feed •OOH/•OH, which are crucial for radical-chain oxidation of organics; conversely, highly dispersed monomeric cations may underperform without an oxygen-transfer bridge. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies improve catalysis, consistent with bridging-assisted oxygen transfer to radicals</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-5">Phase-specific MnO2 sites alter radical initiation rates and product yields in acetone oxidation</cite>.
- Coverage and promoter effects: WO3/MoO3 on V2O5/TiO2 increase Brønsted acidity and adjust electron transfer between NO/NH3 and vanadium centers, increasing N2 formation rates without catastrophic NO2 accumulation by balancing hydroxyl/O–• supply. <cite id="80ef33dc-4">V2O5/TiO2 mixed with WO3 or MoO3 is widely used; mechanisms and performance depend on promoter-induced acid/redox properties</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-5">Promoters facilitate efficient coupling of NO and NH3 oxidation on vanadium sites</cite>.

Design takeaways

- To maximize radical generation without losses to quenching: use reducible metal oxides (MnOx, VOx) with controlled oxygen vacancies and high Mn2+/V4+ exposure; consider ceria or Brønsted acidic frameworks to buffer redox pools and stabilize •OH/•O on surface cations. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies improve reducible oxide catalysis</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancies improve NH3-SCR by enhancing NO/NH3 activation</cite> <cite id="1773a134-5">Mn oxidation state and lattice oxygen govern NOx reduction pathways</cite>.
- To reduce radical over-activity and by-product formation: pair cationic metal sites with electron-rich supports (TiO2, Al2O3) that limit electron density at the oxide, or add redox buffers (CeO2) that store/release oxygen to keep radicals in stoichiometric balance with substrates. <cite id="80ef33dc-4">WO3/MoO3 promoters tune SCR pathway coupling and suppress undesired routes</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-3">Birnessite Mn oxide achieves high N2 selectivity at low T by leveraging layered Mn redox</cite>.
- For hydrocarbon oxidations: favor MnOx/V-based systems with exposed {001} or edge/vacancy faces and tune promoter composition (NbOx–Pt, WOx) to maintain Mars–van Krevelen electron supply while avoiding CO coverage poisoning; for peroxide-based processes, incorporate Fenton-like metal cations (Fe2+/Mn4+) to harvest peroxides and amplify •OH flux. <cite id="2bd05d42-1">NbOx-doped Pt/Al2O3 adjusts intermediates and pathways for effective VOC combustion</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-2">Fe2+ catalyzes H2O2 decomposition to •OH, increasing hydroxyl radical generation rate</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-3">Manganese sources generate •OH both heterogeneously and homogeneously under permanganate/ozone conditions</cite>.

Open questions and trade-offs

- Radical specificity vs. quenching: While higher radical yields generally raise turnover, competing recombination channels (•OOH + NH3 → N2O/N2; •OOH + CO → CO2) can limit selectivity; site-specific EPR/operando spectroscopy is needed to quantify hydroxyl/oxygen radical pools per active site and correlate to TOF. <cite id="80ef33dc-0">Operando DRIFTS shows radical intermediates and pathways can be tuned by vanadium site coupling</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-2">Pathway mapping and trade-offs are documented across SCR mechanisms</cite>.
- Dynamic structure–activity relations: Under reaction, lattice oxygen migrates and metals reduce/re-oxidize; the best catalysts maintain a steady redox couple (e.g., Mn–O–Mn/•OOH) rather than exposing bare metal centers that quench radicals. <cite id="1773a134-3">Dynamic evolution of lattice oxygen on metal oxides in diesel oxidation catalysts highlights structural adaptability needed for sustained activity</cite>.

In summary, the nature of metal species—oxidation state, coordination (M–O–M vs M*), dispersion, and host-driven charge transfer—directly tunes radical generation on catalyst surfaces. Increasing cationic Mn/V sites and oxygen vacancies boosts •OH/O–• and O2•− formation and often translates to higher low-temperature turnover in oxidation/SCR, but the optimal “efficiency” emerges when radical supply is balanced by substrate kinetics and mass transfer; ceria-type redox buffers and Brønsted acidic supports stabilize this balance for high selectivity. <cite id="1773a134-2">Bare metal cations with oxygen vacancies are key radical sites in reducible oxides</cite> <cite id="1773a134-6">Lattice oxygen anion/oxide bonding underlie partial oxidation pathways on metal oxides</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-0">Operando DRIFTS mechanisms on V2O5/TiO2 show how vanadium redox and defect chemistry control radical generation and efficiency</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-1">Oxygen vacancies enhance NH3-SCR by activating NO/NH3 and tuning hydroxyl radical initiation</cite> <cite id="80ef33dc-3">Layered Mn oxides (birnessite) leverage Mn redox for low-temperature SCR, evidencing structured radical pathways</cite> <cite id="7fa5b0c2-2">Fe2+ catalyzes peroxide decomposition to •OH, demonstrating metal-catalyzed hydroxyl radical generation</cite> <cite id="2bd05d42-5">MnO2 phase and structure dictate acetone oxidation TOF, linking metal-site chemistry to radical-driven efficiency</cite>.

Below is an evidence-based picture of how reactant content, surface composition (metal/acid/support/promoters), and site coverage govern a catalyst’s role (which SRPs participate, selectivity) and activity (rates, barriers), with mechanistic explanations and representative case studies.

# Mechanistic Basis: Active Sites, Reactant Binding, and Reaction Pathways

Catalyst “role” arises from which surface reaction pairs (SRPs) are formed and held near each other and the energetics of those steps, determined by site type and composition. <cite id="12c1804a-0">Brønsted acidic sites enhance catalyst activation, reducibility, and metal-support interaction, while Lewis acidic sites facilitate CH4 and CO2 activation</cite>. <cite id="12c1804a-4">Catalyst–support interactions further tune physical and chemical coupling of the active component, altering dispersion, electron density, and accessibility of active sites</cite>. <cite id="12c1804a-3">At the reaction level, catalysts speed rates by bringing reactants together or stabilizing transition states, thereby lowering activation energy</cite>.

Selectivity emerges as different SRPs are favored by site strength/stereochemistry and adsorption thermodynamics. <cite id="c66e120c-0">In many acid–base reactions (esterification, CO oxidation, H2 activation), the Eley–Rideal mechanism—where one species is physisorbed and the other chemisorbed—governs the rate and product formation</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-1">For acid–base coupling such as carbamate formation, an Eley–Rideal model is often better supported than Langmuir–Hinshelwood because the two reactants are inherently strongly dissimilar in binding strength</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-2">The classical Eley–Rideal picture formalizes the interaction between a chemisorbed molecule and a physisorbed molecule as the rate-limiting step</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-7">By contrast, Langmuir–Hinshelwood assumes both species are adsorbed on adjacent sites, often with stronger adsorbates at strong-acid sites and weaker adsorbates at Brønsted/Lewis sites</cite>. Thus, changing reactant content changes which SRPs and mechanisms dominate, altering barrier and product distribution.

# How Reactant Content Changes Activity and Role

Changes in feed composition shift site occupancy, SRP identity, and coupling geometry, which modifies barriers and turnover. <cite id="c66e120c-6">In Eley–Rideal-type oxidation, only one species needs to adsorb for the rate-determining step, so tuning the physisorbed/chemisorbed mix via reactant content can sharply change rate</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-4">At the nanocluster/nanoconfined level, cooperative kinetics (e.g., bridgehead or edge-site cooperativity) further magnifies how co-adsorbate arrangements under ER mechanisms alter activity</cite>.

Competition among mechanisms with changing composition often yields nonmonotonic or threshold behaviors. <cite id="c66e120c-8">For CO oxidation on Cu clusters, the balance between ER and LH pathways changes with coverage and co-adsorbate density, switching dominant rate-controlling SRPs and sensitivity to O2/CO ratios</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-0">In esterification, H2 activation, and alkylation chemistry, ER pathways are prevalent when one reactant binds much more strongly (acid sites), making the weakerly bound component’s “content” (partial pressure or concentration) the controlling variable of rate and selectivity</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-3">When both species co-adsorb (LH pathways), rate surfaces can become concave or cross-inhibitory as adsorption-induced repulsion or side-reactions rise at high coverage</cite>.

# Case Studies Linking Composition to Role and Activity

1) Water–gas shift (WGS) and CO in syngas. <cite id="8623b861-0">On Cu-based catalysts, WGS rate and stability depend on CO content because CO both participates in the productive SRP (CO + *OH → *COOH → products) and competes for strong CO-binding sites</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-2">Operationally, WGS is used to “reduce the carbon monoxide content” of synthesis gas, leveraging the exothermic SRP to extract CO’s toxicity as energy</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-4">Conversely, CO is a poison for base-metal WGS catalysts in dry environments, where CO competes with water for active sites and even inserts into metal–oxygen, reducing turnover</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-5">At low temperatures, WGS rate is controlled by kinetic SRPs where water and CO bind to adjacent active sites; raising CO relative to H2O shifts the rate-determining SRP toward CO-dominated activation, increasing barrier when CO binding is too strong</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-7">CO also poisons iron-based catalysts whereas copper or silver tolerate CO better, evidencing that “role” (where CO participates constructively vs destructively) depends on which SRPs are stabilized on the surface</cite>.

2) CO oxidation on metal catalysts and NO/air composition. <cite id="c66e120c-0">CO oxidation on metals often proceeds via ER mechanisms where O2 is activated at adsorption sites and CO remains largely physisorbed, making rate sensitive to CO/O2 partial pressures and surface acidity</cite>. <cite id="6cbd07c6-8">Introducing NOx into CO/air feeds can convert ER pathways to less selective SRPs (e.g., nitrite/nitrate formation), reducing CO2 selectivity and activity via Eley–Rideal nitrogen transfer to oxygenated intermediates on Lewis acid sites</cite>. <cite id="c66e120c-4">On nanoclusters, site-specific cooperative kinetics predict nonmonotonic dependence of CO2 yield on NO/CO ratios due to bridging-site nitrate and carbonate formation that depends on cluster geometry and coverage</cite>.

3) Methanol-to-olefins (MTO) and acid content in zeolites. <cite id="12c1804a-5">Mechanistic control in RWGS-like dehydrogenation/condensation steps is governed by acid strength and topology; promoters and framework composition tune CHx activation barriers</cite>. <cite id="6cbd07c6-3">In methanol-to-olefins over H-ZSM-5 (MOR), acid site strength/content and structural defects control DME formation and ethene/propene ratios; altering “composition” of Brønsted/Lewis sites reshapes the network of ER and LH SRPs among methanol, DME, and olefins</cite>. <cite id="6cbd07c6-2">Site engineering (e.g., Zn-MOR) suppresses undesired ethanol side reactions (ER-type bifunctional SRPs on strong acid sites), raising acetaldehyde selectivity to 90% by reducing an alternative SRP family</cite>.

7) PEM fuel cell fuels: H2 purity and CO impurity content. <cite id="8623b861-6">CO in hydrogen fuel poisons platinum by forming surface cobalt or CO-oxide SRPs that block active sites and raise overpotentials; mitigation (preferential oxidation) leverages copper or base oxides to oxidize CO at lower cost while preserving H2 activity</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-0">Copper-based slurry catalysts in fuel cells exploit ER pathways where CO remains weakly bound while surface hydroxyls activate water, explaining why even low CO content greatly reduces Pt-only activity but can be tolerated with Cu promoters by diverting SRPs</cite>.

# Promoters and Supports: Tuning the “Role” of a Catalyst

Promoters and supports don’t just add activity; they rewire SRP connectivity and selectivity. <cite id="12c1804a-0">Alkali and transition-metal promoters modify reducibility and the strength/number of acid sites, shifting activation modes (Brønsted vs Lewis), which in turn changes roles in CH4, CO2 activation and overall turnover</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-6">Promoter content also governs susceptibility to poisoning; e.g., Cu-containing WGS promoters resist CO-induced methanation while Fe-based cores activate CO destructively</cite>. <cite id="6cbd07c6-6">In CO hydrogenation, Na/K promote bifunctionality and suppress methane-forming SRPs by tuning hydrogenolysis barriers at acid sites, redefining the role toward chain-growth</cite>. <cite id="12c1804a-8">Strong alkali promoters can even inhibit reduction of oxide catalysts and extend time-on-stream by stabilizing basic oxygen vacancy states and suppressing sintering-related SRPs</cite>.

# Summary

Across catalyst classes, content—of reactants, promoters, supports, and contaminants—reshapes the ensemble of surface reaction pairs by altering adsorption energies, geometry, and coupling between sites. <cite id="c66e120c-0">ER- vs LH-pathway selection, governed by adsorption strength and SRP geometry, changes with reactant content</cite>, while <cite id="12c1804a-0">promoters and supports modulate acid/base strength, reducibility, and site coupling to reprogram selectivity</cite>. <cite id="8623b861-2">Operationally, removing CO via WGS or POX increases activity and shifts role away from CO-poisoning SRPs to productive hydrogenation/shift SRPs</cite>, and <cite id="6cbd07c6-6">alkali additions tune RWGS products by suppressing methane-forming SRPs and favoring C2+ growth</cite>.
