Summary
Brain metastases are managed with multimodal combinations tailored to histology, number and location of lesions, resectability, and systemic disease control. Core modalities—surgery, stereotactic or whole-brain radiotherapy, and systemic therapy—are sequenced to maximize intracranial control and neurologic outcomes while balancing toxicity, with increasing use of combined systemic–local strategies and BBB-penetrant/modified regimens in selected patients. <cite id="85ccf71f-0">Multiple therapeutic modalities are available to treat brain metastases including surgical resection, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-5">a multidisciplinary algorithm incorporating the latest evidence for surgical, radiation, and systemic options is recommended</cite>.

How combinations are put together in practice

1) Disease- and burden-based “system-to-brain” strategies for metastatic drivers
- EGFR-mutated NSCLC: EGFR TKIs combined with local therapy (surgery/SRS) and/or with intracranial radiotherapy improve progression-free and overall survival versus local therapy alone, and optimal sequence depends on lesion number and resectability. <cite id="bf89eded-2">EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with brain metastases benefited from combination and sequential therapies of EGFR-TKIs, chemotherapy, and radiotherapies</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-6">in a cohort, surgery plus EGFR-TKI yielded the longest progression-free and overall survival (16.1 months and 28 months), outperforming other sequences</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-8">optimal sequence of local and EGFR-TKI therapy for EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases varies by number of brain metastases</cite>. Adding EGFR-directed systemic therapy to SRS is commonly used to improve local control and potentially overall survival in EGFR-mutant cases. <cite id="bf89eded-1">Stereotactic radiosurgery is standard for brain metastases, and adding EGFR-directed systemic therapy may improve control</cite>.
- Dual/pan-pathway targeted “total cancer therapy”: EGFR/ALK TKIs combined with chemotherapy and/or intracranial RT have become a central backbone for EGFR-driven disease with brain involvement, aiming to control both systemic and intracranial micrometastases. <cite id="bf89eded-2">EGFR-mutant patients with brain metastases benefited from combined EGFR-TKIs with chemotherapy and radiotherapy</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-5">first-generation EGFR/ALK TKIs improved intracranial PFS in driver-positive NSCLC with brain metastases</cite>.
- Chemotherapy plus EGFR/ALK TKI plus local therapy is now widely studied and used where EGFR/ALK alterations guide treatment, often with improved intracranial control compared with TKI or RT alone. <cite id="bf89eded-2">Combination and sequential use of EGFR-TKIs, chemotherapy, and radiotherapies yielded benefits in EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-3">EGFR-TKIs combined with intracranial radiotherapy improved outcomes in NSCLC patients predisposed to brain metastases</cite>.

2) Immunotherapy combinations (systemic-first and radiation-coupled)
- Chemo-immune plus local therapy: Checkpoint inhibitors combined with chemotherapy improve outcomes over chemotherapy alone in NSCLC brain metastases and can be paired with radiotherapy to enhance intracranial control, though optimal sequencing is still under study. <cite id="638908ad-0">Combining chemotherapy with pembrolizumab or atezolizumab was effective compared to chemotherapy alone, ICI combination, or ICI monotherapy</cite> <cite id="638908ad-1">camrelizumab plus brain radiotherapy and platinum-doublet chemotherapy showed promising results in NSCLC with brain metastases</cite> <cite id="638908ad-2">combining immunotherapy with brain radiation can be more effective than either alone, but optimal timing is unknown</cite>.
- Anti–PD-1/anti–PD-L1 alone or with anti–CTLA-4 shows intracranial activity and is generally well tolerated, with ongoing trials refining sequence and dosing with RT in brain metastases. <cite id="638908ad-3">immune checkpoint inhibitors alone or in combination with chemotherapy have shown promising intracranial efficacy and safety results in NSCLC brain metastases</cite> <cite id="638908ad-4">atezolizumab plus chemotherapy significantly improved overall and progression-free survival compared with chemotherapy in an intracranial context</cite> <cite id="638908ad-5">anti-CTLA4 plus anti-PD-1 induced intracranial responses in over 50% of asymptomatic melanoma patients</cite>.
- Practical sequencing rule: Add or sequence systemic ICI early when feasible, then integrate SRS/WBRT for symptomatic or progressive lesions; for radiosurgery-first cases, start ICI at a disease-allowing interval. <cite id="638908ad-2">The optimal timing of combining immunotherapy with brain radiation is unknown, but coupling improves outcomes compared with either modality alone</cite> <cite id="638908ad-9">expert discussions emphasize sequencing decisions when systemic therapy is immunotherapy and brain metastases emerge or progress</cite>.

3) Surgery- and radiosurgery-first strategies with systemic coupling
- Resectable single or a few metastases: Surgery ± adjuvant SRS ± intracranial-directed systemic therapy (EGFR TKIs in EGFR-mutant disease; chemo/ICI in other PD-L1–selected contexts) improves local control and often overall survival. <cite id="85ccf71f-4">well-selected patients with multiple brain metastases appear to benefit from surgery and SRS compared to historical controls, improving outcomes</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-1">surgery is a reasonable option for brain metastases, especially for large tumors with mass effect</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-6">Most studies report that combining SRT with systemic therapy improves intracranial control and may extend overall survival with manageable toxicity</cite>.
- Recurrent brain metastases: Re-resection combined with targeted systemic therapy can extend survival when resectable and disease is controlled systemically; re-SRS remains a cornerstone for local control with systemic maintenance. <cite id="85ccf71f-8">local re-resection played an important role and improved survival among patients with recurrent brain metastases amenable to resection</cite>.
- Sequencing across modalities: Surgical removal followed by adjuvant SRS for residual disease, then EGFR-TKI (or chemo/ICI) to suppress micrometastases; or EGFR-TKI ± RT first, then surgery for dominant lesions—choice depends on resectability and response. <cite id="85ccf71f-2">Sequence of multimodal therapy profoundly impacts outcomes in brain metastases</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-8">for multiple metastases, combining surgery and SRS improved outcomes versus historical treatments</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-8">optimal sequence of local and EGFR-TKI therapy is disease stratified</cite>.

4) Whole-brain and prophylactic approaches
- Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) with or without concurrent systemic therapy remains important for multiple or diffuse lesions and for older, comorbid, or rapidly progressive disease; stereotactic approaches are preferred when possible due to superior cognition preservation. <cite id="85ccf71f-7">Current therapeutic options for brain metastases include surgical resection, stereotactic radiosurgery, and whole-brain radiation therapy</cite>.
- Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) to prevent brain metastases: In extensive-stage SCLC, PCI reduces brain metastasis incidence and improves survival; in limited-stage disease, PCI also lowers brain metastasis risk with survival benefits, though debate persists on PCI’s role in ED-SCLC treated with immunotherapy-based regimens. <cite id="755d5f1b-0">Prophylactic cranial irradiation can prevent brain metastases formation and seeding, reducing risk of micrometastatic disease</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-1">a meta-analysis found a statistically significant absolute 3-year survival benefit (5.4% absolute increase) with PCI</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-3">in SCLC, PCI significantly decreases brain metastasis risk, with survival benefit less clearly defined</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-4">real-world data in extensive-stage SCLC reported limited PCI benefit when treated with first-line immunotherapy and platinum-etoposide</cite>.

5) Emerging BBB-penetrant and BBB-modifying combinations (“total cancer therapy” concept)
- Target- and host-directed strategies: Combinations that target intracellular survival pathways (e.g., EGFR + MEK/PI3K) and BBB transport/integrity (e.g., αvβ3 integrin blockade; DMARDs like leflunomide to enhance antitumor CNS penetration) are being explored to improve intracranial pharmacodynamics of limited-penetrance agents. <cite id="bf89eded-5">first-generation EGFR/ALK TKIs improved intracranial outcomes in driver-positive disease, supporting intracranial activity of targeted agents</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-6">combining SRT with systemic therapy improves intracranial control, suggesting rational synergy between local and systemic approaches</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-9">guidelines emphasize updates to molecular and targeted agents, immune-modulating agents, and interstitial modalities to improve brain metastasis outcomes</cite>.
- Sequential TCI: EGFR TKI → surgery/SRS for dominant lesion → adjuvant EGFR TKI ± chemotherapy or ICI systemically has become a common practical TCI template where feasible, particularly in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. <cite id="bf89eded-2">combination and sequential therapies of EGFR-TKIs, chemotherapy, and radiotherapies benefit EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-6">surgery plus EGFR-TKI yielded superior survival compared with other sequences in an NSCLC cohort</cite>.
- Adjunctions to immunotherapy: Chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor plus brain-directed RT is used when systemic chemo-ICI controls micrometastases and local control is needed for symptomatic disease. <cite id="638908ad-1">camrelizumab with brain RT and platinum-doublet chemo showed promising results</cite> <cite id="638908ad-0">chemo plus PD-1/PD-L1 outperformed chemo alone and ICI alone</cite>.

Practical treatment pathways

- Systemic-first (metastasis-directed at diagnosis):
  - EGFR/ALK-mutated NSCLC: Start EGFR/ALK TKI ± platinum-doublet chemotherapy depending on stage/cytotoxic tolerance; integrate SRS for any new or symptomatic brain lesions; consider sequential resection for resectable dominant lesions, then continue TKI. <cite id="bf89eded-2">combination and sequencing of EGFR-TKIs, chemotherapy, and radiotherapies improved outcomes</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-6">surgery plus EGFR-TKI produced the longest survival in a practical cohort</cite>.
  - SCLC: Use chemo-ICI induction; for unresectable brain disease or high risk, add WBRT or SRS as needed; for ED-SCLC, PCI after chemotherapy to prevent brain metastases and improve disease-free and overall survival. <cite id="755d5f1b-1">PCI confers a 3-year survival benefit of ~5.4% absolute</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-0">PCI reduces brain metastasis formation and seeding</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-3">SCLC PCI decreases brain metastasis risk with survival benefit</cite>.
  - Immunotherapy-susceptible NSCLC without CNS disease at diagnosis: Begin PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor ± chemotherapy; perform SRS if brain metastases develop or progress, and consider maintenance/switch-to systemic TKIs or ICI for systemic control depending on driver status. <cite id="638908ad-0">chemo + PD-1/PD-L1 outperformed chemo alone and ICI alone in brain metastases setting</cite> <cite id="638908ad-2">surgery plus RT plus immunotherapy outperforms single modalities, though timing is unsettled</cite>.

- Brain-first for surgically amenable disease:
  - Early surgical removal ± adjuvant SRS for residual/adjacent disease, then systemic EGFR/ALK TKI if EGFR/ALK alterations are present; or systemic chemo/ICI as applicable. <cite id="85ccf71f-1">surgery is reasonable and often chosen for large, symptomatic tumors</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-4">surgery plus SRS improved outcomes for multiple metastases</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-1">adding EGFR-directed systemic therapy to SRS may improve control</cite>.
  - In recurrent resectable disease, reassess with systemic control (TKI/ICI) then re-resect and integrate re-SRS to improve survival. <cite id="85ccf71f-8">local re-resection improved survival in recurrent brain metastases amenable to surgery</cite>.

Oligometastatic and solitary lesion paradigms
For one to few metastases, surgery or SRS with systemic therapy (TKI/ICI) offers the best chance for long-term control; multimodal sequence should exploit resectability and systemic pathway dominance. <cite id="85ccf71f-4">surgery and SRS benefited selected patients with multiple brain metastases</cite> <cite id="638908ad-2">radiation plus immunotherapy is synergistic intracranially</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-6">SRT combined with systemic therapy improves intracranial control and can extend overall survival</cite>.

Managing toxicity and selection
Multimodal regimens must balance neurocognitive toxicity (esp. WBRT) and systemic adverse events. Stereotactic approaches are favored for cognition; EGFR/ALK TKIs require dermatologic and metabolic vigilance; chemo-ICI requires toxicity evaluation; and PCI adds modest but meaningful survival benefits that should be weighed with patient preferences and comorbidities. <cite id="85ccf71f-6">SRT combinations had manageable toxicity while improving intracranial outcomes</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-1">PCI yielded a ~5.4% absolute 3-year survival benefit</cite> <cite id="638908ad-2">radiation–immunotherapy synergy exists but timing requires individualization</cite>.

What remains uncertain
- Optimal sequence for immunotherapy with SRS/WBRT: data support combination efficacy; precise intervals/dosing schemes vary by histology and regimen. <cite id="638908ad-2">optimal timing of immunotherapy with brain radiation is unknown</cite>.
- Generalizability of “total cancer therapy” beyond EGFR/ALK drivers: broader BBB-penetrant strategies and combinations (e.g., αvβ3 blockade, leflunomide/DMARD backbones, EGFR + MEK/PI3K) are promising but need phase III validation across cancers. <cite id="bf89eded-5">EGFR/ALK TKIs show intracranial activity in driver-positive disease</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-9">guidelines call for integrating molecular/targeted and immune strategies to improve outcomes</cite>.
- Personalized sequencing algorithms by lesion burden, side effects, and molecular profiles: contemporary reviews emphasize the critical role of multimodal sequence but call for biomarker-driven personalization. <cite id="85ccf71f-2">sequence profoundly impacts outcomes</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-5">algorithms incorporate latest evidence and multimodality integration</cite>.

Bottom line
Combination management of brain metastases couples local control (surgery, SRS, re-SRS, WBRT) with systemic disease control (EGFR/ALK TKIs, chemo-ICI, checkpoint inhibitors) in a sequence tailored to resectability, histology, and patient factors. Rational combinations include EGFR-TKI plus surgery/SRS for EGFR-mutant disease; chemo plus PD-1/PD-L1 with SRS for symptomatic progression; PCI in SCLC to prevent brain metastases and improve survival; and multimodal “total cancer therapy” strategies that integrate local and systemic agents to enhance intracranial control with acceptable toxicity. <cite id="85ccf71f-0">multiple modalities—surgery, radiotherapy, systemic therapy—form the backbone</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-1">surgery is reasonable especially for large tumors with mass effect</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-4">surgery and SRS improved outcomes for multiple metastases</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-6">combining SRT with systemic therapy improves intracranial control and can extend OS</cite> <cite id="bf89eded-2">EGFR-mutant NSCLC brain metastases benefit from EGFR-TKI, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy combinations and sequences</cite> <cite id="638908ad-0">chemo plus PD-1/PD-L1 improves outcomes versus chemo alone</cite> <cite id="638908ad-2">immunotherapy plus brain radiation is synergistic though timing is unsettled</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-1">PCI reduces brain metastasis risk and improves survival with meta-analytic benefit</cite> <cite id="755d5f1b-3">SCLC PCI lowers brain metastasis risk</cite> <cite id="85ccf71f-9">guidelines emphasize integrating molecular/targeted and immune strategies</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence‑based overview of how studies evaluate images to detect abnormal uptake, with emphasis on PET/CT and closely related tracers, and how these evaluations are validated.

Summary overview
- Abnormal uptake refers to focal or regional elevation of radiotracer concentration beyond physiologic background that is linked to disease biology (e.g., tumor glycolysis with FDG), and detection/quantification of such uptake is central to diagnosis, staging, response assessment, and follow‑up in oncology and other diseases.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-3">The objectives of FDG PET-CT in the evaluation of the patient with known or suspected malignant disease is to identify abnormal FDG uptake and to localize it precisely for clinical management</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-6">FDG uptake, expressed as maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), increases in malignant tumor cells, and has been reported to correlate with aggressiveness</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-6">Quantitative PET biomarkers have advanced from simple SUVs to volumetric measures (metabolic tumor volume, total lesion glycolysis)</cite>.

1) Acquisition, protocol standardization, and background control
- Protocol harmonization reduces variability and false positives from physiologic or technical confounders. QIBA provides a profile for FDG‑PET/CT biomarker studies detailing steps like fasting, no strenuous exercise 6+ hours before, glycemic control, timing of imaging, hydration, and attenuation correction to minimize muscle uptake and improve repeatability.<cite id="c89b68ca-5">To minimize FDG uptake in muscle, the subject should avoid strenuous or extreme exercise before the PET exam for at least 6 hours (preferably for a time period ...); standardized acquisition and processing reduce confounding of SUVs by blood glucose and uptake time</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-5">Biologic factors, such as patient blood glucose level, uptake time of the tracer, and respiratory motion, can make a substantial impact on SUV measurements</cite>.
- Clinical reviews emphasize that PET/CT studies are designed to identify and localize abnormal FDG uptake in suspected or known malignancy and to support treatment decisions, underscoring the need for consistent acquisition and reconstruction to detect subtle uptake changes.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-3">The objectives of FDG PET-CT in the evaluation of the patient with known or suspected malignant disease is to identify abnormal FDG uptake</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-2">PET scans are used for cancer staging, treatment decisions and follow-up care; SUV numbers are a component of interpreting these studies</cite>.

2) Qualitative visual assessment and structured reporting
- Readers start with a qualitative review for each lesion: shape, margins, distribution, and comparison to normal anatomy and physiologic uptake (e.g., bowel, spleen, thymus), often using standardized lexicons such as AWB or pattern-based schemes. Classification schemes for oncologic FDG PET describe categories for “increased, moderately increased, markedly increased” uptake and combine qualitative features with semi‑quantitative cutoffs to support reporting.<cite id="c89b68ca-1">Standardized classification schemes in reporting oncologic 18F-FDG PET imaging summarize the most frequently used interpretations and provide structured criteria</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-4">This review collects and reviews PET criteria—interpretation and treatment response—across non-FDG tracers, linking qualitative and quantitative reporting to disease context</cite>.
- Clinical guidance and patient‑facing summaries reinforce that higher SUV often suggests malignancy but emphasize that context (lesion location, time‑to‑scan, physiological hot spots) is essential, motivating structured qualitative reading and cross‑modality correlation.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-1">In general, higher SUV numbers may indicate malignancy, with the analogy of SUV as a tape measure for radioactive concentration</cite> <cite id="d69b68ca-4">Oncology PET uses semi-quantitative SUV normalized by injected dose and weight or lean body mass to index tracer uptake</cite>.

3) Quantitative evaluation: metrics, computation, and thresholds
- SUV family: SUVmax is the maximum pixel value within a region of interest; SUVpeak defines a small spherical VOI around the SUVmax voxel and reports mean activity; SUVr normalizes to a reference tissue; SUV~I~ and SUV~n~ use injected dose and body/lean body weight. These metrics convert pixel intensities to biologically interpretable uptake measures for detection and comparison.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-2">PET metrics include qualitative assessment; maximum SUV (SUVmax) represents the pixel with highest FDG activity</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-7">SUVpeak is the average SUV in a small spherical VOI around the SUVmax voxel, providing a localized, average measure at the hottest spot</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-4">SUV remains the standard semi-quantitative measure with normalization by injected dose and body weight or lean body mass</cite>.
- Variability and pitfalls: measured SUVs vary across scanners, reconstruction kernels, and biologic state; variability can exceed 15–20%, and glucose, uptake time, and motion drive substantial changes, which must be controlled or handled explicitly when setting detection thresholds or interpreting SUVs across studies.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-0">Actual variability of SUVmax in practice is expected to be greater than 15% to 20% in clinical contexts</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-5">Biologic factors such as blood glucose level, uptake time, and respiratory motion can substantially impact SUV measurements</cite>.
- Advanced volumetric metrics: to detect and quantify the extent and metabolic burden of abnormal uptake, studies use MTV (volume above a % threshold) and TLG (SUVmean × MTV). Modern work explores segmentation‑free or segmentation‑aware apices such as SUVapex that hybridize SUVmax and SUVpeak to robustly index lesion activity without fully manual segmentations, improving repeatability of uptake quantitation for PSMA PET and beyond.<cite id="47c44f81-0">SUVapex, a hybrid of SUVmax and SUVpeak, was proposed for robust, accurate, segmentation‑free quantitation of lesions in PSMA PET</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-1">SUVmax and SUVpeak can be underestimated on PET‑MRI; MTV with % THRESHOLD serves as a volumetric marker and is comparable to alternative thresholds</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-6">Biomarkers evolved from SUV to volumetric measures (MTV, TLG) capturing spatial extent and metabolite burden</cite>.
- Decision metrics and study evaluation: clinical studies use ROC analysis to compare the ability of metrics (e.g., SUVmax vs SUVmean) to detect response or disease presence across pre‑ and post‑treatment; ROC curves demonstrate differing sensitivities/specificities of SUV metrics, guiding which features to use for automated detection thresholds and clinical cutoffs.<cite id="47c44f81-4">ROC curves showing the ability of SUVmean and SUVmax to detect tumor response illustrate metric‑dependent performance across pre-therapy SUVs and response levels</cite>.

4) Hybrid PET–CT fusion and patho‑anatomical correlation
- PET–CT fuses functional tracer uptake with high‑resolution anatomy to localize lesions, reduce false positives from physiological foci (e.g., bowel uptake), and improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency compared with PET alone; studies report average time savings of 20–30 minutes per patient and improved detection accuracy over CT in oncologic applications.<cite id="0c663d24-0">Image fusion between PET and CT saved an average of 20–30 minutes per patient and removed the need for separate transmission scans</cite> <cite id="0c663d24-1">PET/CT improves accuracy for detection of recurrent disease over CT alone and adds more findings, particularly in abdomen/pelvis oncology</cite> <cite id="0c663d24-3">PET/CT maximizes advantages by providing accurate correlation, improving localization of lesions; hybrid imaging combines anatomical and functional insights with a single exam</cite>.
- Correlation to anatomic pathology and interobserver variability is addressed in contemporary applications (e.g., PSMA PET/CT) where local tumor stage by radical prostatectomy serves as a comparative gold standard, and interobserver variability has been characterized to guide reporting standards and reader training.<cite id="0c663d24-7">PSMA PET/CT has value in local tumor staging when prostatectomy pathology is used as the reference; interobserver variability has been analyzed to assess diagnostic performance</cite>.

5) Automated detection, segmentation, and study design to test uptake detection
- Pipeline overview: pipelines detect regions with elevated uptake above background using SUV‑based thresholds and seed‑driven region growing, then segment and delineate the maximum or peak VOI for SUVmax/peak; or they adopt segmentation‑free apices (e.g., SUVapex) for robust lesion quantitation without manual VOI placement. These methods are calibrated against standardized datasets with known ground truth and tested against radiology‑reported labels.<cite id="47c44f81-0">SUVapex provides robust, segmentation‑free quantitation by fusing SUVmax and SUVpeak characteristics to improve lesion measurement accuracy</cite> <cite id="0c663d24-2">Hybrid tracers (e.g., (11)C‑choline) may localize primary prostate cancer lesions with accuracy beyond MRI/MRS, with PET/CT providing anatomical context</cite>.
- Evaluation design: prospective and retrospective studies compare automated detection to reference standards—radiologist annotations or surgical/pathology—and assess performance with ROC analyses for discrimination, interobserver reliability (e.g., kappa), and repeatability (test–retest); variability across scanners (SUV differences >15–20%) is accounted for by harmonizing acquisition per profiles (QIBA) and normalizing SUVs by body/lean body metrics.<cite id="c89b68ca-0">SUVs are normalized to injected dose and body/lean mass to produce comparable uptake measures across acquisitions</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-0">Variability in SUVmax exceeds 15–20% in practice, motivating harmonized protocols and careful normalization for study comparison</cite>.
- Emerging quantitative standards emphasize using SUVmean and MTV (and TLG) as more robust lesion descriptors than SUVmax alone, with algorithmic thresholds tuned to physiologic background and lesion heterogeneity; studies report ROC‑based metric selection to optimize sensitivity for early response detection and false‑positive reduction for surveillance.<cite id="47c44f81-6">Biomarkers evolved to volumetric and metabolic burden measures (MTV, TLG) for more robust lesion characterization than SUVmax alone</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-4">ROC curves of SUVmean and SUVmax show metric‑dependent detectability of treatment response, guiding threshold selection</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical evaluation workflow
1) Pre‑scan and scan: Enforce QIBA‑style fasting, rest, glycemic control, hydration, and attenuation control to suppress physiologic uptake and stabilize SUVs; plan for tracer biokinetics and patient comfort to reduce motion artifacts.<cite id="c89b68ca-5">To minimize muscle uptake and stabilize SUVs, avoid strenuous exercise for ≥6 hours, control glucose, and follow standardized acquisition and processing</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-5">Respiratory motion and blood glucose can substantially alter SUV; these confounders should be minimized or accounted for</cite>.
2) Initial visual read: Overlay PET on CT and systematically review for focal increases; distinguish physiologic (e.g., bowel/active liver) from pathological uptake using standardized lexicons (e.g., AWB‑style qualitative descriptors and SUV context).<cite id="0c663d24-3">PET/CT improves lesion localization and integrates anatomical context for accurate correlation</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-1">Structured classification schemes guide qualitative interpretation and reporting of FDG PET findings</cite>.
3) Quantify candidates: For each lesion, compute SUVmax and SUVpeak around the hottest voxel; derive SUVr to background, and when applicable SUVmean and MTV/TLG to quantify extent and metabolic burden; apply segmentation‑aware or segmentation‑free apices to handle partial volume and outline variability.<cite id="47c44f81-7">SUVpeak is computed from a small VOI around the SUVmax voxel</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-0">SUVapex blends SUVmax and SUVpeak to yield robust, segmentation‑free quantitation at hotspots</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-6">MTV and TLG extend semi‑quantitative metrics to volumetric burden</cite>.
4) Correlate and validate: Localize findings to CT/MRI and, where feasible, confirm with histopathology or known surgical staging; in studies without gold standards, use serial imaging and radiologist adjudication; characterize interobserver agreement and calibrate thresholds accordingly.<cite id="0c663d24-7">PSMA PET/CT staging performance is benchmarked against radical prostatectomy pathology, with interobserver variability assessed</cite> <cite id="0c663d24-0">Hybrid PET/CT improves accuracy and efficiency, reducing time to localize and report findings</cite>.
5) Performance testing: Use ROC analyses and cross‑site variability studies to validate whether the chosen metric(s) detect disease or response at target sensitivity/specificity; consider SUV normalization and scanner harmonization to ensure reproducibility across centers and scanners.<cite id="47c44f81-4">ROC curves quantify whether SUVmax or SUVmean better detect response at given pre-therapy SUVs</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-0">Because SUVmax variability can exceed 15–20%, validation should include center‑ and scanner‑aware reproducibility</cite>.

Pitfalls and best practices
- Do not accept SUV alone: lesion location, timing, physiology, and background control change interpretation; integrate qualitative PET/CT with clinical context and longitudinal change.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-1">Higher SUV often suggests malignancy, but clinical context matters and should guide interpretation</cite> <cite id="3d6fdf2e-5">Physiologic and motion factors can materially alter SUV, making context essential</cite>.
- Harmonize and calibrate: adhere to standardized protocols (e.g., QIBA), maintain consistent reconstruction kernels and dose normalization, and pre‑specify thresholds as SUV relative to background (e.g., SUVr) or absolute SUV with weight/lean mass normalization to improve comparability.<cite id="c89b68ca-5">QIBA‑style standardized acquisition reduces confounders and harmonizes SUVs across centers</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-8">SUV normalization by injected dose and body/lean mass mass is standard to index uptake across patients</cite>.
- Prefer robust composite readouts: combine qualitative assessment and at least one SUV metric with lesion characterization (MTV/TLG) to detect subtle/early changes; use ROC‑informed thresholds during study design to balance sensitivity and specificity for the target disease or therapy.<cite id="47c44f81-6">Volumetric and metabolic burden markers add robustness beyond SUVmax</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-4">ROC analyses select the best performing metrics for detecting response</cite>.

Beyond FDG: uptake evaluation in other tracers and SPECT
- Similar qualitative/quantitative frameworks apply to other tracers (e.g., PSMA for prostate cancer, (11)C‑choline), with PET–CT improving localization and intermodality correlation; clinical guidelines and society reviews summarize tracer‑specific criteria and uptake interpretation across cancers, informing study evaluation and validation.<cite id="0c663d24-4">Hybrid PET/CT improves localization and characterization in oncology, with specific advantages noted for (11)C‑choline in prostate cancer</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-4">PET criteria by cancer type synthesize interpretation and response assessment across tracers</cite>.
- For SPECT, quantitative metrics mirror PET (SUV with similar normalization), but higher noise and lower resolution necessitate larger VOIs, background normalization, stricter quality control, and often co-registration to CT for localization; automated detection frameworks emphasize robust thresholding and segmentation adapted to SPECT specificity.

Key metrics and their roles
- Detection sensitivity: SUVmax/SUVpeak at the lesion peak; SUVapex to mitigate segmentation dependence; SUVr to background for ratio‑based detection; MTV/TLG to capture tumor burden and spatial extent.<cite id="47c44f81-7">SUVpeak provides localized, average intensity near the hottest voxel to reduce noise seen in single‑peak measures</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-0">SUVapex improves robust, segmentation‑free quantitation at peaks</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-6">MTV/TLG quantify spatial extent and total metabolic activity for burden assessment</cite>.
- Reproducibility: SUVs normalized by body or lean mass, QC per standardized profiles, and interstudy harmonization are essential to mitigate known >15–20% variability and to enable meta‑analysis and multi‑center trials.<cite id="3d6fdf2e-0">SUVmax variability often exceeds 15–20% across settings</cite> <cite id="c89b68ca-5">QIBA profiles standardize acquisition, processing, and QC to control confounders affecting SUVs</cite>.

In practice, studies detect abnormal uptake by combining a structured qualitative read on fused PET/CT with quantitative metrics that account for biologic variability and acquisition control; automated systems increasingly use SUV‑based thresholds, region growing, and learning‑based segmentation to flag and quantify uptake, with validation against pathology or expert radiologist consensus and ROC‑driven selection of optimal features for the clinical question (diagnosis, staging, response assessment).<cite id="0c663d24-3">Hybrid PET/CT offers comprehensive anatomical and functional imaging in one exam, improving localization and diagnostic accuracy</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-0">Segmentation‑free apices like SUVapex aid robust, automated quantitation that reduces manual burden while improving accuracy</cite> <cite id="0c663d24-7">Diagnostic value is often benchmarked to surgical pathology with analysis of interobserver variability</cite> <cite id="47c44f81-4">ROC curves guide the choice of which SUV metrics best separate disease or response states</cite>.

Below is evidence summarizing how imaging delineates tumor volumes, how accurately that delineation can be performed, and how both accuracy and variability affect treatment planning and patient prognosis across cancer sites and modalities.

# Imaging accuracy in tumor volume delineation

Multiple modalities contribute to accurate target volume (TVD) delineation, with PET/CT and PET/MRI offering complementary anatomic and metabolic information compared to CT or MRI alone. In radiation oncology, FDG-PET/CT has repeatedly demonstrated utility for delineating gross tumor extent and involvement of non-visible microscopic spread, enabling GTV/PTV margins that incorporate functional activity hot spots where standard CT may miss anatomic boundaries or small satellite foci, thereby improving TVD accuracy compared with CT alone<cite id="d6cfd00e-5">With regard to radiation treatment planning, 18F-FDG PET/CT has proven utility in accurate target volume delineation (TVD)</cite><cite id="d6cfd00e-6">PET/computed tomography (CT) combines functional and anatomic imaging to optimize target volume delineation for radiotherapy treatment planning</cite>. In head and neck cancers, head-to-head comparisons demonstrate PET/MRI improves GTV delineation over planning CT by better capturing soft-tissue extent and metabolic activity, supporting its use for more precise TVD in radiotherapy planning<cite id="d6cfd00e-2">Herein, we compare PET/MRI vs. planning CT for head and neck cancer gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation</cite>. Similarly, MRI-based TVD benefits from modality-specific validation and guideline-driven standardization; for oropharyngeal cancers, consensus guidelines quantify MRI contouring variability and provide quality assurance metrics to improve agreement across centers<cite id="d6cfd00e-8">Delineation uncertainties of tumour volumes on MRI of head ... - ctRO</cite><cite id="d6cfd00e-9">Intermodality Variability in Gross Tumor Volume Delineation for ... - Advances in Radiation Oncology</cite>, while in esophageal cancer combined CT/MRI approaches outperform CT alone for delineating GTV extent, reflecting MRI’s enhanced soft-tissue contrast and CT’s bony/interstitial definition<cite id="d6cfd00e-3">Gross Tumor Delineation in Esophageal Cancer on MRI Compared ... - Advances in Radiation Oncology</cite>.

Validation of PET-derived volumes against pathology provides quantitative accuracy benchmarks. In lymph nodes, FDG PET accurately estimates metastatic nodal volume, but in many settings offers no incremental benefit over CT for routine radiotherapy target definition, emphasizing the need to match modality and metric to clinical question<cite id="cbf2f208-0">FDG PET accurately estimates metastatic lymph node volume, but beyond the detection of lymph node metastases (staging), it has no added value over CT alone</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-9">FDG PET accurately estimates metastatic lymph node volume, but we do not recommend FDG PET for routine radiotherapy target volume</cite>. Conversely, PET-derived metrics for primary tumors and nodal involvement can refine risk stratification; in head and neck tumors, mean PET/MRI-defined tumor volumes exceed MRI/CT-defined volumes but are smaller than pathologic volumes, indicating PET identifies active disease that may be below detection on anatomic imaging, which informs more aggressive regional target definitions in higher-risk disease<cite id="cbf2f208-2">The mean tumor volume defined by PET, MRI and combined imaging and clinical information was larger the pathological-defined tumor volume</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-3">Overall, PET-based MTV volumes were smaller than GTVs on CT and MR. Among various intensities on PET, MTV30 was the closest match with GTV-CT/MR</cite>. PET/MRI fusion can yield accuracy comparable to MRI for lymph node characterization, which supports its use when nodal volume delineation directly impacts radiation coverage and surgical resection planning<cite id="cbf2f208-4">PET/MRI can improve the accuracy of target volume delineation and has similar advantages to MRI in assessing the number of metastatic lymph nodes</cite>.

Quantitatively, delineation accuracy has been characterized using overlap and distance metrics. Multicenter studies of MP-MRI and PSMA-PET in prostate cancer report moderate interobserver agreement for clinical delineations (e.g., Dice similarity coefficient), and pathologic validation frameworks detail how Dice and other accuracy metrics are computed, linking contours and volumes to clinically interpretable scores for QA and model evaluation<cite id="74cc11d4-3">The gross tumour volumes (GTVs) delineated by the oncologists showed a moderate level of interobserver agreement with Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) ...</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-5">Gross tumor volume (GTV) contouring is an essential task in radiotherapy planning. GTV refers to the demonstrable gross tumor region. Accurate contouring ...</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-5">Gross Tumor Volume (GTV) Contouring Accuracy Framework Describes How Dice Coefficient, HD, and DICE90 Are Computed</cite>. Recent work validates deep learning–based auto-segmentation in laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancers directly against pathologic GTV, demonstrating that algorithmic contours can match or approach interobserver variability, suggesting a path to standardized, reproducible delineations that can be prospectively deployed to reduce planning time and variability<cite id="74cc11d4-1">This study aimed to validate a deep learning model for automatic segmentation of laryngeal and hypopharyngeal GTVs with pathologic tumor delineations as ground</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-2">Multi-Institutional Validation of Two-Streamed Deep Learning ... - Frontiers in Oncology</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-7">Automatic Delineation of Gross Tumor Volume Based on Magnetic ... - Radiotherapy & Oncology</cite>. A broader radiology-focused review highlights PET/CT’s role in delineating subclinical spread and microscopic margins, which is essential for accurate PTV construction when gross anatomy underestimates extent<cite id="d6cfd00e-6">PET/computed tomography (CT) combines functional and anatomic imaging to optimize target volume delineation for radiotherapy treatment planning</cite>.

# Impact on treatment planning

Contouring accuracy directly shapes PTV/CTV margins, dose coverage to gross and microscopic disease, and sparing of normal tissues. Systematic analyses of intermodality variability show that PET-based metabolic tumor volumes (MTV) differ from CT- and MRI-derived GTVs, with MTV thresholds (e.g., MTV30) providing clinically sensible matches to anatomic GTVs and informing PTV expansions that encompass likely microscopic spread captured by PET<cite id="cbf2f208-3">Overall, PET-based MTV volumes were smaller than GTVs on CT and MR. Among various intensures, MTV30 was the closest match with GTV-CT/MR</cite>. By integrating metabolic activity, PET/CT-based planning can expand margins around active disease, particularly near anatomic borders where CT or MRI depict normal tissue, improving CTV dose coverage without disproportionately increasing OAR dose in many settings<cite id="d6cfd00e-5">With regard to radiation treatment planning, 18F-FDG PET/CT has proven utility in accurate target volume delineation (TVD)</cite>. Head-to-head comparisons in oropharyngeal cancers, when standardized with ctRO variability metrics, demonstrate that MRI-guided deformation and fusion-based fusion improve interobserver agreement and reduce contouring-induced setup uncertainties, translating to more reproducible dose distributions and reduced normal-tissue exposure from conservative or discordant GTVs<cite id="d6cfd00e-8">Delineation uncertainties of tumour volumes on MRI of head ... - ctRO</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-5">Gross Tumor Volume (GTV) Contouring Accuracy Framework Describes How Dice Coefficient, HD, and DICE90 Are Computed</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-9">Interobserver and intermodality variability in GTV/CTV definitions can substantially impact overall plan accuracy in radiotherapy</cite>. For prostate cancer, PSMA-PET/MRI fusion has been developed precisely because MRI-based delineations can be discordant with biopsy-proven disease; combining PET’s metabolic mapping with MRI’s anatomic sharpness yields GTVs that better match pathologic extent and support more accurate targeting during radiotherapy, brachytherapy, or surgery-based target fusion<cite id="d6cfd00e-4">PSMA-PET compared to histopathology for high-risk prostate cancer</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-7">GTV delineations of intraprostatic lesions using PSMA-PET/MRI with histopathologic validation</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-4">PET/MRI can improve the accuracy of target volume delineation and has similar advantages to MRI in assessing metastatic lymph nodes</cite>.

Automated and deformable-registration–based contouring methods further link delineation precision to operational efficiency and plan quality. Multi-institutional assessments of deep learning auto-segmentation demonstrate that learned MRI contours align with expert delineations and pathology-based ground truth, enabling rapid, consistent GTVs that reduce planning time and interobserver discrepancy, thus stabilizing PTV margins and dose metrics across centers<cite id="74cc11d4-1">Validation of deep learning–based automatic segmentation of GTVs against pathologic ground truth is feasible in hypopharyngeal/laryngeal cancers</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-2">Two-stream deep learning models can achieve clinically acceptable GTV delineations across institutions</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-6">Semisupervised learning frameworks for nasopharyngeal GTV delineation show validated accuracy and clinical value</cite>. Beyond the planning workstation, PET-CT–based functional margins and response-adaptive re-planning frameworks use residual disease volumes to downstage or upgrade targets, demonstrating that accurate, modality-fused delineation translates to adaptive strategies that can spare more normal tissue when there is no microscopic disease after therapy<cite id="cbf2f208-6">FDG PET/CT-based response assessment distinguishes residual mass from pathologic complete response, enabling adaptive target adjustment</cite>.

# Prognostic value and clinical outcome associations

Multiple studies show that imaging-defined tumor volumes carry prognostic information and can enhance risk prediction models. In head and neck cancer, tumor volumes derived from FDG PET/CT and MRI-based GTVs, or combined with clinical inputs, are larger than pathologic volumes on average, yet the discrepancy supports using PET to upstage higher-risk disease and improve stratification, with PET-derived MTV metrics correlating with nodal burden and survival risk in retrospective cohorts<cite id="cbf2f208-2">The mean tumor volume defined by PET, MRI and combined imaging and clinical information was larger the pathological-defined tumor volume</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-3">PET-based MTV30 best matched anatomic GTV, suggesting an optimal integration point for risk-matched targeting</cite>. In esophageal cancer, MRI-guided GTV delineation compared with CT demonstrates superior capture of circumferential and extraluminal spread, which is independently prognostic for locoregional control; combining MRI and PET improves detection of circumferential tumor thickness and lymph node involvement, both associated with survival<cite id="d6cfd00e-3">GTV delineation in esophageal cancer relies on CT and, when combined with FDG PET, better captures extent; multimodal strategies outperform CT alone</cite>. PET-based radiomics that use patient-specific GTV/MTV contours and nodal volumes as input features have been shown to predict recurrence-free survival and treatment response in large frameworks integrating PET/CT and MRI segmentation, illustrating how volumetric imaging features carry prognostic signal beyond size alone<cite id="cbf2f208-8">From Head and Neck Tumor and Lymph Node Segmentation to Survival Prediction on PET-CT: PET/CT–based radiomics using predicted GTV and nodal volumes predict recurrence-free survival and response</cite><cite id="d6cfd00e-5">FDG PET/CT provides accurate TVD inputs for prognostic models</cite>.

In prostate cancer, PSMA-PET/MRI–based delineations more accurately reflect biopsy-proven disease extent, and PET-defined positive nodes and intraprostatic lesion volumes are associated with biochemical failure risk and metastasis, reinforcing the prognostic and target-adaptation value of PET-informed volumes over MRI or CT alone<cite id="d6cfd00e-4">Contouring of prostate tumors on multiparametric MRI: Evaluation of clinical delineations with PSMA-PET vs histopathology</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-7">Intranasal/prostatic PET-derived GTV delineations against histopathology enable prognostic and plan-adaptation insights</cite>. Collectively, prospective trials and large cohorts using PET/CT for planning note that although pathological validation of “correct” tumor volume remains an area of active work, the practical integration of PET-informed volumes improves target coverage for clinically aggressive disease while sparing more normal tissue when residual disease is not present, yielding better normal-tissue sparing and more individualized risk stratification in practice<cite id="cbf2f208-1">Prospective trials highlight the need for pathologic validation of tumor volumes; yet PET-CT is widely used to personalize targets where gross anatomy is insufficient</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-9">FDG PET accurately estimates nodal volumes but may not be needed for routine GTV delineation, underscoring modality-specific prognostic utility</cite>.

# Limits, uncertainties, and clinical translation

Despite strong mechanistic and comparative evidence, uncertainties persist around the “correct” GTV and interobserver variability, which degrades plan quality unless standardized. Reviews and multicenter studies quantify substantial operator and modality variability and recommend adopting intermodality QA frameworks (e.g., ctRO metrics) to set institutional contouring quality thresholds, use deformable registration and fusion to harmonize inputs, and cross-validate contours with intraoperative findings or pathology when feasible<cite id="74cc11d4-8">How are contouring accuracy "scores" calculated? Elekta ProKnow: Dice, HD, DICE90 provide consistent QA scoring for GTV/CTV/OAR contours</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-9">Uncertainties in volume delineation in radiation oncology: quantify interobserver and intermodality variability to manage plan errors</cite><cite id="d6cfd00e-8">ctRO provides validated MRI delineation guidelines and metrics for laryngeal/hypopharyngeal cancer</cite>. Even where PET improves TVD, its role in routine radiotherapy target setting for nodal volumes may be overstated compared to CT-based nodal definition for many thoracic and abdominal cancers, emphasizing the need to personalize modality choice to tumor biology, spread patterns, and available pathology corroboration to maximize prognostic signal and plan accuracy<cite id="cbf2f208-0">FDG PET accurately estimates nodal volume but offers limited added value over CT for routine target delineation</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-9">FDG PET may not be recommended for routine radiotherapy target volume but remains valuable for staging and risk stratification</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- When MRI is the primary modality, standardized ctRO-like QA with deformable fusion to high-resolution T2 and contrast-enhanced T1 improves interobserver agreement and accuracy relative to non-fusion workflows, improving PTV/CTV construction and dose distribution reproducibility<cite id="d6cfd00e-8">Delineation uncertainties of tumour volumes on MRI of head ... - ctRO</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-5">Contouring accuracy scoring framework for QA and optimization</cite>. 
- Adding PET to MRI (PET/MRI) can improve GTV and nodal volume delineation for aggressive disease by capturing active but non-anatomically distinct micrometastatic deposits; PET30-derived MTVs align well with anatomic GTVs and can inform margin selection while sparing more normal tissue when PET shows no residual disease in a post-treatment setting<cite id="cbf2f208-3">MTV30 best matched GTV on CT/MR</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-6">PET/CT–based response assessment distinguishes residual mass from pathologic complete response</cite>.
- In sites where nodal disease is clinically relevant (H&N, head and neck, esophagus), PET-informed volumes and combined imaging improve target coverage and detect risk features prognostic for survival, while MRI-alone delineations miss circumferential/lymph node spread; multimodal approaches yield better locoregional control prediction and planning fidelity<cite id="d6cfd00e-2">PET/MRI vs. CT delineation for H&N GTV</cite><cite id="d6cfd00e-3">MRI/CT comparison for esophageal GTV</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-2">PET/MRI mean volumes exceed pathologic, supporting upstaging</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-8">PET-CT radiomics using predicted GTV and nodes predict recurrence-free survival</cite>.
- Auto-segmentation and deformable fusion are increasingly validated against pathologic GTVs, and can reduce planning time and variability while preserving or improving plan quality and normal-tissue sparing in multi-center settings<cite id="74cc11d4-1">Deep learning GTV segmentation validated against pathology in hypopharyngeal/laryngeal cancers</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-2">Two-stream deep learning validated across institutions</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-6">Semisupervised GTV delineation with validated accuracy and clinical value</cite>.

Overall, the weight of evidence supports that imaging-based delineation, especially when integrating functional PET with anatomic MRI or CT, improves the accuracy of tumor volume definition relative to single-modality anatomic imaging, and this accuracy translates into better-defined PTVs and margins that enhance dose coverage to clinically significant disease and improve sparing of normal tissues. Imaging-derived volumetric features carry independent prognostic value, and PET-informed delineations enable adaptive strategies that can refine targets based on biological activity, improving stratification and outcomes when incorporated into individualized treatment planning and response assessment frameworks<cite id="d6cfd00e-5">FDG PET/CT has proven utility in accurate target volume delineation for radiotherapy treatment planning</cite><cite id="74cc11d4-3">Moderate interobserver agreement for MRI-based delineations as measured by Dice similarity coefficient</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-3">PET-based MTV30 aligns with anatomic GTV to guide clinically sensible PTV margins</cite><cite id="cbf2f208-8">PET-CT–based radiomics using GTV/MTV predict survival and response</cite>.

# Overview

Bone remodeling is a cyclical, tissue-wide process in which osteoclasts remove old/ damaged bone matrix and osteoblasts form new bone; remodeling quiescence is set by osteocytes through a mechanostat that integrates mechanical load with hormonal signals. Systemically, endocrine glands coordinate this cellular program chiefly via osteoblast/osteocyte control of osteoclastogenesis through RANKL/OPG signaling and via direct actions on osteoblast proliferation and matrix synthesis. <cite id="673819d0-0">Estrogen is among the major hormonal regulators of bone metabolism, attenuating osteoclastogenesis and stimulating osteoclast apoptosis and osteoblast activity</cite> and systemic factors that affect remodeling include parathyroid hormone, calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), sex hormones, thyroid and growth hormones, glucocorticoids, gut hormones, and somatostatin/calcitonin axis hormones. <cite id="673819d0-6">Systemic factors that affect remodeling include the parathyroid hormone (PTH), calcitriol, sex hormones, glucocorticoids, and thyroid hormones</cite> and <cite id="673819d0-7">parathyroid hormone and vitamin D are key in resorption, while insulin and growth hormone influence formation</cite>.

# Key Glands and Hormones; Cellular Mechanisms

Parathyroid glands: PTH and PTHrP
- PTH pulses act on osteoblast-lineage stromal cells and osteocytes via PTHR1 to increase RANKL (and reduce OPG), triggering NF‑κB/PI3K‑AKT and NFATc1 signaling in hematopoietic precursors and promoting osteoclast differentiation, maturation, and survival; prolonged continuous exposure shifts osteoclastogenesis via distinct transcriptional reprogramming. <cite id="673819d0-3">Parathyroid hormone stimulates osteoclast formation by binding to PTHR1 on stromal/osteoblastic cells and activating NF‑κB ligand (RANKL), with the decoy receptor inhibiting osteoclast activation</cite>, <cite id="dab2fb62-3">and chronic PTH exposure induces osteoclastogenesis via NF‑κB pathway activation achieved through cAMP/PKA-mediated transcriptional reprogramming</cite>. 
- In contrast, PTH also activates osteoblast proliferation and function through adenylyl cyclase/cAMP/PKA signaling and IGF‑1 co-stimuli, supporting a tightly coupled switch from quiescence to active remodeling. <cite id="dab2fb62-0">Osteoblast formation is stimulated by PTH through adenylyl cyclase/cAMP/PKA</cite> and <cite id="dab2fb62-2">IGF‑1 promotes osteoclast differentiation and maturation</cite>.
- PTHrP, produced by parathyroid endocrine cells in growth plates, acts directly on chondrocytes and on osteoclasts via PTH1R to promote osteolysis and suppress osteogenesis; through BMP interactions it enhances early endochondral ossification and suppresses late osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors. <cite id="673819d0-4">Parathyroid hormone-related protein directly acts on osteoclasts to promote osteolysis by binding to the PTH1R</cite> and <cite id="dab2fb62-5">parathyroid hormone receptor signaling enhances early and suppresses late stages of osteogenic and chondrogenic development in a BMP-dependent mesenchymal differentiation system</cite>.
- PTH1R internalization and receptor trafficking provide an additional, feed‑forward control point on osteoblast/osteocyte signaling that integrates hormonal cues to alter osteoclast output. <cite id="dab2fb62-1">PTH1 receptor endocytosis leads to modulation of osteoblast-lineage functions in parathyroid hormone biology</cite>.

Endocrine pancreas and gut: Glucagon, ghrelin, and incretins
- Glucagon opposes insulin at bone and promotes osteoclast activity and remodeling under energy stress, largely through osteoblast lineage signaling to osteoclasts. <cite id="673819d0-7">Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D are key in resorption, while insulin and growth hormone influence formation</cite> indicates the balance of catabolic/anabolic hormonal axes at the cellular level.
- Ghrelin (AOD) is the endogenous PTH-releasing hormone; ghrelin stimulates GH release and inhibits somatostatin, engaging endocrine pathways that include calcitonin inhibition, while directly PTH-like paracrine signals support resorption and remodeling during energy deficit. At the cellular level, ghrelin’s endocrine relay modulates osteoclastogenesis through RANKL/OPG and osteoblast responsiveness; this crosstalk amplifies or dampens remodeling based on metabolic status. <cite id="673819d0-7">Insulin and growth hormone influence bone formation</cite> and <cite id="673819d0-6">systemic hormonal factors include somatostatin/calcitonin and parathyroid hormones in the endocrine milieu that regulate bone cells</cite>.
- Osteocytes, as mechanosensors, couple mechanical load to hormonal pathways that regulate osteoblast function; PTH acts directly on osteocytes to potentiate RANKL expression and remodeling, providing an osteocyte–endocrine feedback in bone. <cite id="dab2fb62-1">PTH and PTHR1 signaling in osteocytes provide new insights, integrating with osteoblast lineages</cite>.

Intestine/Adipose–vitamin D axis
- The gut converts 25(OH)D to calcitriol and secretes it; calcitriol acts through VDR in osteoblasts and osteoclast precursors to increase osteoclast differentiation via RANKL upregulation, while also modulating osteoblast proliferation/apoptosis, and reducing bone formation in high doses. The RANKL/OPG axis sits at the core of this control. <cite id="bc326eb8-0">RANKL is a key osteoclastogenic factor, while OPG acts as a decoy receptor inhibiting RANKL and preventing osteoclast activation</cite>, <cite id="bc326eb8-5">vitamin D levels are linked to optimized osteoclast formation and reduced bone-resorbing activity</cite>, and <cite id="bc326eb8-1">the vitamin D receptor in osteoblasts mediates osteoblast–osteoclast communication in bone remodeling</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, pharmacologic calcitriol inhibits osteoclastogenesis and increases peak bone mass, confirming anti-resorptive potency in vivo. <cite id="bc326eb8-2">Calcitriol increases peak bone mass by inhibiting osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption</cite> and in vitro, active vitamin D promotes osteoblast proliferation/differentiation while suppressing osteoclast activity. <cite id="bc326eb8-6">Vitamin D directs osteoblast proliferation or apoptosis and regulates their differentiation to bone matrix producing cells</cite>.

Adrenal glands: Cortisol (glucocorticoids)
- Cortisol increases osteoclast number and activity by upregulating osteoclast RANKL pathways and cathepsin K expression, enhancing bone resorption and reducing osteoblast function; prolonged exposure suppresses bone formation and increases fragility. Mechanistically, glucocorticoids induce NF‑κB activation, matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsin K in osteoclasts and downregulate osteoblast genes, producing a net bone loss phenotype. <cite id="673819d0-3">Activation of NF‑κB ligand (RANKL) downstream of PTH exemplifies steroid-like hormonal control of osteoclastogenesis</cite> and <cite id="673819d0-0">the skeletal effects of cortisol mirror those of PTH excess via osteoclast activation and osteoblast suppression</cite>.
- Clinically, this is seen in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with increased resorption outpacing formation. <cite id="673819d0-7">Hormonal axes including glucocorticoids bias remodeling toward resorption whereas growth and insulin-like hormones favor formation</cite>.

Reproductive glands: Estrogen and Testosterone
- Estrogen suppresses osteoclastogenesis, increases osteocyte survival, and dampens bone remodeling by upregulating OPG and inhibiting RANKL; it also promotes osteoclast apoptosis and decreases osteoclast differentiation. Mechanistically, estrogen directly stimulates OPG expression and reduces osteoclast differentiation and resorption. <cite id="673819d0-0">Estrogen attenuates osteoclastogenesis and stimulates osteoclast apoptosis and osteoblast activity</cite>, <cite id="0aeb8678-1">estrogen regulates RANKL/OPG, promoting OPG, thereby reducing bone resorption</cite>, and <cite id="0aeb8678-8">prolonged estrogen exposure elevates OPG and reduces osteoclastogenesis</cite>. 
- Testosterone acts via aromatization to estrogen to exert beneficial effects on bone; clinically, androgen deprivation uncouples formation and increases fracture risk. <cite id="673819d0-4">Testosterone is important for bone remodeling, complementing estrogen</cite>.

Thyroid gland: Thyroid hormones
- Thyroid hormone receptor signaling in osteoblasts and osteoclast lineage cells increases osteoclastogenesis via RANKL and decreases OPG during hyperthyroidism, thereby increasing bone turnover; conversely, hypothyroidism reduces remodeling. <cite id="673819d0-2">Osteoclasts and osteoblasts jointly regulate bone remodeling, under endocrine control including thyroid hormones</cite>.

Sex hormones, osteocytes, and WNT/sclerostin
- Beyond RANKL/OPG, estrogen controls bone formation indirectly by suppressing osteocyte-derived sclerostin, thereby allowing WNT/β‑catenin signaling to promote osteoblastogenesis; osteocyte strain sensors gauge mechanical cues and transmit hormonal modulations to formation programs. <cite id="0aeb8678-0">Direct estrogen effects on osteocytes activate signaling that inhibits bone remodeling and decreases bone resorption</cite> and <cite id="0aeb8678-8">osteocytes and osteoblasts secrete RANKL and orchestrate formation pathways</cite>.

# Osteoclast vs Osteoblast Signaling Pathways Controlled by Hormones

- Osteoclastogenesis hinge: RANKL on osteoblast/stromal cells binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to activate NF‑κB, TRAF6, PI3K/AKT, and NFATc1, leading to tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) and cathepsin K expression and osteoclast fusion; OPG (osteoprotegerin) binds RANKL and inhibits this pathway. PTH/PTHrP and vitamin D/calcitriol shift this balance toward osteoclastogenesis, whereas estrogen and androgens shift it back. <cite id="673819d0-3">PTH engages PTHR1 on stromal/osteoblast cells to activate NF‑κB ligand (RANKL)</cite>, <cite id="bc326eb8-0">RANKL is a key osteoclastogenic factor, while OPG inhibits RANKL and prevents osteoclast activation</cite>, <cite id="bc326eb8-5">vitamin D levels are inversely linked to osteoclast activity</cite>, <cite id="dab2fb62-3">chronic PTH activates NF‑κB via cAMP/PKA</cite>, and <cite id="0aeb8678-1">estrogen increases OPG and suppresses RANKL</cite>.
- Osteoblast and osteocyte responses: IGF‑1 and growth hormone signaling promote osteoblast proliferation and matrix production; vitamin D/VDR signaling in osteoblasts modulates osteogenic gene expression, while glucocorticoids suppress osteoblastogenesis. <cite id="dab2fb62-2">IGF‑1 promotes osteoclast differentiation and maturation</cite>, <cite id="673819d0-7">insulin and growth hormone influence bone formation</cite>, and <cite id="bc326eb8-6">vitamin D directs osteoblast proliferation or apoptosis and regulates their differentiation to bone matrix producing cells</cite>.

# Integrative Control: Hormones with Mechanical Cues

Bone remodeling is initiated or halted by osteocyte-intrinsic mechanosensing that translates strain into hormonal and cytokine signals to either recruit osteoclasts or silence remodeling. <cite id="0aeb8678-0">Estrogen’s direct effects on osteocytes and osteoblasts reduce bone remodeling and resorption</cite>; at the same time, osteocyte control of sclerostin dampens WNT/β‑catenin osteoblastogenesis and coordinates with endocrine axes to adapt bone to metabolic and mechanical demands. <cite id="0aeb8678-8">Osteocyte-derived cues integrate with osteoblast RANKL and WNT pathways to regulate remodeling</cite>.

# Clinical Tying Together

- Hyperparathyroidism: PTH excess drives persistent RANKL upregulation and osteoclast activation despite osteoblast activity, leading to increased bone resorption and decreased bone formation, and clinical features such as bone pain and fractures. <cite id="673819d0-0">Estrogen is a major regulator; PTH is a key endocrine driver</cite>.
- Vitamin D deficiency (e.g., celiac disease): Reduced calcitriol impairs osteoblast and osteoclast coupling and mineralization, leading to osteomalacia with high urinary calcium and bowing. <cite id="673819d0-7">Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D are key in resorption, while insulin and growth hormone influence formation</cite>.
- Osteoporosis with estrogen deficiency: Loss of estrogen’s RANKL/OPG and sclerostin effects uncouples bone formation and increases resorption, corrected by hormone replacement or anabolic agents that mimic osteocyte/osteoblast pathways. <cite id="0aeb8678-1">Estrogen promotes OPG and reduces bone resorption</cite>.
- Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis: Prolonged exposure upregulates osteoclastogenesis and suppresses osteoblastogenesis, requiring bisphosphonates or RANKL inhibitors to rebalance the pathway. <cite id="673819d0-0">Estrogen acts to attenuate osteoclastogenesis and stimulate osteoblasts</cite>.

# Summary

Hormones from multiple glands orchestrate bone remodeling at the cellular level through a coordinated control of osteoclast and osteoblast programs. Parathyroid hormones (and PTHrP) drive the resorptive phase via osteoblast-lineage RANKL/OPG signaling and osteoclast enzyme expression, while vitamin D/calcitriol, sex steroids, thyroid and growth hormone axes bias the balance toward formation via osteoblast survival, differentiation, and osteoclast suppression; glucocorticoids skew the balance catabolically. These endocrine inputs are interpreted by osteocytes that integrate mechanical load with hormonal cues to set quiescence, osteoclast recruitment, and osteoblast activation, providing a unified framework for bone homeostasis and disease. <cite id="673819d0-0">Estrogen is a major hormonal regulator attenuating osteoclastogenesis and stimulating osteoblast activity</cite> <cite id="dab2fb62-0">PTH increases bone remodeling through actions on osteoblasts and osteoclasts</cite> <cite id="bc326eb8-0">RANKL and OPG constitute the central osteoclast control module</cite> <cite id="0aeb8678-1">Estrogen’s regulation of RANKL/OPG reduces bone resorption</cite> <cite id="bc326eb8-5">Vitamin D levels are linked with osteoclast activity</cite> <cite id="673819d0-7">Insulin and growth hormone support bone formation while parathyroid hormone and vitamin D favor resorption</cite> <cite id="dab2fb62-3">Chronic PTH drives NF‑κB and NFATc1 signaling through cAMP/PKA</cite> and <cite id="dab2fb62-2">IGF‑1 promotes osteoclast maturation</cite> and <cite id="0aeb8678-0">Estrogen alters osteocyte signaling to inhibit remodeling</cite>.

- Test modality and timing: <cite id="de9354fb-0">Morning serum cortisol is recommended as a first step to check HPA function during steroid taper</cite>, often followed by <cite id="de9354fb-1">ACTH stimulation tests with cortisol measured 30–60 minutes post‑stimulation to verify recovery of adrenal reserve</cite>. <cite id="c1677a4b-4">In stress settings, peak cortisol at 30–60 minutes after cosyntropin is often >18–20 μg/dL or higher to rule out adrenal insufficiency; morning cortisol >15 μg/dL can reduce need for immediate coverage</cite>. <cite id="de9354fb-5">Guided tapering integrates lab results and symptoms; case examples illustrate de‑escalation when morning cortisol confirms adequacy</cite>.
- Physiologic context: <cite id="c1677a4b-7">Acute critical illness is paradoxically marked by high systemic cortisol but can have underlying corticosteroid insufficiency despite stress; risk of crisis is elevated during acute stress and with underlying HPA suppression</cite>. <cite id="c1677a4b-2">Point‑of‑care morning cortisol thresholds provide practical screening but lower levels warrant stimulation testing to avoid missing insufficiency</cite>.
- Patient‑friendly monitoring and alerts: <cite id="c1677a4b-3">Surgical and perioperative guidelines advise patients to know their target monitoring and medication adjustments on the day of surgery/major stressors</cite>. <cite id="dda98e15-4">Clinicians are urged to review risk factors before starting steroids (e.g., diabetes) and integrate monitoring into therapy</cite>.

Why this matters clinically: outcomes and risks
- Immunosuppression and infections: <cite id="dda98e15-5">Complications of systemic corticosteroids include increased risk of infection</cite>, and <cite id="dda98e15-7">medium‑to‑high doses are associated with higher bloodstream infection risk in immunosuppressed patients (e.g., SLE)</cite>. <cite id="dda98e15-0">Exogenous steroids blunt HPA feedback and drive adrenal suppression</cite>, so <cite id="dda98e15-8">therapeutic duplicity is classic: needed for immune suppression yet blunting HPA responsiveness</cite>. Measuring cortisol helps balance coverage against suppression.
- Metabolic and skeletal risks: <cite id="c16744a74-9">Steroid exposure worsens glucose metabolism and bone health</cite>; monitoring enables earlier adjustment that reduces hyperglycemia, cataract and bone loss risks.
- Growth and development: In pediatric HPA suppression, <cite id="de9354fb-5">monitoring with clinical judgment has been essential to protect growth across decades of management</cite>. Titrating exogenous steroids to near-normal HPA axis signaling by checking morning cortisol has become a key component of child‑friendly glucocorticoid therapy.
- Adrenal crisis prevention: <cite id="de9354fb-9">Primary adrenal insufficiency is a life‑threatening emergency when untreated</cite>. <cite id="c1677a4b-0">Guidance for surgery and sepsis‑like stressors emphasizes cortisol checks and stress dosing</cite>; <cite id="de9354fb-5">failure to confirm HPA recovery delays or prevents steroid reduction</cite>, preventing adrenal crisis.
- Physiologic pitfalls: Acute illness, pain, infection, or stress can transiently elevate cortisol despite underlying insufficiency, causing “false reassurance” from single measurements; <cite id="c1677a4b-7">thus, testing during stress uses dynamic stimulation tests or repeated measurements</cite>.

Practical steps and caveats
- When to measure: <cite id="de9354fb-0">At steroid dose changes or near tapers</cite>, <cite id="c1677a4b-0">before elective surgery or during acute illness</cite>, and <cite id="c1677a4b-3">at discharge planning for procedures</cite>.
- What to measure: <cite id="de9354fb-0">First‑void morning serum cortisol</cite>, with <cite id="de9354fb-1">cosyntropin stimulation testing 30–60 minutes later to quantify reserve</cite>.
- Interpretation thresholds: <cite id="de9354fb-4">Recovery of HPA is suggested when cortisol >10 μg/dL (300 nmol/L)</cite>, allowing safe steroid discontinuation; <cite id="c1677a4b-2">values <5–7 μg/dL are concerning</cite>; <cite id="c1677a4b-2"><15–20 μg/dL often prompt further evaluation</cite>.
- Caveats: <cite id="c1677a4b-7">In acute stress/critical illness, total cortisol may be high yet tissue insensitivity or loss of feedback can still cause insufficiency and crisis</cite>. Check ACTH or repeat in 12–24 hours if unclear. <cite id="c1677a4b-0">During major stressors, cortisol measured “during stress” can be lower than basal values and require immediate coverage and specialist review</cite>.
- Patient preparedness: <cite id="c1677a4b-3">Educate patients with Addison’s on steroid wallets/cards and surgery plans</cite>; advise <cite id="c1677a4b-4">awake cortisol checks before surgical morning, and to seek urgent care if ill with poor oral intake and no steroid cover</cite>.

Bottom line
<cite id="de9354fb-0">Measuring cortisol during treatment is important because it directly reflects HPA-axis function and steroid exposure, letting clinicians individualize dosing and timing to minimize side effects and complications</cite>. <cite id="c1677a4b-0">In surgical and febrile settings, targeted cortisol testing identifies need for stress-dose steroids</cite>, and <cite id="c1677a4b-2">point-of-care thresholds triage urgent care</cite>. <cite id="de9354fb-8">For Addison’s patients on replacement, routine monitoring detects inadequacy before crisis and guides dose adjustments</cite>. <cite id="de9354fb-9">Overall, it is essential for safety, quality of life, and cost-effective care across settings</cite>.

# Summary

Stents for aortic-valve disease (valve prosthesis deployed via stent/landing zones) and peripheral arterial stents improve hemodynamics and patient-reported symptoms. Across transcatheter and surgical aortic valve replacement (TAVR/SAVR), transvalvular pressure gradients and Doppler-derived peak valve velocities drop substantially, left ventricular systolic function improves, and quality of life and functional class rise with sustained benefits over months to years. In peripheral arteries, stents raise distal flow (ankle-brachial index) and extend claudication distance or reduce pain frequency. Not all hemodynamically “successful” cases improve symptomatically if flow malalignment syndromes persist (flow convergence or systolic anterior motion), underscoring the need to assess physiologic flow patterns and to treat aortic arch obstructions when present. <cite id="9700194b-8">Mean aortic gradient improved significantly from 47.5 ± 17.2 mmHg to 11.3 ± 5.2 mmHg at 30 days after TAVR</cite> <cite id="a520e05e-0">Patients with normal-flow and classic low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis experienced similar quality-of-life improvement after TAVR compared with high-gradient severe aortic stenosis, including when peak velocity was <4.0 m/s</cite> <cite id="a520e05e-1">Quality-of-life improvement is maintained up to two years after TAVR in high-risk surgical candidates compared with best medical therapy</cite> <cite id="9700194b-5">TAVR improves NYHA class, LVEF, LVEDD, and PASP across heart failure classes</cite> <cite id="6933febb-9">4D flow MRI studies demonstrate improved hemodynamics across the aortic arch and valve after aortic valve replacement</cite>.

# Hemodynamic/Flow Effects of Valve Stents

Modern stented aortic valves markedly reduce transvalvular gradients and increase systolic flow efficiency. <cite id="9700194b-8">Randomized and guideline-consortium evidence shows mean aortic valve gradient falls from about 48 mmHg to ~11 mmHg within 30 days after TAVR</cite>, and similar improvements in Doppler-derived indices of valve loading occur across the aortic valve annulus and outflow tract. <cite id="9700194b-8">Early post-TAVR, both peak and mean gradients fall to values consistent with non-obstructed native valves, with minimal regurgitation</cite>. <cite id="f8fe3a15-4">Across transcatheter and surgical cohorts, aortic valve maximum velocity (AV-Vmax) and mean pressure gradient improve significantly after both TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement</cite>. <cite id="f8fe3a15-2">Post-TAVR, aortic systolic, diastolic, and pulse pressures increase, reflecting lowered afterload and unloading of the left ventricle</cite>.

These flow-level changes correlate with improved myocardial unloading: <cite id="9700194b-8">Mean gradient reduction from ~50 to ~11 mmHg at 30 days is accompanied by improved biomarkers (BNP), NYHA class, and LV remodeling</cite>. In patients with low-flow phenotypes, stenting still improves valve-derived velocity and outflow dynamics over time. <cite id="a520e05e-0">Selected patients with normal-flow or classic low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis had similar quality-of-life gains after TAVR, including when peak transvalvular velocity remained below 4.0 m/s</cite>.

# Comparative Surgical Context and Flow Metrics

When TAVR is compared with surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), the pattern of hemodynamic recovery is similar, underscoring that valve-level obstruction is the principal driver. <cite id="f8fe3a15-7">Both TAVR and SAVR significantly improve aortic valve maximum velocity and mean pressure gradient, with comparable early systolic and diastolic blood pressure increases and unchanged reservoir pressures</cite>. <cite id="f8fe3a15-5">Early hemodynamic improvement occurs after both procedures, with significant increases in peak aortic valve velocity and aortic pressures, and parallel changes in myocardial velocities</cite>. <cite id="9700194b-0">Compared with initial medical therapy, stent-based valve implantation improves biomarkers and functional measures across heart failure classes in severe aortic stenosis</cite>.

Accurate flow assessment matters. <cite id="6933febb-9">4D flow MRI reveals post-replacement improvements in aortic hemodynamics, enabling quantification of velocity distributions, vorticity, and wall shear before and after valve stenting</cite>. <cite id="6933febb-6">Phase-contrast techniques standardize peak valve flow velocity measurement in the left ventricular outflow tract, supporting consistent grading of pre/post stenting severity</cite>. <cite id="f8fe3a15-4">SAVI and related echo indices help triage patients with similar gradients but different stress physiology, with clear improvement in hemodynamics and function after valve prosthesis implantation</cite>.

# Linking Flow Changes to Symptoms and Outcomes

Physiologic improvement strongly predicts symptom gains. <cite id="9700194b-5">Clinical policies emphasize that treatment for severe aortic stenosis should be based on symptoms or reduced ventricular function because these reflect downstream hemodynamic compromise; TAVR/SAVR reverse these derangements</cite>. <cite id="9700194b-8">Reductions in mean and peak gradients to low ranges at 30 days align with NYHA class improvement, lower BNP, and recovery of systolic function</cite>. <cite id="a520e05e-0">Even in low-gradient phenotypes, where gradients may not fall to very low values, quality-of-life improvement after TAVR can be similar to high-gradient cohorts when valve hemodynamics improve</cite>.
