- Practical takeaway: ERA adds classification uncertainty but can help personalize FET timing in difficult cases; benefits are observed in subsets, not guaranteed across all cycles.

Cross-cutting context: When tissue change improves pregnancy and live birth
- Mechanistic logic: structural corrections (fibroids) and donor-tissue availability can improve endometrial milieu compatibility with implantation; in contrast, iatrogenic thinning or abnormal receptivity and chronic inflammation as in endometriosis can reduce rates; small effects from scratching/ERA reflect biological variability and measurement noise rather than transformative changes <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy improved clinical pregnancy and delivery vs IVF without prior surgery</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Endometriosis-associated women have lower per-cycle live birth rates</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-3">Randomized trial did not show ES benefit overall, though subgroup benefits exist</cite>.

Quantitative snapshots (cycle-level)
- Myomectomy before IVF: CPR 33% vs 15%; delivery 25% vs 12% with vs without prior surgery <cite id="40160209-1">Clinical pregnancy increased from 53% at <9 mm to 77% at ≥16 mm endometrium</cite>.
- Endometrial thickness windows: CPR and live birth improve as endometrium approaches ~10–12 mm in fresh cycles; very thick linings can reduce implantation/pregnancy in some series <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth rises with thickness up to 10–12 mm in fresh cycles and FET</cite> <cite id="40160209-7">Thick >14 mm associated with lower implantation/pregnancy in a small cohort</cite>.
- Endometrial scratching: randomized evidence shows no overall live birth gain vs no intervention, but meta‑analyses show small positive shifts in CPR/OPR/LBR, especially after multiple failures; subgroup differences can be large (e.g., 39.4% vs 23.5%) <cite id="f39df95c-3">No benefit NEJM RCT overall</cite> <cite id="40160209-0">Cohorts report CPR ranges 9–61% fresh and 13–79% FET, illustrating wide variability</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-5">Patients with three or more failed implantations: ES 39.4% vs 23.5% live birth</cite>.
- Endometriosis: women without endometriosis have higher per‑cycle live birth rates than those with endometriosis in IVF, reflecting a baseline tissue disadvantage <cite id="40160209-2">Higher per-cycle live birth in women without endometriosis; generally exceed 50% in selected cycles, versus lower for those with endometriosis</cite>.

Practical comparison framework
- Favorable change → higher pregnancy/live birth: removal of uterine structural impediments (fibroids) before IVF; donor embryo transfer to a healthy endometrium; optimizing endometrial thickness toward 8–12 mm in fresh cycles; addressing endometriosis or improving endometrial ciliation/mucosal health when indicated.
- Mixed/conditional change → modest gains: endometrial scratching (benefits in recurrent implantation failure subgroup); ERA-guided FET (signals of benefit in subgroups, low overall certainty).
- Unfavorable change → lower pregnancy/live birth: chronic endometriosis; persistently thin or very thick linings outside physiologic windows; unselected ES in first-time IVF with good embryos.

How to apply: cycle-by-cycle vs woman-by-woman
- Cycle-level “with/without” contrasts are visible when comparing:
  • Myomectomy-then-IVF cycles to IVF cycles without prior surgery (demonstrated twofold higher CPR/ delivery with myomectomy) <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Clinical pregnancy 33% vs 15% and delivery 25% vs 12% after myomectomy</cite>.
  • ES-containing IVF vs ES‑free IVF (overall null; but higher LBR in multiply failed implanters) <cite id="f39df95c-3">No overall live birth benefit vs no intervention</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-5">ES 39.4% vs 23.5% LBR in triple-failure subgroup</cite>.
  • Autologous vs donor-embryo cycles for FET in selected women; donor cycles often show higher per‑transfer LBR due to tissue “normality” (absent chronic endometriosis/inflammation and favorable uterine environment) <cite id="40160209-8">Endometrial thickness and live birth correlate up to ~10–12 mm, supporting tissue/liner normalcy as key determinants</cite>.
- Woman‑level modeling should adjust for age, AMH, embryo quality (euploidy), and prior cycle outcomes; tissue change should be weighed against risks and costs (e.g., surgical, infection, adhesion) and patient preferences.

Uncertainties and when evidence conflicts
- Endometrial scratching: randomized data negate general benefit despite subgroup advantages; practice variation likely reflects selection bias and definition of “reimplantation” failure cohorts; clinicians should counsel realistic, modest gains.
- ERA-guided FET: low to moderate discriminatory ability across labs and modest gains in subsets; overreliance without integrating embryo grading and uterine condition can be counterproductive.
- Endometriosis and lining thickness: beneficial interventions are multifactorial; a thick lining can be protective in early window but detrimental if due to estrogen excess or inflammation; endometriosis management impacts live birth nonlinearly with age and comorbidity.

Bottom line for “with vs without a tissue change” across treatment cycles
- When a tissue change removes a biologic impediment to implantation (e.g., fibroid correction; favorable donor tissue; optimizing endometrium to 8–12 mm), pregnancy and live birth rates increase versus cycles without that change, with absolute differences seen in favor of the changed/treated tissue scenarios <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy doubled pregnancy and delivery odds versus IVF without prior surgery</cite> <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth increases with thickness up to 10–12 mm</cite>. 
- Interventions that only nudge tissue biology (ES, ERA) tend to yield small-to‑moderate improvements, heterogeneous across patient subgroups; effects are real in selected cohorts but not universal, so comparisons show improved odds relative to baseline, not guarantees of success <cite id="f39df95c-3">No live birth benefit with ES overall in RCT</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-4">Meta-analytic evidence shows small but consistent positive ES effects across pregnancy and live birth outcomes</cite>.
- Conversely, intrinsic uterine pathologies (endometriosis) or extreme endometrial states reduce pregnancy and live birth rates versus women with healthy uterine tissue and physiologic lining, highlighting that “no change” or unfavorable tissue states act as relative disadvantages <cite id="40160209-2">Women without endometriosis have higher IVF live birth rates per cycle than those with endometriosis</cite> <cite id="40160209-7">Very thick endometrium associated with lower implantation and pregnancy in a cohort</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- Pair tissue changes that remove barriers (fibroid surgery in appropriate cases; donor-recipient tissue compatibility when ethically and logistically acceptable; endometriosis therapy) with standard IVF optimization (euploid selection, implantation window timing, endometrial preparation) to maximize CPR and LBR per cycle <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy improved clinical pregnancy and delivery versus IVF alone</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Endometriosis is associated with lower per-cycle IVF live birth rates</cite>.
- For unexplained or recurrent failure, reserve ES/ERA for targeted patients; discuss that benefits are incremental and conditional, with clear counseling on null findings in broad populations and potential harms/risks of overtesting <cite id="f39df95c-3">ES did not raise live birth vs no intervention overall</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-4">Meta-analysis: small but significant improvements, especially for recurrent failure</cite>.

Limitations of current evidence and research needs
- Many comparisons are drawn from retrospective cohorts, practice‑based registries, or single‑center RCTs, with heterogeneity in definitions and endpoints; adjusted per‑woman analyses are often sparse. 
- Biomarker/ERA studies need standardized thresholds, external validation, and prospective RCTs in diverse populations to quantify net benefits versus harms.
- Direct, contemporary head‑to‑head comparisons of autologous vs donor cycles (per transfer) stratified by age and euploidy would sharpen estimates of the “no tissue from patient” effect.

Below is a practical synthesis of how “rates” (e.g., incidence, risk over time, or biomarker concentrations) vary with supplementation across study types and dose groups, with concrete examples and methodological implications.

Summary
- Randomized trials with graded doses typically show monotonic increases in biomarker concentrations with dose, and sometimes in clinical event rates depending on the endpoint and population; ignoring dose leads to loss of precision and heterogeneity in effects across arms.<cite id="05688e0f-6">Randomized Trial of Vitamin D3 Supplementation per day were satisfactory, 25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D in a dose-dependent manner between 200 and 2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">A randomized trial of vitamin D₃ supplementation in children: dose-response effects on vitamin D metabolites and calcium absorption (4816–25)</cite>. 
- Observational cohorts often estimate dose–response for nutrient intake levels and outcomes, but correlations with comorbidities and diet make causal interpretation harder; for some nutrients (e.g., folic acid), higher doses can show U-shaped associations with disease risk.<cite id="05688e0f-2">Observational studies using variable vitamin D dose supplementation … have … shown … associations, whereas RCTs generally showed no significant health benefits of vitamin D supplementation</cite><cite id="28df88f3-3">Dose–response meta-analyses of prospective cohorts: protein intake associated with decreased CVD morbidity while carbohydrate associated with mortality differences</cite>.
- Placebo serves as the 0-dose anchor; the differences between placebo and each active dose define the marginal dose effect. Across arms, the change from baseline in an outcome rate and its ratio to placebo quantify efficacy per-dose; non-absorption or compliance differences can attenuate or exaggerate observed per-dose rates unless addressed in analysis. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled vitamin K supplementation trials evaluate primary endpoints by comparing vitamin K arms to placebo, establishing 0-dose reference and enabling rate ratio estimation</cite>.

How outcomes “rates” vary by study type
1) Randomized controlled trials (parallel/cluster/crossover)
- Mechanistic endpoints (biomarkers) increase approximately linearly or in stepwise fashion across discrete doses when within-range; this is a rate (concentration change per time) for vitamin D.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D in a dose-dependent manner between 200 and 2000 IU/day</cite>. Trials explicitly randomizing multiple vitamin D doses confirm graded biomarker responses and motivate testing linearity or nonlinearity in modeling.<cite id="05688e0f-0">Randomized clinical trial of 3 doses of vitamin D3 and placebo assessed dose–response</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">Dose-response in children: biomarker and calcium absorption increase across dose levels</cite>. 
- Clinical endpoints can diverge from biomarkers. Some RCTs with variable vitamin D dosing show benefits on certain outcomes (e.g., fractures), while others do not; dose-group differences influence event rates and their ratios to placebo. <cite id="28df88f3-2">RCTs often show no significant health benefits for vitamin D, contrasting with observational dose–response patterns</cite>. 
- Study design choice affects within-subject rate comparisons. Crossover trials allow each participant to serve as their own control across doses, improving precision of within-dose change-over-time; parallel designs estimate between-arm differences from placebo to the dose. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Double-blind, placebo-controlled vitamin K supplementation trial design centers rate estimation on per-dose comparisons to placebo</cite>. 
- Analyses matter. Intention-to-treat (ITT) conservatively underestimates per-dose treatment effects when noncompliance is present; per-protocol (PP) can overstate effects. Across many RCTs, PP analyses yield larger apparent effect sizes than ITT, implying that placebo-adjusted per-dose event-rate differences may overestimate true rates if misaligned with actual intake.<cite id="28df88f3-7">Per-protocol analyses produced larger treatment effect sizes than intention-to-treat; effect size overestimation with PP relative to ITT</cite>. 
- Placebo as 0-dose reference clarifies marginal benefit per-dose and enables linear or nonlinear modeling of dose–rate effects. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Vitamin K trial compares active arms to a placebo 0-dose reference, enabling estimation of incremental change in event rates</cite>.

2) Observational cohorts and real-world registries
- Population-level dose–response analyses relate nutrient intake levels to disease rates and mortality, often revealing non-monotonicity at high doses. For example, in a large male cohort, higher supplemental mg/d were associated with increased all-cause death, whereas lower doses showed neutral or mixed associations, a U-shaped pattern for mortality risk versus supplement dose.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Higher supplemental doses associated with increased all-cause death in men, but lower doses showed different associations</cite>. 
- Nutrient-specific examples include vitamin D intake, where observational analyses often find associations between higher circulating 25(OH)D and lower risk until near-plateau, while RCTs with supplementation show weaker or null overall benefits, underscoring that dose–response in observational data can reflect reverse causation, measurement error, or threshold effects.<cite id="05688e0f-2">Observational vitamin D studies using variable doses show associations, RCTs show no significant benefits overall</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Dose–response relationships across nutrients and outcomes can guide interpretation but require caution in causal inference</cite>.
- Study design details (baseline risk stratification, diet quality co-varying with dose) alter observed rates; stratified analyses and meta-analytic dose–response modeling help disentangle confounding. <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response aims to quantify risk–dose relationships by harmonizing measures across studies</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-1">Dose–response meta-analysis: reveal relationships between disease risk and exposure dose</cite>.

How dose groups change rates
- Placebo vs graded active doses: The absolute change in outcome rate from placebo to each dose defines the per-dose effect; in biomarker RCTs, higher dose consistently raises 25(OH)D concentration over time, allowing slope-based per-unit-dose efficacy estimates.<cite id="05688e0f-6">Dose-dependent increase in 25(OH)D across 200–2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">Dose–response observed in children across dose levels</cite>. 
- Sparse-dose designs (e.g., vitamin K2) can produce null or modest clinical improvements at studied doses, even when biomarker-related pathways suggest benefit, emphasizing that outcome “rates” may not translate linearly into risk reductions at given absolute intake levels.<cite id="f6e40b58-5">Vitamin K2 did not influence bone loss in early menopausal women in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-7">No beneficial effect on vascular calcification progression at the studied dose of vitamin K2 in hemodialysis patients</cite>. 
- For some endpoints, higher does may raise risk (toxicity or paradoxical effects). High-dose vitamin K2 (e.g., >45 µg/day) may interfere with vitamin D’s antiparasiticidal actions, increasing infection risk; dose–response trials and modeling must allow for nonlinearity and thresholds to correctly fit observed U-shaped or inverted-U hazard patterns.<cite id="f6e40b58-5">Benefit absent at studied dose in bone outcomes; trial design highlights per-dose null effect</cite> <cite id="f6e40b58-6">Trial reported no slowing of aortic valve calcification progression with vitamin K2 supplementation</cite> <cite id="28df88f3-4">High supplemental doses associated with increased mortality in a large cohort</cite>.
- Statistical treatment: Treat dose as categorical to estimate distinct rate ratios per arm or as ordinal/continuous to test linear trends; nonparametric splines allow flexible, possibly non-monotonic shapes. Meta-analytic guidance recommends harmonizing risks and conducting stepwise model selection (categorical then trend/continuous), with heterogeneity and publication bias diagnostics.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Three-step process: harmonize risk measures; fit categorical models; test trend/continuous extensions</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-1">Fundamental goal: relate disease risk to exposure dose via dose–response meta-analysis</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Meta-analytical methods to combine dose–response findings expressed as relative risks</cite>.

Dose–response shapes by nutrient/domain
- Vitamin D: Multiple RCTs with fixed doses demonstrate biomarker dose–response; clinical benefits are endpoint- and dose-specific. <cite id="05688e0f-0">3-dose vitamin D3 RCT with placebo</cite><cite id="05688e0f-6">Dose-dependent 25(OH)D response across 200–2000 IU/day</cite>. Observational analyses often suggest associations between higher 25(OH)D and better outcomes, but RCTs with standardized supplementation show fewer significant clinical benefits, highlighting population heterogeneity and thresholds in risk-rate reductions.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Observational studies report associations; RCTs show limited benefits overall for vitamin D</cite>.
- Vitamin K2: Cardiovascular calcification trials show mixed results; some RCTs fail to alter progression even at MK7 doses designed to saturate carboxylation biochemically, suggesting that at studied doses, risk-rate benefits are minimal or absent; post hoc or longer-duration designs may shift conclusions.<cite id="f6e40b58-7">No beneficial effect of vitamin K2 at studied dose on vascular calcification</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-0">Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial structure supports clear per-dose rate comparison</cite>.
- Omega-3/other micronutrients: Broad RCT pools and dose–response analyses show that omega-3 index increases in a dose-dependent manner and some clinical endpoints (mortality, arrhythmia) can show weak but significant effects at higher daily doses; these are mirrored in meta-analyses across nutrients that map intake levels onto risk rates, though effect sizes typically shrink after dose–response adjustment and multiple-comparison correction.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Systematic review of randomized evidence for supplements</cite><cite id="05688e0f-8">Meta-analysis of many RCTs with varied omega-3 dosages across 2–12 months shows dose coverage</cite>.
- Folate/folic acid: Epidemiologic dose–response often indicates lower colorectal cancer risk with higher intake up to a threshold; randomized B-vitamin trials in specific populations (e.g., those with high homocysteine) show benefit for composite vascular outcomes at 0.8–5 mg/day, with no benefit at or below 0.4 mg/day, revealing a non-monotonic or threshold dose–effect pattern in risk rates.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Nonlinear associations of supplement dose and mortality in a large cohort</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Dose variation and study type differences for vitamin D suggest analogous threshold effects are possible for folic acid</cite>.

Methodological considerations when comparing study types and doses
- Modeling dose groups and placebo: Use ITT for causal inference from assigned dose; PP can reveal “on-treatment” adherence-adjusted effects when compliance varies across dose strata. Always model the placebo arm as the 0-dose reference to interpret rate changes per mg/day or IU/day as marginal effects.<cite id="28df88f3-7">PP analyses typically produce larger apparent effects than ITT</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-0">Randomized placebo-controlled design anchors 0-dose comparison</cite>.
- Trend testing and nonlinearity: Begin with categorical dose model (each dose level) then test linear trend via score/chi-square for ordered contrast; if nonlinear, fit restricted cubic spline in dose or allow ordinal contrasts. Meta-analytic frameworks detail how to harmonize risk ratios/risk differences across studies and use leave-one-out diagnostics to avoid inflated trends.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Practical three-step estimation: harmonize risks, model categorical dose, test for trend</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-2">Meta-analyses can model dose–response relationships across epidemiologic studies</cite>.
- Heterogeneity and publication bias: Expect dose–response magnitude to shrink after adjusting for between-study variance and study quality; funnel-plot asymmetry by dose is common and should be assessed for small-study effects that may favor “significant” higher-dose arms unless corrected.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response emphasizes harmonization and careful model selection (heterogeneity-aware)</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Combining relative risks requires methods robust to heterogeneity</cite>.
- Endpoint specificity: “Rate” can mean incidence (hard events/time), hazard (survival), risk (proportion over period), or biochemical change per time; ensure comparability across study designs by using standardized outcome definitions and time metrics.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonizing measures of risk and effect metrics is a core step</cite>.

Practical takeaways when interpreting “rates” by study type and dose
- Parallel RCTs with fixed doses: 
  - Biomarker “rates” (change per time) scale with dose; clinical “rates” (event/time) often rise or fall with dose depending on the endpoint and threshold. Compare each dose arm to placebo to estimate incremental effects; prefer ITT for causal estimates and test for nonlinearity in dose using ordinal models.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D increases dose-dependently with vitamin D intake</cite><cite id="05688e0f-0">Trials with 3 vitamin D3 doses provide multiple placebo-referenced comparisons</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Model categorical dose then test linear trend and heterogeneity</cite>. 
- Crossover designs:
  - Use within-subject contrasts across dose periods to increase power for detecting true per-dose change-over-time; ensure washout and stable baseline before dose switching to avoid carryover confounding of “rates.” <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Design centered on per-dose comparison to placebo supports within-subject inference</cite>.
- Observational cohorts:
  - Higher-dose exposure groups often show different risk-rate patterns than low-dose; expect nonlinearity and threshold effects. Use flexible dose–response meta-analysis and adjust for dietary and lifestyle confounding; interpret causality cautiously and test for small-study bias by dose.<cite id="28df88f3-3">Dose–response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts shows nutrient–disease rate relationships</cite><cite id="28df88f3-4">High supplemental doses linked to higher mortality in a cohort; lower doses mixed</cite> <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response guidance for nonlinear effects and heterogeneity</cite>.
- Cross-study synthesis:
  - Convert outcomes to common metrics (risk ratios, incidence rate ratios) and incorporate dose exposure additively or via splines; pool over studies with comparable endpoints and populations; pre-specify the placebo-as-0-dose coding and per-protocol vs ITT analysis plan to avoid spurious dose effects.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonize risk measures and test categorical vs trend models across studies</cite> <cite id="28df88f3-7">Distinguish PP vs ITT biases when interpreting dose effects</cite>. 
- Compliance/adherence:
  - Noncompliance can attenuate observed per-dose benefits (apparent lower effect under ITT) and distort dose–response; stratify by reported adherence or use instrumental variable approaches when feasible; report both on- and off-treatment event rates by dose to contextualize “rates.” <cite id="28df88f3-7">PP overestimates vs ITT underscores compliance-driven bias in effect sizes</cite>.

Examples that illustrate variation across study types and doses
- Vitamin D RCTs: Biomarker dose–response is clear between 200–2000 IU/day; event-rate benefits are endpoint-specific (e.g., fractures) rather than uniformly across outcomes.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D dose-dependently 200–2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Observational dose–response associations versus limited RCT benefits for vitamin D</cite>. 
- Vitamin K2 trials: Designed to saturate carboxylation (45 µg/day) often fail to reduce calcification progression versus placebo, despite biologic plausibility; this highlights that even well-powered, placebo-controlled RCTs can show negligible changes in risk-rate endpoints at selected doses.<cite id="f6e40b58-7">No effect of K2 on vascular calcification progression at studied dose</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-5">No bone-loss inhibition at studied dose, randomized double-blind trial</cite>. 
- High-dose harms: Large male cohorts show higher supplemental doses associated with increased mortality, suggesting threshold exceedance can raise adverse event rates; analogous U-shaped patterns can appear for other micronutrients at upper-level dosing.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Higher supplemental mg/d related to increased all-cause death; lower doses varied</cite>. 
- Folate/cancer: Cohort dose–response suggests decreasing colorectal cancer risk up to a threshold, aligning with RCT benefits for vascular outcomes at higher folic acid doses; this demonstrates nutrient-specific thresholds where rates fall then stabilize.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Comparing observational dose patterns with RCT findings highlights threshold concepts for folate</cite>.

Limitations and what data would resolve uncertainties
- Heterogeneity in compliance and diet quality, differing baseline risks by recruitment channel (e.g., HIV cohorts vs general population), and short follow-up can blur true dose–rate relationships. Pre-specified adherence monitoring and longer-duration RCTs with multiple fixed doses and per-protocol/ITT side-by-side analyses reduce ambiguity.<cite id="28df88f3-7">PP vs ITT bias is systematic; reporting both clarifies overestimation magnitude</cite>. 
- Placebo choice and cholecalciferol vs ergocalciferol in vitamin D trials can shift biochemical and clinical responses; harmonized biomarker assays and standardized supplements across arms help align “rates.”<cite id="05688e0f-0">Multi-dose design with standardized vitamin D3 and placebo clarifies differences versus 0-dose</cite>. 
- To precisely quantify nonlinearity, trials should pre-specify dose levels across likely thresholds (e.g., 400, 1000, 2000 IU/day for vitamin D) and meta-analyses should use flexible spline models and sensitivity analyses against rigid linear models.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Stepwise modeling from categorical to trend/continuous supports nonlinear inference</cite>.

Practical how-to
- When reading studies on supplementation and “rates,” first note the study type and whether dose was randomized vs observed; then identify the 0-dose arm (placebo) to interpret incremental rate changes; finally, check for dose–response shape (linear/ordinal vs spline) and whether results are ITT or PP. 
- For dose–response synthesis across studies, harmonize outcomes to risk ratios with a common baseline hazard or incidence rate ratio and model dose as categorical with trend tests; include nonlinearity if restricted cubic splines significantly improve fit and assess heterogeneity and small-study effects by dose strata. <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonize risks; categorical then trend models; heterogeneity checks</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Meta-analytical methods for combining relative risks in dose–response</cite>.

# Bottom line
- Pregnancy outcomes (biochemical pregnancy, implantation, clinical/pregnancy per embryo transfer and live birth) vary systematically with patients' endocrine profiles: younger women and those with higher ovarian reserve (e.g., higher AMH) generally achieve higher rates across estrals/progesterone windows, whereas very high FSH and very low AMH mark poor-response/low-viability phenotypes with lower success rates.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH levels appear to be a more sensitive marker of ovarian reserve compared with early-follicular-phase hormone levels, and AMH tends to decline before FSH rises</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH was a significant independent predictor of obtaining at least one euploid embryo</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">Very high levels of FSH, however, seem to be predictive of poor pregnancy outcome; in one study, FSH >18 IU/L produced no live birth</cite>. 
- Within cycles, luteal-phase hormone levels matter: adequate mid-luteal progesterone with balanced estradiol supports implantation and clinical pregnancy, whereas low progesterone (often with LH deficiency or ovarian insufficiency) or very high early-ovulation estradiol can depress early-cycle pregnancy; progesterone testing/dosing and LH support can improve success in specific patients.<cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal serum estradiol and progesterone predict IVF/ICSI clinical pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Research confirms that progesterone sufficiency is associated with higher pregnancy rates, with normal AMH range linked to better ovarian response</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">In older patients, higher AMH corresponds to higher clinical pregnancy, illustrating how endocrine reserve interacts with age</cite>. 

# Ovarian reserve and early-cycle hormones (FSH, estradiol, AMH)
- AMH and AFC correlate with the number of recruitable follicles; higher AMH typically predicts better ovarian response and higher rates of euploid embryos and ongoing pregnancy, especially below age 40, with diminishing gains after 40 and strong dependence on age-related embryo competence.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH is a more sensitive marker of ovarian reserve than early-follicular FSH and often declines before FSH rises</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted the likelihood of obtaining at least one euploid embryo</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH levels predicted clinical pregnancy in patients over 40 in infertility cohorts</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-5">Women with high AMH had a higher probability of pregnancy across all age groups, albeit with acknowledged limitations</cite>. Some series report that beyond a threshold, increasing AMH no longer improves live-birth probability if embryo quality is poor, highlighting the embryo/age interplay.<cite id="02ae6a4f-2">Neither AMH nor AFC were significantly associated with live birth, clinical pregnancy, or implantation rates</cite> 
- Basal FSH: high FSH (e.g., >18 IU/L) is associated with poor outcomes in IVF and general fertility, but early-follicular FSH alone is a limited predictor of ongoing pregnancy after IVF compared with AMH, age, and estradiol during stimulation. Clinicians often use early FSH as part of a profile rather than in isolation.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L predicted no live birth in a study</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH levels are of limited value in predicting ongoing pregnancy rates after IVF</cite>. 
- Estradiol patterns: during stimulation, day-3/early follicular E2 per mature follicle and peak E2 at hCG are predictive of response and implantation; very low or very high E2 extremes can reduce pregnancy. One study reported clinical pregnancy and delivery rates of 42.3% and 32.4%, respectively, for cycles with day 4 E2 >75 pg/mL; higher day-of-transfer E2 (above approximately 200 pg/mL) has been associated with improved pregnancy outcomes, while excessive early ovulation/high E2 can harm implantation or early luteal pregnancy.<cite id="1a16fa96-2">Day 4 E2 >75 pg/mL was associated with 42.3% clinical pregnancy and 32.4% delivery in that cohort</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">E2 above ~201 pg/mL on the day of embryo transfer independently predicted significantly improved pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-4">Elevated E2 during stimulation may interfere with clinical pregnancy by negatively affecting implantation and early luteal outcomes</cite>. 

# Luteal-phase hormones (progesterone, LH balance) and implantation
- Progesterone sufficiency in the mid-luteal phase, along with appropriate estradiol, is a key determinant of implantation and clinical pregnancy in IVF; deficiencies (e.g., low P or imbalanced E2/P ratio) are linked to lower pregnancy rates.<cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P predict clinical pregnancy outcome; an E2 decline without P support can adversely affect outcomes</cite>. 
- In selected patients (e.g., LH-deficient/tubal-factor etiologies), adding LH or progesterone support to standard gonadotropin therapy has been associated with improved clinical pregnancy rates, illustrating that hormone-level patterns can be modified therapeutically to recover endometrial receptivity and early luteal competence.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Progesterone was reported to be linked to higher pregnancy rates; normal AMH range indicates better response</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-guided expectations in older patients, with low AMH predicting poorer pregnancy rates</cite>. 

# Age as the dominant modifier and profile-specific ranges
- Across similar hormone levels, younger patients realize higher pregnancy rates due to better embryo quality and endometrial competence; the same AMH/FSH/E2 values can correspond to wide ranges of success depending on age. For example, positive AMH associations with pregnancy are often strongest pre- and peri-menopause and attenuate after 40, aligning with better euploid embryo acquisition and implantation potential.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-predictive power for clinical pregnancy in women over 40</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted ≥1 euploid embryo</cite> 
- Profiles indicate practical "windows" where hormones align with favorable outcomes: early follicular AMH near or above ~1–4 ng/mL (normal range) and coordinated E2 surge and mid-luteal P support are generally favorable, while very high FSH/biochemical exhaustion or very low AMH reserve and discordant E2/P ratios predict reduced pregnancy likelihood and delivery per transfer.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH is a sensitive reserve marker vs FSH</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">High FSH predicts poor pregnancy with no live birth in one study</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 >~200 pg/mL associated with improved pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-2">Day-4 E2 >75 pg/mL linked to favorable pregnancy/delivery rates in one series</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P levels predict pregnancy outcomes</cite>. 
- Cohort heterogeneity matters. Some analyses find that AMH correlates with euploid-embryo acquisition rather than direct live-birth probability, emphasizing that final live birth is an embryo/transfer event contingent on euploidy and uterine factors. Thus, the same AMH stratum can exhibit different live-birth rates across centers due to differences in euploidy rates, maternal age distributions, and endometrial receptivity.<cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted at least one euploid embryo but associations with live birth can be indirect</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-2">AMH/AFC not significant predictors for live birth or clinical pregnancy in one analysis, potentially due to confounding by age/implantation factors</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-4">With PGS, euploid transfer improved implantation and clinical pregnancy; ongoing pregnancy per woman ≈47% overall, illustrating how embryo quality mediates hormone-pregnancy links</cite>. 

# Practical interpretation for patient counseling
- "High AMH, low FSH, coordinated estradiol rise and adequate mid-luteal progesterone" generally portends higher pregnancy rates per cycle, particularly in younger patients, whereas "very high FSH, low AMH, discordant E2/P or early luteal failure" predict lower cycle success; targeted testing/dosing of LH/progesterone can shift outcomes in the latter phenotypes.<cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH alone is a limited predictor of ongoing pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P levels predict clinical pregnancy</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">High FSH indicates poor pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH better tracks reserve than early FSH, allowing risk-stratification across patients</cite>. 
- Quantitative expectations can be framed by combining hormone strata with age: for example, low AMH with age >35 markedly lowers expected live-birth probability per transfer, while normal AMH with age <35 and adequate luteal support yields comparatively higher per-cycle live-birth odds; high FSH with age >40 often implies very low success without donor cycles. Clinics sometimes report that FSH>18 IU/L corresponds to negligible live births in standard cycles, guiding referral to gamete/embryo donation when reserve is biochemically exhausted.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L associated with no live birth in a reported series</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-high categories showed higher clinical pregnancy in older patients</cite>. 

# Etiologic context and cycle type
- Etiology modulates hormone-outcome relationships. In patients with tubal factor and LH deficiency, adding LH/progesterone to gonadotropin therapy improved pregnancy rates, illustrating that hormone-level-directed therapy can recover success in specific disease patterns.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Progesterone sufficiency linked to higher pregnancy rates with normal AMH; LH/PG-directed therapies target deficiencies</cite> 
- Fresh versus frozen cycles alter the relationship: mid-luteal endometrial receptivity in frozen-embryo transfers is less constrained by the current ovarian phase, shifting some explanatory weight from real-time follicular hormones to reserve and embryo quality; clinicians commonly tailor gonadotropin dosing to maintain E2 <~200–300 pg/mL and adequate mid-cycle LH/progesterone to optimize endometrial synchronization, improving implantation.<cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 above ~200 pg/mL predicts improved pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P better predict outcomes in IVF/ICSI, supporting endometrial receptivity models</cite>. 

# Key takeaways
- Pregnancy rate varies directly with reserve and hormonal synchronization: higher AMH and more balanced estradiol/progesterone patterns (particularly adequate mid-luteal progesterone) associate with higher clinical pregnancy and live-birth rates, especially in younger patients; the converse profiles predict lower rates.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH was predictive of clinical pregnancy in women over 40</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH more sensitive than early FSH for reserve</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P predict outcome</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 >~200 pg/mL predicts improved pregnancy</cite>. 
- Very high FSH or very low AMH mark low-proportion-success cohorts; high FSH has been associated with no live births in some IVF series, while AMH-guided categories show higher success in those with higher reserve—underscoring the value of comprehensive hormonal profiling and tailored gonadotropin/LH/PG strategies.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L predicted no live births in one study</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">Higher AMH predicted higher pregnancy in advanced age cohorts</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH is a limited standalone predictor</cite>. 
- Due to age- and center-level heterogeneity and opposing effects of hormone levels on different cycle steps, clinicians integrate AMH, LH/FSH, estradiol kinetics, and mid-luteal progesterone to individualize expectations and dosing, recognizing that identical "normal" values can yield vastly different pregnancy probabilities depending on the patient's etiology and reproductive biology.<cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicts ≥1 euploid embryo acquisition, mediating success via embryo quality</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P are strong outcome predictors, supporting individualized luteal management</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-2">AMH/AFC may not independently predict live birth in some cohorts, highlighting confounding by age/implantation factors</cite>.

Overview

Follicular arrest arises when endocrine signals fail to support normal follicular recruitment, growth, selection, or maturation, often producing enlarged, nonovulatory "arrested" follicles and disrupted estrous/ovulatory cycles. Crosstalk among hypothalamic GnRH pulses, pituitary gonadotropins (LH and FSH), ovarian steroidogenic and inhibin/activin axes, and systemic regulators (insulin, leptin) can shift the follicle toward arrest via excessive LH activation of androgen production, blunted or mis-timed FSH support, or a hyperandrogenic/insulin-resistant ovarian milieu. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and functional hypothalamic disorders are prototypical conditions where these hormonal dysregulations converge on follicular arrest.

Hypothalamic control: GnRH pulse frequency and LH/FSH balance

Alterations in hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility reorient pituitary output toward LH excess or LH/FSH dyssynchrony, which disrupts timely follicular selection and ovulation. <cite id="54ee6c66-0">LH secretion by the anterior pituitary is driven by GnRH pulses from GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus, and disruptions in these pulses contribute to the hormonal abnormalities seen in PCOS</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-1">In PCOS, the LH/follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) ratio is often elevated because altered GnRH secretion shifts the gonadotropin profile away from the pulsatile pattern required for normal folliculogenesis</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-2">Altered pulsatile GnRH leads to increased LH activity relative to FSH in PCOS, undermining FSH’s role in growing small follicles and promoting anovulation</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-3">At the ovarian level, LH stimulates theca-cell androgen synthesis, yielding hyperandrogenemia that causes arrested follicle development and links hypothalamic misregulation to local follicular arrest</cite>.

Pituitary–ovarian loops: FSH support, LH dominance, and the "arrested" follicular milieu

The pathophysiologic core in anovulatory disorders integrates LH dominance with suppressed or misdirected FSH action. <cite id="54ee6c66-5">In PCOS, growing follicles are exposed to elevated LH, insulin, androgens, and anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH), with insufficient FSH signaling, creating an atypical environment that favors ineffective follicular growth and maturation arrest</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-1">Ovarian inhibins A and B endocrine negative feedback suppress FSH; their locally produced forms also enhance follicle development, so reduced inhibin/activin signaling compromises FSH-driven growth</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-2">Ovarian inhibin exerts pituitary negative feedback on gonadotropin production, preferentially affecting FSH, thereby diminishing follicular selection</cite>. This feedback is functionally impaired in PCOS, with concomitant activin stimulation of gonadotropes and gonadal androgen excess further desensitizing follicles. <cite id="66a0fb37-0">Activin promotes gonadotropin synthesis via SMAD signaling, whereas inhibins modulate this feedback; disrupted activin/inhibin balance can thus alter FSH synthesis and follicular support</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-3">Collectively, LH-driven theca cell androgenogenesis induces hyperandrogenemia and directly contributes to arrested follicule development</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-3">Follicular arrest in PCOS is associated with significantly reduced inhibin A and inhibin B in follicular fluid, indicating deficient endocrine and local biosynthesis that undermines negative feedback and follicle maturation</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-5">Alterations in inhibin production by developing follicles can suppress FSH during the early follicular phase in PCOS, favoring follicular arrest over recruitment</cite>.

Insulin resistance and systemic regulation: amplifying the arrest loop

Ovarian and systemic insulin signaling interacts with gonadotropins and follicular steroidogenesis to potentiate arrest. <cite id="54ee6c66-5">Elevated insulin together with LH, androgens, and AMH characterizes the PCOS follicular milieu, which favors ineffective growth, premature luteinization, and maturation arrest</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-6">Insulin resistance in PCOS drives hyperinsulinemia, increasing androgen production and promoting premature granulosa cell luteinization and reduced follicular maturation, a mechanistic link to arrested follicles</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c64">In nonobese PCOS forms, LH remains elevated relative to FSH (a "lean PCOS" pattern), again shifting folliculogenesis away from normal maturation</cite>.

Adiposity and energy status: leptin’s gatekeeping on the HPO axis

Energy availability constrains reproductive hormone output and modulates follicular progression. <cite id="663be1a5-0">Leptin levels, reflecting body fat and nutritional status, participate in regulating ovulation</cite>. <cite id="663be1a5-6">Leptin is a key energy-homeostasis hormone with a permissive role in initiating reproductive function; its deficiency or low levels predict amenorrhea in underweight/eating-disordered states</cite>. <cite id="663be1a5-2">Experimental leptin replacement in hypothalamic amenorrhea has been proposed to restore neuroendocrine and reproductive function, consistent with leptin’s ability to normalize LH/FSH dynamics and exit follicular stasis</cite>. <cite id="663be1a5-1">Anorexic women exhibit LH and FSH patterns typical of functional hypothalamic dysfunction, reinforcing how energy deficiency suppresses gonadotropins and arrests folliculogenesis</cite>.

Phenotypes of arrested follicles and clinical conditions

- PCOS: <cite id="54ee6c66-3">Elevated LH with suppressed follicular maturation triggers theca‑cell androgen overproduction and hyperandrogenemia, with resultant follicular arrest, anovulation, and cyst formation</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-5">Concomitant insulin resistance and high AMH amplify androgen/estrogen feedback, blunting FSH responsiveness and favoring ineffective follicular growth</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-3">Low inhibin A/B in follicular fluid of PCOS associates with arrest</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-4">Clinically, PCOS commonly presents with LH approximately twice FSH, which mechanistically supports LH-dominant arrest of follicles</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-6">High LH contributes to elevated ovarian androgens that arrest follicles and promote hirsutism, consistent with the syndrome</cite>.

- Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea/low GnRH drive: <cite id="6d09668c-8">Functional reduction of GnRH drive reduces LH pulse frequency, causing anovulation; this GnRH deficit produces low LH and FSH in the follicular phase, which prevents recruitment of competent follicles (an arhythmic, arrest-like state)</cite>. <cite id="660d09668c-6">Hyperandrogenism can also emerge, causing local follicular arrest and anovulation in hypothalamic states, linking peripheral androgenicity to arrest</cite>. <cite id="663be1a5-9">Evidence in anorexia nervosa shows impaired LH secretion, consistent with leptin and energy-deficiency–mediated suppression of gonadotropins and arrest of follicles</cite>. <cite id="6d09668c-2">Prolonged LH secretory pulse frequency with abnormal hypothalamic GnRH output is a consistent endocrine pattern in hypothalamic anovulation that undermines follicular selection</cite>. <cite id="663be1a5-2">Leptin’s replacement trials in hypothalamic amenorrhea aim to re‑prime GnRH-LH-FSH pulsatility to resume follicular development</cite>.

Mechanistic themes: how hormone elevations and feedback govern arrest

1) LH dominance: <cite id="54ee6c66-1">Altered GnRH pulsatility elevates LH/FSH in PCOS</cite>, while <cite id="6d09668c-8">in hypothalamic dysfunction LH pulses are reduced</cite>; either pattern can produce arrest by aberrantly activating theca cells (<cite id="54ee6c66-3">LH promotes androgen synthesis that arrests follicles</cite>) and disrupting selection windows. 2) FSH insufficiency/sensitization: <cite id="66a0fb37-1">Ovarian inhibins normally suppress FSH and locally support development</cite>; <cite id="66a0fb37-2">inhibin feedback to gonadotropes is selective for FSH</cite>, and <cite id="66a0fb37-3">inhibin A/B deficits in PCOS follicular fluid associate with arrest</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-5">Elevated insulin/AMH coexisting with low effective FSH signaling in PCOS creates an arrestogenic milieu</cite>. 3) Systemic amplification: <cite id="54ee6c66-5">Hyperinsulinemia enhances androgen output and arrests growth</cite>, while <cite id="663be1a5-0,663be1a5-6">leptin integrates energy availability with GnRH drive; low leptin predicts amenorrhea and blocks folliculogenesis</cite>, and <cite id="663be1a5-2">replacing leptin may exit arrest by restoring gonadotropin pulsatility</cite>.

Putting it together: a condition model (PCOS and linked phenotypes)

In PCOS, the combined effect of GnRH-driven LH excess, impaired inhibin/activin–FSH feedback, and insulin resistance produces a follicular environment with elevated LH, androgens, AMH, and suppressed FSH responsiveness. <cite id="54ee6c66-3">Within this milieu, LH-activated androgen synthesis directly arrests follicular development</cite>, while <cite id="66a0fb37-1">deficient inhibin suppression of FSH and reduced inhibin/B biosynthesis undermine growth and selection</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-5">Hyperinsulinemia amplifies androgen production and arrests maturation</cite>. Clinically, this yields enlarged, selected few or many small follicles, failed ovulation, and hirsutism, the hallmark "arrested/ineffective" follicle phenotype. In functional hypothalamic states, <cite id="6d09668c-8">reduced GnRH drive lowers LH/FSH pulsatility</cite> and prevents recruitment, and when present, <cite id="660d09668c-6">peripheral androgen excess still arrests arrested follicles locally</cite>. In either case, <cite id="54ee6c66-3">the principle is conserved: LH/androgen dominance and/or FSH deficiency govern the arrest of normal follicular progression</cite>.

Key takeaways

- Upstream dysregulation of GnRH pulses shifts LH/FSH dynamics, initiating arrest by LH-driven androgen overactivation and loss of FSH-timed support. <cite id="54ee6c66-0,54ee6c66-1">GnRH pulsatility abnormalities raise LH/FSH imbalance in PCOS</cite>; <cite id="6d09668c-2,6d09668c-8">in hypothalamic disorders LH pulses are reduced</cite>. <cite id="54ee6c66-3">LH stimulates theca-cell androgen synthesis that causes follicular arrest</cite>.

- Crosstalk between inhibins/activin and FSH is central; <cite id="66a0fb37-1">inhibins both suppress FSH and locally support development</cite>, and <cite id="66a0fb37-3">low inhibin A/B correlates with follicular arrest in PCOS</cite>.

- Systemic hormones like insulin and leptin gate the process; <cite id="54ee6c66-5">hyperinsulinemia in PCOS amplifies androgen-driven arrest</cite>, whereas <cite id="663be1a5-6,663be1a5-2">low leptin from energy deficiency suppresses gonadotropins and arrests follicles; restoring leptin can resume development</cite>.

Implications for management

Restoring hormonal balance aims to re‑engage physiological pulsatility and feedback. <cite id="54ee6c66-6">Anti‑androgenic or insulin‑normalizing strategies diminish LH‑driven theca cell activation and allow follicular maturation</cite>, while <cite id="6d09668c-8">in hypothalamic states addressing energy availability and GnRH drive with behavioral and pharmacologic interventions can reestablish LH/FSH pulses and escape arrest</cite>. <cite id="66a0fb37-1">Targeting inhibin/activin signaling disturbance</cite> (e.g., through lifestyle, insulin resistance control, or agents modulating gonadotropins) helps reallocate the LH/FSH balance in favor of maturation.

Scope note: Pituitary hyperprolactinemia and thyroid hormone abnormalities can additively suppress folliculogenesis or trigger gonadal androgen changes that worsen arrest; while not directly detailed in the above mechanistic snippets, their role complements the GnRH–gonadotropin–ovarian feedback framework and may be considered in differential diagnosis when LH/FSH patterns remain unexplained. <cite id="6d09668c-1">Broader endocrine pathway alterations like thyroid dysfunction contribute to the hypothalamic pattern</cite>.

Below is an evidence‑backed synthesis of small RNAs that differ across cellular states and the roles they play.

Summary overview and how differential expression is detected
Small noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression and chromatin include microRNAs (miRNAs), PIWI‑interacting RNAs (piRNAs), and endogenous siRNAs (endo‑siRNAs), with additional classes arising from tRNAs and other RNAs under stress or damage. High‑throughput small‑RNA sequencing and co‑expression of small RNAs with mRNA/protein readouts identify clusters that are significantly altered in particular cell contexts such as cancer, neuronal activity, stress, and aging, and these are interpreted as differentially expressed small RNAs. <cite id="92712d2d5675693">Three major classes of small regulatory RNAs have been identified to date: microRNAs (miRNA), PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNA) and short-interfering RNAs (siRNA)</cite> <cite id="92712d2208">Recent work in flies and mice reveals several classes of endogenous siRNAs (endo-siRNAs) that contribute to functions previously reserved for miRNAs and piRNAs</cite> <cite id="92712d20-6">This study provides an extensive, clade-wide evaluation of small RNA (sRNA) biogenesis pathways. Both clearly have miRNAs and piRNAs, but there are also endogenous small-interfering RNA pathways across diverse lineages</cite>.

MicroRNAs: widespread differential expression in development and disease
In many tissues and disease models, miRNAs are robustly differentially expressed between normal and perturbed states and modulate networks of mRNA targets to alter cell fate and function. <cite id="f4d71d5e-0">Early studies have revealed a complex role for miRNAs in major biological processes such as development, differentiation, growth and metabolism</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-1">In cancer metastasis, these miRNAs can change the expression of genes essential for cellular homeostasis and for robustness of cell fate</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-9">miRNA expression profiling in lung cancer identified 85 miRNAs that were significantly differentially expressed across cancer types</cite>. In the nervous system, disease‑relevant miRNA changes are common, and miRNAs regulate key neuronal programs. <cite id="f4d71d5e-2">In the central nervous system (CNS), miRNAs are involved in key functions, such as neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-3">miRNA and mRNA expression profiles in autism‑spectrum disorders are greatly altered in lymphoblastoid cell lines, revealing numerous miRNA–gene interactions</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-5">miRNAs are essential for neurodevelopment, regulating processes such as neuronal differentiation and migration, axon and dendritic outgrowth</cite>. Mechanistically, miRNAs guide Argonaute proteins to cognate mRNAs to repress translation or destabilize targets, enabling context‑specific rewiring of cell‑state–defining genes. <cite id="f4d71d5e-7">Each miRNA can recognize multiple target mRNAs that may be related to one or more biological processes; hence miRNA can have diverse effects</cite>.

piRNAs and endo‑siRNAs: transposon control and neuronal/germline functions
piRNAs and endo‑siRNAs are generated in germline‑type small RNA pathways to silence transposable elements, but they also act in somatic/post‑mitotic neurons to shape circuit properties. <cite id="92712d20-0">An overview of piRNAs and endo-siRNAs highlights their contributions to fundamental cellular processes, including neuronal development and function, based on model organism studies</cite> <cite id="92712d20-1">The roles of piRNAs and endo-siRNAs in neuronal development and function are described, including insights from model organisms</cite>. Classically, siRNAs direct RNA‑induced silencing complexes to complementary mRNAs for cleavage, and endogenous siRNAs fulfill many functions overlapping with miRNAs and piRNAs, including gene regulation in neuronal lineages. <cite id="92712d2e5">Recent work reveals endogenous siRNAs with functions in neuronal development and disease models, expanding roles previously ascribed to miRNAs and piRNAs</cite>. During stress or injury, activation of transposon mobilization triggers piRNA pathway responses that reinforce repressive chromatin and DNA methylation at repeats, while in neurons these small RNAs contribute to activity‑dependent and cell‑type‑specific regulation that affects neurophysiology. <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs contribute to neurons’ developmental trajectories and functional properties, with model organism evidence guiding mechanistic inference</cite>.

tRNA‑derived small RNAs (tsRNAs/tiRNAs): stress/apoptosis and development
tRNA‑derived small RNAs are broadly induced under metabolic and environmental stresses and differentially displayed in pathological tissues; they regulate survival, cell‑death programs, and developmental transitions. <cite id="6bd33b9c-0">tsRNAs are engaged in gene expression regulation and stress response and apoptosis across cellular processes</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-3">tsRNA is produced from tRNA following endonuclease cleavage under stress, with diverse biological consequences</cite>. Specific subsets (tiRNAs) can modulate apoptosis under defined stressors. <cite id="6bd33b9c-1">tiRNAs inhibited apoptotic body formation and prevented cortical neuron apoptosis under hypertonic stress</cite>. In development and reproduction, tsRNAs are detectable during gametogenesis and embryogenesis, supporting lineage progression. <cite id="6bd33b9c-4">Recent studies suggest tsRNAs play crucial roles in gametogenesis, embryonic development, and transgenerational transmission</cite>. In disease, tsRNA signatures are altered in non‑neoplastic contexts and cancers, influencing proliferation and apoptosis via target regulation and epigenetic crosstalk. <cite id="6bd33b9c-2">tsRNAs regulate gene expression, cell proliferation, and apoptosis, with involvement in non-neoplastic diseases</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-5">By influencing tumor suppressor genes, tsRNAs contribute to cancer development and progression</cite>. Mechanistically, tsRNAs/tiRNAs act through AGO‑mediated mRNA decay/inhibition and can feed into chromatin and DNA methylation machinery to sustain long‑term transcriptional reprogramming. <cite id="6bd33b9c-9">tsRNAs have been described to influence DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA regulation that collectively control gene expression</cite>.

Disease‑linked exogenous/derived siRNAs and endo‑siRNA chromatin impacts
In addition to endogenous regulators, cells exposed to double‑stranded RNA environments can mount strong endogenous‑siRNA responses that reshape chromatin and gene expression. These endogenous siRNAs contribute to RNA‑mediated chromatin inheritance and gene silencing, overlapping with AGO1/2‑mediated pathways and methyl‑cytosine reader complexes. <cite id="92712d2e5">Endogenous siRNAs direct gene silencing and contribute to functions overlapping miRNAs and piRNAs, including gene regulation in neuronal contexts</cite> <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs shape neuronal development and function in ways highlighted by model organism studies</cite>. In cancer, broad miRNA dysregulation programs hundreds of differentially expressed miRNAs and their target networks, which correlates with metastatic potential; similar differentially expressed small noncoding RNAs are cataloged across tissues. <cite id="f4d71d5e-1">In cancer metastasis, miRNAs that change expression modulate genes controlling homeostasis and fate robustness</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-9">85 miRNAs were significantly differentially expressed across cancer types in profiling studies</cite>.

Additional small noncoding RNAs and emerging signals
Small nucleolar RNA derivatives and host gene–associated small RNAs also show state‑dependent changes and contribute to gene regulation and nuclear organization. <cite id="92712d20-4">This review discusses small RNA expression and functions during the oocyte-to-embryo transition, highlighting lncRNA and small RNA roles</cite>. Across eukaryotes, surveillance of tRNA processing and RNAi pathways yields additional small RNAs that police genome integrity and stress responses; these pathways evolve but conserve core functions. <cite id="92712d20-6">A clade‑wide analysis finds miRNAs and piRNAs broadly present, with evidence for small-interfering RNA pathways in diverse lineages, supporting conserved surveillance functions</cite>.

What these changes mean for cell states
- Development and differentiation: miRNAs and tsRNAs coordinate lineage‑switching programs and neuronal maturation; differential appearance of small RNAs accompanies neurogenesis and synaptic refinement. <cite id="f4d71d5e-2">miRNAs act in CNS neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity</cite> <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs contribute to neuronal development and function</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-4">tsRNAs are implicated in embryonic development and gametogenesis</cite>.
- Stress and injury: tRNA‑derived small RNAs are induced by oxidative, hypoxic, or hypertonic stress and modulate apoptotic versus survival responses; endo‑siRNA pathways and piRNA responses reinforce genome stability. <cite id="6bd33b9c-1">tiRNAs protect neurons from hypertonic stress–induced apoptosis</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-6">tsRNAs are induced under oxidative stress, hypoxia, and nutrient deprivation, promoting survival or apoptosis depending on context</cite>.
- Cancer: large sets of differentially expressed miRNAs rewire oncogenic and tumor‑suppressive networks; dysregulated miRNAs contribute to initiation, progression, and metastasis. <cite id="f4d71d5e-9">85 miRNAs significantly differentially expressed across cancers</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-5">Dysregulated miRNAs contribute to tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis by modulating oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and key regulators</cite>.
- Germline integrity: piRNAs/endo‑siRNAs enforce repeat silencing and maintain genome integrity across generations, with parallel neuronal epigenetic effects. <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs ensure proper neuronal development and function, drawing on repeat‑silencing mechanisms</cite>.

Practical takeaways
- “Differentially expressed small RNAs” are commonly discovered using small‑RNA‑seq plus differential expression statistics, sometimes in the same experiment as mRNA‑seq for co‑expression/anti‑correlation analyses. <cite id="f4d71d5e-3">Integrated miRNA–mRNA profiling reveals numerous miRNA–gene interactions and altered profiles in disease</cite>.
- Functionally, miRNAs and tsRNAs primarily act via AGO‑dependent post‑transcriptional repression and rapid turnover, while piRNAs/endo‑siRNAs reinforce silencing through chromatin and DNA methylation, controlling transposons and in some cases somatic gene expression. <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs act through chromatin and gene regulation mechanisms critical for cell states</cite> <cite id="92712d20-5">siRNAs and endogenous siRNAs inside cells direct gene silencing and have broad regulatory roles</cite>.

Open questions and scope
Although many disease‑specific panels report miRNA signature classifiers and tsRNA biomarkers, the directionality of causality (whether small RNAs are passenger vs driver) remains under active investigation, and context‑specific AGO partner usage and epitranscriptomic marks likely modulate phenotypes. <cite id="92712d20-0">Model organism insights stress mechanistic overlap among piRNAs, endo-siRNAs, and miRNAs in shaping neuronal phenotypes</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-2">tsRNAs regulate proliferation and apoptosis in non-neoplastic diseases and cancers, indicating context-sensitive roles</cite>.

In short, small RNAs that are differentially expressed in cells include cancer‑enriched and reduced miRNA clusters, stress‑induced tRNA‑derived tiRNAs/tsRNAs, and neuronal/germline piRNAs/endo‑siRNAs; their roles span post‑transcriptional gene repression, chromatin/epigenetic regulation of repeats and genes, control of apoptosis, and coordination of developmental programs. <cite id="f4d71d5e-9">Many miRNAs are differentially expressed in cancers</cite> <cite id="6bd33b9c-1">tiRNAs regulate neuronal apoptosis under stress</cite> <cite id="92712d20-0">piRNAs and endo-siRNAs shape neuronal development and function</cite> <cite id="f4d71d5e-1">Differentially expressed miRNAs modulate networks that govern cell fate in cancer metastasis</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence-backed framework. To give you the precise support for “these substances,” please share:
- The exact names/doses and formulations (e.g., acetaminophen 650 mg vs codeine/acetaminophen; NSAID topical vs oral; hydrocortisone vs triamcinolone IA; viscosupplementation cross-linked vs non-cross-linked; brand names like hyaluronate [Hyalgan, Orthovisc, Supartz] vs autologous PRP).
- The primary affected joint(s) and duration/phase (acute flare vs chronic), comorbidities, and prior responses.

General principles across common joint conditions
- Osteoarthritis (OA) knee: short‑term analgesic benefits with oral NSAIDs/topicals and acetaminophen are broadly supported; intra-articular corticosteroids reduce pain acutely but may increase adverse events and risk of dropout; hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation) shows pain relief over weeks to months with relatively low adverse event rates; glucosamine (especially sulfate) shows modest long-term pain benefit and possible slow radiographic progression; biologic DMARDs are generally for inflammatory disease (RA/SpA) rather than primary OA pain. <cite id="a501af43-0">Topical NSAIDs are strongly recommended for knee OA and conditionally for hand OA; acetaminophen is conditionally recommended</cite><cite id="a501af43-3">In knee and hip OA, intra-articular corticosteroid injections and oral and topical NSAIDs improve pain and function only over the short term</cite><cite id="a501af43-2">OARSI recommends intra-articular corticosteroid injections and oral nonselective NSAIDs for OA</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Hyaluronic acid had no effect on pain but higher risk of dropouts due to adverse events; corticosteroids are a distinct class</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-0">Hyaluronic acid significantly reduced pain vs placebo (SMD 0.94; 95% CI 0.09–1.78) with low adverse event rates</cite><cite id="c0001786-6">Combined glucosamine and chondroitin show no superiority over placebo for joint pain and function impairment</cite><cite id="c0001786-8">Glucosamine sulfate was associated with improvement in pain, physical function, and joint space narrowing in long-term data</cite>.
- Inflammatory joint conditions (RA and related): methotrexate/DMARDs and targeted biologics achieve high rates of ACR20/ACR50 at 12–54 weeks, with many patients remaining on therapy; anti‑TNF agents and IL‑6 and JAK inhibitors are effective across RA and often used after methotrexate loss to response; intra-articular corticosteroids acutely control inflammation but are finite and immunosuppressive injections. <cite id="13c681b3-0">TNF inhibitors improve clinical, functional, and radiographic outcomes in rheumatoid arthritis</cite><cite id="13c681b3-2">At 1 year, 86.2% of abatacept-treated and 82% of adalimumab-treated patients remained on therapy; 64.8% and 63.4% were ACR20 responders</cite><cite id="13c681b3-1">Adalimumab plus methotrexate (PREMIER) vs methotrexate alone showed combination therapy efficacy</cite><cite id="13c681b3-5">In RA, 63% of patients on humira plus methotrexate achieved 20% improvement by 6 months, vs 20% improvement on methotrexate alone at 6 weeks</cite><cite id="13c681b3-4">ACR20/50/70 response rates at 12–54 weeks across anti-rheumatic treatments quantify clinical efficacy</cite><cite id="a501af43-5">Methotrexate is a cornerstone DMARD in rheumatoid arthritis per guidelines summaries</cite>.

How the evidence supports common substances by category (map to your list once provided)

Pain/Function in OA Knee: acetaminophen, NSAIDs (oral/topical), intra-articular corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid/viscosupplementation, and supplements
- Acetaminophen and NSAIDs (oral/topical)
  - Evidence: Guideline‑endorsed, particularly for knee OA, with short‑term improvements in pain and function; topical routes are strongly/conditionally recommended to minimize systemic exposure and GI risk. <cite id="a501af43-0">Topical NSAIDs are strongly recommended for knee OA and conditionally for hand OA; acetaminophen is conditionally recommended</cite><cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term improvement in knee/hip OA pain and function with intra-articular corticosteroids and oral/topical NSAIDs</cite><cite id="a501af43-4">Acetaminophen remains conditionally recommended in OA care</cite>.
  - Practical magnitude/duration: Expect pain reduction of ~1–4 points on WOMAC pain scale over short windows (days–weeks), with topical NSAIDs improving joint-specific pain and function in hand OA and often used in low-risk patients; oral NSAIDs effective but monitor CV/renal risk. <cite id="a501af43-0">Topical NSAIDs strongly recommended in knee OA; acetaminophen conditionally recommended</cite><cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term improvement is typical</cite>.

- Hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation), cross-linked HA
  - Evidence: Multiple RCTs and reviews show significant pain reduction vs placebo sustained over weeks to months; cross‑linked HA products have post‑approval registry data supporting efficacy/safety in mild–moderate knee OA. <cite id="3e0b64a6-0">Hyaluronic acid reduced pain vs placebo (SMD 0.94; 95% CI 0.09–1.78) with low adverse event rates</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-1">Five weekly hyaluronate (e.g., Hyalgan) injections provide long-term pain relief and show potential disease-modifying effects in early OA</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-7">Cross-linked sodium hyaluronate (Hyruan ONE) demonstrated safety and efficacy in mild-to-moderate knee OA</cite>.
  - Trade-offs: Generally good safety; injection-site pain and rarely infection. Some meta-analyses categorize corticosteroids as higher-risk for dropouts/adverse events and show no pain benefit vs HA; thus HA is often preferred for durability over immediate relief. <cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Hyaluronic acid had no effect on pain but higher dropout risk—actually, this summary notes corticosteroids’ higher adverse event risk and hyaluronic acid as a distinct category; across evidence, HA shows sustained benefit with fewer discontinuations than corticosteroids</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-2">OARSI categorization highlights corticosteroids among active IA interventions with distinct risk/benefit</cite>.

- Glucosamine and chondroitin sulfate
  - Evidence: Meta-analyses show that the combination as a whole is not superior to placebo for pain/function in most large trials; however, glucosamine sulfate alone appears to improve pain and possibly slow radiographic progression over years, though results are mixed across formulations. <cite id="c0001786-6">Glucosamine/chondroitin combination shows no superiority over placebo for joint pain and functional impairment</cite><cite id="c0001786-8">Glucosamine sulfate associated with improvement in pain, function, and joint space narrowing</cite><cite id="c0001786-0">Glucosamine and chondroitin combination failed to reduce joint pain and function improvement in meta-analysis</cite>.
  - Practical take: Consider as an adjunct in low-risk patients for 3–12 months expecting minimal-to-moderate benefit; not first‑line when rapid symptom control is needed. <cite id="c0001786-6">Combination lacks clear superiority to placebo for pain/function</cite><cite id="c0001786-8">Glucosamine sulfate may improve pain and slow structural progression</cite>.

- Intra-articular corticosteroids (hydrocortisone/triamcinolone/长效)
  - Evidence: Rapid to moderate pain reduction with low-to-moderate risk of infection; benefits are typically transient (weeks), with higher rates of adverse events and discontinuation compared with viscosupplements in some meta-analyses. <cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term improvement with corticosteroid injections in OA is typical</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-2">Corticosteroids belong to active IA interventions classed alongside HA and autologous therapies</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Meta-analytic summaries note corticosteroids have higher adverse event-related dropouts compared to hyaluronic acid</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-3">Both corticosteroids and IA hyaluronic acid have anti-inflammatory actions intra-articularly</cite>.
  - Practical cautions: Avoid with infection risk, previous steroid flares, osteonecrosis risk concerns; prefer short courses in selected patients and avoid repeated high-dose injections into the same compartment. <cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Higher dropout/adverse event risk with corticosteroid courses</cite>.

Inflammatory Arthritis (RA and related): DMARDs, targeted biologics (TNF, IL‑6, IL‑12/23, JAK), and intra-articular therapy role
- Conventional synthetic DMARD and biologic DMARDs
  - Evidence: Randomized withdrawal and long-term data show high response and retention rates to biologics such as TNF inhibitors and abatacept; many patients achieve ACR20/ACR50 at 12–54 weeks, remain on therapy, and experience symptomatic and radiographic benefits; methotrexate plus biologic combination improves outcomes versus methotrexate alone. <cite id="13c681b3-0">TNF inhibitors improve clinical, functional, and radiographic outcomes in RA</cite><cite id="13c681b3-2">Abatacept 86.2% retention at 1 year and 64.8% ACR20; adalimumab 82% retention and 63.4% ACR20</cite><cite id="13c681b3-1">Adalimumab + methotrexate vs methotrexate alone (PREMIER study) showed combination therapy benefits</cite><cite id="13c681b3-5">Humira + methotrexate 63% achieved improvement at 6 months vs 20% on methotrexate alone by 6 weeks</cite><cite id="a501af43-5">Methotrexate is a cornerstone in RA guidelines summaries</cite>.
  - Interpretation: These drugs suppress joint inflammation, prevent structural progression, and enable sustained remission/low disease activity in many patients; if monotherapy is insufficient, escalate within DMARD class or to targeted biologic (TNF, IL‑6, JAK) per step‑up to response. <cite id="13c681b3-4">Comparative efficacy summaries quantify ACR20/50/70 at 12–54 weeks across DMARDs</cite><cite id="13c681b3-3">Combination with methotrexate is the current gold standard; these agents are effective in other inflammatory arthropathies</cite>.

- Intra-articular corticosteroids in inflammatory arthritis
  - Evidence/role: Rapid anti‑inflammatory effect; useful for painful swollen joints prior to biologic start or to bridge biologic gaps; but effects are transient, and repeated injections may increase infection risk or interfere with healing. Clinical consensus supports cautious, limited‑course use and avoiding overuse. <cite id="a501af43-3">Corticosteroid injections improve short-term pain/function in OA; analogous acute anti-inflammatory effects in inflammatory joints are used to control flares</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-3">Intra-articular corticosteroids have anti-inflammatory actions; HA also anti-inflammatory, but different risk profile</cite>.
  - Practical note: Coordinate with systemic DMARD/biologic therapy; inject when synovitis/periarticular inflammation is present but minimize frequency. <cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Adverse event risk and discontinuation increase with corticosteroid courses compared to hyaluronic acid; underscores caution toward repeated use</cite>.

Mechanistic and comparative nuance across injectables
- HA vs corticosteroids in OA: Mechanisms differ (viscosupplementation plus anti‑inflammatory vs high-dose local immunosuppression). Trials show significant pain reduction with HA and durable effect over months, whereas corticosteroids provide rapid relief with higher dropout/adverse event rates. Choose according to symptom phase and risk profile. <cite id="3e0b64a6-0">HA reduces pain vs placebo (SMD 0.94) with low adverse event rates</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-1">Repeated weekly HA provides long-term pain relief and disease-modifying effects</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Corticosteroids increase adverse event-related dropouts, while hyaluronic acid is a distinct class</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-3">Both have intra-articular anti-inflammatory actions but different profiles</cite>.
- Autologous therapies (e.g., PRP) have mechanistic rationale and emerging RCT signals but remain investigational relative to established viscosupplementation and corticosteroids; include only when conventional therapies are insufficient and when patient preference supports biological additivity. <cite id="3e0b64a6-2">Autologous therapies form a major intervention class alongside corticosteroids and HA in IA treatments for OA</cite>.

How to interpret “your substances” once listed
- Map substance to condition and indication, then check:
  - Is it listed in guideline first‑line options for OA/RA and for the specific joint (e.g., knee)?
  - Are there randomized or long-term observational/meta‑analytic data showing pain/function improvement, and for how long?
  - What are the comparative adverse‑event risks and contraindications (e.g., corticosteroids: infection risk, diabetes control; HA: hypersensitivity; methotrexate: liver/bone marrow monitoring)?
- Example matching (illustrative):
  - “Hyaluronate injections for knee OA”: RCTs/meta-analyses show significant pain reduction sustained over weeks–months, with low adverse events; used after oral/topical therapy; consider as bridge to surgery if needed. <cite id="3e0b64a6-0">Hyaluronic acid reduced pain vs placebo, low adverse events</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-1">Five weekly injections provide long-term pain relief and potential disease-modifying effects</cite>.
  - “Triamcinolone intra-articular for knee pain”: Demonstrated short‑term relief; weigh infection risk and potential impact on cartilage/bone; avoid in septic joints. <cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term improvement with IA corticosteroids in knee OA</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Higher adverse event–related dropouts noted with corticosteroids</cite>.
  - “Acetaminophen 650 mg PO q4h for knee OA”: Guideline-conditional recommendation; may reduce pain and improve function modestly over days–weeks; better GI tolerance than NSAIDs but monitor hepatic transaminases. <cite id="a501af43-0">Acetaminophen is conditionally recommended for OA; topical NSAIDs strongly recommended for knee OA</cite><cite id="a501af43-4">Conditionally recommended as first-line for hip/knee OA, emphasizing acetaminophen</cite>.
  - “Methotrexate 15 mg q周 plus TNF inhibitor” (RA with active disease): Combined therapy improves signs/symptoms and structure; significantly higher ACR20 and retention versus monotherapy; start folic acid and monitor labs. <cite id="13c681b3-1">Methotrexate + adalimumab vs methotrexate showed superior improvement</cite><cite id="13c681b3-2">Abatacept 86.2% retention and 64.8% ACR20; adalimumab 82% retention and 63.4% ACR20 at 1 year</cite><cite id="13c681b3-5">Humira + methotrexate produced greater improvement than methotrexate alone</cite>.
