Practical decision guide you can apply now
- When to consider each:
  - First‑line OA pain/function: acetaminophen; NSAIDs (oral/topical); acetaminophen-based combination for persistent pain. <cite id="a501af43-0">Topical NSAIDs strongly recommended, acetaminophen conditionally recommended</cite>.
  - Rapid pain relief/OA flare: short course intra-articular corticosteroid; consider infection risk. <cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term improvement with corticosteroid injections in knee/hip OA</cite>.
  - Structural preservation and prolonged relief: hyaluronic acid/viscosupplementation; consider early disease and patient preference for injectables. <cite id="3e0b64a6-0">HA pain reduction vs placebo (SMD 0.94), low adverse events</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-1">Week-by-week injections provide durable relief and potential disease modification</cite>.
  - Supplements: trial glucosamine sulfate (especially) for minimal-to-moderate benefit; not for acute need. <cite id="c0001786-8">Glucosamine sulfate associated with improved pain and slowed joint space narrowing</cite><cite id="c0001786-6">Combination shows no clear superiority over placebo</cite>.
- Inflammatory joint disease with swelling/pain:
  - Start or optimize disease‑modifying therapy (methotrexate, TNF, IL‑6, JAK) and monitor labs; consider intra-articular steroids for local flare control pending systemic DMARD optimization. <cite id="13c681b3-0">TNF inhibitors improve clinical, functional, and radiographic outcomes in RA</cite><cite id="13c681b3-3">Combination DMARD/biologic therapy is the gold standard</cite><cite id="13c681b3-1">Methotrexate + biologic improves outcomes vs methotrexate alone</cite>.

Examples you can check against your list
- Hyaluronate (Hyalgan, Orthovisc, Supartz): RCTs show SMD ~0.94 pain reduction vs placebo; repeated weekly dosing yields months-long relief; infection rates ~1–2% depending on product; consider if patient wants to avoid oral NSAIDs. <cite id="3e0b64a6-0">SMD 0.94 improvement in pain vs placebo, low adverse events</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-1">Five weekly injections: long-term pain relief and possible disease modification</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-2">Categorized as an active intra-articular therapy</cite>.
- Triamcinolone IA: rapid reduction of pain and swelling for 4–8 weeks; higher risk of infection and peri-articular fat necrosis; avoid if infection, diabetes, or prior necrosis; do not exceed 2–3 courses per compartment per year. <cite id="a501af43-3">Short-term pain and function improvement with IA corticosteroids</cite><cite id="3e0b64a6-6">Higher adverse events/dropouts compared with hyaluronic acid</cite>.
- Etanercept/adalimumab/ustekinumab/tocilizumab: RA RCTs show high ACR20 and retention versus placebo or methotrexate control; used across inflammatory arthropathies; induce sustained remission and slow structural progression with monitoring; escalate within class if insufficient. <cite id="13c681b3-2">Abatacept and adalimumab produced high retention and ACR20 rates over 1 year</cite><cite id="13c681b3-0">TNF inhibitors improve clinical and radiographic outcomes</cite><cite id="13c681b3-4">ACR20/50/70 quantification across agents supports efficacy-guided escalation</cite>.
- Glucosamine/chondroitin: combination not clearly superior to placebo across the board; glucosamine sulfate may help pain and radiographic progression; try for 3–12 months in low-risk patients or as adjunct after surgery. <cite id="c0001786-6">Combination lacks superiority over placebo</cite><cite id="c0001786-8">Glucosamine sulfate associated with pain and structure benefits</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence‑based checklist of factors to consider before initiating therapy for patients with chronic inflammatory conditions. Items are organized to guide a shared decision‑making conversation and a safe, individualized handoff to treatment.

1) Confirm diagnosis and define disease burden and trajectory
- Anchor treatment in a clear diagnosis and exclude mimics using current criteria and needed confirmatory tests; document clinical severity and extra‑articular manifestations where relevant. <cite id="78dc2513-6">Rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria emphasize persistent synovitis without a better explanation to guide diagnosis and downstream management</cite>. 
- Use disease activity measures to decide whether immediate treatment is warranted; treat to target sustained remission/low disease activity when feasible. <cite id="78dc2513-7">Rheumatology guidelines advise starting disease‑modifying antirheumatic drugs early</cite> and <cite id="2f884eaf-1">treatment should be aimed at reaching a target of sustained remission or low disease activity in every patient</cite>. <cite id="2f884eaf-0">ACR/EULAR endorsed Boolean and index‑based remission criteria provide standardized definitions and measurement tools</cite>. 
- In inflammatory bowel disease, start biologics after correlating endoscopic/typologic findings with symptoms and severity scales; weigh risks versus benefits by comorbidity and disease course. <cite id="c5e53588-0">The decision to start anti‑TNF in IBD hinges on disease severity, comorbidities, and the balance of benefits and risks</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-5">AGA living guidelines stratify therapy selection by prior exposures and disease activity to aid decision making</cite>.

2) Evaluate organ risk and comorbidity profile (infection, malignancy, cardiovascular, hepatic)
- Screen for infections before immunosuppression: latent tuberculosis (including IGRA and TST with risk‑adapted interpretation), viral hepatitis B and C, and consider mycobacterial/tuberculous exposures with travel/history. <cite id="d08a1af3-0">Prior to anti‑TNF, evaluate latent TB, HBV, and typically HCV</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-2">Hepatotoxicity risks necessitate pre‑treatment HBV/HCV screening and monitoring</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-3">National guidelines outline TB prophylaxis and critical pre‑initiation information for anti‑TNF</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-6">Baseline TB screening, with attention to exposure and symptoms, is mandatory for psoriasis biologics</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-8">ACR recommends latent TB screening in RA patients before biologic therapy</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-1">TB/HCV risk assessment should include travel, residence, and birthplace with targeted skin testing</cite>.
- Document baseline CBC, creatinine, transaminases, ESR/CRP, and consider chest radiography with risk‑based TB evaluation to individualize start and monitoring. <cite id="d08a1af3-4">Recommended baseline workup includes CBC, creatinine, AST/ALT; HBV screening is required for rheumatic patients before immunosuppressive therapy</cite>. 
- Identify patients with high infection risk or active infections and defer or de‑escalate immunosuppression; institute empiric therapy and re‑assess timing. <cite id="c5e53588-1">A focused physical and history, with attention to travel and international birthplace, helps identify infection risks before immunosuppression</cite>.
- Integrate cardiovascular and malignancy risk assessment, particularly with IL‑6/i‑cyclooxygenase pathway inhibitors and prolonged corticosteroid exposure; manage modifiable risk factors before and during therapy. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Rheumatology guidelines catalog drug classes, contraindications, and adverse events to inform individualized risk assessments</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-6">Expert commentary notes immunosuppression in neurology carries relatively high risk, requiring careful quality and safety evaluation frameworks</cite>.
- Check for contraindications and active hypersensitivity to targeted agents; favor alternatives when severe allergies (e.g., to mAb Fc moieties) are present. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Rheumatoid arthritis guidance recognizes infections and medication contraindications as salient issues when considering csDMARDs</cite>.

3) Vaccination and travel status (preventive care as precision immunomodulation)
- Optimize immunization prior to or early in therapy; separate live and non‑live vaccine timelines from immunosuppressants. <cite id="d08a1af3-2">Screening for hepatitis B/C before immunosuppressive treatment is mandatory, and hepatotoxicity requires careful monitoring</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-3">Shared decision‑making improves patient‑clinician interactions in chronic illness management</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-4">Travel guidance for immunocompromised patients emphasizes disease duration, stability, and level of immune competence</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-3">ASGE scan highlights SDM’s role in choosing therapy in patients with chronic liver disease</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-5">TB evaluation should follow positive or symptomatic screening results, underscoring preventive measures for travelers</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-6">Baseline TB screening is required in psoriasis biologic candidates before treatment</cite>.
- Counsel on prophylaxis when indicated (e.g., LTBI with anti‑TNF/MTX exposure, pneumocystis prophylaxis in high‑risk IBD flares with azathioprine), and provide written plans. <cite id="d08a1af3-3">National anti‑TNF guidelines include prophylaxis strategies and critical patient education before initiation</cite>. 
- For patients with chronic hepatitis B, consider nucleos(t)ide analog cover when switching to TNF inhibitors. <cite id="d08a1af3-0">IBD anti‑TNF algorithms recommend HBV screening and, when positive, specialist involvement and consideration for antiviral prophylaxis</cite>.

4) Patient preferences, values, and social context
- Engage patients in shared decision‑making early to align therapy with goals (symptom control, prevent disability/flare, preserve function/quality of life); tailor intensity by preferences. <cite id="c5e53588-3">Shared decision‑making is a cornerstone for managing chronic illnesses</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Guidelines emphasize patient engagement when choosing therapies and monitoring strategies</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-3">ASGE scan reports SDM improves therapy selection in chronic liver disease</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-2">ACR reproductive health guidance encourages preconception discussion of medications with rheumatology colleagues</cite>.
- Discuss expectations, realistic timelines, and the trade‑offs of higher‑risk agents (response speed, durability, safety) versus step‑up therapy. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Rheumatology guideline panels include patients and weigh benefits, risks, and burdens when formulating conditional recommendations</cite>.

5) Reproductive planning, contraception, and lactation
- Before conception and during childbearing years, plan medications and contraception with both medical and sexual health counseling; avoid teratogenic combinations. <cite id="78dc2513-2">Rheumatology reproductive guidance recommends medication review and future family planning discussions pre‑conception</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-5">Contraception choice should be tailored to safety and effectiveness in rheumatic disease</cite>. 
- Counsel on fertility window considerations during biologic exposure and spacing after drug elimination half‑lives; arrange for close follow‑up. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Rheumatology clinical practice guidelines enumerate drug‑specific contraindications and adverse events relevant to reproductive counseling</cite>.

6) Drug–drug interactions and adherence factors
- Identify interactions with over‑the‑counter meds, supplements (e.g., St. John’s wort), anticonvulsants, and proton pump inhibitors that reduce biologic levels or corticosteroid efficacy. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Rheumatoid arthritis guideline recommendations explicitly address drug safety and interactions during csDMARD/DMARD selection and use</cite>.
- Plan a simplified regimen and problem‑solve barriers (dosing complexity, needle phobia) before initiation; provide educational materials and written schedules. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Guidelines incorporate patient preferences and medication adverse events and emphasize patient participation in choosing regimens</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-1">Adequate patient education is embedded in pre‑biologic evaluation and counseling cycles</cite>.

7) Safety monitoring blueprint and escalation pathways
- Establish baseline labs and a cadence (CBC, creatinine, transaminases; adjust with drug and risk); screen for TB with CXR and symptom evaluation; consider prophylaxis when exposure/susceptibility is high. <cite id="d08a1af3-4">Baseline CBC, creatinine, AST, and HBV screening are required before rheumatic immunosuppression</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-6">All psoriasis biologic candidates need baseline TB screening and management of LTBI exposure</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-5">TB screening and diagnosis algorithms incorporate symptoms and positive testing</cite>. 
- Counsel on medication adverse‑effect recognition (GI perforation alarm features with TNF inhibitors, fatigue/edema with JAK inhibitors, visual changes with MTX); arrange rapid access pathways. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Rheumatoid arthritis guideline recommendations detail adverse events and management for csDMARDs and bDMARDs to support early detection and escalation</cite>. 
- For patients with prior or extensive skin/mucosal disease or immunoglobulin abnormalities, include ophthalmologic screening and ENT evaluation as part of baseline and surveillance. <cite id="78dc2513-1">In psoriasis care, pre‑biologic workup integrates comorbidity assessment and anticipatory guidance for ocular disease and other complications</cite>.

8) Quality of life, function, and comanagement
- Incorporate patient‑reported outcomes (symptoms, function) and address social determinants that impact adherence and disease expression; schedule early, frequent reassessments during titration to target. <cite id="c5e53588-3">Shared decision‑making improves interactions and choices in chronic gastrointestinal disease therapy</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Involving patients in therapy selection and monitoring improves engagement and adherence</cite>.
- Coordinate with subspecialists as appropriate (gynecology/reproductive endocrinology, dermatology, gastroenterology, infectious disease) to optimize preconception/teratogen‑free strategies and manage complex multimorbidity. <cite id="78dc2513-2">Reproductive planning requires joint discussion of rheumatologic and contraception/teratogen risks</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-1">Infection screening for dermatologic immunosuppression should be thorough and subspecialty‑informed</cite>.

9) Practical pre‑treatment checklist (to customize per disease)
- Diagnosis confirmation and prognosis overview. <cite id="78dc2513-6">Use RA classification and disease activity measures to connect diagnosis with treatment intensity</cite>.
- Disease activity benchmarking and treatment threshold discussion (e.g., remission/low activity as targets; step‑up when DAS28 or equivalent remains high). <cite id="2f884eaf-0">ACR/EULAR remission criteria provide consistent thresholds for remission/low activity</cite>. <cite id="2f884eaf-1">Patients should be treated to sustained remission or low disease activity</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-0">IBD candidates for anti‑TNF should be clearly stratified by severity and comorbidity</cite>.
- Physical exam focusing on infection signs (adenopathy, fever) and constitutional status. <cite id="c5e53588-1">Thorough history and targeted systems review (including travel and exposure) are required before immunosuppressive dermatology therapy</cite>.
- Baseline labs and imaging including CBC, creatinine, transaminases, ESR/CRP, CXR (with TB workup), and organ‑specific tests (e.g., IBD endoscopy/serologies; RA DAS28). <cite id="d08a1af3-4">CBC, creatinine, AST, HBV screen are baseline requirements for rheumatic immunosuppression</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-6">TB screening precedes biologic initiation for psoriasis</cite>. 
- Vaccination status and travel plans; optimize immunization and plan prophylaxis (TB, HBV, VZV) and contraception. <cite id="c5e53588-3">Shared decision‑making guides therapy choice and adherence in inflammatory bowel disease</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-2">HBV/HCV screening and hepatotoxicity monitoring are mandatory</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-5">Symptomatic or positive TB screening requires disease evaluation and treatment</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-2">Discuss medications with future plans to conceive and contraceptive method safety</cite>.
- Contraindications, prior hypersensitivity, malignancy history, TB exposure, and current infections; defer if active/severe infection or malignancy until safety case made. <cite id="c5e53588-1">Risk‑focused physical and history mitigate peri‑therapy infections in dermatologic immunosuppression</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Rheumatology guidance explicitly addresses patient safety and adverse events in treatment selection</cite>. 
- Patient education and written plan including adverse‑event red flags, dosing schedule, and follow‑up timetable; arrange first post‑treatment check and labs. <cite id="78dc2513-1">Comprehensive pre‑biologic counseling and education are standard in dermatologic care pathways</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-3">National anti‑TNF algorithms provide patient education and prophylaxis guidance prior to therapy</cite>.
- Reproductive and psychosocial assessment and agreement on monitoring intensification if pregnancy is planned or occurs. <cite id="78dc2513-2">Medication review and family planning discussions preconception are recommended</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-5">Contraception method safety in rheumatic disease is addressable with shared choices</cite>.
- Willingness to engage in “treat‑to‑target” with home monitoring (DAS28, PROMs) and readiness to escalate or biologica‑ize step‑up therapy if needed. <cite id="2f884eaf-1">Treatment targets are sustained remission/low disease activity in every rheumatologic patient</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Patient participation in monitoring and therapy selection is emphasized to improve adherence</cite>.

10) Special scenarios and how to sequence decisions
- Active infection: treat infection first; cover with sulfonamides if TB is suspected; reassess immunosuppression timing with ID input. <cite id="d08a1af3-6">All biologic candidates must be screened for TB exposure and managed accordingly before starting</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-4">Travelers with chronic inflammation require careful assessment of immune competence and travel risks</cite>. 
- Low disease activity but functional/patient‑reported impairment: consider non‑pharm and PT/OT; if goal remains unmet, trial a targeted biologic with an agreed escalation plan if remission not achieved within expected timeframes. <cite id="2f884eaf-1">Patients may target sustained remission or low disease activity; intensity is individualized</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-3">SDM helps align therapy with patient values and improves decisions for symptom‑focused care</cite>.
- High shared risk (malignancy/CV/hepatic) and uncertain benefit: delay, de‑risk (screen and treat comorbidities), and retry when risk profile shifts (age, smoking cessation, HLD control), or favor narrow, tight step‑up with rigorous surveillance. <cite id="78dc2513-8">Rheumatology guidelines explicitly weigh risk, adverse events, and patient participation before selecting less preferred but necessary therapy</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-6">Immunossuppression requires a framework for quality and safety evaluation</cite>.

Caveat and monitoring enhancements
- Re‑assess pharmacovigilance in the first 3–6 months more often if disease activity is high or prior adverse events occurred; consider imaging or organ‑specific labs per drug and comorbidity. <cite id="78dc2513-0">Conditioning recommendations in rheumatology reflect need to manage infections, laboratory abnormalities, drug reactions, and other adverse events</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-4">Ophthalmic baseline screening and monitoring of liver enzymes accompany HBV screening and immunosuppression in rheumatic care</cite>.
- Counsel that while rare, drug‑associated malignancies occur in susceptible patients; weigh with cumulative dose, exposure duration, and smoking; maintain multidisciplinary surveillance. <cite id="78dc2513-6">Guidelines acknowledge elevated risk in neurologic immunosuppression and require careful evaluation, suggesting heightened vigilance for safety signals</cite>.

Summary starter sheet (custom to each disease)
- Diagnosis and trajectory: confirm with latest criteria; estimate likely disease course and need for early aggressive therapy. <cite id="78dc2513-6">RA diagnosis uses clinical synovitis criteria</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-7">Start DMARDs early in RA</cite>.
- Activity/burden: quantify with DAS28/IBD indices; discuss thresholds for treatment/intensification toward remission or low activity. <cite id="2f884eaf-0">Remission definitions support quantifying targets</cite>. <cite id="c5e53588-0">IBD severity and comorbidity drive anti‑TNF decision making</cite>.
- Safety: TB/LTBI screen, HBV/HCV screen, CBC/creatinine/AST, baseline CXR if indicated, and infectious foci treatment. <cite id="d08a1af3-0">IBD and rheumatology anti‑TNF require TB/HBV/HCV screening</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-4">CBC/creatinine/AST are baseline requirements</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-5">TB workup acts on symptoms and positive screening</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-2">HBV monitoring/mitigation is mandatory</cite>.
- Preferences/values: SDM on risks/benefits, preferred intensity, fertility/contraception, work/school disruption, and willingness to self‑monitor and escalate. <cite id="c5e53588-3">SDM improves therapy choice and adherence in chronic inflammatory disease</cite>. <cite id="78dc2513-2">Preconception and contraception planning with rheumatology is emphasized</cite>.
- Plan of care: agreed timeline to target, first post‑treatment visit and labs, adverse‑event hotline, and comanagement list (ID, oncology, obstetrics, GI/hep) when applicable. <cite id="d08a1af3-3">National anti‑TNF algorithms include detailed pre‑treatment counseling and prophylaxis planning</cite>. <cite id="d08a1af3-1">Biologic start requires specific medical tests including TB, hepatitis</cite>.

These elements provide a safe, patient‑centered template to decide “when to start” and “how to start,” with timely escalation and shared ownership—principles echoed across rheumatology, gastroenterology, and dermatology guidelines and summarized in the ACR and EULAR treat‑to‑target paradigms. <cite id="78dc2513-8">ACR emphasizes shared decision‑making and patient engagement in therapeutic choices</cite> and <cite id="2f884eaf-1">treat‑to‑target aims at sustained remission or low disease activity</cite>.
