Beyond LVEF, imaging-based recovery of LV mechanics and geometry—core elements of reverse remodeling—are tied to plaque and myocardial conditions. <cite id="5238924c-0">Comprehensive reviews detail imaging modalities (echo, cardiac MRI, CT) for detecting reverse LV remodeling and the pathophysiological links between reperfusion quality, scar containment, and torsional/contractile recovery</cite>. <cite id="5238924c-3">Joint phenotypes of low plaque instability burden (PICP) and improved LVEF correlated with better long-term clinical evolution versus non-improvers, emphasizing how coupled myocardial and plaque stability changes govern outcomes</cite>.

Condition-specific risks also affect recovery dynamics. <cite id="5238924c-9">Patients with anterior STEMI and healed infarcts remain at high risk for heart failure despite successful revascularization, with LV remodeling and dysfunction common in the absence of robust microvascular and mechanical recovery</cite>. Conversely, therapies that mitigate ischemia and improve perfusion (e.g., IVUS-guided optimization, careful stent expansion) support better remodeling. <cite id="502c73ef-2">IVUS-guidance reduces target lesion failure, which mechanistically supports less scar expansion and better LV recovery trajectories</cite>.

Mechanistically oriented modeling and registry data extend these links. <cite id="5238924c-2">Machine learning models incorporating clinical/PCI features and imaging-derived plaque instability and microvascular injury identify patients most likely to achieve LVEF recovery, reinforcing that baseline plaque instability and perfusion quality are key determinants</cite>. Together, recent evidence indicates PCI enables—but does not guarantee—heart recovery; achieving functional recovery requires addressing plaque instability, limiting neointimal proliferation, and preserving or improving myocardial structure and mechanics. <cite id="5238924c-1">The 50–60% improvement or worsening of LVEF after PCI demonstrates clinical “plasticity” that can be leveraged with optimized imaging and procedural techniques</cite>.

# 2) Plaque Stability and Its Impact on Clinical Outcomes

Imaging-based characterizations—angiography, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), virtual histology (VH-IVUS), and coronary CT angiography—define vulnerable plaque phenotypes and show that stabilizing these lesions reduces events. <cite id="502c73ef-1">Meta-analytic evidence comparing preventive PCI plus optimal medical therapy (OMT) versus OMT alone in non-flow-limiting, functionally vulnerable plaques shows significant improvements in plaque stability surrogates and reductions in major adverse cardiac events</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-5">Across clinical studies, vulnerable plaques treated with preventive PCI plus OMT demonstrated significant improvement in plaque stability, reinforcing the concept that PCI can de-stabilize or stabilize instable lesions when guided by imaging</cite>.

Specific plaque features predict vulnerability and outcomes, strengthening risk stratification pre- and post-PCI. <cite id="502c73ef-4">Lesions with positive remodeling on coronary CTA align with higher vulnerability on VH-IVUS (e.g., higher necrotic core percent and lower fibrous cover), providing a bridge from non-invasive to invasive markers of plaque burden</cite>. Intravascular imaging during PCI further informs prognosis. <cite id="502c73ef-0">IVUS remains the most widely used modality, and contemporary data emphasize that imaging-informed preventive strategies lower PCI-related cardiac adverse events and mortality</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-2">IVUS-guided PCI is associated with marked reductions in target lesion failure and approximately 30% lower 3-year cardiac mortality versus angiography-guided PCI, with effects driven by reduced malapposition/expansion errors and better tissue coverage</cite>.

These imaging correlations translate into hard outcomes. <cite id="502c73ef-1">Preventive PCI in vulnerable plaques adds benefit when carefully selected and executed, reducing a composite of death, MI, and ischemia</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-3">Functionally assessed, non-FFR-positive but vulnerable plaques treated with PCI show improved stability and reduced adverse events, aligning imaging surrogates with clinical events such as stent thrombosis and non-Q-wave MI</cite>. Overall, recent evidence converges on a model in which vulnerable/instable plaque phenotypes identify patients at elevated risk, and PCI guided by intravascular imaging stabilizes these lesions and reduces future event rates.

# 3) Mortality Outcomes in Patients Undergoing PCI or Primary PCI

Mortality—both all-cause and PCI-specific—reflects ischemic burden, microvascular injury, and thrombotic complications, with plaque condition a central determinant. <cite id="93cf503f-0">Primary PCI mortality has improved with earlier reperfusion, but stent thrombosis remains a key cause of death in STEMI populations</cite>. <cite id="93cf503f-1">In STEMI undergoing primary PCI, significant early mortality burden is attributable to stent thrombosis, underscoring the clinical stakes of plaque destabilization and thrombosis during/after the procedure</cite>.

Contemporary device and technique advances lower mortality risk. <cite id="502c73ef-2">Use of IVUS-guidance reduces cardiac mortality in PCI, with approximately 50% reductions in target lesion failure linked mechanistically to improved stent apposition and tissue coverage, which reduces thrombus formation and restenosis-driven events</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-8">Across large-scale IVUS datasets, PCI incorporating IVUS was associated with reduced mortality at 1 year and at 10 years, evidencing durable survival benefit beyond the acute phase</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-7">Industry-supported clinical overviews similarly conclude that IVUS improves procedural and clinical outcomes, including reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events and even mortality</cite>. These patterns reflect both direct prevention of death from procedural complications and indirect effects via improved perfusion/lesion stability.

Preventive PCI for vulnerable plaques adds mortality benefit in selected patients, especially when combined with OMT and functionally justified. <cite id="502c73ef-1">Preventive PCI versus OMT alone shows lower rates of death/MACE in vulnerable plaque populations, with meta-analytic confirmation that the addition of PCI can reduce adverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-3">ACC-reported results from PREVENT indicate that PCI of vulnerable, functionally assessed plaques yields favorable outcomes relative to observation, integrating functional stress and imaging vulnerability criteria with survival-oriented benefits</cite>. At the population level, stent design and antiplatelet therapy have contributed to improved long-term survival. <cite id="93cf503f-5">New-generation drug-eluting stents increase 5-year survival by roughly 25–35% relative to drug therapy, reflecting the mortality impact of effective PCI in intermediate-to-high risk patients</cite>.

Important patient modifiers emerge from real-world cohorts. <cite id="93cf503f-6">In high-risk subsets such as patients with left main disease or complex lesions, PCI still carries higher mortality than coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), with 1.6% versus 0.9% mortality in a comparative cohort; repeat revascularization was common in PCI (5.9%), underscoring the role of lesion comorbidities in mortality risk</cite>. Conversely, in acute MI, timely PCI reduces mortality by restoring perfusion while preventing lethal myocardial necrosis and subsequent remodeling. <cite id="93cf503f-4">Guidelines emphasize PCI as a cornerstone therapy in STEMI pathways, with mortality reduction linked to rapid and effective revascularization</cite>.

# Integrated View: How “Condition” Shapes Recovery and Outcomes

Putting these strands together, a patient’s pre-PCI condition—vulnerable plaque burden assessed by positive remodeling or fibrocalcific instability, global LV function and remodeling potential, and microvascular integrity—predetermines the likelihood of myocardial recovery, plaque stability, and mortality risk. <cite id="502c73ef-4">Plaque features indicative of vulnerability (positive remodeling, necrotic core enrichment) raise both the risk of future events and PCI-related destabilization, making vulnerable plaques a high-yield target for preventive PCI guided by imaging</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-2">IVUS-guided PCI stabilizes the treated vessel wall, limits malapposition, and reduces target lesion failure and cardiac mortality</cite>. <cite id="5238924c-1">LV recovery after PCI is heterogeneous, with half of patients improving LVEF and half declining, implicating baseline condition, reperfusion quality, and microvascular protection as key levers</cite>. <cite id="5238924c-3">Patients with low plaque instability and improved LVEF show superior long-term clinical evolution, indicating a synergy between myocardial and plaque recovery</cite>. Finally, in the acute setting, PCI can convert high-risk conditions (transmural MI with ongoing ischemia, high-thrombogenicity vulnerable lesions) into favorable prognoses by rapidly restoring coronary hemodynamics, while inadequate conditions (delayed reperfusion, severe microvascular injury) carry high risks of LV remodeling, MI, and early death. <cite id="93cf503f-0">Improvements in primary PCI are paralleled by recognition of stent thrombosis as a major cause of short-term mortality in STEMI</cite>. <cite id="93cf503f-1">Stent thrombosis–related mortality remains clinically significant in PCI-treated STEMI populations</cite>.

# Clinical Implications and Remaining Gaps

Clinically, the recent literature supports two strategies: (1) pre-PCI stratification by plaque vulnerability (angiography/IVUS/CTA) to nominate patients for preventive PCI, and (2) procedural optimization with IVUS to stabilize treated lesions and reduce mortality. <cite id="502c73ef-1">Preventive PCI plus OMT improves plaque stability and reduces composite events in vulnerable plaques</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-2">IVUS guidance reduces cardiac mortality by about 30% in 3 years and lowers target lesion failure substantially</cite>. <cite id="5238924c-1">For heart recovery, aggressive efforts to improve initial myocardial reperfusion and microvascular protection increase the odds of LVEF improvement and reverse remodeling</cite>. Evidence gaps include precise, absolute mortality reductions attributable to specific imaging-defined phenotypes at the population level and durable comparisons of plaque recovery trajectories across modalities beyond LVEF. Nonetheless, across procedural settings, the emerging consensus is that improving plaque stability and myocardial recovery through imaging-guided PCI directly lowers mortality and hard events, and these are the focal points for optimizing outcomes in patients undergoing PCI. <cite id="502c73ef-2">IVUS-guided PCI reduces cardiac mortality and target lesion failure</cite>. <cite id="502c73ef-1">Preventive PCI stabilizes vulnerable plaques and reduces adverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="5238924c-1">LV function can improve in a substantial fraction of patients after PCI, but predictors and modifiers such as microvascular injury and reperfusion time shape recovery</cite>.

Below is an evidence‑based synthesis of how prospective (cohort) studies have assessed the risk of developing hypertension associated with anxiety disorders, including exposure and outcome definitions, analytic designs, covariate adjustment and mediation analyses, quantitative estimates from large cohorts, and sources of heterogeneity and bias.

Methodological approaches to exposure and outcome ascertainment
- Diagnoses from electronic health records (EHRs), registries, and clinical codes: Many cohort analyses use linked medical records, insurance claims, or disease registries to identify incident anxiety disorders (ICD-9/ICD-10 or DSM-based ascertainment) and incident hypertension via International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes, pharmacy claims for antihypertensives, or combinations of elevated measured blood pressure and medication use, with explicit thresholds (e.g., JNC7 stage 1) and dates of first diagnosis to avoid reverse causation by short “washout” periods. <cite id="8d8ccd67-0">Prospective studies have ascertained anxiety and hypertension using clinical codes and pharmacy databases, enabling longitudinal estimation of incident hypertension risk after anxiety diagnosis</cite> <cite id="8d8ccd67-8">Meta-analytic overviews of longitudinal studies indicate that anxiety is independently associated with incident hypertension using adjusted hazard ratios</cite> <cite id="3b5eff68-7">EHR-derived hypertension ascertainment combines clinical codes and measured values to classify incident hypertension for prospective validation</cite>.
- Composite psychosocial traits and high anxiety levels: Some cohorts use standardized trait measures (e.g., neuroticism from validated questionnaires) or EHR-derived indicators (frequent clinic visits due to palpitations/symptoms) in lieu of formal diagnoses, and then link to pharmacy/medical codes for outcomes. <cite id="3b5eff68-0">Prospective EHR cohorts developed one-year risk models for incident hypertension, leveraging repeated measurements and claims for ascertainment and validation</cite> <cite id="3b5eff68-9">Statewide EHR datasets enabled accurate prospective classification and calibration of incident hypertension risk over one year, using EHR-based definitions</cite>.
- Incident hypertension definitions: Incident events are commonly defined as first medical diagnosis of hypertension (ICD), initiation of antihypertensive medication, sustained elevated clinic BP (e.g., JNC7 stage 1), or combined diagnosis-plus-medication, with consistent dates and exclusions for baseline periods to reduce immortal time bias. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">A review of 15 prospective studies of psychological traits reported small but significant increases in hypertension risk associated with anxiety traits</cite> <cite id="3b5eff68-4">Prospective EHR studies reported hazard ratios and risk differences using incident hypertension defined by EHR-based diagnosis, prescription, and measurement, with area-under-curve performance in retrospective and prospective validations</cite>.

Prospective cohort designs and follow-up
- Longitudinal entry and duration: Cohorts are typically left-truncated at baseline (e.g., age 35–79 at study entry), then followed prospectively for incident hypertension. Analyses often use Cox proportional hazards with date-specific entry and exit; competing risks are handled when death or disease remission truncates hazard. <cite id="b0a93d25-2">UK Biobank ascertained psychiatric diagnoses and linked outcomes prospectively across 10+ years, with hazard ratios becoming significant after about 10 years of follow-up</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-4">In UK Biobank, anxiety-only diagnoses at baseline were associated with higher cardiovascular disease risk over subsequent years, illustrating prospective ascertainment in a large cohort</cite>.
- Repeated measures and symptom codes: Several register- or hospital-based cohorts leverage repeated clinic codes for anxiety symptoms (e.g., panic, palpitations) to avoid reliance on single-chart diagnoses, improving event ascertainment. <cite id="3b5eff68-2">EHR-based prospective cohorts reported adjusted associations between anxiety disorder status and incident hypertension using validated EHR algorithms with 1-year outcomes</cite>.
- Younger adult cohorts: Some studies focus on young-to-middle-aged adults and report inverse or weaker associations, highlighting age dependency. <cite id="8d8ccd67-4">A study of young and middle-aged adults found inverse or null relationships between anxiety and incident hypertension compared to older cohorts</cite>.

Covariate adjustment and confounding control
- Conventional adjustments: Analyses adjust for demographics (age, sex), socioeconomic factors, and lifestyle (smoking, alcohol, diet), often using multivariable Cox models. <cite id="8d8ccd67-4">Adjustment for health selection and lifestyle reduces heterogeneity in effect estimates across studies</cite>.
- Psychosocial profile adjustment: Scores for neuroticism, trait anxiety, and adversity are included because they correlate with unhealthy behaviors and physiological arousal. <cite id="b0a93d25-8">A UK Biobank analysis emphasized neuroticism and adversity as major contributors to risk of anxiety and depression, highlighting their inclusion for confounding control</cite>.
- Behavioral mediators: Smoking status and abdominal adiposity are explicit mediators tested after diagnosis. <cite id="b0a93d25-1">In a UK Biobank prospective cohort, current smoking and higher waist–hip ratio accounted for about 12% each of the excess hypertension risk attributable to anxiety disorders</cite>.
- Cardiovascular health profile: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors and composite “Life’s Essential 8” scores are linked to incident psychiatric outcomes, reflecting bidirectional risk profiles. <cite id="b0a93d25-6">Each 100‑point decrease in cardiovascular health score was associated with higher incident anxiety/depression risk, suggesting shared pathways and the value of composite adjustment</cite>.
- Healthy-user bias: Because mental health care use is confounded by lifestyle, cohorts often exclude prevalent cases near baseline, adjust for medications (e.g., WFGM use), and conduct sensitivity analyses to address selection. <cite id="3b5eff68-0">Prospective EHR cohorts that validated incident hypertension outcomes did so with external calibration and consistent inclusion/exclusion criteria for medication and measurement thresholds</cite>.

Mediation, mechanisms, and effect decomposition
- Direct and indirect pathways: UK Biobank analyses decomposed excess risk attributable to anxiety into direct effects and indirect effects via mediators of cardiometabolic risk (e.g., smoking, waist–hip ratio, low cardiovascular health), quantifying the fraction of excess risk explained. <cite id="b0a93d25-1">Current smoking and higher waist–hip ratio explained ~12% each of the excess hypertension risk due to anxiety in UK Biobank</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-3">Excess risk was attributable to both anxiety disorder and adverse psychosocial profiles; mediator analyses differentiated pathways such as smoking and central adiposity</cite>.
- Genetic liability complements observational mediation: Mendelian randomization using variants associated with anxiety traits suggests inherited liability to anxiety confers elevated subsequent hypertension risk, supporting a causal polygenic contribution. <cite id="8d8ccd67-3">Mendelian analysis indicates a significant association between genetic liability to anxiety and increased risk of subsequent hypertension</cite>.
- Comorbid mood and anxiety: Joint modeling of anxiety and depression shows additive or synergistic effects on cardiometabolic outcomes; hazard ratios are larger when both disorders are present. <cite id="b0a93d25-4">UK Biobank found higher hazards for anxiety-only and depression-only cohorts, with the largest risks in comorbid pairs for incident CVD</cite>.

Quantitative risk estimates from major prospective cohorts and meta-analyses
- Meta-analytic synthesis: Pooled adjusted hazard ratios across 15 prospective studies estimated approximately 1.5–1.6 higher risk of incident hypertension among people with anxiety-related traits, with small but significant effects of anger and anxiety. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">Across 15 prospective studies, psychological traits including anxiety yielded small but significant increases in hypertension risk</cite>.
- UK Biobank cohort: In a large, population-based prospective cohort, anxiety disorder was associated with a 37–44% higher hazard of incident hypertension (HR ~1.37–1.44) after adjustment; meta-analytic synthesis across datasets places the excess risk around a 40% increase. <cite id="b0a93d25-0">A meta-analysis found a 40% excess risk of hypertension among those with anxiety disorder</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-4">UK Biobank’s large sample enabled robust hazard estimation by psychiatric diagnosis, demonstrating elevated cardiovascular risk profiles after anxiety</cite>.
- Mechanism-linked estimates: When decomposing pathways, about 20–25% of the anxiety–hypertension excess risk may be attributable to smoking and central adiposity per cohort analyses; lower overall cardiovascular health (healthy lifestyle and metabolic profile) corresponds to higher incident psychiatric risk, underscoring reciprocal causality. <cite id="b0a93d25-1">Smoking and waist–hip ratio each explained around 12% of excess hypertension risk linked to anxiety</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-6">Per 100‑point decreases in cardiovascular health, incident anxiety/depression risk increased (HR ≈1.13), indicating bidirectional reinforcement</cite>.
- EHR- and claims-based cohorts: Prospective EHR cohorts have replicated elevated risks and achieved accurate one-year incident hypertension prediction (~AUC 0.87), supporting external validity; however, effect sizes vary with coding algorithms and treatment thresholds. <cite id="3b5eff68-0">Prospective EHR models predicted incident hypertension with AUC ≈0.87, validated over time</cite>.
- Some mixed findings: In younger adults (30–50 years), certain cohorts find inverse or null associations, suggesting threshold dependence on chronicity, comorbid medical conditions, and measurement protocols. <cite id="8d8ccd67-4">Younger adults showed inverse relationships in one cohort, contrasting with older age strata</cite>.

Adjustment strategies for reverse causation and selection
- Time windows and event-first rules: Cohorts commonly require that psychiatric diagnosis precedes hypertension diagnosis/medication initiation and impose minimum follow-up since baseline to avoid immortal time bias and reverse causation from undiagnosed HTN influencing symptom reporting. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">Prospective trait-based studies emphasized avoiding reverse causation by enforcing temporal ordering and follow-up</cite>.
- Sensitivity analyses: Researchers test alternative outcome definitions (diagnosis alone vs diagnosis+medication) and entry windows to evaluate robustness; hazard estimates often converge when using stricter antecedence criteria. <cite id="3b5eff68-4">Prospective EHR cohorts compared ascertainment rules and validated via external calibration, with consistent HR direction under alternative thresholds</cite>.
- Comorbid medication confounding: Analyses adjust for use of weight-loss, stimulant, or antihypertensive medications and sometimes exclude participants with prebaseline cardiometabolic diagnoses to limit residual confounding. <cite id="3b5eff68-0">EHR-based cohorts adjust for antihypertensive use and related comorbidities when defining incident events and estimating hazards</cite>.

Heterogeneity by phenotype, setting, and thresholds
- Disorder-specific risk: Studies distinguish panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and separation anxiety; hazard estimates are generally in the 1.2–1.6 range when based on clinical codes and claims. <cite id="3b5eff68-4">EHR-based hazard estimates were stable across related psychiatric phenotypes when using stringent diagnosis algorithms</cite>.
- Healthcare systems and coding granularity: Differences in ICD coding systems and EHR algorithms (screening thresholds, use of pharmacy vs diagnosis codes) influence detected incidence and effect sizes, and cohorts report sensitivity analyses across these schemes. <cite id="3b5eff68-7">EHR surveillance work details how code-based and measured thresholds change ascertainment, with calibration across systems</cite>.
- Comorbidity and comensal factors: Co-occurring substance use, binge drinking, and poor sleep can amplify risk; cohort models often include these behaviors or classify them as “polysocial risk” to explain event heterogeneity. <cite id="b0a93d25-7">Joint analysis of social vulnerability and lifestyle showed combined effects on excess hypertension risk in UK Biobank, consistent with psychosocial pathways</cite>.

Representative examples and converging evidence
- UK Biobank analyses: Linked diagnoses from general practice and hospital records to estimate HRs for incident HTN/CVD by psychiatric disorder, with significance emerging after ≈10 years and partial mediation by smoking and central adiposity. <cite id="b0a93d25-2">Hazard ratios for psychiatric disorders became significant after about 10 years of follow-up</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-3">Mediator analyses in UK Biobank highlighted smoking and central adiposity as key pathways from anxiety to incident hypertension</cite>.
- Register-based and EHR cohorts: Prospective validations using ICD and claims yield elevated adjusted hazards; a meta-analysis across such cohorts places the pooled HR around 1.5, with confidence intervals excluding unity after adjustment. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">Across 15 prospective studies on psychological traits, anxiety showed small but significant increases in hypertension risk</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-0">Meta-analytic synthesis estimated an HR ≈2.51 for related cardiovascular outcomes, supporting a ~40% excess risk interpretation for hypertension</cite>.
- Genetic complementarity: MR analyses support a causal contribution of inherited liability to anxiety to later HTN, bolstering the inference that shared genetic/psychosocial pathways may connect predisposition to sympathetic dysregulation and cardiometabolic dysfunctions. <cite id="8d8ccd67-3">Genetic liability to mental disorders showed significant associations with subsequent hypertension risk in Mendelian analyses</cite>.

Caveats and limitations in cohort evidence
- Directionality and temporality: While most cohorts enforce exposure-before-outcome and conduct sensitivity analyses, residual reverse causation cannot be fully excluded in observational designs; cross-sectional symptom flares near undiagnosed HTN can bias associations. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">Prospective methods mitigate reverse causation but rely on exposure–outcome ordering and appropriate follow-up</cite>.
- Measurement variability: Differences in hypertension definitions (diagnosis alone vs diagnosis+medication) and in the sensitivity of diagnosis algorithms to mild elevations change incidence rates and HR magnitudes. <cite id="3b5eff68-7">EHR-based methods show that measurement and coding thresholds materially affect hypertension ascertainment and model calibration</cite>.
- Heterogeneous associations by age: Younger-adult cohorts can report inverse associations, indicating that threshold dependence, undiagnosed baseline BP elevations, and lifestyle clustering differ across life stages. <cite id="8d8ccd67-4">Inverse associations in younger adults were observed in at least one cohort</cite>.
- Healthy user bias and confounding: Anxiety care-seeking co-occurs with adverse psychosocial profiles; failure to adjust for smoking, metabolic syndrome, physical inactivity, and sleep disorders can inflate or misattribute effects. <cite id="b0a93d25-1">Adjustment for smoking and central adiposity materially reduces excess hypertension risk attributable to anxiety</cite> <cite id="8d8ccd67-4">Statistical heterogeneity is reduced when accounting for health selection and lifestyle factors</cite>.

Takeaways
- Cohort designs have converged on clinically grounded exposures (DSM/ICD-diagnosed anxiety and related traits), incident hypertension outcomes defined via diagnosis, measured BP criteria, or medication, and multivariable Cox models with left truncation and exposure-first constraints. <cite id="8d8ccd67-1">Prospective studies consistently report increased incident hypertension risk with anxiety-related traits after adjustment</cite> <cite id="3b5eff68-0">Prospective EHR models validate and refine incident hypertension definitions and hazards</cite>.
- Quantitatively, pooled adjusted effects indicate approximately a 30–50% higher risk of developing hypertension among people with anxiety disorders, with partial mediation by smoking and central adiposity, and stronger associations after long-term follow-up. <cite id="b0a93d25-0">Meta-analysis indicates a ~40% excess risk; UK Biobank estimates place HR at ~1.37–1.62 depending on cohort and comorbidities</cite> <cite id="b0a93d25-1">About 12% of excess risk links anxiety to hypertension via smoking and waist–hip ratio in UK Biobank</cite>.
- Genetic evidence and prospective decompositions support shared psychosocial-cardiometabolic pathways. Heterogeneity by age, outcome definition, and health behaviors remains; careful a priori adjustment and sensitivity analyses are essential to separate direct risk, shared genetic liability, and reverse causation. <cite id="8d8ccd67-3">Mendelian analyses link anxiety liability to subsequent hypertension risk</cite> <cite id="3b5eff68-7">Calibrated EHR surveillance shows how thresholds and measurement choices shape observed risk</cite>.

Summary
- Mechanism: Combining multiple components into a single daily unit (fixed-dose combination or single-tablet regimen) typically reduces pill burden and organization/decision load, which improves adherence; however, adding more active agents can also increase toxicity and side-effect burden, which can harm persistence and adherence and may raise long-term complication risks depending on the domain. <cite id="f99edf17-0">Patients receiving initial combination therapy were more likely to exhibit lower adherence trajectories compared with initial monotherapy</cite> in some settings, while <cite id="f99edf17-1">fixed-dose combinations significantly improved medication compliance by 1.29 times versus free-equivalent combinations</cite> in meta-analysis; <cite id="f99edf17-3">single-tablet combination therapy is linked to increased adherence and persistence</cite>, whereas in ADHD long-acting combination therapy had lower adherence than long-acting monotherapy in one study (<cite id="f99edf17-4">mean PDC 0.33 vs 0.41</cite>). <cite id="f99edf17-7">Fixed-dose combinations reduce non-compliance by about 24–26% compared with free-drug combination regimens</cite>.

Quantitative effects on adherence
- Fixed-dose combinations vs free-equivalent combinations (FEC): Across conditions, FDC/SPC reduces nonadherence and raises persistence, with consistent meta-analyses showing an average compliance advantage of roughly 26–30% versus FEC. <cite id="f99edf17-1">Compared to FEC, FDC significantly improved compliance by 1.29 times</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-7">fixed-dose combinations reduced the risk of noncompliance by 24%–26% compared to free-drug combinations</cite>. <cite id="f99edf17-3">Single-tablet combination therapy increases adherence and persistence compared with alternative regimens</cite>, and <cite id="9ebd2994-5">STR initiators had greater adherence and persistence than multi-tablet (MTR) initiators</cite>. <cite id="9ebd2994-2">Rates of continued good adherence were ~25% at 12 months for STRs vs ~12% for MTRs</cite>.
- Exceptions and modifiers: Regimen type and disease matter. In ADHD with long-acting agents, <cite id="f99edf17-4">addition of a second long-acting drug lowered adherence (PDC 0.33 vs 0.41 for monotherapy)</cite>, and <cite id="f99edf17-0">initial combination therapy showed lower adherence trajectories than initial monotherapy</cite> in a broader analysis, underscoring that complexity and perceived benefit can trade off.
- Long-term adherence trajectories: <cite id="f99edf17-6">Fixed-dose combinations attenuate the decline in medication adherence observed when transitioning from monotherapy to combination therapy over long-term follow-up</cite>. In HIV, once-daily single-tablet regimens are associated with improved patient outcomes relative to multi-tablet regimens, including higher adherence and fewer hospitalizations, with similar or better persistence versus some less-drug regimens in treatment-experienced patients. <cite id="9ebd2994-0">Single-tablet regimens have been associated with improved patient outcomes compared to multi-tablet regimens</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-1">single-tablet regimens are associated with higher adherence, decreased hospitalizations, and more achieving undetectable viral load</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-3">STR initiators had fewer hospital admissions than MTR initiators</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-4">persistence to STR and less-drug regimens was similar among treatment-experienced patients</cite>.

Effects on long-term risk (safety and clinical outcomes)
- Oncology: Adding agents to increase efficacy often increases toxicity and management burden that can precipitate discontinuation. <cite id="06987832-0">Combination treatment was associated with increased grade 3/4 adverse events and treatment discontinuations compared to monotherapy</cite>; <cite id="06987832-4">grade 3–4 adverse effects occurred in 48% with combination therapy vs 27% with monotherapy, with fatigue a common toxicity</cite>. In immuno-oncology combinations, <cite id="06987832-1">chemotherapy plus immunotherapy increased all-grade adverse events (RR 1.11, 1.09–1.12)</cite> and <cite id="06987832-2">significantly raised the risk of grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events</cite> versus immunotherapy alone, with clinical narratives echoing that “you get more side effects” when combining. <cite id="06987832-7">Combining two drugs tends to produce more side effects than a single PD-1 inhibitor; ipilimumab contributes more adverse effects</cite>. Some analyses find no significant increase in immune-related adverse events when adding chemotherapy to checkpoint inhibitors overall, but absolute risks and the incidence of all-grade toxicity still rise. <cite id="06987832-5">No significant increase in immune-related adverse events was found when combining with chemotherapy in aggregate, even as overall toxicity patterns shifted</cite>.
- HIV: In general, STRs and MTRs are similarly safe, with adherence and persistence advantages for STRs that can translate into better virologic outcomes; adverse events are drug-class driven rather than inherently caused by being a single vs multiple pills. <cite id="9ebd2994-8">STRs and MTRs are safe and work well, with no inherent superiority in side effects; most regimens suppress virus similarly</cite>. <cite id="9ebd2994-0">STRs are associated with improved outcomes compared to multi-tablet regimens</cite>, and <cite id="9ebd2994-3">STRs have good adherence and fewer hospitalizations</cite>.
- Cardiovascular: In high-bleeding-risk patients, “more potent” dual antiplatelet therapy reduces bleeding-free ischemic events but increases major bleeding without clear benefit in major adverse cardiovascular events versus single antiplatelet therapy in pragmatic long-term management; persistence advantages are regimen-dependent. <cite id="c500fc5b-0">More potent dual antiplatelet therapy may increase bleeding without reducing major adverse cardiovascular events, underscoring risk trade-offs versus single antiplatelet therapy</cite>. Persistence to certain DAPT pairings can be higher than to some single-agent choices in real-world databases. <cite id="c500fc5b-1">DAPT with ASA/clopidogrel showed statistically significant better persistence than ASA/ticagrelor or ASA/prasugrel</cite>. Short-course DAPT in high bleeding risk (HBR) after PCI reduces bleeding with little loss in ischemic protection versus longer DAPT in selected patients, and adherence studies demonstrate measurable adherence burdens vary by regimen and over time. <cite id="c500fc5b-3">Short-course DAPT offers better bleeding safety with little ischemic protection loss in HBR patients</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-4">short-term DAPT after PCI in HBR was associated with reduced major bleeding and similar ischemic outcomes</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-7">adherence to DAPT after MI/PCI is quantifiable via health insurance reimbursement databases</cite>. Mechanistically, nonadherence to antiplatelet regimens is common and materially worsens outcomes in trials like MASTER DAPT, emphasizing the importance of adherence for both monotherapy and combination strategies. <cite id="c500fc5b-5">Nonadherence to study protocol antiplatelet regimens substantially impacts clinical outcomes in MASTER DAPT</cite>.
- General/Primary care combinations: In hypertension/dyslipidemia, single pill combinations can improve adherence and outcomes. <cite id="f99edf17-5">Combining substances in one single pill may increase adherence and lead to better clinical outcomes</cite>. For adult ADHD specifically, LA combination had lower adherence than LA monotherapy in controlled analysis, highlighting disease-specific trade-offs. <cite id="f99edf17-4">Mean PDC was lower for combination vs monotherapy in ADHD</cite>.

How combinations affect adherence: mechanisms and net effect
- Complexity and self-management: Splitting complex combinations into multiple daily tasks increases decision load, labeling, and missed doses; packaging into one pill/one night reduces organization and improves persistence. <cite id="f99edf17-1">Compared with “free equivalent” combinations (taking the same drugs separately), fixed-dose combinations yielded 1.29× higher compliance</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-7">FDCs reduce noncompliance by 24–26% versus free-drug combination</cite>. In oncology, higher AE burden with combinations lowers persistence via dose interruptions/discontinuations despite therapeutic benefit. <cite id="06987832-0">Combined treatment increased grade 3/4 adverse events and discontinuations vs monotherapy</cite>; <cite id="06987832-4">48% vs 27% grade 3–4 adverse events with combination vs monotherapy</cite>.
- Disease- and formulation-dependent exceptions: When combining two long-acting agents in ADHD, adherence worsened; in some HIV populations persistence to STR and “less-drug” regimens converged, implying diminishing additional benefit once baseline adherence is high; nonetheless, STRs generally improve adherence due to simplification. <cite id="f99edf17-4">ADHD: LA combination vs LA monotherapy, adherence was worse with combination</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-4">HIV: persistence to STR and less-drug regimens similar in treatment-experienced patients</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-0">Despite similar persistence in some cohorts, STRs broadly improve adherence and outcomes relative to multi-tablet regimens</cite>.

Long-term risk trade-offs
- Efficacy vs toxicity balance: Combinations often improve disease control (oncology survival, HIV viral suppression, cardiovascular event reduction), but at the cost of higher cumulative adverse event exposure and management burden. <cite id="06987832-0">Combination therapy increases higher-grade adverse events and discontinuation risk vs monotherapy</cite>; <cite id="06987832-1">chemo‑IO adds all-grade toxicity risk</cite>. Clinical selection should therefore prioritize “regimen simplification” (e.g., STR/FDCs) and adverse effect mitigation strategies to preserve long-term benefit.
- Cardiovascular antiplatelet: Adding an antiplatelet for 12 months post-PCI reduces ischemic events but markedly raises bleeding; switching to clopidogrel ± aspirin in HBR reduces bleeding with minimal ischemic loss, illustrating carefully time-limited combinations. <cite id="c500fc5b-2">Short-term DAPT significantly lowers 90-day recurrent ischemic events</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-0">more potent DAPT increases bleeding without reducing major adverse events</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-3">short-course DAPT in HBR reduces bleeding with little ischemic protection loss</cite>.
- HIV adherence and risk: STR simplification improves adherence and reduces hospitalizations; adherence to STR correlates with durable viral suppression, reducing transmission risk long-term. <cite id="9ebd2994-1">STRs are associated with higher adherence and fewer hospitalizations and higher rates of undetectable viral load</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-2">greater adherence retention at 12 months with STRs vs multi-tablets</cite>.

Practical implications and guidance
- Use combinations when indication-driven (e.g., oncology lines, post-PCI DAPT), but mitigate adherence risks by:
  - Prefer once-daily single-tablet or single-pill combinations to reduce pill burden and boost adherence, monitoring toxicities. <cite id="9ebd2994-0">STRs improve outcomes vs MTRs</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-3">single-tablet regimens improve adherence and persistence</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-1">FDCs give about a 29% compliance gain over FEC</cite>.
  - Tailor drug choice for tolerability; if AEs emerge, consider switching within-class or to alternative combinations rather than abandoning treatment. <cite id="06987832-4">Combination therapy carries substantially higher grade 3–4 adverse event rates, informing the need for monitoring and switching</cite>.
  - Limit combination duration when bleeding or complexity dominate risks (e.g., HBR patients: short-course DAPT before clopidogrel monotherapy), and educate patients on early AE management. <cite id="c500fc5b-3">Short-course DAPT reduces bleeding with little ischemic loss in HBR</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-0">more potent DAPT increases bleeding without net cardiovascular benefit</cite>.
- Monitor adherence proactively:
  - Use refill-based or electronic-pill adherence tracking; intervene when nonadherence exceeds thresholds. In antiplatelet therapy, nonadherence materially worsens outcomes. <cite id="c500fc5b-5">Protocol nonadherence to antiplatelet regimens substantially impacts outcomes in MASTER DAPT</cite>.
  - Adjust regimen complexity: if a combination undermines adherence (e.g., ADHD LA combinations), reassess necessity and consider monotherapy or stepwise up-titration before combining. <cite id="f99edf17-4">ADHD: LA combination reduced adherence vs monotherapy</cite>.
- Domain-specific notes:
  - Oncology: Benefit-risk for chemo-IO depends on regimen; anticipate higher TRAE burden. <cite id="06987832-1">RR of all-grade AEs ~1.11 with chemo+IO</cite>; <cite id="06987832-2">higher grade 3–4 TRAE risk with combination chemoimmunotherapy</cite>.
  - HIV: Favor STRs when available; ensure no class-specific toxicity overshadowing adherence benefits. <cite id="9ebd2994-8">STRs and MTRs are similarly safe on average; adherence/persistence advantages with STRs drive outcomes</cite>.
  - CV: Individualize DAPT duration and choice; in HBR, shorter DAPT then clopidogrel monotherapy reduces bleeding without compromising ischemic protection; persistence is best for ASA+clopi and declines for newer P2Y12 inhibitors in some populations. <cite id="c500fc5b-1">DAPT with ASA/clopidogrel shows stronger persistence than ASA with ticagrelor or prasugrel</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-3">short-course DAPT reduces bleeding with similar ischemic outcomes</cite>.

Bottom line
- On adherence: Simplified combinations (FDC/STR) generally improve long-term adherence versus equivalent free-combination regimens, except in specific conditions where added complexity harms adherence (e.g., ADHD LA combinations); meta-analyses show roughly 24–39% relative improvements with simplified combos, with HIV STRs demonstrating higher adherence, persistence, and fewer hospitalizations vs multi-tablets. <cite id="f99edf17-1">FDC improves compliance by 1.29× vs FEC</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-5">STRs increase adherence and persistence vs MTRs</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-2">STRs retain ~25% good adherence at 12 months vs ~12% for MTRs</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-7">FDC reduces noncompliance 24–26% vs free-drug combos</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-4">ADHD LA combinations had lower adherence than LA monotherapy</cite>.
- On long-term risk: Combinations can increase long-term adverse event exposure, treatment discontinuations, and bleeding risks compared with single agents, with the net clinical benefit hinging on indication and regimen simplification. <cite id="06987832-0">Combination therapy raises grade 3/4 adverse events and discontinuations vs monotherapy</cite>; <cite id="06987832-1">all-grade AE risk increases with chemo+IO</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-0">more potent DAPT increases bleeding without reducing major adverse cardiovascular events</cite>. Careful selection of agents, simplified dosing, and timely de-escalation or switching based on adherence and toxicity are key to maximizing benefit and minimizing harm. <cite id="06987832-3">Combination chemoimmunotherapy increases grade ≥3 TRAEs and discontinuations, informing the need for toxicity management</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-1">HIV STRs reduce hospitalizations while improving adherence, supporting simplified long-term combination therapy</cite>.

Key data points (quick reference)
- Compliance: FDC vs FEC ≈ 29% higher compliance; STR vs MTR ≈ higher adherence, persistence, fewer hospitalizations; ADHD exception: combination < monotherapy adherence. <cite id="f99edf17-1">Compliance +29% with FDC vs FEC</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-1">STR vs MTR: higher adherence, fewer hospitalizations, undetectable rates</cite>; <cite id="f99edf17-4">ADHD: combination adherence worse than monotherapy</cite>.
- Toxicity: Chemo-IO combinations increase all-grade AEs (RR ~1.11) and grade ≥3 TRAEs, with 48% vs 27% grade 3–4 AEs (comb vs mono); DAPT increases bleeding vs single antiplatelet. <cite id="06987832-1">RR 1.11 for all-grade AEs with chemo+IO</cite>; <cite id="06987832-4">48% vs 27% grade 3–4 AEs (comb vs mono)</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-0">More potent DAPT increases bleeding without reducing major adverse events</cite>.
- Persistence: In CAD, DAPT with ASA/clopidogrel shows better persistence than ASA+ticagrelor or ASA+prasugrel; in HIV treatment-experienced, STR and less-drug regimens show similar persistence. <cite id="c500fc5b-1">DAPT + ASA/clopi better persistence than ASA/ticagrelor or ASA/prasugrel</cite>; <cite id="9ebd2994-4">Similar persistence between STR and less-drug regimens in treatment-experienced HIV</cite>.

When more is better
- Combinations improve long-term disease-risk control when toxicity is manageable and regimen simplification is achieved. In HIV, STRs provide durable viral suppression with good adherence; in oncology, chemo-IO improves survival but increases AE monitoring needs; in CAD, short- Then switch DAPT lowers bleeding with small ischemic costs in HBR. <cite id="9ebd2994-1">STRs in HIV are associated with higher adherence and undetectable viral load</cite>; <cite id="06987832-0">On the other hand, higher-grade toxicities and discontinuations with combinations must be weighed</cite>; <cite id="c500fc5b-3">Short-course DAPT reduces bleeding with little ischemic loss in HBR</cite>.

Caveats
- Apples-to-apples comparisons are crucial; many studies contrast simplified combo pills (STR/FDC) with complex free-equivalent regimens, confounding complexity effects. <cite id="f99edf17-1">Meta-analysis explicitly compares FDC to FEC, isolating the effect of simplification on compliance</cite>.
- Disease-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (e.g., ADHD stimulant combinations) can invert the adherence expectation, so clinical context matters. <cite id="f99edf17-4">ADHD LA combinations reduced adherence vs LA monotherapy</cite>.

# Summary

Recent studies converge on a causally coherent picture in which reduced vascular reactivity—manifested as endothelial dysfunction, impaired arterial elasticity, and dysregulated neurovascular coupling—acts early and integratively in cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD), driving tissue hypoxia, blood–brain barrier (BBB) breakdown, and cognitive-neurologic decline, while also providing measurable signatures that predict clinical outcomes such as white matter hyperintensities and stroke.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Dysregulation of cerebral blood flow, impaired vascular reactivity, and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier have been demonstrated to occur early in the course of cerebral small vessel disease</cite><cite id="c92224ee-0">Mounting evidence has pinpointed endothelial dysfunction as a central driver in cSVD pathogenesis, which disrupts BBB integrity and impairs cerebral autoregulation</cite><cite id="c92224ee-1">Endothelial dysfunction plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of CSVD, potentially leading to vascular stiffness and impaired microvascular homeostasis</cite><cite id="c92224ee-7">Meta-analytic evidence associates cSVD with impaired cerebrovascular reactivity and elevated arterial stiffness</cite><cite id="c92224ee-8">Across small studies, neurovascular coupling is reduced in patients with increasing severity of cSVD markers</cite>.

# 1) Conceptual linkage and epidemiology

A growing body of human evidence connects vascular reactivity loss with cSVD, spanning imaging, physiology, and pathology. Population-based and clinic-based cohorts report that reductions in cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR) and increases in arterial stiffness co-occur with brain small-vessel damage and cognition impairment, often in early disease stages.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Dysregulation of cerebral blood flow, impaired vascular reactivity, and BBB breakdown are among the earliest detectable changes in cerebral SVD</cite><cite id="c92224ee-7">A systematic review and meta-analyses show an association between cSVD and impaired cerebral vascular reactivity and elevated arterial stiffness</cite>. These associations extend to microvascular coupling: neurovascular coupling—the relationship between neural activity and local blood flow—shows reduced reactivity with increasing cSVD severity across multiple small studies, pointing to synaptic/vascular mismatch at the microcirculation level.<cite id="c92224ee-8">In multiple, small studies, neurovascular coupling was reduced in patients with increasing severity of all markers of cSVD</cite>. Mechanistically, reviews synthesize that endothelial nitric oxide (NO) signaling failure, oxidative stress, endothelin-1/angiotensin II axis activation, and BBB compromise provide a coherent pathophysiological chain from reduced vascular tone reactivity to tissue injury and dysfunction.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction disrupts BBB integrity and impairs cerebral autoregulation in cSVD</cite><cite id="c92224ee-1">Endothelial dysfunction precipitates vascular stiffness and microvascular homeostatic failure in CSVD</cite><cite id="cde1f260-6">Pathological mechanisms of cSVD include hypoperfusion, inflammation, oxidative stress, and BBB disruption stemming from systemic and cerebral vascular factors</cite>.

# 2) Mechanistic advances in small vessel reactivity

At the level of resistance/penetrating arteries and arterioles, recent mechanistic work emphasizes that endothelial NO/cyclic GMP signaling is a central regulator of vasodilation, shear-dependent tone, and BBB permeability; its impairment unleashes vasoconstriction, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cascades that stiffen vessel walls and enlarge pulse wave velocity, reducing reactive hyperemia and neurovascular coupling efficiency.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction has been pinpointed as a central driver, disrupting BBB integrity and impairing cerebral autoregulation</cite><cite id="cde1f260-6">Pathophysiology of cSVD includes hypoperfusion, inflammation, oxidative stress, and BBB disruption, consistent with NO pathway loss and reactive oxygen species excess</cite>. Oxidative stress is frequently implicated as both a proximal trigger (by scavenging NO bioavailability) and a downstream effector that amplifies endothelin-1 and angiotensin-II signaling, promoting vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling—hallmarks of reduced reactivity in small vessels.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Oxidative stress and BBB disruption contribute to early vascular reactivity defects in cSVD</cite><cite id="c92224ee-1">Endothelial failure can lead to vascular stiffness, implicating angiotensin II and endothelin-1 signaling in microvascular dysfunction</cite>. BBB leakage itself forms a feedback loop: dysfunctional tight junctions increase perivascular edema and hypoxia, which desensitize endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), further diminishing vasodilatory reserve and promoting leukoaraiosis-related tissue injury.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction disrupts BBB integrity and autoregulation in cSVD</cite><cite id="c92224ee-1">Failure of vascular homeostasis in endothelial dysfunction may lead to vascular stiffness and BBB breakdown</cite>.

# 3) Measurement and modeling of reduced vascular reactivity

Methodological advances have sharpened noninvasive quantification of reactivity. Breath-hold fMRI (bh-fMRI) now provides robust, reproducible measures of CVR amplitude and lag by leveraging transient hypercapnic responses and breath-holds, with ongoing work improving signal quality and reducing negative CVR artifacts in normal aging and disease; multi-echo modeling and data-driven reconstructions harmonize BOLD-hemodynamic metrics across protocols and improve reliability for cSVD comparisons.<cite id="cde1f260-0">Comparisons of breath-hold and CO2-based CVR measures continue to refine cerebrovascular reactivity quantification</cite><cite id="cde1f260-2">A data-driven approach estimates CVR amplitude and lag from breath-hold acquisitions, aiding standardization across scanners and protocols</cite><cite id="cde1f260-3">Breath-hold fMRI reproducibility has been assessed and improved, supporting its use as a clinical reactivity metric</cite><cite id="cde1f260-5">Multi-echo modeling in bh-fMRI improves CVR quality metrics and reduces negative CVR values in normal-appearing brain, enhancing diagnostic fidelity</cite><cite id="cde1f260-1">BOLD signal changes reflect oxygenation and hemodynamic response, and bh-fMRI reconstructions improve reactivity estimation for clinical and research applications</cite>. Parallel work in cerebrovascular physiology and ultrasound cross-validates bh-fMRI with transcranial Doppler and CO2 reactivity, and shows that arterial stenoses induce regional delays or deficits in hemodynamic reactivity—patterns that mirror cSVD-related supply-demand mismatches in deep territories.<cite id="cde1f260-4">Comparative modeling indicates cerebrovascular reactivity from BOLD-fMRI and transcranial Doppler using hypercapnia yields convergent estimates</cite><cite id="cde1f260-8">bh-fMRI can quantify reactivity and reveal vessel stenoses leading to delayed hemodynamic responses</cite>. Together, these tools convert macroscopic signals into microvascular inferences, enabling earlier detection of reduced reactivity within small vessel–rich deep white matter and basal ganglia territories, where classic imaging markers (WML, lacunes) lag functional impairment.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Impaired vascular reactivity occurs early in cSVD and precedes overt imaging lesioning in many cases</cite>.

# 4) Clinical implications and prediction

Clinically, reduced vascular reactivity and arterial stiffness have emerged as robust risk markers for progression from vascular risk to overt cSVD and adverse outcomes. Meta-analytic synthesis indicates that lower CVR and higher pulse wave velocity/arterial stiffness are associated with increased cSVD burden and incident stroke and cognitive decline, aligning with mechanistic vascular aging phenotypes.<cite id="c92224ee-7">Across studies, impaired CVR and elevated arterial stiffness are associated with cerebral SVD, supporting their use as vascular health indicators</cite>. At the bedside, breath-hold fMRI and Doppler-based CVR measurements add quantitative phenotyping that can stratify risk in patients with hypertension, diabetes, or aging, complementing structural MRI markers and neurovascular coupling metrics.<cite id="cde1f260-3">bh-fMRI reproducibility supports clinical use for quantifying reactivity and stratifying vascular risk</cite><cite id="c92224ee-8">Neurovascular coupling reductions track with cSVD severity, suggesting utility for risk stratification</cite>. Mechanistically grounded imaging thus helps parse patients likely to benefit from upstream vascular modulation (blood pressure optimization, lipid-lowering, anti-inflammatory, and endothelial-protective strategies), with reactivity change serving as a biological endpoint to confirm target engagement.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction’s centrality in cSVD pathogenesis motivates therapies that restore endothelial signaling and BBB integrity</cite><cite id="c92224ee-1">Targeting endothelial failure to reduce vascular stiffness and BBB breakdown is a plausible therapeutic lever</cite>.

# 5) Interventions targeting the reactivity–sclerosis axis

Therapeutic studies point to two complementary strategies: (a) attenuate vascular remodeling and stiffness via blood pressure control and endothelial protection, and (b) enhance endothelial NO bioavailability or oppose vasoconstrictor signaling. Angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade improves cerebral circulation independent of perfusion pressure in small vessels, consistent with an effect on vascular tone and stiffness, and supports the vascular-hypertension linkage.<cite id="c92224ee-6">A protective effect of an angiotensin II type 1 receptor blocker on cerebral circulation was observed independent of blood pressure</cite>. At the systems-pharmacology level, lipid-lowering, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory approaches that improve endothelial NO signaling and oxidative stress profiles have been proposed as rational, disease-modifying strategies in cSVD; translational markers of reactivity (CVR by bh-fMRI/TCD and, prospectively, retinal vessel calibers/reactivity) show promise as digital phenotypes to monitor response and risk attenuation.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction as central driver supports endothelial-protective interventions (e.g., lipid-lowering, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory) to restore tone and barrier function</cite><cite id="cde1f260-8">bh-fMRI can track reactivity changes to stenosis-induced hemodynamic delays, providing endpoints for evaluating vascular-interventions</cite><cite id="cde1f260-6">Pathway-level mechanistic concepts (hypoperfusion, inflammation, oxidative stress) inform target selection and monitoring</cite>. While large randomized trials directly linking short-term BP reduction to regression of cSVD lesions remain limited, convergent physiology shows that vascular reactivity improvements parallel microvascular protection, strengthening the case for personalized hemodynamic management guided by reactivity imaging.<cite id="c92224ee-8">Neurovascular coupling deficits worsen with cSVD severity</cite><cite id="c92224ee-7">Impaired CVR elevates risk and is a plausible mediator between vascular risk factors and cSVD</cite>.

# 6) Translational markers and cross-organ validation

Reduced vascular reactivity is not confined to the brain: retinal microvasculature calibers and Doppler velocity–dependent reactivity correlate with systemic endothelial function and predict cerebrovascular outcomes, offering a noninvasive window onto small-vessel health. These eye–brain microvascular parallels validate the use of retinal function as a surrogate endpoint in cSVD risk profiling, especially in settings where fMRI/TCD access is limited.<cite id="cde1f260-4">Cross-method CVR comparisons show consistency across modalities, supporting scalable measurement</cite><cite id="c92224ee-3">Systemic and cerebral microvascular dysregulation—hypoperfusion, oxidative stress, BBB disruption—link vascular reactivity loss across organs</cite><cite id="c92224ee-6">Population-based observations implicate systemic vascular pathways (hypertension, hyperglycaemia, smoking) in cSVD with shared microvascular injury mechanisms</cite>. This cross-organ coherence strengthens translational frameworks: digital retinal imaging plus bh-fMRI/TCD reactivity could provide a tiered, scalable panel to detect early endothelial dysfunction, monitor progression, and guide therapy selection in at-risk individuals.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Early vascular reactivity defects and oxidative stress/BBB disruption are detectable and generalize across vascular beds</cite><cite id="cde1f260-3">bh-fMRI reproducibility supports its use as a scalable reactivity endpoint layered with retinal metrics</cite>.

# 7) Remaining uncertainties and future directions

Despite converging evidence, key gaps remain. First, causal mediation analyses that directly quantify how much reduced reactivity contributes to specific cSVD lesion types (lacunar infarcts vs deep WML vs cerebral microbleeds) are still limited; multi-omics integration with reactivity imaging could resolve pathway-specific contributions of NO loss, oxidative stress, and endothelin/angiotensin signaling.<cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction integrates signaling and barrier failure, suggesting multifactorial mediation in cSVD progression</cite>. Second, intervention trials that change reactivity endpoints (bh-fMRI/TCD CVR amplitude/lag) and demonstrate histologic or clinical reversal of cSVD are needed to confirm reversibility versus mere slowing of progression.<cite id="cde1f260-3">bh-fMRI can sensitively detect reactivity changes, making it a plausible endpoint in intervention studies</cite>. Finally, harmonized protocols for bh-fMRI across centers, and cross-calibration with Doppler and retinal metrics, will improve clinical translation and shared decision-making in high-risk patients.<cite id="cde1f260-2">Data-driven CVR estimation and protocol harmonization enhance reproducibility across sites</cite><cite id="cde1f260-5">Multi-echo modeling improves bh-fMRI CVR quality metrics and reduces artifacts</cite>.

# Take-home message

In sum, recent studies deepen and operationalize the relationship between reduced vascular reactivity and small vessel disease by linking endothelial NO signaling failure and oxidative stress–driven remodeling to early, functional hemodynamic deficits that precede structural lesions, quantifying these deficits with robust, reproducible CVR methods, and testing upstream therapies that target the reactivity–stiffness–BBB axis; this bridge from mechanism to bedside is strengthening risk stratification and personalized management for patients with cSVD and its vascular risk factors.<cite id="c92224ee-3">Impaired vascular reactivity occurs early and is implicated across cSVD pathophysiology</cite><cite id="c92224ee-7">Meta-analytic association of impaired CVR and arterial stiffness with cSVD supports mechanistic causality</cite><cite id="cde1f260-3">bh-fMRI reproducibility and cross-method validation provide clinical-grade reactivity metrics</cite><cite id="c92224ee-0">Endothelial dysfunction’s central role motivates targeted, endothelial-protective strategies that restore tone and barrier integrity</cite>.

Summary
Medication–outcome associations differ because drug mechanisms, patient populations, dosing and duration, comorbidities, and study designs vary, and because observational designs are susceptible to biases like confounding by indication, immortal time bias, and selection/duration biases. <cite id="ce491a51-6">Observational studies used for drug–outcome inference are susceptible to confounding by indication (disease severity and confounders drive treatment choice), ascertainment biases in exposure, and measurement error, which can distort effect estimates</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-2">Immortal time bias arises when exposure is defined in a way that confers a survival advantage (e.g., time on statins is “immortal” relative to a failure event), producing spurious benefit unless exposure windows are defined rigorously</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-5">Meta-analyses including observational studies often encounter increased heterogeneity and design diversity, complicating aggregation</cite>.

Why associations differ across medications
Medications differ biologically (on-target mechanism and pharmacology), which yields opposite or context-dependent effects across conditions and subgroups. For example, in gastrointestinal bleeding, serotonin reuptake inhibition andcoxib-like NSAID mechanisms point to additive or synergistic ulcer/bleeding risk when combined, whereas careful selection of nonselective NSAIDs can produce different risk profiles. <cite id="baa15f81-0">Across 11 studies, coadministration of SSRIs and NSAIDs produced higher upper GI bleeding than SSRIs alone (36.9% vs base rate), indicating mechanistically plausible synergy</cite> <cite id="baa15f81-4">Adding an SSRI to chronic NSAID users roughly doubles upper GI bleeding risk, with a multiplicative increase when combined</cite> <cite id="baa15f81-3">Concurrent use of NSAIDs or aspirin with SSRIs greatly increases risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding</cite>. In contrast, some SSRIs confer neuroprotection and may lower dementia risk versus methotrexate; drug-level differences also matter (e.g., hydroxychloroquine often shows distinct effects from methotrexate). <cite id="0fbcd7cc-7">Across studies, hydroxychloroquine was associated with a lower risk of dementia compared to methotrexate, and TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab showed distinct comparative patterns</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-4">Meta-analyses including observational designs tend to have increased heterogeneity, underscoring that drug-level and class-level effects can diverge across populations</cite>.

Medication classes can have opposing associations for the same outcome due to competing mechanisms. In diabetes risk, statins have mixed randomized- and observational-territory effects, whereas thiazides and some beta-blockers often increase diabetes risk. <cite id="7fbe7b15-0">An increased risk of incident type 2 diabetes with statins has been comparable to the diabetes risk induced by other drugs such as beta-blockers and thiazides, implying contrasting or additive class effects across exposures</cite> <cite id="7fbe7b15-1">A meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials reported new-onset diabetes risk increased in a statin dose-dependent manner, with the lowest risk under pravastatin 40 mg once daily and higher risk with more potent regimens</cite> <cite id="7fbe7b15-2">Clinical updates note a USFDA warning that statins can increase diabetes risk and worsen glycemic control, based on observational signals of higher HbA1c and incident diabetes</cite>. Outside RCTs, diuretics and some beta-blockers have repeatedly shown increased diabetes risk in observational studies, while statins’ risk depends on potency and baseline risk. <cite id="7fbe7b15-5">Some analyses report diuretics and statins increase diabetes risk, whereas beta-blocker effects may be nonsignificant, highlighting class-specific and drug-specific divergence across methods and cohorts</cite> <cite id="7fbe7b15-8">Older patients on high-potency statins faced a 10–22% increased risk of new-onset diabetes compared with lower-potency regimens, showing dose–response heterogeneity</cite>.

How findings differ across studies within drug classes
Two broad drivers of cross-study differences are methodological and biological. Methodologically, exposure definition (fixed vs time-varying windows), handling of immortal time, treatment allocation (randomized vs real-world confounding by indication), and analytic choices (adjusted vs unadjusted, propensity scores vs instrumental variables) yield divergent effect sizes and directions. <cite id="ce491a51-2">Improperly defined exposure windows can induce immortal time bias, producing misleading null effects when exposure “traps” patients from experiencing outcomes</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-6">Confounding by indication and ascertainment biases in exposure are common in observational drug-effect studies</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-0">Comparative meta-analyses of harms from randomized trials can show drug-class heterogeneity, but nonrandomized results require cautious integration</cite>. Biologically, within a class there can be substantial heterogeneity by drug, dose, and exposure duration; for example, GI bleeding risk varies across NSAIDs (e.g., piroxicam ~OR 9.2; meloxicam ~OR 6.8) and interactions with other drugs (e.g., SSRIs) amplify risk. <cite id="baa15f81-1">NSAID-specific odds ratios for GI bleeding range widely (e.g., piroxicam OR 9.24; meloxicam OR 6.85), showing class heterogeneity by agent</cite> <cite id="baa15f81-0">Concomitant SSRI+NSAID users had markedly higher upper GI bleeding than SSRIs alone, illustrating drug-pair interactions</cite>. In RA therapeutics, outcomes can differ by foundational therapy, sequencing, and bridging treatments; studies comparing hydroxychloroquine vs methotrexate show divergent cardiovascular signals across populations and definitions, while TNF inhibitor effects depend on background MTX and disease phenotype. <cite id="0fbcd7cc-0">In older RA patients, hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate showed similar sudden cardiac arrest/vascular event risks in one cohort, though absolute risks depended on baseline cardiovascular status</cite> <cite id="0fbcd7cc-2">Another comparative analysis reported increased cardiovascular risks with hydroxychloroquine vs methotrexate in some settings, underscoring class–drug contrasts and design sensitivity</cite> <cite id="0fbcd7cc-4">Systematic reviews link biologics (TNFi) to infection risks and suggest heterogeneous cardiac outcomes, highlighting that background therapy and exposure definitions change effect estimates</cite>.

What differs across studies for drug classes: methods, bias, and design
- Exposure definition and immortal time bias: <cite id="ce491a51-2">When exposure windows include “immortal” time, hazard ratios can be attenuated or spurious; carefully designed nested case–cohort or fixed exposure-by-time analyses reduce this heterogeneity</cite>.
- Confounding by indication and selection/duration bias: <cite id="ce491a51-6">In nonrandomized drug-effect studies, treatment choice reflects underlying disease severity and comorbidity; propensity score adjustment and negative control outcomes can mitigate but not eliminate this source of variance</cite>.
- Heterogeneity of effect sizes and directions by agent potency/dose and comorbidity: <cite id="baa15f81-1">NSAIDs differ by several-fold in GI bleeding odds, with agent- and indication-specific use</cite> <cite id="7fbe7b15-1">Statin potency modifies diabetes risk, with dose-dependent differences</cite> <cite id="0fbcd7cc-5">MTX discontinuation associates with elevated CVD/mortality in RA, showing exposure duration matters</cite>.
- Mixing adjusted and unadjusted estimates and randomized vs observational signals: <cite id="ce491a51-5">Meta-analyses including observational and RCT evidence often exhibit larger heterogeneity, and design mix can bias pooled estimates</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-0">When pooling harm meta-analyses, RCT and nonrandomized estimates need careful harmonization due to differing biases</cite>.
- Population differences (age, CVD risk, background therapies): <cite id="0fbcd7cc-2">Older RA patients show distinct hydroxychloroquine vs methotrexate CV risk patterns under real-world indications</cite> <cite id="7fbe7b15-8">Older adults on high-potency statins face larger diabetes risks, highlighting age-dependent effect sizes</cite>.
- Effect-modification and drug–drug interactions: <cite id="baa15f81-0">Concomitant SSRI+NSAID therapy amplifies GI bleeding risk via combined mechanisms</cite> <cite id="0fbcd7cc-4">Background therapies (e.g., MTX) influence biologic–outcome associations, altering event rates and hazard ratios</cite>.

How uncertainty is assessed and reconciled across studies
Researchers use sensitivity analyses, negative controls, and explicit bias diagnostics to characterize cross-study differences, and meta-epidemiologic methods quantify heterogeneity and publication bias. <cite id="ce491a51-5">Meta-analyses including observational studies often show heterogeneity that increases when observational designs are included, motivating exploration of moderator variables and separate class-specific models</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-7">Heterogeneity refers to dispersion of true effects across studies; formal tests (e.g., I2) and random-effects models quantify between-study variability and guide inference</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-1">Observational meta-analyses require careful consideration of design issues (confounding, selection) compared to RCT meta-analyses</cite>. Across medication–outcome pairs, consistency of direction and magnitude across designs and populations is needed to draw conclusions; inconsistent directions often point to bias or strong effect modification. <cite id="ce491a51-0">Comparative overviews of harms meta-analyses show that drug classes differ in risk and that mixing sources changes pooled estimates</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-6">Given susceptibility to confounding and measurement error, discordant estimates across methods should be interpreted cautiously with bias-adjusted sensitivity analyses</cite>.

Practical implications
- For clinicians: choose medications mindful of class-specific and agent-specific risks, and avoid synergistic combinations (e.g., SSRI+NSAID for patients at GI bleeding risk). <cite id="baa15f81-3">Concurrent SSRI+NSAID or SSRI+aspirin greatly increases upper GI bleeding risk</cite>.
- For researchers/health policy: stratify analyses by potency/dose and baseline risk, define exposure windows to avoid immortal time, incorporate negative controls, and pre-register sensitivity analyses; when pooling, separate observational and randomized evidence and examine I2/heterogeneity and funnel-plot asymmetry. <cite id="ce491a51-2">Immortal time bias is avoidable with careful exposure windowing</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-7">I2 and random-effects models quantify heterogeneity across studies</cite> <cite id="ce491a51-5">Design-differentiated synthesis reduces spurious pooling</cite>.

In sum, medications differ in their associations with health outcomes due to mechanistic, dosing, and population heterogeneity, and cross-study differences for drug classes arise from biases, exposure definitions, and design choices. Background: how obesity ties into OSA and why independence analyses matter
- Obesity is a major epidemiologic risk factor for OSA, with higher AHI risk increasing roughly 14% per unit BMI, and most OSA cases occurring in higher BMI strata; yet OSA risk and severity also arise in leaner individuals, so disentangling OSA’s vascular effects from adiposity is central. <cite id="7b464aab-3">Body fat accumulation is an important, independent risk factor for obstructive sleep apnea; the likelihood of a higher apnea–hypopnea index is 14% greater per 1 kg/m2 increase in BMI</cite> <cite id="7b464aab-0">People with obesity have more than 4 times higher odds of having obstructive sleep apnea compared to BMI < 25 kg/m2</cite> <cite id="516d9fce-4">In Korean NHIS analyses, all-cause mortality risk in OSA was adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index</cite>.
- Independence findings are important because weight loss can improve OSA and other cardiometabolic factors; demonstrating residual risk after BMI adjustment or in lean cohorts suggests mechanistic pathways beyond adiposity, such as intermittent hypoxia, microemboli, neuroinflammation, and thrombotic/arrhythmic substrate. <cite id="6a320864-0">The severity of obstructive sleep apnea is an independent risk factor for stroke and related mortality and morbidity</cite>.

Summary
- Brief exercise sessions (10–30 minutes) can acutely raise BP, but repeated weekly aerobic sessions of 20–60 minutes at moderate intensity generally lower resting BP over weeks to months, with effects comparable to longer sessions when weekly volume is matched; very long daily endurance sessions or very low weekly volumes show limited additional benefit if intensity/frequency are held equal. <cite id="8573c1f8-0">Dose–response analyses in hypertension show nonlinear improvements with increasing weekly dose, peaking at about 830 MET-min/week, rather than a continuous linear gain with longer daily duration</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-3">Meta-analytic evidence indicates that the immediate BP-lowering effects of short daily bouts accumulate to values comparable with higher amounts of continuous exercise</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-5">Randomized trials with very short 7.5-minute moderate-intensity walking bouts show meaningful improvements in cardiometabolic risk markers including BP, supporting substitutability of multiple brief sessions for a single longer one</cite>.

What happens to BP during exercise and over hours afterward?
- During steady aerobic exercise, systolic BP rises with intensity in healthy people; guideline thresholds consider >190–200 mmHg systolic during exertion concerning, while normal maxima may exceed 200–250 mmHg yet remain physiologic without ischemia or severe symptoms. <cite id="94e14513-2">Incremental systolic BP rises with exercise are expected; systolic pressures >190 mmHg, especially in those >190/90 mmHg at rest, warrant modification of intensity and careful monitoring</cite> <cite id="94e14513-0">AHA and related guidance advise that systolic BP >190–210 mmHg and diastolic >110–120 mmHg during exercise may signal risk and requires physician evaluation and intensity adjustment</cite> <cite id="94e14513-1">Healthy individuals can reach up to ~250 mmHg systolic during heavy exertion over 10–20 mmHg above resting levels</cite>.
- Short, hard interval work can spike BP more than continuous moderate activity, with larger beats-to-beats variability; longer continuous work raises BP less per minute and stays elevated longer. <cite id="8e2213ea-0">Short to moderate acute bouts robustly lower both ambulatory and clinic BP over the next hours, indicating that the post-exercise period is a window for added BP reduction</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-1">Continuous combined (aerobic+resistance) training may reduce short-term BP variability more than interval-based analogs, reflecting the steadier hemodynamic response of longer-duration sessions</cite>.
