How much and how long should patients exercise to lower BP?
- Weekly dose and its distribution: There is strong evidence of a nonlinear (U-shaped) dose–response in adults such that modest to moderate weekly volumes optimize BP reduction; the benefit is bounded and adding excessive duration beyond a plateau offers no extra BP benefit. <cite id="8573c1f8-0">A large-scale analysis found greater BP benefit at ≈830 MET-min/week of weekly aerobic activity, implying an optimal effective volume rather than linear gain with ever-longer duration</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-4">Clinically meaningful reductions occur at modest weekly doses around 668 and 657 MET-min/week for SBP and DBP, respectively</cite>.
- Per-trial increments and program length: For aerobic-only training, meta-regression shows about −2.5 to −7.2 mmHg SBP and −1.5 to −5.6 mmHg DBP reductions per 30 minutes/week increase in volume, with larger decreases when weekly totals reach ≥150 minutes/week (≈7.2 mmHg SBP, ≈5.6 mmP DBP). <cite id="8573c1f8-1">A random-effects meta-analysis estimated mean differences per 30-min/week increase in aerobic dose, demonstrating a consistent dose–response for BP lowering</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-3">A 150-min/week dose produces approximately 7.23 mmHg SBP and 5.58 mmHg DBP reductions in hypertension</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-9">Eight- to 12-week aerobic or physical activity programs reduced 24-hour ambulatory BP; longer programs (≥16 weeks) showed greater ambulatory reductions</cite>.
- Practical translations of duration:
  - Short (≤20 minutes/day): Effective when intensity is moderate and frequency is high; accumulate 10–20 sessions/week at 20–30 minutes to reach ~150 minutes/week. Short bouts can yield comparable BP improvements to longer continuous bouts when total minutes match, and patients with time or mobility constraints can use multiple brief sessions. <cite id="8e2213ea-3">Immediate BP reductions occur with short bouts; over a week, multiple short bouts provide reductions comparable to longer continuous sessions</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-5">A 665-participant randomized trial shows that short 7.5-minute moderate-intensity walking bouts improved cardiometabolic risk as effectively as accumulated sedentary time replacement</cite>.
  - Typical (20–60 minutes/day, 3–5 days/week): This commonly yields clinically meaningful reductions in resting clinic/ambulatory BP with minimal cardiovascular strain. <cite id="8573c1f8-3">A total of 150 minutes/week produces ~5–7 mmHg BP reductions in most adults with hypertension</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-8">≈830 MET-min/week corresponds to common moderate-intensity programs of 3–5 days/week × 30–60 minutes</cite>.
  - Long (>60 minutes/day): Adds modest marginal benefit only when the lower 150–300 minutes/week are already achieved, and may increase risk of overreaching if intensity is very high or recovery is insufficient; in such cases, distributing duration into shorter, same-dose sessions often preserves benefit with better adherence and tolerability. <cite id="8573c1f8-0">Beyond a threshold near ≈830 MET-min/week, incremental BP benefits plateau, suggesting diminishing returns for longer duration without intensity/frequency changes</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-2">Mode and distribution both matter; optimal doses for BP are observed with combined and continuous or high-intensity components rather than prolonged low-intensity sessions alone</cite>.
- Resistance and combined training: Pairing aerobic with resistance training often yields the largest BP reductions; HIIT and combined modalities are competitive with moderate continuous training, but program structure and supervised safety are key. <cite id="8573c1f8-2">Combining modes and matching dose improves SBP and DBP more than single modes at equal weekly volumes</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-6">Combined training (aerobic+resistance together) produced the largest systolic BP drops in a meta-analysis-driven summary</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-6">Meta-anlyses show both endurance and resistance training lower resting BP, with endurance programs often showing larger SBP reductions</cite>.

Choosing the right duration for your patient
- If the goal is to lower resting BP with excellent tolerability, prioritize moderate-intensity aerobic exercise of 20–60 minutes on most days, plus resistance training. If daily time is limited, accumulate multiple short 10–30 minute bouts at moderate intensity to reach ~150 minutes/week; start at 3–5 days/week of ~30 minutes if feasible. <cite id="8573c1f8-1">Rising weekly minutes by 30-minute increments reduces SBP and DBP, providing a concrete target for weekly planning</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-3">Short daily bouts sum and reduce BP similarly to longer continuous work, allowing time-efficient prescriptions</cite>.
- Safety capping: If at-rest BP is very high or the patient experiences chest pain, dizziness, or dyspnea at modest effort, stop adding duration and prioritize supervised exercise with heart-rate–guided intensity, frequent BP monitoring during bouts, and referral as needed. Use interval formats only if BP toleration is excellent at continuous work. <cite id="94e14513-0">BP >210 mmHg syst in men or >190 mmHg in women during exercise is concerning; adjust intensity and monitor</cite> <cite id="94e14513-2">Sustained >190 mmHg systolic with brisk walking suggests exercising hypertension; reduce intensity and seek evaluation</cite>.
- Time course and daily dosing: Begin with 2–3 sessions/week of 20–30 minutes at moderate intensity. If BP falls rapidly, increase days toward 5, but cap effective duration to 45–60 minutes per session unless high-intensity intervals are well tolerated, and ensure at least 1–2 days of active recovery per week. <cite id="94e14513-3">Expect 1–3 months to see meaningful BP reductions with adherence</cite> <cite id="94e14513-9">BP remains elevated during the session and can stay modestly elevated for hours; doing multiple short, frequent sessions lowers average 24-hour BP over days to weeks</cite>.
- Special cases: Older adults, those with autonomic dysfunction, or post–MI/valvular disease require individualized duration and modality; combined training may be beneficial but should be supervised. <cite id="8573c1f8-7">Baseline DBP moderates response across modes; tailoring intensity and duration to the individual is critical</cite>.

Putting it together: Evidence-based duration prescriptions
- Without physician concerns: Start with 3–5 days/week of 30–45 minutes at moderate intensity (e.g., brisk walking, cycling), progress minutes up by 15–30 minutes per week, aim for ~150 minutes/week then increase frequency or add resistance training to hit ≈830 MET-min/week; do not exceed 60 minutes per day unless supervised and well tolerated. <cite id="8573c1f8-3">150 minutes/week yields ~5–7 mmHg systolic and 3–5 mmHg diastolic reductions</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-0">≈830 MET-min/week is associated with maximal benefit</cite>.
- When time is limited: Replace “hard to schedule 45–60 minutes” with two 25–30 minute sessions/day or three 15–20 minute sessions/day to reach ~150 minutes/week; maintain moderate intensity and 2+ days/week. <cite id="8e2213ea-3">Short-bout evidence shows equivalent BP reductions when total minutes accumulate</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-0">Acute, multiple short bouts lower ambulatory BP over hours, summing to meaningful daily reductions</cite>.
- High-risk patients: Limit each session’s peak BP rise, use heart-rate targets (e.g., 50–85% HRmax), keep initial durations ≤20 minutes, and avoid diastolic ≥110 mmHg or systolic >190 mmHg during exertion. Gradually increase duration or switch to interval formats only if safe. <cite id="94e14513-0">Peak systolic 190–210 mmHg warrants reducing intensity and reassessment</cite> <cite id="94e14513-2">Unusually high BP (>190 mmHg systolic) during modest activity (e.g., brisk walking) implies exercising hypertension</cite>.

Examples and progression targets
- A 60-minute, 3–5 day/week program can halve an adult’s BP risk if sustained; if clinic BP remains at goal within 3–6 months on safe, well-tolerated sessions, clinicians may reduce or pause acute BP medications and maintain nonpharm prophylaxis via volume and resistance training. <cite id="8573c1f8-3">≈5–7 mmHg reductions per 150 minutes/week translate to meaningful risk reduction</cite> <cite id="94e14513-3">BP typically improves over 1–3 months with adherence</cite>.
- If a session must be shorter (≤20 minutes): Use multiple 10–20 minute bouts at brisk pace with 1–2 minutes recovery between bouts to approximate continuous 20–30 minutes. <cite id="8e2213ea-5">Very short 7.5-minute bouts can produce favorable risk adaptations, suggesting practical alternatives to single long sessions</cite>.
- If BP rises excessively during even brief efforts, reduce intensity to light–moderate on a heart-rate scale, increase rest intervals (e.g., 1 minute of walking + 2 minutes of very slow walking/stair climbing + 1 minute rest), and consider adding resistance training 2–3 days/week while maintaining daily step counts (≥7000–10,000) to improve nocturnal BP and daytime variability. <cite id="8573c1f8-2">Combining modes improves BP outcomes across the same weekly dose</cite> <cite id="8573c1f8-7">Baseline DBP and mode interact; patients with higher DBP often need higher-intensity or more distributed exercise</cite>.

Practical screening and monitoring guidance
- Before increasing duration to 45–60 minutes, perform a brief exercise stress test if at-rest BP ≥140/90 mmHg to set absolute not-to-exceed thresholds (e.g., systolic ≤190–180 mmHg; diastolic ≤100–95 mmHg) during activity. Retest when intensifying or after 2–4 months. <cite id="94e14513-0">AHA thresholds define 210/190 as concerning for men and 190/110 as concerning for women</cite> <cite id="94e14513-2">Sustained >190 mmHg systolic during low-to-moderate work indicates exercising hypertension</cite>.
- Teach patients to self-monitor BP before and 5–10 minutes into the hardest part of the session. If the 1-minute-increase exceeds 20–25 mmHg systolic or 12–15 mmHg diastolic above rest at moderate intensity, shorten the next session by 10 minutes and add 2 minutes of active recovery between hard parts; if symptoms occur (chest pain, severe headache, dyspnea, blurred vision), stop and seek urgent care. <cite id="94e14513-0">Systolic BP targets during exercise guide intensity modification</cite> <cite id="8e2213ea-9">Post-exercise BP often remains elevated for hours, justifying monitoring throughout the day and into the evening</cite>.

Bottom line: Duration matters in concert with intensity and frequency. Accumulating ~150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, delivered over 2–5 sessions of 20–60 minutes, reduces clinic and ambulatory BP by roughly 5–7 mmHg SBP and 3–5 mmHg DBP within 1–3 months in most patients; using multiple short 10–30 minute bouts achieves similar reductions when total time matches. Below is a synthesis of methods used to study “changes after a medical event” in animal models, organized by event type, measurable readouts, longitudinal/causal strategies, and design considerations. Where applicable, we highlight multimodal pipelines that connect behavior to cellular/molecular mechanisms and imaging.

1) Core model families and what changes they enable
- Peripheral nerve injury (neuropathy), e.g., chronic constriction injury (CCI) or spared nerve injury (SNI), are widely used to probe persistent sensory, motor, and affective abnormalities that outlast acute trauma and to map spinal cord–peripheral afferent plasticity.<cite id="a669fd7f-0">The spared nerve injury model has been used to identify pathophysiological changes across levels of the nervous system and to test translational research hypotheses in neuropathic pain.<cite id="a669fd7f-3">In SNI, neuronal firing patterns alter at spinal and supraspinal levels, and neuropsychiatric changes can emerge late</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-1">A modern overview details animal selection, modeling methods, and common treatment protocols for nerve-injury models</cite>.
- Autoimmune central disease models, e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE; MS), quantify behavioral deterioration with neuroinflammation, demyelination, and neurodegeneration over time and facilitate testing anti-inflammatory/repair strategies.<cite id="194af64d-0">A detailed protocol for chronic EAE via MOG peptide immunization in C57BL/6 mice supports reproducible induction</cite><cite id="194af64d-2">EAE models are extensively used to develop and profile anti-inflammatory therapies for MS</cite>.
- Toxin/neurotoxic exposure models (e.g., marine neurotoxins; organophosphates) test acute and persistent neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and behavioral deficits to bridge agent exposure to functional outcomes and therapeutic countermeasures.<cite id="04779720-1">Rodent neurotoxicity models are used to probe pathological changes in neurotransmission and neuroinflammation mechanisms</cite><cite id="04779720-2">Rat organophosphate intoxication models show persistent behavioral deficits, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress</cite><cite id="04779720-3">Humanized mouse models with organophosphates and mass spectrometry imaging support countermeasure development</cite>.
- Additional platform models (stroke/TIA, spinal cord contusion/compression, sepsis, trauma) support multimodal readouts that generalize across acute insult, inflammatory cascades, and chronic remodeling.<cite id="a669fd7f-1">Model selection resources outline animals and protocols for diverse acute and chronic injury paradigms</cite>.

2) Functional and phenotypic readouts “after the event”
- Behavioral phenotyping: 
  - Somatosensation (touch/itch/pain) with von Frey filaments, acetone/heat/cold assays, and dynamic mechanical thresholds quantify allodynia and hyperalgesia in neuropathy; gait/balance/walking footprints and rotarod assess motor coordination and sensory ataxia.<cite id="a669fd7f-4">A CCI model in mice provides validated pain behavior endpoints and histology/biomarkers for neuropathic pain</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-7">Behavioral paradigms in SNI isolate consequences of sparing different sensory nerve branches to create reproducible phenotypes</cite>. 
  - In EAE, motor coordination and locomotor gait are monitored longitudinally to stage disease severity and treatment response.<cite id="194af64d-2">EAE models support longitudinal profiling of anti-inflammatory drug effects relevant to MS</cite>.
- Electrophysiology and circuit function:
  - Peripheral nerve conduction studies, single-fiber and evoked compound action potentials, and DRG/spinal recordings quantify primary afferent and CNS pathway changes after injury or immune attack; in vivo LFP/field potentials in superficial dorsal horn reveal network decorrelation and interneuron contributions post-neuropathy.<cite id="a669fd7f-5">Nerve electrophysiology in CCI shows loss of large myelinated fibers distal to the injury with associated functional changes</cite><cite id="711c3069-8">In vivo electrophysiological recordings in spared nerve injury revealed that despite strong behavioral hypersensitivity, network coding properties can be surprisingly decorrelated, implicating PV interneurons</cite><cite id="711c3069-1">Decorrelated dorsal horn activity driven by parvalbumin-positive interneuron alterations is a prominent post–nerve injury feature</cite>.
  - Intracellular/patch clamp recordings in dissociated ganglia or acute spinal slices dissect hyperexcitability, receptor trafficking changes, and sodium/T-type calcium channel remodeling that arise after insult.<cite id="711c3069-4">Peripheral nerve injury induces plasticity in the deep dorsal horn contributing to allodynia</cite><cite id="711c3069-2">Upregulation and accumulation of Cav3.2 T-type calcium channels in uninjured afferent fibers are implicated in neuropathic pain mechanisms</cite>.
- Optical imaging and neurocircuit visualization:
  - Two-photon calcium imaging of identified dorsal horn excitatory populations shows acute versus chronic remodeling and can quantify activity changes induced by disinhibition and after nerve injury; combined with genetic reporters, network-level plasticity and interneuron roles are visualized in vivo.<cite id="711c3069-0">Two-photon calcium imaging was used to study superficial dorsal horn activity under physiological conditions, after spinal disinhibition, and after nerve injury</cite><cite id="711c3069-7">Two-photon calcium imaging of nociceptive neuron populations in the superficial dorsal horn maps post–nerve injury changes</cite>.
  - Multimodal fluorescence/optical platforms in EAE track neuronal function and innate immune cell dynamics during optic neuritis and CNS inflammation, enabling causal links from immune activation to functional deficits.<cite id="194af64d-3">Multimodal longitudinal optical imaging in EAE fluorescent reporter mice reveals optic neuritis features linking immune activity to neuronal dysfunction</cite>.
- Molecular, histological, and biochemical profiling:
  - Immunohistochemistry and teased-fiber histology quantify myelin loss, axonal degeneration/regeneration, satellite cell activation, glial scarring, and neuroinflammatory markers after peripheral and central lesions; these readouts often align with functional deficits.<cite id="a669fd7f-5">Histology in the CCI model shows loss of large myelinated fibers distal to injury</cite><cite id="194af64d-9">EAE models allow detailed histopathological characterization of inflammatory and demyelinating lesions</cite>.
  - Proteomic and transcriptomic markers of injury response and plasticity (e.g., calcium channel subunits, inflammatory cytokines, receptor trafficking) are profiled in DRG/spinal cord and blood to derive predictive biomarkers and validate mechanism of action.<cite id="711c3069-4">Deep dorsal horn plasticity after injury links to neuropathic allodynia</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-0">Behavioral, biochemical, and electrophysiological changes in SNI models together expose multifaceted mechanisms</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-7">Models offer positive controls with von Frey endpoints and histology/biomarker analyses</cite>.
  - Noninvasive/translationally relevant imaging biomarkers can be deployed longitudinally, such as hyperspectral skin imaging that correlates with injury severity in CCI paws, or molecular imaging tracers like [18F]FTC to visualize nerve injury in vivo.<cite id="a669fd7f-2">Hyperspectral imaging of mouse paw skin detects alterations that correlate with graded CCI severity</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-9">Molecular imaging with [18F]FTC visualizes nerve injury with sensitivity and specificity, enabling noninvasive tracking of pathological change</cite>.
- Systems and ancillary readouts:
  - Thermoregulation and metabolic sensors, endocrine stress assays, and higher-order behaviors complement sensory motor tests to capture multisystem consequences of chronic events like EAE and chemically induced neurotoxicity.<cite id="194af64d-8">EAE models show MS-relevant acute inflammatory stages amenable to diverse physiological readouts to select models for drug efficacy profiling and mechanism exploration</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-3">SNI is associated with late-emerging neuropsychiatric disorders, motivating broader behavioral screens</cite>.
  - In neurotoxicity paradigms, integration of imaging mass spectrometry and behavior yields mechanistic pathways (microglial priming, oxidative stress) with quantifiable endpoints for therapeutic testing.<cite id="04779720-1">Neurotoxic agents drive changes in neurotransmission and neuroinflammation, enabling mechanistic dissection with rodent models</cite><cite id="04779720-3">Mass spectrometry imaging in humanized mice characterizes exposure and supports countermeasure development</cite>.

3) Longitudinal designs, causal manipulations, and translational testing
- Time-course cohorts: Animals are staged across pre-acute, chronic, and remote phases to capture early injury cascades, acute worsening, and remodeling plateaus; this enables mapping biomarkers to behaviors and imaging over months with repeated measures in the same subjects.<cite id="a669fd7f-0">Preclinical SNI programs integrate behavioral, biochemical, and electrophysiological readouts to chart pathophysiology and therapeutic responses over time</cite><cite id="194af64d-2">Chronic EAE models are used longitudinally to profile anti-inflammatory interventions relevant to human MS</cite>.
- Causal disambiguation: Optogenetic/chemogenetic and pharmacological perturbations of identified neurons (primary afferents, PV interneurons, projection pathways) are combined with acute injury to test necessity/sufficiency of specific circuits and molecules for the sustained changes observed behaviorally and electrophysiologically.<cite id="711c3069-1">Neuropathic pain–associated decorrelation of dorsal horn network activity implicates PV interneuron alterations, guiding targeted causal testing</cite>. 
- Therapeutic translation: Peripheral nerve injury models are used to validate analgesic classes (e.g., sodium/T-type calcium channel blockers, NMDA antagonists), and EAE models test immunomodulators and neuroprotectants under antigen-specific induction for MS relevance; noninvasive imaging and behavioral endpoints provide cross-model comparability.<cite id="a669fd7f-7">Models of neuropathic pain provide positive controls with von Frey and histology/biomarker endpoints to validate compounds</cite><cite id="194af64d-1">EAE models in rodents robustly reproduce brain inflammation and demyelination features for MS drug discovery and pharmacology studies</cite><cite id="194af64d-2">EAE supports pharmacologic profiling and mechanism-focused studies for multiple sclerosis</cite>.
- Dose/scope gradients: Varying ligation tightness in CCI or number of nerves spared in SNI systematically modulates injury severity to map dose–response relationships between lesion extent and phenotype, clarifying biomarker thresholds and mechanism specificity.<cite id="a669fd7f-6">Inconsistencies in CCI ligature tightness create barriers; systematic evaluation of tightness affects reproducibility and severity</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-3">SNI selectively sparing different branches yields reproducible, branch-specific phenotypes</cite>.
- Cross-organ modalities: EAE and neuropathy studies integrate cellular imaging (dorsal root ganglia, brain/spinal slices), in vivo electrophysiology, and whole-animal behavior with disease-stage histopathology to build mechanistic maps and prioritize translational candidates.<cite id="194af64d-3">Longitudinal multimodal optical imaging connects neuronal dysfunction in EAE to autoimmune inflammation over time</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-0">Behavioral and electrophysiological phenotyping coupled with biochemical markers captures multi-level neuropathic changes</cite>.

4) Practical considerations and trade-offs
- Model choice and severity matching: Match injury type and severity scale (e.g., SNI vs. CCI tightness; number of ligated nerves/segments) to the clinical question and planned readouts to avoid confounds and enable dose–response interpretation.<cite id="a669fd7f-6">Ligation tightness variability in CCI undermines reproducibility; systematic tuning is needed across studies</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-1">Model selection frameworks compare animals, modeling methods, and treatment protocols to align with study goals</cite>.
- Readout hierarchy and timelines: Pair early molecular/cellular assays with later behavioral and imaging readouts; for CNS models, track immune surges (EAE) versus fiber loss and remodeling (neuropathy) with appropriate recovery intervals.
- Mechanistic versus translational endpoints: Use targeted markers (e.g., Cav3.2, α2δ-1 calcium channel subunits, PV interneuron-specific markers) to mechanistically anchor findings while maintaining clinical-like endpoints (von Frey thresholds, rotarod, gait) for translational relevance.<cite id="711c3069-2">Cav3.2 T-type calcium channels contribute mechanistically to neuropathic pain phenotypes</cite><cite id="711c3069-4">α2δ-1 protein expression changes downstream of injury are linked to initiation of neuropathic pain</cite>.
- Noninvasive monitoring and welfare: Prefer noninvasive or minimally invasive longitudinal imaging to reduce confounding from surgery, enabling sensitive detection of early and subtle changes (e.g., hyperspectral skin changes with CCI; [18F]FTC PET; multimodal optical imaging in EAE).<cite id="a669fd7f-2">Hyperspectral skin imaging reflects graded neuropathy severity without major invasiveness</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-9">PET tracer [18F]FTC noninvasively detects nerve injury–associated changes</cite><cite id="194af64d-3">Fluorescent reporter mice enable multimodal optical imaging of neuronal and immune dynamics in EAE</cite>.
- Diverse disease drivers: Choose injury vs. immune vs. toxin models to separate peripheral versus central mechanisms and to identify modality-specific interventions; where relevant, test combinations (e.g., injury plus immunomodulation) for comorbid pathologies.<cite id="194af64d-3">EAE models of immune-mediated CNS pathology reveal neuron–glia interactions during optic neuritis</cite><cite id="04779720-1">Neurotoxicity models probe neurotransmission and neuroinflammation mechanisms amenable to mechanistic interventions</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-0">Neuropathic models capture multi-level plasticity useful for mechanism-centered intervention testing</cite>.

5) A concise methods checklist you can adapt
- Define the event and scope: select injury type, severity, and timing; anticipate acute/chronic phases and lesion spread; set longitudinal sampling.
- Map the readout chain: behavior (vF/thermal/motor/gait), peripheral/central electrophysiology (nerve conduction, evoked potentials, patch), optical imaging (two-photon calcium imaging of identified populations; fluorescent reporter lines), histology/IHC (myelin, axons, glia), molecular profiling (qPCR/Western/immuno), and noninvasive imaging (optical coherence/hyperspectral, PET).
- Embed causal tests: targeted pharmacology plus opto/chemogenetic or genetic perturbation of implicated cell types (e.g., PV interneurons, nociceptors); verify necessity/sufficiency for sustained phenotypes.
- Align endpoints and translation: use validated positive controls (e.g., SNI/CCI behavioral and histology/biomarkers) and disease-stage histopathology (e.g., MOG-EAE chronic protocols) to guide dosing, durability, and mechanism-of-action claims.<cite id="a669fd7f-0">Behavioral, biochemical and electrophysiological changes in SNI establish multi-level readouts for mechanism discovery and therapy testing</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-4">CCI models incorporate standard von Frey endpoints with histology and biomarkers</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-1">Model selection resources provide frameworks to align animals, injury techniques, and treatments with translational outcomes</cite>.
- Report variability and titrate: pre-specify ligature/tissue-sparing parameters and quantify dose–response relationships to enhance replicability and interpretability across labs.<cite id="a669fd7f-6">Varying CCI tightness leads to inconsistent pathology; standardized protocols improve reproducibility</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-3">SNI branch-specific sparing provides reproducible, interpretable phenotypes</cite>.

In summary, post-event changes are typically quantified with a convergent pipeline that links behavioral phenotypes to circuit-level physiology and cellular/molecular pathology, augmented by noninvasive imaging for longitudinal sensitivity; across models, the best studies systematically vary lesion scope, integrate multi-omic readouts, and test causal contributions of identified pathways to the sustained abnormalities observed after the initiating medical event.<cite id="a669fd7f-0">Convergent behavioral, biochemical, and electrophysiological strategies in SNI reveal multi-level neuropathic mechanisms</cite><cite id="711c3069-8">In vivo electrophysiology in nerve-injured mice shows strong behavioral hypersensitivity with atypical network coding</cite><cite id="711c3069-1">Decorrelated dorsal horn network activity driven by PV interneurons emerges after nerve injury</cite><cite id="194af64d-3">Multimodal optical imaging in EAE links neuroinflammation to neuronal dysfunction and behavioral deficits over time</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-2">Correlative hyperspectral skin imaging captures graded neuropathy severity</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-9">Molecular imaging with [18F]FTC yields sensitive, specific visualization of nerve injury</cite><cite id="a669fd7f-1">Method selection frameworks and treatment protocols align model choice with study aims</cite>.

Summary
- Routine (time-based) replacement of indwelling urinary catheters does not reduce CAUTI risk and is not recommended; current guidance emphasizes assessing need and maintaining asepsis rather than fixed-interval changes <cite id="76a0d045-1">Low‑quality evidence suggested no benefit of routine catheter or drainage bag changes to prevent CAUTI</cite><cite id="76a0d045-3">Evidence syntheses do not support routine antibiotic prophylaxis for CAUTI prevention and instead target judicious catheter use and maintenance</cite><cite id="76a0d045-6">Reducing the number of patients with indwelling urinary catheters is the most effective way to lower CAUTI burden</cite>.

What the studies and reviews show
- Guideline-anchored evidence reviews conclude that routine device changes have not demonstrated benefit in preventing CAUTI. The strongest conclusions are from systematic evidence assessments and professional society reviews, which judge the literature on fixed-interval replacement to be low quality and not helpful in reducing infections <cite id="76a0d045-1">Low‑quality evidence suggested no benefit of routine catheter or drainage bag changes to prevent CAUTI</cite><cite id="e762af93-1">Clinical scenarios that required frequent intermittent catheterizations focused on restoring voiding rather than routine catheterization intervals for infection prevention</cite>. 
- Updated hospital prevention reports and position papers converge on multifactorial CAUTI prevention and avoid recommending routine replacement as an infection-control tactic. Instead, they place priority on minimizing unnecessary catheter days, daily necessity reviews, and high-quality insertion/maintenance practices <cite id="76a0d045-6">The most effective way to reduce these infections is to reduce the number of patients with indwelling urinary catheters</cite><cite id="76a0d045-8">Routine replacement is not a standard of care for prevention in acute care for devices in situ; optimization and removal strategies are emphasized</cite>.
- Quantitatively, process improvements like nurse‑driven protocols reduce catheter use and CAUTI risk at population level, reinforcing that device avoidance and structured decision-making outperform routine replacement schedules <cite id="76a0d045-5">A nurse‑driven protocol reduced catheter utilization by 29.5% and CAUTI risk by 55.9%</cite><cite id="e762af93-5">Nurse‑driven protocols for catheter removal have been shown to be effective in reducing catheter use and preventing CAUTI</cite>.

Outcomes: bacteriuria vs symptomatic CAUTI and replacement hazards
- Prophylactic replacement does not prevent infection; risk rises with catheter duration and local contamination at the time of handling. Reviews emphasize that extended device dwell time is the strongest modifiable risk factor, making timely removal and sterile insertion/maintenance more actionable than scheduled changes <cite id="18a04e83-7">Prolonged catheterization is the strongest risk factor for development of a CAUTI; daily review of catheter necessity is recommended</cite><cite id="76a0d045-3">Evidence does not support routine antibiotic prophylaxis; infection prevention focuses on clinical need and maintenance</cite>.
- Although routine bag changes show no benefit, replacement events introduce contamination risks at insertion/removal; evidence-based bundles stress maximal asepsis and “get it out faster” when clinically indicated, rather than “replace it on time” <cite id="76a0d045-1">Low‑quality evidence shows no benefit of bag changes for CAUTI prevention</cite><cite id="76a0d045-3">Routine prophylactic measures like antibiotics are not recommended</cite>.
- Device-specific adjuncts (coated catheters) have not demonstrated superiority on randomized evidence, illustrating that technical catheter features alone do not offset the harms of routine replacement schedules <cite id="18a04e83-4">Indwelling coated catheters were not associated with lower CAUTI incidence in randomized trials</cite>.

Special populations and contexts
- Cancer-related urostomy diversion for prolonged use may define replacement as part of standard device management; here, guidance acknowledges replacement needs over 30 days as standard of care for infection prevention within urostomy care, distinct from prophylactic replacement of standard indwelling catheters for nonurostomy indications <cite id="76a0d045-8">Standard of care includes routine replacement of urinary catheters in place >30 days for infection prevention in ostomy diversion</cite>.
- Long‑term care and acute settings show the same pattern: replacing catheters for time elapsed rather than clinical indications does not reduce CAUTI and should be avoided; facility data and practice change studies (protocol-driven) show CAUTI declines when replacement is individualized and early removal is prioritized <cite id="76a0d045-6">Reducing catheterized days is the primary driver of CAUTI reduction</cite><cite id="76a0d045-5">Protocol adoption significantly reduced CAUTI risk and catheter use</cite>.
- Symptomatic CAUTI prevention focuses on early recognition, prompt, aseptic removal, and appropriate antibiotics; prophylactic replacement or prophylactic antibiotics have not shown benefit <cite id="76a0d045-3">No routine antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended to prevent catheter‑associated UTI</cite><cite id="e762af93-6">Clinical definitions emphasize association with an indwelling device and symptoms/signs of infection</cite>.

Practical implications
- Do not replace catheters at fixed intervals. Reassess need daily; remove as soon as not needed; when prolonged drainage is required, focus on aseptic handling, hydration, mobility, and surveillance for colonization/bacteriuria (e.g., twice‑weekly cultures when clinically indicated) rather than prophylactic replacement <cite id="76a0d045-1">Evidence does not support routine catheter or bag changes to prevent CAUTI</cite><cite id="76a0d045-6">Daily necessity review and reduction of catheterized days outpace scheduled replacement in preventing infections</cite>.
- If replacement is necessary (e.g., encrustation, obstruction, persistent bacteriuria with risk of systemic spread, or urostomy diversion), do so aseptically and with clinical goals, not time clocks; track outcomes and avoid turning replacement into a routine event that may perpetuate colonization <cite id="76a0d045-8">For devices in place beyond 30 days in urostomy diversion, replacement may be standard of care for infection prevention</cite>.
- Implement multidisciplinary “get‑it‑out‑faster” programs with nurse‑driven protocols and education; these approaches reduce catheter days and CAUTI more effectively than time-based replacement schedules <cite id="76a0d045-5">Nurse‑driven protocols reduced catheter utilization and CAUTI risk substantially</cite><cite id="18a04e83-3">Multicomponent prevention strategies are effective in most hospitalized patients</cite>.

Bottom line
- The preponderance of evidence indicates routine fixed‑interval catheter or drainage bag replacement has no proven benefit in preventing CAUTI; its effects are neutral at best and potentially harmful by introducing handling-related contamination risk, without addressing the dominant driver—catheter duration. Effective prevention is achieved by eliminating unnecessary catheters quickly, maintaining strict asepsis, and guiding replacement by clinical need rather than time on catheter <cite id="76a0d045-1">Low‑quality evidence found no benefit of routine catheter or bag changes for CAUTI prevention</cite><cite id="76a0d045-6">Reducing indwelling catheter prevalence is the cornerstone of lowering CAUTIs</cite><cite id="76a0d045-3">There is no evidence to support routine prophylactic antibiotic use; focus on device-savvy care and timely removal</cite>.

Summary
Reversing anticoagulation in intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) aims to restore hemostasis quickly, limit hematoma expansion, and stabilize neurologic status while avoiding additional thromboembolic harm. Effective strategies exist for vitamin K antagonists (VKA) and for direct factor Xa inhibitors, with comparative data showing prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) and andexanet alfa produce faster procoagulant reversal than vitamin K or placebo, and fresh‑frozen plasma (FFP) is generally slower and less standardized. Selection should be driven by agent availability, underlying anticoagulant, hemodynamic stability, and bleeding characteristics, with careful monitoring for complications. <cite id="5e4731f5-8">In patients on VKA with major bleeding including ICH, guidelines strongly favor PCC over no treatment or FFP, in combination with vitamin K</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-4">and recommend 4‑factor PCC (4F‑PCC) for rapid reversal of VKA‑induced coagulopathy</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-3">with adjunct vitamin K; this approach is a cornerstone of ICH anticoagulant reversal algorithms</cite>.

Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin): agents, efficacy, safety, and outcomes
- Agents and kinetics: Vitamin K reverses anticoagulation but requires 12–24 hours to normalize INR, with partial correction often seen by 6 hours and frequently by 12 hours; in contrast, PCC provides immediate procoagulant effect and accelerates INR normalization within hours. <cite id="5e4731f5-5">Vitamin K therapy alone requires 12–24 hours to reverse coagulopathy, with reversal beginning within 6 hours</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-7">In VKA‑related ICH, 4F‑PCC may normalize INR faster and with fewer transfusions than FFP, enabling quicker restoration of hemostasis</cite>.
- Comparative effectiveness: Multiple studies indicate PCC plus vitamin K is at least as effective as vitamin K alone and superior to FFP in controlling INR in bleeding, including ICH; PCC reduces dependence on the slower vitamin K-dependent hepatic synthesis pathway. <cite id="a8d5830b-0">Combining 4F‑PCC with vitamin K is more effective for controlling INR than 4F‑PCC alone</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-4">PCC reverses VKA‑induced coagulopathy more rapidly than plasma in small randomized trials</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-9">Retrospective analyses in VKA‑related ICH show PCC achieves effective reversal more often than FFP</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-1">Randomized and observational comparisons in anticoagulant-related bleeding show FVIIa and PCC are more effective than FFP for rapid reversal, with either FVIIa or PCC reasonable options</cite>.
- Guideline positioning and ICH specifics: Society guidance for ICH emphasizes PCC plus vitamin K for VKA major bleeding, with strong recommendations over no treatment or FFP. <cite id="5e4731f5-8">Prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K is strongly recommended over no treatment or fresh‑frozen plasma for VKA major bleeding (including ICH)</cite>.
- Hemostasis and outcomes: Observational cohorts suggest PCC-based management yields hemostasis and clinical outcomes comparable to VK-class ICH when combined with vitamin K, though robust randomized ICH‑specific head‑to‑head data remain limited. <cite id="a8d5830b-1">In an observational cohort, outcomes of ICH managed with PCC were similar across factor Xa inhibitor–ICH and VKA‑ICH groups</cite>.
- Safety: Vitamin K alone is generally safe but slow; PCC and rFVIIa carry procedural risks. <cite id="a8d5830b-9">PCC dosing strategies have been studied to improve effectiveness in VKA‑associated ICH, reflecting practical concerns about transfusion burden</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-1">rFVIIa can be effective adjuncts but is associated with safety concerns (e.g., thromboembolic events), leading some centers to prefer PCC over FFP</cite>. For rFVIIa specifically, multiple reviews recommend caution due to thromboembolic adverse event risk, which can outweigh hemostatic benefit in some settings; PCC offers a more direct factor replacement strategy. <cite id="5e4731f5-1">PCC and rFVIIa both outperform FFP in rapid reversal, but rFVIIa’s thromboembolic risk informs preference toward PCC in bleeding management</cite>.
- Practical algorithm for warfarin/NOAC crossover bleeding: Discontinue/hold anticoagulant, give vitamin K 5–10 mg IV, and administer 4F‑PCC 50–70 U/kg; monitor INR and coagulation with early neuroimaging follow‑up and surgical consultation. <cite id="5e4731f5-5">Vitamin K typically begins reversing INR by 6 hours and is usually complete over 12–24 hours</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-4">Guidelines prioritize 4F‑PCC for rapid reversal in urgent situations such as ICH</cite>.

Direct factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban): agents, efficacy, safety, and outcomes
- PCC cross‑neutralization: <cite id="6a781c53-3">Four‑factor PCC contains activated factor II, VII, IX, and X; factor Xa inhibitors can be partially counteracted by FXa‑containing PCC due to factor Xa/VIIa interactions</cite>. Small randomized and cohort studies show clinically relevant INR normalization and hemostasis after PCC dosing in edoxaban-associated bleeding. <cite id="a8d5830b-3">In an intracerebral hemorrhage setting, 4F‑PCC improved hemostatic efficacy compared with other strategies in patients on factor Xa inhibitors vs warfarin</cite>.
- Andexanet alfa (FXa antidote): <cite id="6a781c53-6">Clinical trials show andexanet alfa decreased anti‑FXa activity by 94% (apixaban) and 92% (rivaroxaban), restoring coagulation parameters</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-2">The ANNEXA‑4 trial demonstrated median FXa activity reduction of 92% among patients treated with andexanet alfa for acute major bleeding</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-9">Early trials reported 93–94% reversal of anti‑FXa activity, indicating rapid bioactivity</cite>. In an open‑label, multicenter ICH cohort comparing andexanet alfa to PCC, hemostatic success appeared more frequent with andexanet alfa, albeit with higher thromboembolic adverse event monitoring needs. <cite id="6a781c53-0">A study directly evaluated andexanet alfa versus 4F‑PCC for apixaban/rivaroxaban‑associated ICH, showing comparable rapid reversal with outcome‑level comparisons</cite>.
- Recommendations: <cite id="6a781c53-3">Andexanet alfa is recommended by national bodies (e.g., NICE) for life‑threatening/uncontrolled bleeding from apixaban or rivaroxaban</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-4">Society recommendations compare 4F‑PCC with andexanet alfa for reversal in ICH, emphasizing agent availability and bleeding severity</cite>.
- Safety: <cite id="6a781c53-0">As with other antidotes, andexanet alfa carries risks such as thromboembolic events, vascular complications, and potential hypersensitivity, necessitating informed risk‑benefit assessment</cite>. <cite id="6a781c53-2">Large phase studies documented near‑complete reversal of anti‑FXa activity but required careful monitoring for adverse effects</cite>.
- Practical algorithm for FXa inhibitor ICH: Confirm drug and duration, obtain rapid imaging/ICU consult, stop anticoagulant if safe, and administer andexanet alfa/andexanet omega (if available) or 4F‑PCC with vitamin K in combination, with adjunct vitamin K for apixaban/rivaroxaban where appropriate; repeat coagulation checks and plan neurosurgical intervention. <cite id="6a781c53-3">Andexanet alfa has been recommended as an option for apixaban/rivaroxaban reversal in life‑threatening bleeding</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-8">Prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K is strongly recommended over no treatment or FFP for ICH</cite>.

Comparative effectiveness and outcomes across agents
- Warfarin/ICH: <cite id="a8d5830b-0">Adding vitamin K to 4F‑PCC improved INR control versus PCC alone</cite>, supporting combination therapy to leverage rapid PCC effects with sustained vitamin K repletion. <cite id="a8d5830b-7">4F‑PCC normalized INR faster than FFP in VKA‑related ICH</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-9">and was associated with improved outcomes compared with FFP in warfarin-associated bleeding</cite>.
- Hemostasis rates: <cite id="6a781c53-8">A meta‑analysis/summary noted good or excellent hemostasis occurred more frequently with andexanet alfa than with PCC (87.8% vs 81.8%) in factor Xa inhibitor bleeding</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-1">whereas rFVIIa and PCC outperformed FFP in rapid warfarin reversal</cite>.
- Neurologic/hematoma outcomes: In observational cohorts, PCC-based reversal in ICH has shown clinical outcomes comparable to VK-group ICH cohorts, though definitive randomized ICH‑focused superiority trials remain limited. <cite id="a8d5830b-1">PCC‑treated FXa inhibitor ICH and VKA ICH cohorts had similar overall outcomes</cite>.
- Time sensitivity: Rapid reversal likely reduces time to hemostasis and may mitigate hematoma expansion; guidelines emphasize urgency and early neurosurgical consult for ICH. <cite id="a8d5830b-8">Two small randomized trials and broader trials show PCC reverses VKA coagulopathy more rapidly than alternatives</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-3">with intracerebral hemorrhage benefits demonstrated for 4F‑PCC</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-8">and society guidance stresses prompt reversal in bleeding ICH</cite>.

Safety and adverse effects
- Vitamin K: Generally safe but slow; contraindicated in vitamin K–dependent clotting defects and pregnancy risks debated; hemodynamic support and monitoring required while INR normalizes. <cite id="5e4731f5-5">Vitamin K’s INR reversal is gradual (12–24h), which may delay hemostasis</cite>.
- PCC (4F): Rapid, effective, but may precipitate thromboembolic events and carries theoretical risks of hypersensitivity/circulatory overload with rapid bolus; benefits often justified in life‑threatening bleeding but dosing must be weight‑based and hemodynamically supported. <cite id="a8d5830b-8">Despite general benefits, concerns about thromboembolic risk and circulatory overload drive careful monitoring</cite>.
- rFVIIa: High hemostatic potency outside the liver synthesis pathway; thromboembolic adverse events occur in a subset, requiring cautious selection and anti‑coagulation interruption. <cite id="5e4731f5-1">rFVIIa is effective but associated with higher thromboembolic risk, informing preference for PCC in many centers</cite>.
- Factor Xa antidote (andexanet alfa/omega): Near‑complete bioactivity reversal in trials; risks include thromboembolic events, vascular access complications, and possible anaphylaxis; availability and cost/logistics limit universal adoption. <cite id="6a781c53-6">Trials show 92–94% anti‑FXa reversal</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-0">with comparative outcome analyses demonstrating efficacy but necessitating safety surveillance</cite>.

Practical management algorithms and thresholds
- Indications to reverse: Elevated INR with clinical bleeding, including ICH, GI bleeding, hemodynamic instability, active surgery, or thrombosis risk. <cite id="a8d5830b-4">Guidelines recommend 4F‑PCC for rapid reversal when urgent control is required</cite>.
- Immediate steps for ICH:
  1) Stabilize with airway/BCPM/ICU; obtain head CT; neurosurgical consult. 
  2) If on VKA and bleeding active/hemodynamically unstable: give IV vitamin K 5–10 mg with 4F‑PCC 50–70 U/kg; repeat INR in 4–6 h, consider repeat PCC if INR not trending upward and bleeding persists. <cite id="5e4731f5-5">Vitamin K begins to reverse INR within 6 h and typically completes by 12–24 h</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-7">while 4F‑PCC achieves faster INR normalization than FFP</cite>.
  3) If on FXa inhibitor and bleeding is active: prefer andexanet alfa/andexanet omega if available; otherwise 4F‑PCC with vitamin K, with apixaban‑specific idarubicin considered where validated and available. <cite id="6a781c53-3">Andexanet alfa is recommended for apixaban/rivaroxaban reversal in life‑threatening/uncontrolled bleeding</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-8">and 4F‑PCC remains a preferred option over no treatment or FFP in ICH</cite>.
- Monitoring: Repeat coagulation tests (INR/FXa activity), D‑dimer trends, hemoglobin, neurologic status, and imaging as clinically indicated. Consider anti‑Xa measurement for direct‑acting agents to guide adjunct vitamin K and repeat reversal if needed. <cite id="6a781c53-2">Rapid bioactivity reduction by andexanet alfa supports targeted follow‑up of anti‑FXa activity</cite>.
- Timing to surgery/DTI: If surgical/DTI is planned for life‑threatening bleeding under INR control, PCC or rFVIIa can bridge hemostasis with vitamin K for sustained reversal, individualizing by patient factors, bleeding severity, and device specifics. <cite id="5e4731f5-0">In emergency surgery, guidelines recommend 4‑factor PCC with vitamin K for rapid reversal</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-1">and rFVIIa as an alternative adjunct, recognizing its thromboembolic risk</cite>.

What this means for effectiveness and safety
- Effectiveness: Across modern evidence, rapid reversal agents (4F‑PCC or andexanet alfa) achieve quicker coagulopathy correction and higher hemostatic success in ICH than vitamin K or FFP, with outcomes in observational ICH cohorts favoring PCC-based management comparable to VKA ICH when appropriately resourced. <cite id="a8d5830b-7">4F‑PCC normalizes INR faster than FFP in VKA‑related ICH</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-0">and improves INR control when combined with vitamin K</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-8">andexanet alfa showed higher hemostatic success than PCC in factor Xa inhibitor bleeding</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-8">while guidelines endorse PCC plus vitamin K over no treatment or FFP in ICH</cite>.
- Safety: Benefit must be balanced against thromboembolic risk (notably with rFVIIa) and infusion-related complications (hypersensitivity/circulatory overload with PCC), with careful patient selection and hemodynamic monitoring. <cite id="5e4731f5-1">rFVIIa’s thromboembolic risk informs preference for PCC in bleeding contexts</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-8">and practical concerns about circulatory overload with PCC drive cautious, weight‑based dosing and monitoring</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-0">andexanet alfa requires vigilant ADR surveillance despite rapid efficacy</cite>.

Evidence gaps and individualized care
ICH‑focused randomized head‑to‑head trials across all anticoagulants are limited; many data derive from small RCTs, observational cohorts, and perioperative algorithms. Decisions should therefore integrate: agent availability, anticoagulant type, time from injury, bleeding source, neurosurgical plan, thromboembolic risk (e.g., atrial fibrillation), and patient comorbidities and preferences. <cite id="a8d5830b-9">Retrospective analyses highlight practical adaptations in dosing and monitoring to optimize reversal effectiveness in warfarin-associated ICH</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-0">andexanet alfa studies provide direct comparisons to PCC but require ongoing evaluation for safety and outcomes in real world ICH</cite>.

Bottom line
- For warfarin-associated ICH, PCC plus vitamin K is effective and rapidly normalizes coagulopathy with better hemostatic control than FFP; vitamin K alone is slow but safe, and rFVIIa can be reserved for selected cases given thromboembolic risk. <cite id="5e4731f5-8">Guidelines strongly support PCC with vitamin K over FFP or no treatment for ICH on VKAs</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-7">4F‑PCC normalizes INR faster than FFP and supports timely hemostasis</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-5">Vitamin K requires 12–24h for full INR reversal, informing bridge to surgery and monitoring</cite>.
- For factor Xa inhibitor ICH, andexanet alfa/omega achieves near‑complete bioactivity reversal rapidly and can outperform PCC on hemostasis measures, but requires careful safety monitoring; 4F‑PCC with vitamin K remains a broadly available effective alternative. <cite id="6a781c53-6">Andexanet alfa reduces anti‑FXa activity by ~94% (apixaban) and 92% (rivaroxaban)</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-8">andexanet alfa achieved higher hemostatic success than PCC in factor Xa inhibitor bleeding</cite> <cite id="a8d5830b-3">4F‑PCC confers hemostatic benefit in intracerebral hemorrhage patients on factor Xa inhibitors</cite>.
Overall, in the acute ICH setting, rapid reversal with PCC or agent‑specific antidotes is generally effective and often safe when appropriately selected and monitored; vitamin K alone is safe but slow and often insufficient by itself in ICH, whereas rFVIIa carries notable thromboembolic risk and is not universally recommended. <cite id="5e4731f5-1">VIIa and PCC were more effective than FFP for rapid warfarin reversal but with safety considerations</cite> <cite id="5e4731f5-8">and prothrombin complex with vitamin K is strongly preferred over no treatment or FFP</cite> <cite id="6a781c53-3">andexanet alfa is recommended for apixaban/rivaroxaban in life‑threatening bleeding</cite>.

Practical tips for reversing INR and managing outcomes in anticoagulant-related ICH
- Immediate: Stop/hold anticoagulant; secure airway and hemodynamics; neurosurgery consult; head CT; targeted reversal based on drug.
- Warfarin: IV vitamin K 5–10 mg + 4F‑PCC 50–70 U/kg; reassess INR in 4–6 h; consider repeat PCC if bleeding persists; plan repeat INR daily to trend upward.
- FXa inhibitor: If antidote available, andexanet alfa/omega per local protocol; otherwise 4F‑PCC 50–70 U/kg + vitamin K; consider apixaban-specific idarubicin where validated; anticipate monitoring for thromboembolic and infusion-related complications.
- Bridging to surgery/DTI: Use PCC or rFVIIa to secure hemostasis while vitamin K ensures sustained reversal; avoid rFVIIa in high thromboembolic risk anatomy if possible.
- Outcome monitoring: Serial INR/anti‑FXa, neurologic exams/hemoglobin, repeat imaging if needed; early rehabilitation planning.

Overview: What the lactate/pyruvate ratio captures
- The lactate-to-pyruvate (L:P) molar ratio reflects the balance between cytosolic lactate production (from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase) and mitochondrial utilization (conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA in the PDH complex and oxidative steps in the tricarboxylic acid [TCA] cycle), along with NADH/NADPH redox constraints and tissue perfusion for clearance. An elevated L:P is a broad signal that lactate production exceeds mitochondrial conversion and downstream oxidation, and it is widely used as a screening marker for mitochondrial and other inborn errors, although it is not diagnostic on its own. <cite id="ad0185eb-0">The lactate-to-pyruvate ratio is proposed to be a better screening test for mitochondrial disorders, with elevated lactate or ratio suggestive but not diagnostic</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-2">An elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio may indicate inherited disorders of the respiratory chain, TCA cycle, and pyruvate metabolism</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-6">The lactate:pyruvate ratio is considered a helpful but not diagnostic tool in mitochondrial disease evaluation</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-8">It is useful to calculate lactate-to-pyruvate ratio because an elevated ratio suggests mitochondrial disease in infants/children</cite>.

Mechanisms: How metabolic pathway defects raise L:P

1) Impaired mitochondrial oxidative metabolism (electron transport chain and TCA defects)
- When mitochondrial respiration is limited (e.g., complex I/III/IV deficiencies or broader respiratory chain defects), the mitochondrial NADH/NADPH oxidizing capacity is reduced. Pyruvate is shunted to lactate by cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase because the reduced mitochondrial PDH complex/complex I cannot consume NADH, leading to elevated lactate and relatively preserved or decreased pyruvate, thereby elevating L:P. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">An elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio may indicate inherited disorders of the respiratory chain</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-1">Mitochondrial complex I involvement was associated with an elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, consistent with a mitochondrial disorder</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-8">Elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio suggests mitochondrial disease</cite>.
- In infants with respiratory chain defects that cause congenital lactic acidosis (e.g., SDH4-associated complex II deficiency), elevated L:P is a typical discriminant because pyruvate oxidation is limited while glycolysis persists; clinical onset in early months and hepatic involvement can guide suspicion. <cite id="89a7fe07-0">Infants with untreated TRMU deficiency typically become symptomatic between two and four months with transient acute liver injury, within a context of mitochondrial dysfunction that predisposes to lactic acidosis</cite>.

2) Defects in pyruvate entry into the mitochondrial citric acid cycle (PDH complex and upstream intermediates)
- Primary PDH complex deficiency (PDCD) blocks conversion of pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA, which both increases plasma lactate (from glycolytic overflow) and diminishes mitochondrial oxaloacetate anaplerosis, increasing pyruvate levels paradoxically. The resulting pattern is inappropriately high lactate with relative preservation or elevation of pyruvate, often yielding a high L:P and severe neonatal/early infantile lactic acidosis. <cite id="1d1a4015-0">Primary pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency is a mitochondrial disorder of carbohydrate oxidation that chiefly affects brain energy metabolism</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-5">PDH converts pyruvate to acetyl‑CoA as the first step into the citric acid cycle</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-2">PDC deficiency causes lactic acidosis, brain malformations, and developmental delay</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-3">PDCD is a rare neurodegenerative disorder tied to abnormal mitochondrial metabolism</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-7">PDCD is a heterogeneous mitochondrial inborn error in carbohydrate oxidation manifesting as congenital lactic acidosis</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-6">Diagnoses in the neonatal period are often spurred by unrelenting lactic acidosis, with PDCD as a common cause of congenital lactic acidosis</cite>.
- Quantitatively, PDH defects present with marked lactic acidosis and often a high L:P ratio in blood or CSF; however, some cases show a near-normal L:P on occasion (rationalized by variable pyruvate elevation and lactate escape): <cite id="1d1a4015-4">PDC deficiency is associated with lactic acidosis, and lactate:pyruvate ratio studies document low normal to low ratios in some cohorts, underscoring heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-9">A neonatal case reported elevated blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate but a normal lactate‑pyruvate ratio despite PDCD, highlighting assay-level and case-to-case variability</cite>. Clinically, PDH complex deficiency is among the most common inborn errors elevating lactate in infants. <cite id="89a7fe07-3">The most common inborn error in neonates causing elevated lactate is PDHC deficiency</cite>.
- Downstream TCA dehydrogenase defects and anaplerosis limitations also elevate lactate or pyruvate in distinctive ways. Loss of succinate dehydrogenase (complex II deficiency) causes lactic acidosis with elevated pyruvate and L:P >1; α‑ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (KGDHC) defects can likewise raise lactate with variable pyruvate depending on upstream PDH flux and NADH redox. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Raising lactate-to-pyruvate ratio may indicate TCA cycle disorders</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-3">Lactate and pyruvate, and their ratio, serve as accessible biomarkers; in IEM with lactic acidosis the key question is the source of elevated lactate</cite> <cite id="7abcf467-7">Mitochondrial α‑keto acid dehydrogenase complexes integrate with redox balancing and NADPH/NADH demands; their defects contribute to lactic acidosis via impaired TCA flux</cite>.
- Thiamine-responsive defects (e.g., RARS2/thiamine‑responsive mitochondrial encephelomyopathy and KGDHC complex defects) show lactate/pyruvate elevations responsive to thiamine or thiamine pyrophosphate cofactor restoration, reflecting sensitivity of PDH/KGDH enzymes to TPP. <cite id="7abcf467-6">A TPDS2-like human disorder due to thiamine pyrophosphokinase deficiency produced encephalopathy with response to thiamine and mechanistic link to TPP activation of α‑keto acid dehydrogenase complexes</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Laboratory patterns point to pyruvate metabolism and dehydrogenase complex involvement in disorders elevating the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio</cite>.

3) Cytosolic glycolysis and redox balance (NADH overflow, GAPDH and phosphoglycerate kinase, PPP shunting)
- When glycolytic enzymes in the cytosol (e.g., glyceraldehyde‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase) are deficient or when NADH sinks are impaired, reducing equivalents accumulate and force pyruvate to be converted to lactate rather than exported or oxidized, elevating plasma L:P; conversely, if NADPH-producing PPP is shunted (e.g., fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency), reduced cofactors can divert NAD(H) redox balance and also favor lactate production or impair mitochondrial uptake. <cite id="ad0185eb-3">In inborn errors where energy metabolism is impaired, critical sources of elevated lactate include metabolic diversion and impaired oxidation, with lactate/pyruvate useful for initial screening</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-6">An increased lactate/pyruvate ratio can result from aspartate deficiency impairing mitochondrial redox, illustrating how amino acid–linked redox balance and pyruvate dehydrogenase activity modulate lactate/pyruvate pools</cite>. In pediatric lactic acidosis reviews, both PDHC deficiency and broader mitochondrial dysfunction are primary drivers, with cytosolic glycolytic redox overflow contributing when tissue oxygenation and PDH capacity are limited. <cite id="89a7fe07-3">Neonatal lactic acidosis reviews identify PDHC deficiency as the most common inborn error but also consider broader mitochondrial causes elevating lactate due to impaired oxidative capacity</cite>.

4) Non‑mitochondrial, tissue and systemic causes with characteristic L:P patterns
- Global tissue hypoxia/ischemia, sepsis, and shock reduce mitochondrial oxidative capacity and perfusion, causing glycolytic NADH accumulation and lactate efflux with pyruvate retention, which raises L:P acutely. These states can be distinguished by context, kinetics, and the simultaneous rise of CK‑MB/lactate in myocardium, blood gas/metabolic acidosis type, and supportive labs; however, because L:P is nonspecific, measurement is most informative when integrated with clinical features. <cite id="ad0185eb-0">Elevated lactate and L:P are suggestive of mitochondrial disease but require clinical correlation</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-9">Elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio indicates mitochondrial dysfunction or lactic acidosis, but such laboratory rules are general and must be interpreted with clinical detail</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-8">Large cohort analysis defines abnormal thresholds (lactate ≥22 mg/dL, pyruvate ≥1.4 mg/dL, L:P >25) to flag lactic acidosis, highlighting that extreme values often point to mitochondrial or severe systemic causes</cite>.
- Endocrine and maternal-dietary factors can shift the ratio. Hypoglycemia and fasting states can lower acetyl‑CoA and pyruvate availability, increasing lactate/low pyruvate ratios in neonates; conversely, maternal carbohydrate load increases fetal lactate export and can raise maternal/pyruvate ratio. These transient changes underscore that L:P is dynamic and condition-dependent. <cite id="ad0185eb-8">Lactic acidosis can arise from multiple mitochondrial and non-mitochondrial causes; calculation of L:P is a useful part of a metabolic survey in infants</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-3">Elevated lactate/pyruvate and their ratio reflect sources of lactate production and impaired oxidation, and are influenced by state conditions including feeding and glycemia</cite>.
- Certain specific IEMs elevate pyruvate with lactate (e.g., pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, biotinidase deficiency with dicarboxylic aciduria) or cause mixed patterns, which can lower or raise the ratio depending on organ compartmentation and flux. Thus, L:P by itself is insufficient to assign etiology. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Pyruvate, lactate, and the ratio must be interpreted within inherited disorders of the respiratory chain, TCA cycle, and pyruvate metabolism</cite>.

Infant and pediatric-specific considerations
- Neonatal/early-infantile onset of symmetrical L:P elevation with profound, persistent lactic acidosis is a red flag for PDCD, SDH4 (complex II) deficiency, and other early-onset mitochondrial disease; neuroimaging and developmental regression often corroborate the diagnosis. <cite id="1d1a4015-6">Neonatal diagnoses are spurred by relentless lactic acidosis, with PDCD a frequent congenital cause</cite> <cite id="1d1a403c6">In congenital lactic acidosis, PDCD and complex I/II dysfunctions are prototypical causes with elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratios</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-0">Elevated lactate/L:P is proposed as an improved screening signal for mitochondrial disorders and used practically in pediatrics</cite>.
- Clinical scenarios common in infants that raise L:P include sepsis, birth asphyxia/ischemia-reperfusion, hypoglycemia, and fructose exposure; each has characteristic timelines and accompanying markers that differentiate them from inherited defects. Pediatric neonatal reviews emphasize that PDHC deficiency is the single most common IEM elevating lactate; the L:P helps triage but not finalize etiology. <cite id="89a7fe07-3">The most common IEM causing elevated lactate is PDHC deficiency; neonatal lactic acidosis reviews guide workups integrating L:P ratios and clinical context</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-8">Pediatric metabolic survey includes lactate-to-pyruvate ratio to suspect mitochondrial disease within a broader differential</cite>.
- Quantitative “rules of thumb” used in clinical practice mark abnormal L:P when lactate exceeds ~20 mmol/L and pyruvate exceeds ~1.4 mmol/L, giving a ratio typically >25; however, thresholds vary with age, acidaemia, and sampling. <cite id="89a7fe07-8">Lactate ≥22 mg/dL, pyruvate ≥1.4 mg/dL, and lactate-to-pyruvate ratio >25 define abnormality in one clinical cohort</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-0">Elevated lactate/L:P indicates increased risk of mitochondrial disease but requires confirmation</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-6">Clinicians consider the ratio helpful yet non-diagnostic; thresholds should be interpreted in context</cite>.

Practical diagnostic use of L:P in infants and patients
- Raising the ratio: increases likelihood of defects limiting mitochondrial NADH oxidation (complex I/II/III/IV deficiencies), PDH/KGDH complexes, PDCD, global ischemia, sepsis, hypoglycemia, or cytosolic glycolytic redox overflow; also occurs with certain amino acid/redox imbalances and neonatal metabolic stresses. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Rising lactate-to-pyruvate ratio indicates respiratory chain, TCA cycle, and pyruvate dehydrogenase disorders</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-6">Laboratory catalogs list elevated L:P as a supportive marker; targeted biochemical tests and genetics confirm etiology</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-1">Complex I involvement is associated with elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratios in disease</cite>.
- Lowering or normal ratio with elevated lactate: can occur when pyruvate is also elevated (as in some TCA-cycle defects, PDH-independent pyruvate overproduction), in sepsis with mixed systemic lactic acidosis, or with fructose-induced enzyme instability; a normal L:P does not exclude mitochondrial disease because flux can be rerouted or coenzyme availability differs. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Disorders of the TCA cycle and pyruvate metabolism may show lactate rise with variable pyruvate elevations rather than high L:P</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-9">PDCD case with normal L:P despite both lactate and pyruvate elevations illustrates that some PDCD cases do not show classic ratio elevation</cite>.
- Workup: confirm with sequential lactate/pyruvate in blood and CSF, metabolite acylcarnitines and dicarboxylic acids, lactate dehydrogenase/alpha‑hydroxybutyric acid ratios, NADH/NADPH-linked fluorescence, respiratory exchange ratio, muscle biopsy for PDH complex, and next-generation sequencing of mitochondrial/energy genes; do not rely on the ratio alone. <cite id="ad0185eb-6">Mayo Clinic labs advise that the L:P ratio is helpful but not diagnostic for mitochondrial disease; comprehensive workup is required</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-8">Pediatric diagnostic algorithms incorporate L:P within metabolic surveys and follow with specific tests for mitochondrial disease</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Deficiencies that reduce mitochondrial oxidative consumption of pyruvate (complex I/II/III/IV defects, KGDHC, PDCD, and thiamine-sensitive dehydrogenases) force cytosolic conversion of pyruvate to lactate, raising L:P; many infants with early-onset lactic acidosis and elevated L:P harbor PDHC or complex II/III defects, or other mitochondrial gene defects. <cite id="ad0185eb-2">Rise in L:P points to respiratory chain/TCA/pyruvate dehydrogenase involvement</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-1">Complex I involvement correlates with elevated lactate-to-pyruvate</cite> <cite id="1d1a4015-0">PDCD blocks glucose oxidation at the PDH step with severe lactic acidosis</cite> <cite id="7abcf467-6">Thiamine-responsive disorders demonstrate the dependence of α‑keto acid dehydrogenases on TPP and respond to thiamine</cite>.
- Cytosolic glycolytic enzyme defects that increase NADH production (GAPDH) or shifts through the PPP also elevate lactate relative to pyruvate, and common neonatal stresses (asphyxia, sepsis, hypoglycemia) mimic or amplify these patterns, requiring clinical context and longitudinal/confirmatory testing. <cite id="89a7fe07-6">Redox imbalances (e.g., aspartate deficiency) can increase lactate/pyruvate via impaired mitochondrial redox balance</cite> <cite id="89a7fe07-3">Sepsis and other systemic insults are frequent causes of neonatal elevated lactate with variable L:P</cite> <cite id="ad0185eb-9">Clinicians treat elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio as suggestive but non-specific, integrating it with broader metabolic findings and clinical picture</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of common study types and outcome measures used to evaluate treatment efficacy in clinical medicine, with examples and practical guidance on selection and interpretation.

Overview
Across medical conditions, treatment efficacy is typically evaluated using combinations of study designs and outcomes tailored to disease endpoints, patient-centered impact, and feasibility, and results are interpreted with attention to bias, confounding, and surrogate validation.<cite id="e6dfe315-0,e6dfe315-3">Observational designs (case-control, cohort, cross-sectional) monitor outcomes without manipulating treatment assignment, and are used to measure intervention effects when controlled experimentation is infeasible, while experimental designs (especially randomized controlled trials) directly compare treatments under concurrent control for concurrent comparators and blinding</cite>.

Types of studies used to evaluate treatment efficacy
- Randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
  - Core design: allocation to test and comparator treatments in comparable groups, enabling causal inference on treatment effects; trial outcomes are directly compared to estimate efficacy and effectiveness.<cite id="f4428579-7">All randomized trials assess outcomes for group comparison, with several outcomes considered but some more important than others for answering the primary question</cite>.
  - Role of endpoints: RCTs commonly use surrogate endpoints to substitute for clinically meaningful outcomes when faster or more feasible measures predict benefit; reporting guidance emphasizes defining primary outcomes and ensuring adequate follow-up and adjudication of endpoints (surrogate or clinical).<cite id="f4428579-0">Randomized controlled trials commonly use surrogate endpoints to substitute for a target outcome when the direct outcome is impractical</cite><cite id="f4428579-4">Reporting trials using surrogate endpoints as primary outcomes requires clear explanation and elaboration</cite><cite id="f4428579-2">Clinical outcomes directly measure whether people feel or function better, in contrast to surrogate endpoints that predict benefit without demonstrating direct clinical gain</cite>.
  - Regulatory and disease areas: Drug approvals have used validated surrogate endpoints as primary efficacy endpoints in specific indications; for example, cancer trials may use progression-free or overall survival, and hematologic malignancy trials may use complete remission categories and depth of response.<cite id="f4428579-1">FDA maintains a table of surrogate endpoints used as primary efficacy endpoints for approval across drugs</cite><cite id="c10cd947-0">ACR50 and ACR70 define ≥20% and ≥50% improvement in tender and swollen joint counts, and are composite responders used in rheumatoid arthritis RCTs</cite>.

- Nonrandomized (observational) comparative studies
  - Case-control and cohort designs compare exposed/unexposed or treated/untreated cohorts on an outcome; when appropriately constructed, they can evaluate effectiveness in routine care, but are susceptible to confounding and selection bias.<cite id="e6dfe315-0">Case-control, cohort, and cross-sectional designs are core observational approaches in which outcomes are measured without manipulation, allowing measurement of interventions’ efficacy in non-experimental settings</cite><cite id="e6dfe315-3">Observational studies monitor outcomes without intervention manipulation, which constrains causal inference compared with randomized designs</cite>.
  - Historical controls: These are special, often single-arm, cohort comparisons to earlier care; they are used when randomized controlled trials are ethically or logistically prohibitive but are prone to time-period and practice-bias and require careful sensitivity analyses.<cite id="e6dfe315-7">Case-control designs nested within defined cohorts combine elements of cohort and case-control designs to improve external validity while retaining comparative efficiency</cite>.

- Pragmatic and real-world evidence (RWE) studies
  - Purpose: Evaluate effectiveness in everyday clinical practice rather than maximal efficacy, often including routine outcomes (survival, utilization, adherence), broader eligibility, and mixed care settings; they complement RCTs by addressing external validity and context of use.<cite id="cc6e3117-1">RCTs and pragmatic trials are two approaches to evaluating efficacy, safety, and effectiveness, with pragmatic trials designed to answer questions in real-world settings</cite><cite id="cc6e3117-5">Pragmatic studies use typical clinical settings to examine real-world outcomes such as survival, healthcare utilization, and pharmacotherapy outcomes</cite><cite id="cc6e3117-7">Pragmatic clinical trials aim primarily to assess effectiveness (as opposed to efficacy) in routine care</cite>.
  - RWE ecosystems and embedded designs: Networks and embedded PCTs integrate evaluations into routine care workflows to collect comparative outcomes across diverse populations and sites.<cite id="cc6e3117-4">An embedded pragmatic clinical trial ecosystem aligns study design and delivery with routine care to generate real-world evidence</cite><cite id="cc6e3117-0">Pragmatic trials have grown in importance to complement traditional randomized designs and improve applicability of findings</cite>.

- Disease-specific and specialized designs
  - Crossover trials and N-of-1 trials: Used for conditions with fluctuating symptoms and periods of stability, allowing within-patient comparison across active treatment periods (washout) on symptom scales, relapse rate, or time-to-worsening; N-of-1 designs aggregate within-patient cycles to estimate treatment effects for the individual, particularly in chronic diseases and symptomatic conditions.
  - Observational longitudinal cohorts and registries: Useful for rare diseases and long natural history conditions to assess survival, quality of life, and safety over time when interventional trials are scarce, relying on routine outcome capture and case-level comparisons.

Outcome measures used to evaluate efficacy
- Clinical vs surrogate endpoints
  - Clinical endpoints directly reflect patient benefits (function, symptoms, remission) and are preferred for regulatory approval and patient-relevant conclusions; surrogate endpoints accelerate trials but require validation that effects on the surrogate predict effects on the clinical outcome of interest.<cite id="f4428579-2">Clinical outcomes directly measure whether people feel or function better, whereas surrogates predict benefit without necessarily representing direct clinical benefit</cite><cite id="f4428579-8">Surrogate endpoints can be used if randomized trials show that effects on the surrogate predict effects on the clinical outcome of primary interest</cite><cite id="f4428579-3">Many outcome measures used in clinical research are indirect surrogates rather than clinically meaningful endpoints</cite><cite id="e6dfe315-6">Trial outcome selection should align with the research question, and the hierarchy of study designs includes trade-offs that affect outcome validity and interpretability</cite>.
  - Examples: In oncology, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) serve as primary endpoints in late-phase trials; in hematologic malignancies, complete response (CR), complete hematologic recovery (CRh), and cytogenetic/cytogenetic complete response (CRg/CRcg) and molecular response durations are used; composite efficacy endpoints may include imaging progression and symptomatic deterioration.<cite id="f4428579-1">Regulatory tables include disease-specific surrogate endpoints used as primary efficacy endpoints across cancers and other areas</cite><cite id="c10cd947-8">The ACR50/70 Responder Index and ACR composite responder categories aggregate clinical, laboratory, and functional measures in RA</cite>.

- Survival and time-to-event endpoints
  - Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), disease-free survival (DFS), and time-to-relapse/time-to-event primary endpoints are estimated with hazard ratios, median survival, and censoring-aware methods, prioritizing long follow-up and adjudication for clinical relevance.<cite id="cc6e3117-5">Pragmatic studies typically examine survival and healthcare utilization outcomes in real-world settings</cite><cite id="f4428579-3">Time-to-event outcomes and related surrogates are common in trials, with careful distinction between clinically meaningful endpoints and indirect surrogates</cite>.
