- Metabolic re-wiring: Alternative respiratory pathways (e.g., extr respiratory electron transfer to nitrate/manganese) and enhanced ATP expenditure for ion transport reduce efficiency; carbon metabolism suffers from Na+ toxicity to Calvin cycle enzymes and mitochondrial electron transport, reinforcing growth suppression. <cite id="12b71e05-6">Some of the alternative NADH dehydrogenases are transcriptionally responsive to salt stress the oxidation of external NADH is stimulated by salt</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-1">Salt stress reduces plant growth by affecting the rate and amount of CO2 fixation by RuBisCo and other enzymes in the Calvin cycle</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-8">High concentrations of Na+ and Cl− in the soil result in both osmotic and ionic stress, which decrease plants' capacity to take up water and nutrients</cite>. 

Practical Implications: What to expect in plants exposed to high soil salt
- Water uptake declines relative to osmotic demand; Na+ and Cl− accumulate in roots first, then leak into xylem and shoots, lowering water and nutrient delivery to leaves. <cite id="110926b9-7">Salts in the soil provide nutrients to plants. However, an excess of salt can interfere with water uptake</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-8">High concentrations of Na+ and Cl− in the soil result in both osmotic and ionic stress, which decrease plants' capacity to take up water and nutrients</cite>. 
- Ion uptake distortions: K+ and Ca2+ influx is curtailed; Na+ and Cl− displace beneficial cations, impairing membrane excitability, stomatal function, and nutrient bioavailability; nitrate reductase activity is compromised via ROS and electron transport interference. <cite id="110926b9-2">Salt stress impairs the uptake of Ca2+, potassium (K+), and water into plant cells</cite> <cite id="110926b9-4">Plants can sense K+/NO3– levels in soils and adjust accordingly the uptake and root-to-shoot transport</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-2">Na+ toxicity, Nitrite reduction may occur during mitochondrial electron transport, probably via cytochrome c oxidase and/or reductase</cite>. 
- Enzymatic impacts manifest as reduced photosynthesis (RuBisCO and Calvin enzymes), mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation defects (cytochrome oxidase sensitivity to Na+), and heightened ROS that must be detoxified enzymatically at energetic cost. <cite id="12b71e05-1">Salt stress reduces plant growth by affecting the rate and amount of CO2 fixation by RuBisCo and other enzymes in the Calvin cycle</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-2">Na+ toxicity, Nitrite reduction may occur during mitochondrial electron transport, probably via cytochrome c oxidase and/or reductase</cite> <cite id="6f2c111c-8">Salt stress may result in excessive uptake of unwanted ions into plant tissues leading to the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS)</cite>. 
- Salt-tolerant genotypes mitigate damage via strengthened Na+ exclusion (HKT1;5/HKT1;2) and extrusion (SOS1), vacuolar sequestration (NHX1), antioxidant induction, and metabolic reconfiguration, but these adaptations incur fitness costs that limit yield at high salinity. <cite id="110926b9-5">Arabidopsis plants utilize SOS1 to achieve Na+ efflux at the root</cite> <cite id="110926b9-9">HKT1;2 plays a significant role in tomato Na+/K+ homeostasis</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-6">Alternative NADH dehydrogenases are transcriptionally responsive to salt stress</cite>. 

Key uncertainties and context
- Enzyme-specific inhibition magnitudes (e.g., IC50 for cytochrome oxidase or nitrate reductase under defined NaCl) vary across genotypes, salinity regimes, and tissues; many studies focus on directional changes (increase/decrease) rather than dose–response kinetics. <cite id="12b71e05-1">Salt stress reduces plant growth by affecting the rate and amount of CO2 fixation by RuBisCo and other enzymes in the Calvin cycle</cite> <cite id="6f2c111c-9">The level of antioxidative enzymes increases when plants are exposed to oxidative stress including salinity</cite>. 
- Transporter-mediated trade-offs (e.g., inverse SOS1/HKT1 regulation) suggest genotype-specific balances between cytosolic Na+ tolerance and xylem Na+ loading; this heterogeneity affects both ion uptake phenotypes and enzymatic stress impacts. <cite id="110926b9-5">Inverse regulation of SOS1 and HKT1 protein localization and stability by</cite>. 
- Soil chemical context (e.g., carbonate/sulfate interference with root hydrogen adsorption and nutrient availability) modulates effective osmotic and ionic stress, with implications for uptake and enzymatic stress burdens; the listed mechanisms are robust across NaCl-dominant systems but may differ in complex soils. <cite id="110926b9-0">The mechanisms by which salinity impairs plant growth involve complex interactions among osmotic stress, ion toxicity, and secondary oxidative stress</cite>. 

In short, high soil salt levels depress ion uptake by collapsing osmotic gradients and imposing ionic toxicity, force plants to rewire transport systems and energy metabolism, and overwhelm enzymatic machinery—especially photosynthetic and mitochondrial enzymes—through ROS and metal-catalyzed damage, ultimately constraining growth unless adaptive transport and antioxidant capacities are adequate. <cite id="110926b9-7">An excess of salt can interfere with water uptake</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-8">High concentrations of Na+ and Cl− in the soil result in both osmotic and ionic stress, which decrease plants' capacity to take up water and nutrients</cite> <cite id="6f2c111c-8">Salt stress may result in excessive uptake of unwanted ions into plant tissues leading to the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS)</cite> <cite id="12b71e05-1">Salt stress reduces plant growth by affecting the rate and amount of CO2 fixation by RuBisCo and other enzymes in the Calvin cycle</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of the main chemical classes in leaves and why measured proportions differ across studies and techniques.

Summary of major constituents
- Leaves are predominantly water and carbohydrates, with substantial protein and fiber, and lower but notable lipid, ash, and secondary metabolite contents. <cite id="4848555d-2">Proximate analysis of plant tissues separates these into moisture, ash, crude fiber, crude protein, crude fat/lipids, and carbohydrate fractions</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-8">Across leaves, carbohydrates commonly constitute the largest proportion, followed by protein, ash, fiber, moisture, and lipids</cite>.
- Water is highly variable and often dominates “fresh” leaf weight; dry-matter normalization is critical. <cite id="4848555d-1">In Amaranthus graecizans leaves, moisture reached 40.8 g/100 g with ash up to 24.7 g/100 g, illustrating leaves can be far drier or wetter depending on species and conditions</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-0">Across herbs, moisture commonly spans ~6.1–10.5% in some datasets, highlighting broad divergence when comparing fresh vs. dry weights</cite>.

Proximate composition and typical ranges
- Dry matter: protein and sugars/fiber/ash rise relatively. <cite id="4848555d-0">Crude protein tends to vary widely among leaves—about 2.55–23.14% on a dry-matter basis—with lipids roughly 0.67–4.00%, fiber 4.18–14.42%, and ash 3.05–12.05%</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-6">An example set reports 5.7% moisture, 10.39% protein, 0.83% fat, 9.06% fiber, and 4.03% ash in total NFE (nitrogen-free extract), exemplifying typical distributions when moisture is low</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-7">Another example yields 14.74% moisture, 12.52% ash, 4.94% protein, 17.65% fat, 10.58% fiber, and 39.50% carbohydrate, underscoring high variability even within “leaves” across species and conditions</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-8">Many studies still generalize that carbohydrates top the list, followed by protein, ash, crude fiber, moisture, and fat</cite>.
- Carbohydrate classes (sugars, starch) differ by leaf ontogeny and function. <cite id="b3b5bcca-1">HPLC-based methods show fructose and glucose contents of 27.7–31.8 g/100 g in some perennials (e.g., onion and chestnut tissues), indicating sugar levels can be high in storage/assimilate-rich organs</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">In mature leaves, starch typically accounts for about 5.7% of total sugars while sucrose is ~63.5%, with glucose and fructose comprising the remainder, reflecting a bias toward sucrose export and limited local starch storage in fully photosynthetic foliage</cite>.
- Analytical coverage and repeatability: <cite id="b3b5bcca-0">Validated HPLC/MS methods quantify sucrose, fructose, and glucose in plant tissues, demonstrating precision and sensitivity for leaf sugar profiling</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-3">UPLC-MS enables rapid, direct quantification across sample matrices, supporting comparable measurement of simple sugars and oligosaccharides in leaves</cite>.

Secondary metabolites and phenolics
- Phenolics, terpenoids (flavonoids, phenolic acids), and other specialized metabolites are abundant and vary widely by plant group and tissue. <cite id="9d779b53-1">Phenolic compounds are among the most abundant secondary metabolites in plants, contributing diverse bioactivities</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-4">In horticultural plants, phenolics are structurally diverse—flavonoids, simple phenols, stilbenes—and are prominent in leaves</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-5">Leaf phenolics include hydroxycinnamic acids, flavonols like quercetin, and condensed tannins, exemplifying the breadth of compounds that differ among species and leaves</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-3">Across plant residues, leaves often show high phenolic consistency within residue groups, but absolute levels vary by species and processing (e.g., brewing/fermentative losses)</cite>.

Why proportions differ across analyses
1) Biological drivers (species, organ, age, environment, function)
- Hydration state strongly shifts percent composition. <cite id="4848555d-1">Leaves of Amaranthus spp. measured near 40% moisture and 25% ash—far drier and ashier than tropical fruit leaves—and illustrate that species ecology and tissue age dominate composition</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Mature vs. developing leaves differ: sucrose makes up ~63.5% of total sugars in mature leaves, with starch ~5.7%, whereas younger, growing leaves tend to accumulate more fructose/glucose and less exported sucrose</cite>.
- Ontogeny, productivity, and storage. <cite id="b3b5bcca-1">Sugar concentrations can be very high in metabolically active or storage organs (e.g., up to 30 g/100 g fructose and glucose in certain tissues), and comparable high sucrose levels appear in leaves when assimilate loading is strong</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-5">Phenolics and terpenoids increase in stress/defense responses (e.g., quercetin, juglone), so composition shifts under biotic/abiotic stress</cite>.
2) Measurement technique and analytical protocol
- Technique sensitivity and calibration. <cite id="fc5cd275-6">Near-infrared reflectance is “governed primarily by leaf moisture content,” so NIR-based composition maps will over- or underestimate other fractions when moisture calibration is poor</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-0">For sugars, targeted HPLC/MS methods separate sucrose, fructose, and glucose with high specificity, whereas colorimetric screens may sum reducing sugars and thus compress sucrose signals</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Starch quantification often requires enzymatic or acid hydrolysis prior to GLU/FRU measurement, and analytical choice affects reported “sugar” vs “starch” proportions</cite>.
- Sampling and normalization. <cite id="4848555d-0">Reporting “as-is” vs. dry-matter percentages leads to large disparities (e.g., >30% differences in protein/ash due to water dilution), so cross-study comparisons should align on basis and method</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-2">Proximate methods differ in definition (e.g., crude fiber via acid-base digestion), introducing method-specific biases when comparing across labs</cite>.
- Specimen heterogeneity. <cite id="9d779b53-9">Leaves are heterogeneous—blade vs petiole can differ; internal gradients from midrib to margin carry distinct metabolite profiles—so sampling strategy affects measured proportions</cite>.
3) Ecological and agricultural context
- Nutrients and environment shape mineral and metabolite pools. <cite id="4848555d-1">High-ash leaves (e.g., Amaranthus) reflect heavy mineral uptake; nutrient-rich soils elevate K, Ca, Mg signatures</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-5">Leaf-specific phenolics and allelochemicals (e.g., juglone) arise from genotypes and microhabitats, producing variation alongside broader secondary-metabolite classes</cite>.

Putting the numbers together: what to expect in “typical” leaves
- Fresh weight (hydrated leaves)
  • Water: dominant (often >50% and sometimes >80% in herbaceous, high-water tissues; species and season modulate this). <cite id="4848555d-0">Moisture as low as ~6% occurs in dried datasets and as high as ~41% in some fresh leaves</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-6">Examples from herbs show ~5–15% moisture after drying</cite>.  
  • Total sugars + starch: high in photosynthetic organs; mature leaves skew toward sucrose export. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Sucrose ~63.5% of total sugars, starch ~5.7% in mature leaves; glucose and fructose together the remainder</cite>.  
  • Protein, lipids, ash, fiber: lower than sugars but tissue-dependent. <cite id="4848555d-0">Protein 2.6–23.1% (dm), crude fat 0.7–4.0% (dm), crude fiber 4.2–14.4% (dm), crude ash 3.1–12.1% (dm)</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-7">One leaf set reported fat 17.65% with 39.5% carbohydrate, showing variability when species are mesophyll-rich or lipid/phenolic–loaded</cite>.
- Dry matter (normalized)
  • Carbohydrate classes: sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose) and starch constitute a major share; enzyme-starch fraction depends on age/assimilate export. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Mature leaves: starch 5.7%/sucrose 63.5% of total sugars</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-1">Sugar totals can reach >27 g/100 g in some tissues; leaves of storage/bud flushes can be similar</cite>.  
  • Protein: varies widely with nitrogen status and species; hemicellulose/pectin vs lignin fractions shift fiber indices. <cite id="4848555d-0">Protein remains variable (≥2% common), but species with C4/photosynthetic adaptations can be high-protein/low-ash</cite>.  
  • Ash and minerals: correlates with soil and leaf litter traits; many leaves show moderate mineral content. <cite id="4848555d-1">High-ash leaves (e.g., Amaranthus) reach ~25% ash in fresh weight and ~12% in dry weight, illustrating strong species effects</cite>.  
  • Phenolics and terpenoids: present from low to high; total phenolics and flavonoids can be prominent in many leaves. <cite id="9d779b53-4">Simple phenols and flavonoids comprise a sizable secondary-metabolite fraction in horticultural leaves</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-1">Phenolics are among the most abundant secondary metabolites and thus contribute significantly to “non-protein/non-sugar” residues</cite>.

Practical guidance for reading literature and designing experiments
- Harmonize baselines: check whether values are “fresh” vs “dry,” and whether fiber was measured enzymatically vs by acid-detergent/neutral detergent protocols. <cite id="4848555d-2">Crude fiber methods vary and shift lignin-inclusive vs cell-wall inclusive readings</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-0">Species-spanning comparisons need dry-matter normalization to compare protein/ash/starch fractions</cite>.
- Consider technique footprints: NIR-based inventories emphasize moisture; wet chemistry screens may miss sucrose or sum sugars; HPLC/MS yields more specific sugar profiles; starch requires hydrolysis/assay. <cite id="fc5cd275-6">Leaf moisture dominates NIR sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-0">Validated HPLC/MS quantifies sucrose/fructose/glucose in plant tissues</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Starch assays inform total sugar allocation to storage vs export</cite>.
- Expect large ecological variation: C3 vs C4 species, temperate vs tropical habitats, and nutrient-rich vs poor soils shift mineral and secondary-metabolite loads. <cite id="9d779b53-5">Leaf phenolics span terpenoids and polyphenols and vary with genotype and stress</cite>. <cite id="4848555d-1">High-mineral leaves can show moisture ~40% and ash ~25% in fresh weight</cite>. 

Examples that illustrate proportion differences
- A tropical woody hanger: “carbs first, then protein, ash, fiber, moisture, and fat.” <cite id="4848555d-8">Carbohydrates highest in proportion among proximate classes; protein next; ash and fiber lower; moisture and fats least in mature, mesophyll-rich leaves</cite>.  
- An Amaranthus leaf: water-dominant with high ash and protein. <cite id="4848555d-1">Leaves with ~40.8% moisture and ~24.7% ash and moderate protein exemplify mineral-rich, well-watered species</cite>.  
- A high-sucrose/mature-leaf profile: <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Sucrose constitutes ~63.5% of total sugars and starch ~5.7% in mature leaves, implying a pronounced bias toward sucrose export compared to storage</cite>.  
- A sugar-heavy storage tissue benchmark: <cite id="b3b5bcca-1">Perennial storage systems can reach 27–32 g/100 g total sugars (fructose/glucose) and high sucrose, setting upper bounds relevant to certain leaf flushes</cite>.

In short, leaves typically consist of water plus a major carbohydrate fraction (sugars and often starch), with substantial fiber and lower protein, ash, and lipids; phenolic and terpenoid secondary metabolites add variable “non- primary” mass. <cite id="4848555d-1">Measured proportions vary enormously—moisture can be 10–40% of fresh weight or more, ash 3–25%, protein 2–20%, fiber 4–14%, and lipids ≤4%—and these ranges contract when comparing on a dry-matter basis</cite>. <cite id="b3b5bcca-8">Within dry matter, mature leaves tend to favor sucrose export (sucrose ≈63% of total sugars, starch ≈6%) and accumulate little starch locally</cite>. <cite id="9d779b53-1,9d779b53-4,9d779b53-5">Secondary metabolites are abundant and species- and stress-specific, further widening inter-study differences</cite>. <cite id="fc5cd275-6">Techniques like NIRS are moisture-dominant, while targeted HPLC/MS and enzymatic assays reveal sugar and starch allocations, explaining numerical discrepancies across analyses</cite>.

Below is a concise overview of commonly used plant trait indices, categorized by the trait they estimate, with mathematical formulations and practical notes. Formulas follow conventional reflectance-band notations (NIR, Red, Red-edge, SWIR, Green; ρ denotes band reflectance; L and C are calibration/sensor-specific constants). Indices are grouped by sensing modality and trait.

Remote-sensing canopy “greenness,” vigor, and nitrogen status
- NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index; broadleaf crops, cereals)
  - Trait: canopy vigor, biomass, leaf area density/greenness.
  - Formula: NDVI = (ρNIR − ρRed)/(ρNIR + ρRed) <cite id="4ef4bf02-2">Standard NDVI is computed as (NIR − red)/(NIR + red)</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">NDVI is among the most widely used indices with the normalized ratio between red and NIR</cite>.
  - Practical notes: red-edge or green variants can be more sensitive to nitrogen or senescence than red NDVI.

- GNDVI (Green NDVI; chlorophyll/N; precedes senescing browning)
  - Trait: chlorophyll/N content (less confounded by senescing brown pigments than red-based NDVI).
  - Formula: same ratio structure as NDVI but with Green and Red: GNDVI = (ρGreen − ρRed)/(ρGreen + ρRed) <cite id="4ef4bf02-2">Interpretation varies by crop condition; NDVI ratio form generalizes to other bands, including green vs red for chlorophyll emphasis</cite>.
  - Use: widely interpreted as higher GNDVI with higher greenness/chlorophyll; declines before harvest (senescence) <cite id="4ef4bf02-2">How NDVI varies with crop condition informs interpretation of green-based ratios for vigor and nutrient status</cite>.

- SAVI (Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index; agriculture with sparse-to-dense canopies)
  - Trait: aboveground biomass/vigor with reduced soil reflectance bias.
  - Formula: SAVI = [(ρNIR − ρRed)/(ρNIR + ρRed + L)] × (1 + L), where L is a soil adjustment factor (e.g., 0 in dense vegetation to 0.25–0.3 for sparse) <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">SAVI = [(NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red + L)] × (1 + L)</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI uses a multiplicative gain G and a red-edge correction, but SAVI directly incorporates soil factor L</cite>.

- EVI (Enhanced Vegetation Index; dense canopies and fractional vegetation)
  - Trait: canopy greenness/density with atmospheric/soil correction; suitable for LAI proxies.
  - Formula: EVI = G × [(ρNIR − ρRed)/(ρNIR + C1×ρRed − C2×ρBlue + L)], with typical coefficients G=1, C1=6, C2=7.75 and L=1 for surface reflectance; L=0 when using TOA reflectance <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI = G × [(NIR − Red)/(NIR + C1×Red − C2×Blue + L)], commonly with G=1, C1=6, C2=7.75, L=0–1 per reflectance domain</cite>.

- NDRE (Normalized Difference Red-Edge; senescence/vigor where red-edge sensitivity matters)
  - Trait: chlorophyll content and vigor in mid–late season; penetrates leaf tissue and tracks nitrogen and senescence earlier than red band.
  - Formula: NDRE = (ρNIR − ρRedEdge)/(ρNIR + ρRedEdge); RedEdge typically near 730–740 nm <cite id="636f6541-7">NDRE = (NIR − RedEdge)/(NIR + RedEdge), RedEdge commonly around 730–740 nm</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-0">NDRE measures chlorophyll in plants and is used in mid and late crop seasons</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-3">NDRE uses red-edge radiation and is formulated as (NIR − RED EDGE)/(NIR + RED EDGE)</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Compared to NDVI/SAVI, newer indices are designed to be more dissimilar yet sensitive to specific biochemical traits</cite>.
  - Notes: requires a red-edge band; widely used for nitrogen deficiency and vigor mapping <cite id="636f6541-4">NDRE requires a red-edge band and is formulated from NIR and red-edge</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-6">NDRE is particularly effective for detecting nutrient deficiencies in crops</cite>.

Water content and stress indices
- NDWI (Normalized Difference Water Index; crops, turf, orchards)
  - Trait: canopy/foliage water content and moisture stress; less sensitive to background.
  - Formula variants: (1) (ρNIR − ρSWIR)/(ρNIR + ρSWIR); (2) (ρMoisture − ρDry)/(ρMoisture + ρDry); water channel band near 1250–1450 nm often used as SWIR1 for vegetation, or 1900–2300 nm for water absorption; red band is also used <cite id="bb36acd8-6">NDWI proposed for vegetation liquid water with a normalized form (NIR − SWIR)/(NIR + SWIR)</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-1">Water indicators often relate to leaf fresh/dry weight per area and LAI, motivating NDWI use to reflect crop water content</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-8">NDWI contrasts with NDVI for vegetation; NDWI better responds to water content under many conditions</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-4">Compared to NDII and NDVI, WI/NDWI better reflected crop canopy water content due to sensitivity to canopy water content</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-5">NDWI is used to monitor crop water status and identify moisture deficits</cite>.
  - Notes: band choice is critical; water band NDWI (1300–1400 nm) distinguishes water from dry biomass, while red-band NDWI is a vegetation/soil-adjusted proxy <cite id="bb36acd8-8">Operational NDWI variants differ by index bands; vegetation vs water-specific implementations explain differing behavior</cite>.

- CWSI (Crop Water Stress Index; field crops, irrigation management)
  - Trait: plant water stress level (0=nondrought, 1=severe drought).
  - Formula: CWSI = [(Ts − Tair)/(Tc − Tair)] where Ts is canopy/leaf temperature and Tc is temperature under full canopy evapotranspiration (emitted/thermal band); Tair is air temperature. Temperature-based, often combined with an NDVI threshold to detect active transpiration stress <cite id="bb36acd8-2">CWSI uses the temperature difference between plants and air to measure water stress more precisely</cite>.
  - Notes: requires thermal imagery and empirical calibration of Tc per crop/variety/season; NDVI or NDWI used to confine stress to transpiring canopies and reduce soil confounding <cite id="bb36acd8-2">CWSI relies on thermal differences and is widely operationalized for irrigation scheduling</cite>.

LAI, fAPAR, and canopy structure proxies
- Empirical LAI proxies from greenness indices
  - Trait: Leaf Area Index and fraction of photosynthetically active radiation absorbed (fAPAR).
  - Green LAI relationship: Green LAI ≈ C × EVI + D; fAPAR ≈ A × EVI + B, with coefficients derived per site/season/cover type; EVI is preferred over NDVI due to blue/soil correction, yielding stronger linear relationships for LAI in dense canopies <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI includes a gain and red-edge correction, enabling improved LAI/cover estimation versus NDVI</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Modern reviews catalog formulations across indices where NDVI/SAVI/EVI differences map to trait sensitivity, enabling regression to canopy traits</cite>.
  - Empirical band-ratio LAIs: ND70-style or NDVI-based linear models fAPAR ≈ k1×NDVI + k2 or fAPAR ≈ k2×EVI + k1; calibrated R2 often >0.75 in agriculture when using cloud/fog-masked data and seasonal harmonics <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Index families differ in mathematical formulation and sensitivity, which underpin empirical regressions to fAPAR and LAI</cite>.

- LAI and biomass estimation from indices and crown measurements
  - Trait: LAI (structure) and aboveground biomass (trait-to-yield proxy).
  - Crown/size-based vigor and LAI estimators: vigor index from ground measurements often combines crown width/height/area with allometric relationships to predict LAI and biomass (e.g., regressions using height and vegetation indices; product models reduce error vs single predictors) <cite id="c28edca9-1">Bivariate and multivariate models combining plant height and hyperspectral indices improved barley biomass estimation</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-0">Ground and remote-sensing fusion estimated LAI with associated vigor metrics; height and vigor show significant interaction</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-3">Crown dimension/allometric equations predict tree sizes and leaf area; crown width, height, diameter relate to leaf area and LAI</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-7">Leaf area is a robust predictor of biomass and yield; LAI widely used and estimated across species and ages</cite>.
  - Height–NIR/VI models: Biomass ~ a*(Height*b + c*VI + d)^p, with root-mean-square error reductions when fusing height and VI relative to each alone <cite id="c28edca9-1">Barley biomass improved with joint height–index models, illustrating polynomial/linear fusion for trait estimation</cite>. Practical, rapid methods also use single-stem dimensions (e.g., main stem length) where calibration across species and growth stages is critical <cite id="c28edca9-4">Farmer-friendly method estimating cereal cover crop biomass from main-stem length illustrates low-cost proxy with need for calibration</cite>.

- fAPAR from canopy reflectance
  - Trait: photosynthetic active radiation absorption, key driver of primary productivity.
  - Two-source/empirical methods: fAPAR estimated from greenness/LAI proxies and land-surface algorithms (e.g., MODIS BRDF-adjusted fAPAR), or inversion of reflectance spectra with greenness indices; EVI-based and red-edge indices offer higher accuracy in dense, clumping canopies due to reduced soil/background mixing <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Index selection impacts downstream trait inference like fAPAR; differences in formulation (e.g., NDVI vs SAVI vs EVI) alter sensitivity and accuracy</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI’s blue/soil correction and red-edge term improve vegetation greenness in dense cover, aiding fractional cover retrievals</cite>.

Nitrogen deficiency and senescence/browning
- Nitrogen-sensitive indices and formulas
  - GNDVI and NDRE as nitrogen indices: higher GNDVI/NDRE in early-to-mid greenness with declining values as nitrogen becomes limiting and senescence progresses; NDRE can precede red-NIR decline due to red-edge sensitivity <cite id="636f6541-6">NDRE is particularly effective for detecting nutrient deficiencies in crops</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-0">NDRE is a chlorophyll-measuring method applicable in mid and late seasons for nitrogen monitoring</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-2">GNDVI/NDVI behavior varies by crop condition and nutrient status, guiding nitrogen decision support</cite>.
  - Additional nitrogen proxies: RGRI = 1 − (ρRed/ρNIR + ρRed/ρRedEdge); ratios where small denominators indicate high chlorophyll, or indices with Green-NIR emphasize N differently than RedNIR; tuning depends on sensor bands and crop red-edge placement <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Indices share similar mathematical families across spectral combinations, and trait interpretation (e.g., nitrogen) differs accordingly</cite>.

- PRI (Photochemical Reflectance Index; early stress/physiology)
  - Trait: chlorophyll photochemistry and nitrogen status prior to canopy-level greenness change.
  - Formula: PRI = (ρ531 − ρ570)/(ρ531 + ρ570) (or similar blue–green bands, e.g., 490–580 nm). Declines under senescence or nitrogen stress before NDVI shifts; used for early detection and yield/quality prediction <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Broad review outlines spectral-band-specific indices (e.g., blue/green combinations) whose formulation maps to biochemical traits like PRI for chlorophyll physiology</cite>.

Structural traits and management indices in crops/forestry
- Canopy cover/height/crown metrics
  - Crown area (CA), crown width (CW), tree/cover height (H), and crown projection area (CPA) summarized into vigor indices (e.g., CA, CW, CP/H and dimensionless CP/H3), widely used in forestry to quantify growth/vigor and extrapolate to LAI/wood production; empirical allometry relates diameter and height to biomass and leaf area <cite id="c28edca9-3">Equations for predicting tree sizes (diameter, height, crown width) and leaf area enable vigor and LAI estimation</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-5">Accurate LAI estimation related to sapwood area and crown structure underpins growth/efficiency modeling</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-0">Plant vigor and height show significant interaction in modeling LAI and vigor</cite>.
  - Simplified vigor index (VIg) in crops: plant height times crown width divided by diameter at base (or by area), used for early growth monitoring; regression to biomass improves when fused with VIg and canopy reflectance metrics <cite id="c28edca9-1">Fusing plant height and spectral indices provided improved biomass estimations versus single predictors</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-0">Empirical ground–air fusion estimated vigor along with LAI</cite>.
  - Rapid biomass estimation: single-stem metrics (e.g., main-stem length) with stage-specific calibrations provide fast, scalable proxies for within-field biomass mapping; validation with destructive sampling recommended <cite id="c28edca9-4">Main-stem length used to estimate cereal cover-crop biomass with farmer-friendly, robust methods; calibration is essential</cite>.

Relationships and implementation cautions
- Band definitions and calibration: Many indices are sensitive to sensor bands (Red ≈ 630–700 nm, Red-edge ≈ 730–750 nm, NIR ≈ 780–900 nm, SWIR1 ≈ 1300–1450 nm). Variations in bandpass/wavelength shift numeric behavior; use vendor-provided “atmospheric/soil-corrected reflectance” for EVI and calibrate site-specific coefficients for biomass/LAI regression <cite id="bb36acd8-8">Operational NDWI behavior depends on index band selection (vegetation vs water) and whether TOA or surface reflectance is used</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-7">Red-edge band placement around 730–740 nm is typical for NDRE</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI’s multiplicative gain and red-edge correction require consistent use of surface reflectance with defined constants</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Mathematical dissimilarity among NDVI, SAVI, EVI supports improved feature separation in crop trait modeling</cite>.
- Trait interpretation and thresholds: Indices vary by crop, phenology, and background. NDRE and GNDVI rise during early green-up, peak in mid-season, and drop as senescence and N limitation increase; CWSI uses canopy temperature and should be paired with NDVI to confine stress to actively transpiring canopies; water-channel NDWI (1300–1450 nm) tracks canopy moisture whereas red-band NDWI is soil-confounded <cite id="636f6541-6">NDRE detects nutrient deficiencies effectively</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-2">CWSI measures water stress via canopy-air temperature differences</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-8">Water indices differ in band selection and intended use (vegetation vs water bodies), affecting interpretation</cite>.

Practical index selection checklist
- Biomass/vigor and greenness in dense, uniform canopies: EVI or NDRE, then calibrate to green LAI and fAPAR; consider GNDVI for chlorophyll/N during early-to-mid season <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI and SAVI differ in soil/soil-mix handling; EVI is favored in dense canopies for greenness and LAI regressions</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-7">NDRE formulation allows sensitive tracking of chlorophyll and vigor</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Formulation differences among indices influence downstream trait estimation (e.g., biomass)</cite>.
- Sparse or early-season vegetation or dry conditions: SAVI with soil factor L, and NDWI (water band) to separate moisture constraints from chlorophyll decline; NDRE available where red-edge sensors exist <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">SAVI’s soil factor L reduces soil brightness influence for biomass/vigor in sparse vegetation</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-6">NDWI’s spectral design targets vegetation liquid water; use requires water-band data</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-4">NDRE requires red-edge; otherwise prefer NDVI when only red/NIR are available</cite>.
- Water stress mapping and irrigation scheduling: NDWI (1300–1450 nm) plus thermal CWSI for active stress detection; avoid NDVI-heavy methods during senescence or chlorophyll stress <cite id="bb36acd8-2">CWSI uses thermal stress differences to quantify crop water stress</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-4">In crops, WI/NDWI show improved sensitivity to canopy water content compared to NDVI/NDII</cite>.
- Structural/vigor and LAI in forestry/cereals: combine ground-measured crown dimensions and height with remote-sensing indices; use allometric equations and LAI–height regressions; fAPAR can be predicted from EVI and used in productivity models <cite id="c28edca9-3">Crown width, height, and leaf area equations underpin vigor metrics and LAI inference</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-1">Height plus spectral indices improve biomass estimation via fusion models</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Index selection and formulation affect downstream LAI/fAPAR-based productivity models</cite>.

Summary
- Commonly used plant trait indices are organized around spectral, thermal, and structural formulations, each mapping to a mechanistic trait (chlorophyll, water, structure) and a crop stage. The NDVI/SAGBI–EVI family quantify canopy greenness and density; NDRE/GNDVI emphasize chlorophyll/N and early senescence; NDWI and CWSI assess water content and stress; crown-based vigor indices and height–index models estimate LAI and biomass; and physiological indices like PRI capture early nitrogen/senescence changes. Each has a simple algebraic form grounded in band reflectance or geometry, but proper interpretation requires attention to sensor bands, vegetation density, phenology, and site-specific calibrations <cite id="4ef4bf02-2">NDVI uses a simple NIR–Red ratio and varies with crop condition</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-0">EVI and SAVI incorporate red-edge and soil terms to improve LAI and biomass inference</cite>. <cite id="636f6541-7">NDRE is (NIR − RedEdge)/(NIR + RedEdge) with RedEdge ~730–740 nm</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-6">NDWI uses (NIR − SWIR)/(NIR + SWIR) for vegetation water content</cite>. <cite id="bb36acd8-2">CWSI maps thermal stress to a 0–1 scale for water deficits</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-0">Vigor and height interact strongly in LAI estimation models</cite>. <cite id="c28edca9-3">Crown dimensions and allometries relate directly to leaf area and LAI</cite>. <cite id="4ef4bf02-6">Mathematical dissimilarity among indices improves their collective sensitivity to plant traits in modeling</cite>.

Below is an overview of major chemical compound types found in different plant parts, with concrete examples and organ-localization notes.

Roots
- Primary storage and transport metabolites: starch and sugars (glucose, sucrose), amino acids, and fatty acids accumulate in root tissues as energy and nutrient reserves; root exudates also contain organic acids and amino acids that interact with soil microbiota <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies plants with small molecules such as simple sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids—compounds ubiquitous across the plant—involved in growth, development, and transport</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Primary metabolites are involved in respiration and photosynthesis and maintain physiological functions</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites and specialized products:
  - Alkaloids (e.g., ephedrine/ephedrines in Ephedra; berberine and aristochinones in Berberis) and their glycosides often concentrate in roots and root-derived tissues, contributing to defense and medicinal value <cite id="c3047a02-0">Plant secondary metabolites include phenolic compounds, alkaloids, glycosides, and terpenoids, stored in specialized structures such as latex</cite> <cite id="c3047a00-8">Secondary metabolites are variously distributed in the plant kingdom; their organ-specific functions are species- and tissue-dependent</cite>.
  - Some latex-producing species (e.g., Ficus elastica) exude milky latex rich in hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipids; rubber (cis‑1,4‑polyisoprene) is synthesized in rubber tree (Hevea) latex, coagulated by lectins and other proteins <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy fatty acids are common constituents of cell surface glycosphingolipids in plants</cite> <cite id="81f633df-7">Hevea brasiliensis rubber particles contain rubber-specific proteins; latex coagulation involves a rubber particle protein-specific lectin</cite>.
  - Tannins and phenolics can also appear in root exudates and outer root tissues, contributing to rhizosphere interactions and defense <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolites such as phenolics and glycosides are stored in specialized structures (e.g., latex)</cite>.

Stems, Bark, and Wood (Xylem/Phloem/Cork)
- Structural and transport metabolites: lignin in xylem provides mechanical strength and hydrophobicity to tracheary elements; cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin dominate cell walls alongside variable lignin content by species and tissue (xylem vs. phloem vs. cork) <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin imparts mechanical strength to stems and trunks, and hydrophobicity to water-conducting vascular elements</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">The composition and structure of lignin differ among phellem (cork), phloem, and xylem (wood) within the same species</cite>.
- Phenolics and tannins: procyanidins and other condensed tannins are prominent in bark and wood, varying with monolignol subunit ratios (S:G:H) across species and ontogeny; monolignol S:G ratios correlate with functional wood traits (e.g., embolism resistance) <cite id="c087f4e9-8">Across tissues and species, monomeric lignin composition (S:G) is a key wood attribute affecting functional traits</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-0">Lignin composition and structure differ across wood and other plant materials, across species and tissues</cite>.
- Storage and secondary metabolites coexisting: in tree latex systems (e.g., Ficus, Euphorbia), rubber particles co-exist with phospholipids and polyphenols (gallic, naphthoic acids, flavonoids), illustrating mixed-phase secondary storage in stem appendages and trunks <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipids are characteristic components of rubber particles in Hevea and related latex-producing species</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex contains polyphenols including gallic acid, naphthoic acid, quercetin, chlorogenic acid, and rutin</cite> <cite id="81f633df-8">Hevea latex is a natural polymer system used medically, illustrating composition and utility</cite>.
- Organ-level mapping in Cannabis stems and roots: UPLC‑QTOF‑MS profiling shows secondary metabolite profiles differ among inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots, highlighting tissue-specific specialization (e.g., terpenes, phenolics, nitrogen-containing alkaloids) <cite id="c3047a02-4">Secondary metabolites profiled across Cannabis inflorescences, leaves, stem barks, and roots demonstrate organ-specific chemistries</cite>.

Leaves (Green Tissue, Trichomes, Stomatal Complexes, Latex/latexifers in some)
- Photosynthetic pigments: chlorophylls a/b and carotenoids dominate leaf biochemistry for light capture; these pigments, chloroplast-derived lipids, and sugar metabolites define “green tissue” chemistry <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies simple sugars as key photosynthetic end products</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Photosynthesis and respiration underpin primary metabolite flow in leaves</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites and specialized structures:
  - Glandular trichomes on leaves are common factories for terpenoids, phenolics, and alkaloids; nicotine is a well-known alkaloid stored on leaf surfaces in Nicotiana species, illustrating defense in epidermal structures <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes commonly store metabolites on the plant surface; nicotine is a well-known example</cite>.
  - In Cannabis leaves, inflorescences, stems, and roots show overlapping but distinct secondary metabolite profiles, with terpenoids (ent-copalyl/abeo-17-ene derivatives), flavonoids, and nitrogen-containing alkaloids varying by organ <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific secondary metabolite profiles (terpenes, phenolics, alkaloids) are documented in Cannabis leaves and inflorescences</cite>.
  - Some leaves (e.g., citrus) concentrate phenylpropane-derived metabolites in peel/epidermis: limonoid triterpenes, flavonoid glycosides, and essential oils in secretory cells or glandular trichomes; tannins (catechins/condensed proanthocyanidins) are prominent in tea leaves <cite id="c3047a02-0">Terpenoids and phenolics are typical secondary metabolites stored in specialized secretory structures (glands, latex)</cite>.
  - Glucosinolates (e.g., glucoinsulfrates in Brassica) and their sulfur-rich degradation products are characteristic leaf metabolites, often sequestered in vacuoles and contributing antimicrobial/herbivore deterrence; leaf peels accumulate phenylpropane glycosides and wax esters <cite id="07d77ca4-0">Secondary metabolism yields phenolics and alkaloids widely present in plant tissues such as leaves</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Flavonoids and phenolics are representative secondary metabolites localized to leaf cells</cite>.

Flowers
- Terpenoids and phenolics predominate: floral volatiles (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes) from glandular trichomes drive pollinator attraction and pathogen defense; flavonoids, naringenin glycosides, anthocyanidins, and flavonols decorate petals and sepals <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes store terpenes and related secondary metabolites on floral surfaces</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific metabolite profiling shows distinct terpenoid, phenolic, and alkaloid patterns across flower/leaf/stem/root tissues</cite>.
- Alkaloids and glycosides may occur in perianths and styles depending on species (e.g., tropane/coralarine alkaloids in some Solanaceae), while amino acids/sugars supply energy to pollinators <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolites such as amino acids and sugars serve growth and signaling while secondary metabolites provide specialized defense</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Alkaloids and terpenoids (secondary) are synthesized via modified primary pathways and tissue-restricted deposition</cite>.

Fruits and Seeds (including Seed Coats/Husks, Aleurone/Endosperm)
- Storage compounds: dry-seed storage features triacylglycerols (oils) in embryos and endosperms (e.g., flaxseed oil), while seed coats and husks commonly concentrate tannins and phenolics (hydrolysable and condensed types) for protection; proteins/peptides and free amino acids are prevalent in non-oil-seeds and seedlings <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism provides fatty acids; storage triacylglycerols accumulate in seeds</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Proteins and amino acids are primary metabolite–derived storage forms supporting germination</cite>.
- Phenylpropane-rich seed coatings: fruits and坚果 husks often display high condensed-tannin/proanthocyanidin levels (e.g., hazelnut husks, rose hips, chestnuts), with proanthocyanidin subunit patterns influencing astringency and protection <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol-derived phenolics structure lignin-like phenylpropane polymers with tissue- and species-dependent compositions</cite>.
- Sugars, organic acids, and aroma volatiles accumulate in fleshy fruits; terpenoids and esters drive aroma; anthocyanins and betalains color pericarps; alkaloids may localize to placenta or inner pericarp in some genera (e.g., solanaceous tomatos/peppers) <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolite classes (phenolics, terpenoids, alkaloids) are synthesized via modified primary pathways and stored in fruits</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific metabolomics confirm tissue differences, e.g., terpenes and phenolics enriched in inflorescences and leaves with differences in roots</cite>.
- Aleurone layers in cereal grains store carbohydrates (amylopectin in aleurone) and synthesize storage proteins; endosperm contains storage starch in aleurone-rich kernels; these layers also accumulate phenylpropane-derived cell-wall phenolics <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Starch and sugars are primary metabolite end products that can be re-allocated as storage within seeds</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Aleurone and endosperm function via primary metabolic pathways for carbohydrate storage</cite>.

Across Plant Parts: Specialized Secretory Systems
- Latex and cellulosic secretory canals: many taxa secrete latex in ducts; Hevea and related species store rubber polymers alongside phospholipids and phenolic antioxidants, with latex coagulation proteins indicating specialized biosynthesis/secretion routes <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex contains gallic, naphthoic acids, flavonoids, and other polyphenols</cite> <cite id="81f633df-6">Rubber particles in Hevea and related species display characteristic lipid/glycosphingolipid compositions</cite> <cite id="81f633df-7">A rubber particle protein-specific lectin mediates latex coagulation</cite>.
- Glandular trichomes: epidermal glands synthesize and store terpenoids (monoterpenes, diterpenes), phenolics (flavonoids, tannins), and sometimes alkaloids; Cannabis, Solanum, and Nicotiana exemplify organ- and species-specific trichome chemistry (cannabinoids, tropanes, nicotine) <cite id="c3047a02-3">Nicotine is a well-known alkaloid stored in leaf surface trichomes</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Cannabis glandular trichomes show metabolite profiles distinguishing inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots</cite>.
- Cork, laticifers, aril/seed-coat cells, and parenchyma rays can exhibit tissue-specific accumulation of monolignols/phenolics, generating species-typical tannins, cork acetates, essential oil droplets, and resin phenolics <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol-derived lignin composition differs among cork (phellem), phloem, and xylem (wood), emphasizing tissue-specific phenylpropane metabolism</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Plant latexes are widely distributed in bark, stems, roots, fruits, and leaves, hosting diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

Examples by Compound Class and Tissue
- Phenolics and tannins: condensed and hydrolysable tannins rich in (+)-catechin/prodelphinidin subunits occur in seed coats and fruit husks (e.g., Rosaceae drupes,坚果), while cork and wood store suberin/lignin phenylpropane polymers that differ among tissues and ages <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Lignin and related phenylpropane structures differ among xylem, phloem, and cork in a single species</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-8">Monolignol S:G ratios relate to xylem embolism resistance, reflecting phenylpropane chemistry in functional traits</cite>.
- Terpenoids (isoprenoids): plastidial MEP and MEP-derived volatiles dominate floral and foliar aromas and defense; diterpenes form ginkgolides in Ginkgo leaves, while resin acids/copalane diterpenoids appear in conifer resins and galls <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes store monoterpenes and diterpenes such as nicotine and terpenoids</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary isoprenoid precursors feed secondary terpenoid pathways</cite>.
- Alkaloids and their glycosides: tropane/coralarine alkaloids (hyoscyamine/scopolamine in nightshade leaves/fruits), benzoylisoquinoline morphine and codeine in Papaver somniferum latex/berries, and purine alkaloids (caffeine in leaves/beans, ephedrine in Ephedra) exemplify tissue-specific distributions—often leaves, stems, or latex ducts—correlated with biosynthetic pathways <cite id="c3047a02-0">Alkaloids are characteristic secondary metabolites synthesized via modified primary pathways in specific tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-1">Secondary metabolites vary by tissue and species, with functions tied to organ localization</cite>.
- Glucosinolates and other nitrogenous glycosides: Sulfur- and nitrogen-rich gluco‑ and isothiocyanate derivatives are typical Brassica leaves and peels; they deter herbivores and pathogens, with hydrolyzable nitriles and isothiocyanates released upon tissue damage <cite id="c3047a02-0">Glucosinolates and alkaloids represent classic secondary metabolite classes in plant tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-8">Glandular trichomes and secretory cells store nitrogenous secondary metabolites and their aglycones</cite>.
- Starch and storage proteins/lipids: root (carrot, sweet potato, corm) and caryopsis aleurone store starch in amylose/amylopectin granules; embryos and endosperms accumulate oils; storage proteins (globulins/albumins) localize to cotyledons/aleurone based on species—maize aleurone stores starch in granules while aleurone phenolics co-localize with storage proteins <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism yields sugars and fatty acids, which are sequestered as starch and triacylglycerols in seeds and root tissues</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Proteins and amino acids participate in growth and storage; storage allocation is driven by primary metabolism</cite>.
- Rubber and latex lipids: cis‑1,4‑polyisoprene rubber synthesized in specialized cells/particles in Hevea, Parthenium, Ficus, and Euphorbia; rubber particles co-exist with phospholipids (PC/PI/PE major fractions) and polyphenolic antioxidants/oxidants, enabling coagulation and long-term storage <cite id="81f633df-6">Hevea rubber particles are defined by hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipid compositions</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex includes phenolic antioxidants (e.g., chlorogenic acid, rutin)</cite> <cite id="81f633df-0">Phospholipid classes (PC, PI, PE) dominate latex and rubber particles’ lipidomes</cite>.
- Photosynthetic pigments and carotenoids: chlorophylls a and b, pheophytin, and carotenoids (carotenes/xanthophylls like lutein, zeaxanthin) are concentrated in mesophyll/chloroplasts of leaves; some fruits store carotenoids as pigments (beta‑carotin, lycopin) <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Photosynthesis-based primary metabolism produces chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments essential for light harvesting</cite>.

How to interpret the “types” and “examples”
- Primary metabolites (ubiquitous, growth/development): carbohydrates (sucrose, starch, sugars), amino acids/proteins, fatty acids/triacylglycerols, energy intermediates (ATP, sugars), and cell-wall polymers (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin), with tissue-specific accumulation in roots, green tissue, seeds, and vascular tissues <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids essential for plant growth</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Primary metabolites are central to respiration and photosynthesis and underpin tissue development</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites (defense/toxicity/attraction): phenolics and tannins, lignin and suberin, terpenoids (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes), alkaloids (pyrrolidine, indole, tropane, purine), and glycosylated derivatives (glucosinolates, glycosides) that often localize to vacuoles, specialized cells, trichomes, laticifers, seed coats, and secretory structures; these often vary by organ and species and can be highly enriched in specific parts (e.g., latex ducts in Ficus/Hevea; glandular trichomes on Cannabis leaves; alkaloid-rich leaves/peels in nightshades/Brassica) <cite id="c3047a02-0">Plants synthesize secondary metabolites such as phenolic compounds, alkaloids, glycosides, and terpenoids as chemical diversity for defense and signaling</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-1">Secondary metabolites show species- and organ-specific distributions with defined ecological functions</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes and latex are common organ-specific depots for alkaloids and terpenes</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latexes occur widely across bark, stems, roots, fruits, and leaves, carrying diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

Practical mapping summary
- Roots: starch/sugars, amino acids, fatty acids as reserves; alkaloids/phenolics/tannins in exudates/outer tissues; rubber/latex and rubber particle lipids present in some latexiferous roots (e.g., Ficus elastica) and rubber tree exudate <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy-fatty-acid/glycosphingolipid-rich rubber particles occur in latexiferous root tissues</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex polyphenols exemplify organ-rich phenolics in root-derived latex</cite>.
- Stems/bark/wood: structural polysaccharide–lignin composites in tracheary elements; tissue-specific monolignol compositions (xylem vs phloem vs cork); phenolics/tannins; storage starch or oils in pith; latex in some stems (Ficus/Artocarpus) <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin gives stems and trunks mechanical strength and hydrophobicity</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol compositions differ across stem tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latex distribution spans bark and stems widely</cite>.
- Leaves: pigments plus primary metabolites; trichome-derived terpenoids/phenolics/alkaloids; glucosinolates and other glycosides in Brassica leaves; essential oils and anthocyanins in peels/peripheral tissues <cite id="c3047a02-3">Nicotine and trichome-stored terpenoids exemplify leaf surface defenses</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Flavonoids and phenolics are characteristic leaf secondary metabolites</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Cannabis leaves show organ-resolved secondary metabolite profiles</cite>.
- Flowers: terpenoid-rich volatiles, flavonoids/anthocyanins in perianths; alkaloids in some perianth/stigmatic tissues; amino acids/sugars support pollination <cite id="c3047a02-4">Floral tissues differ in terpenoid, phenolic, and alkaloid profiles relative to leaves/stems/roots</cite>.
- Fruits/seed: sugars, acids, aroma terpenoids/esters; anthocyanins and betalains; seed storage lipids (oil bodies) and proteins in aleurone/endosperm; tannin-rich husks/coats (hazelnut/rose hip/chestnut); lignified placenta/seed coats; latex in non-tomato Solanaceous fruits (capsaicin-bearing placenta exemplifies pericarp/seed-tissue enrichment) <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolites supply sugars and amino acids to fleshy tissues</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Storage proteins/amino acids are central to germination reserves</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Phenylpropane-derived polymers vary across fruit-derived tissues</cite>.

Notes on variability and species specificity
- Many compounds are tissue-restricted within a species and absent from others; e.g., tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae, benzoylisoquinoline alkaloids and morphine/codeine in Papaver, limonoid triterpenes and essential oils in Rutaceae peels, and ginkgolides unique to Ginkgo leaves <cite id="c3047a02-1">Organ-level distributions and functions of secondary metabolites are species- and tissue-specific</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolite classes arise from modified primary pathways and are stored organ-selectively</cite>.
- Ontogeny and environment modulate levels (e.g., ethylene elevates latex yield in Hevea), with tissue-specific responses and co-regulation of primary and secondary metabolism <cite id="81f633df-5">Ethylene induces latex yield via multi-omic reprogramming in Hevea rubber trees</cite>.

What’s less commonly emphasized
- Some metabolites bridge multiple organs: for example, linseed oil provides seed-storage lipids while flax stem/seed-coat tissues concentrate lignan-derived tannins; cannabis inflorescences concentrate terpenes and cannabidiol, yet roots and stems carry detectable alkaloid/phenolic signals, underscoring long-range metabolite transport and organ-specific sinks <cite id="c3047a02-4">Inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots each show distinct secondary metabolite profiles in Cannabis</cite>.

Key takeaways
- In roots, expect reserve carbohydrates/proteins/lipids and alkaloids/phenolics; in stems/wood, expect lignin and tissue-contrast phenylpropane polymers, plus occasional latex; in leaves, expect pigments with trichome-associated terpenoids/phenolics/alkaloids and leaf-vacuolar glucosinolates; in flowers, expect terpenes and phenolics; in fruits and seeds, expect sugars/acids/aroma volatiles, seed-coat tannins, and storage starch/protein/oil in aleurone/endosperm. <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism underpins reserves (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) found across roots, stems, leaves, and seeds</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin’s physical roles fix the structural chemistry of stems and trunks</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-3">Trichomes serve as organ-specific factories and depots for alkaloids/terpenoids</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latex distribution across multiple organs links secretory biology to diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

Overview and definitions
Regeneration level in plants is typically operationalized as the capacity of excised tissues or whole plants to re-establish meristems, reorganize cells, and form new organs or entire plants after injury or in vitro wounding. This is often measured by presence/formation of shoot or root apical meristems (SAMs), efficiency of de novo shoot/root organogenesis, restoration of growth/survival after incision, or molecular markers of competence, and can be inferred indirectly via physiological, biochemical, and hormonal readouts that track recovery and tissue reprogramming. <cite id="b9d22b9e-3">Plant regeneration is defined as the process by which plants recover from injury through mechanisms that involve oriented cell divisions, acquisition of new organ identity, and developmental reprogramming</cite> <cite id="b9d22b9e-9">De novo formation of shoot apical meristems that give rise to lateral organs is central to successful regeneration</cite>.

Direct methods for determining regeneration level
Direct methods measure regenerative status by observing or quantifying actual tissue/organ formation and cellular re-entry into meristematic activity.

- Histology and meristem/tissue readouts: Presence or re-emergence of functional SAMs and root apical meristems (RAMs), and subsequent organ outgrowth, are core direct readouts of regeneration capacity. <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Plant shoots and roots retain apical meristem functions even after part of the meristem is removed, enabling regrowth via organogenesis</cite> <cite id="b9d22b9e-2">Regeneration protocols score shoot clusters with obvious apical meristems and subsequent elongation into new stems</cite> <cite id="e01d9d06-2">Successful lateral root formation requires reactivation of a functional lateral root apical meristem after injury</cite>. Quantitative endpoints include number of shoots per explant, frequency of meristem formation, and survival/elongation thresholds; for example, shoot regeneration frequencies below 10% have been reported in some stem explants, while optimized conditions can yield 50% maximum regenerative response, providing concrete, countable “levels” of competence. <cite id="a496e5d9-3">Excised tissues can regenerate new shoot apical meristems, but regeneration rates and organogenesis frequencies can be variable and context-dependent</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-6">The maximum regenerative response of 50% was observed for Arabidopsis cotyledon-plus-shoot-apex explants, illustrating quantitative benchmarking of shoot regeneration</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-5">Some protocols achieve shoot frequencies below 10% per explant with subunitary average shoot numbers, underscoring the need for optimization</cite>.

- Reporter- and imaging-based competence assays: Genetic reporters of the developmental and hormonal pathways that gate regeneration provide spatially resolved, in situ readouts of competence and activity. DR5 (SAG:19:GUS/GFP) is widely used as an auxin-response reporter to visualize regenerative wave patterns and competence gradients during de novo shoot meristem assembly; low DR5 signal precludes meristem initiation, while high DR5 accompanies organogenic outgrowth. <cite id="e01d9d06-3">Areas of low DR5 signal are associated with blocked shoot meristem initiation, whereas induction of new shoot meristems and organ formation is observed where DR5 reporter activity is elevated</cite>. However, DR5-reporter systems can be bottlenecks in high-throughput breeding/selection because not all tissues show strong DR5 responsiveness, and reporter dynamics must be carefully timed. <cite id="e01d9d06-4">The DR5:GFP auxin-signaling reporter is a major bottleneck in applying new plant breeding technologies and for shoot meristem development studies</cite>. ER8::GUS and GRF-MCS:GFP reporters similarly mark competence nodes in Arabidopsis regeneration via shoot meristem re-specification and cytokinin-auxin cross-talk, providing direct functional evidence of regenerative competence. <cite id="e01d9d06-7">Auxin- and cytokinin-regulated transcription factors and reporters govern the de novo assembly and lateral organogenesis in regenerating tissues</cite>. Chemical inhibitor assays can disambiguate pathway dependence: for example, compounds affecting regeneration while leaving DR5 or ARR5 reporter activities unchanged indicate effects on transport or injury signaling rather than direct auxin/cytokinin mimicry, directly linking reporter signals to competence metrics. <cite id="e01d9d06-6">Decreased regeneration without changes in DR5::GUS or ARR5::GUS reporter activities suggests effects are not due to direct auxin or cytokinin-like activities, establishing causal links between reporters and pathway-specific competence</cite>.

- Functional organogenesis assays and wounding tests: Regeneration level is often scored by the efficiency of de novo shoot or root formation from explants under defined hormones and light/temperature regimes. Standard two-step shoot regeneration uses root segments on auxin-rich callus-inducing medium followed by cytokinin-rich shoot-inducing medium; efficient shoot bud number per explant (e.g., >15 shoots/root explant) directly quantifies competence. <cite id="a496e5d9-1">Shoots can be regenerated from root explants via a two-step protocol: callus induction on auxin-rich medium followed by shoot differentiation on cytokinin-rich medium</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-7">An optimized shoot regeneration method produced 15.2 shoots per root explant in Populus ussuriensis, providing a quantitative endpoint for regeneration level</cite>. Explant choice and pre-treatments (e.g., removing cotyledons or shoot apex) systematically modulate regenerative frequency, enabling graded measurement of competence across genotypes/treatments. <cite id="a496e5d9-6">Removing both cotyledons and the shoot apex maximized shoot regeneration frequency (50%), demonstrating explant manipulation as a lever to read competence levels</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-3">Excised explants’ shoot regeneration capacity is sensitive to explant identity and light conditions, and shows variable base rates that must be standardized in assays</cite>. Local wound signaling and jasmonate/auxin crosstalk are directly assessed by incision assays that quantify callus and organ outgrowth timelines after tissue damage. <cite id="a496e5d9-0">Wounding rapidly triggers jasmonate signaling at injury sites and is accompanied by de novo root regeneration, enabling wound-assay readouts of tissue repair and regenerative competence</cite>.

Indirect methods for determining regeneration level
Indirect methods infer regenerative capacity from physiological, biochemical, hormonal, and systems-level signals that track injury response vigor and the reprogramming trajectory, often without requiring direct organ formation in the same assay.

- Physiological and redox-based readouts: Wounding elicits rapid, spatially organized ROS bursts at the injury site and systemically, which can be imaged live to quantify injury severity, recovery dynamics, and systemic reprogramming; robust whole-plant ROS imaging in soil-grown or intact plants has been established and used to study “ROS waves.” <cite id="b5573fe5-1">Wounding induces reactive oxygen species such as H2O2 in Arabidopsis leaves</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-2">Whole-plant imaging detects rapid ROS increases at wound sites and systemically after injury</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-5">Live whole-plant imaging of ROS levels shows a systemic ROS wave accompanying injury, enabling quantitative redox analyses during recovery</cite>. Proline accumulation and transport play key roles in wound-induced signaling and ROS homeostasis during tissue repair and organ regeneration, acting as both biomarkers and regulators; manipulating wound-induced proline transport alters the balance between immunity and regeneration, linking proline dynamics to competence. <cite id="b5573fe5-0">Wound-induced proline transporters and the interplay between SA-mediated immunity and regeneration highlight proline, ROS homeostasis, and signaling as axes balancing immunity and tissue repair</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-3">Proline is crucial in stress responses and development, offering mechanistic links between osmolyte accumulation and regenerative processes</cite>. These redox/osmotic markers can thus flag submeristem-level injury handling and recovery capacity, which correlate with successful later organogenesis. <cite id="b5573fe5-4">Stress-induced ROS signaling activates senescence, but regenerative responses can temper or divert these pathways to avoid growth loss</cite>.

- Developmental and hormonal systems-level proxies: Regeneration competence is strongly gated by auxin and cytokinin signaling, including local auxin biosynthesis, transport inhibition, and cytokinin-mediated positive feedback loops; these can be probed by exogenous hormone manipulations and pathway-inhibitor screens to gauge competence thresholds without scoring every organ. <cite id="a496e5d9-2">A cytokinin-signaling positive feedback ensures efficient de novo shoot organogenesis and can be targeted to overcome low regeneration rates</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-0">JA signaling is rapidly activated after wounding, and de novo root regeneration emerges as a typical wound response, linking hormones to injury-triggered competence</cite>. Auxin-pathway reporters (DR5/ARR5) integrated into inhibition tests distinguish whether a compound enhances regenerative competence via hormonal mimicry versus via transport or injury-signal amplification, providing indirect yet mechanistic assessments. <cite id="e01d9d06-6">Changes in regeneration without concomitant changes in DR5::GUS or ARR5::GUS activities indicate that effects are not due to direct auxin or cytokinin-like actions, clarifying indirect pathway involvement</cite>.

- Phenotypic and transcriptomic/organismic proxies: Post-regeneration survival, growth rate, and chlorophyll fluorescence recovery/photoinhibition indices can indirectly reflect competence and photosynthetic reactivation after injury. <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Sustainable regrowth requires maintenance of meristem function and successful organogenesis, where growth recovery is a downstream proxy for regeneration efficiency</cite>. In practice, indirect high-throughput pipelines quantify wound-induced whole-plant redox dynamics and hormonal perturbations to triage genotypes for further direct regeneration assays, balancing speed and mechanistic interpretability. <cite id="b5573fe5-8">Whole-plant live imaging of ROS provides a robust, straightforward method for phenotyping injury and recovery dynamics, which can be integrated with downstream organogenesis tests</cite>.

Direct vs. indirect comparisons: what each buys you, with trade-offs
- Resolution and causality: Direct assays directly quantify regeneration endpoints (meristem presence, organ number/elongation, survival) and thus give precise, organismic-level measures of “level,” enabling unambiguous benchmarking across genotypes and treatments. They capture competence as manifested in tissues and organs but can be labor-intensive and explant-dependent, with variable baselines and growth conditions shaping outcomes. <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Retention of apical meristem function allows direct readout of regrowth capacity after tissue removal</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-3">Light and explant source strongly influence baseline regeneration rates in tissue culture, requiring standardization</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-6">Explant manipulations (cotyledon and apex removal) yield stepwise increases in shoot regeneration frequency, providing quantitative controls</cite>. In contrast, indirect assays measure mechanistic intermediates (ROS waves, proline fluxes, auxin/cytokinin signaling via reporters or perturbations) that are causally involved in competence acquisition; they can prioritize lines or conditions for optimization but may mislead if disentangled from context-specific injury physiology. <cite id="b5573fe5-0">Wound-induced proline transport connects immunity and regeneration, showing that “regeneration level” is intertwined with stress signaling</cite> <cite id="e01d9d06-6">Auxin/cytokinin-like mimics can confound reporter-based competence readouts, necessitating pathway-specific controls</cite>.

- Throughput and cost: Reporter-based imaging and organogenesis screens strike a practical balance—automatable for medium-to-high throughput, but still explant-centric. Reporter-based systems are powerful but can be bottlenecks if signals are weak or timing is off, whereas physiology-based ROS imaging scales to whole-plant phenotyping and can quickly fractionate regenerators from non-regenerators. <cite id="e01d9d06-4">DR5:GFP can become a bottleneck for breeding and functional mapping due to limited responsiveness or timing constraints</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-8">Live whole-plant ROS imaging is straightforward and scalable across mature plants grown in soil</cite>.

- Interpretability and mechanistic leverage: Indirect, signaling-level methods offer mechanistic levers for boosting regeneration—e.g., cytokinin-positive feedback or JA/ET–auxin crosstalk—and can reveal trade-offs (immunity vs. repair). Direct methods confirm that the mechanism translated into successful organogenesis. Together they form a feedback loop: indirect assays triage candidates and tune hormonal/tissue contexts, while direct assays validate conversion into regenerates with quantified efficiency. <cite id="a496e5d9-2">Cytokinin signaling positive loops can be harnessed to ensure efficient de novo shoot formation</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-0">Proline transporters and SA–regeneration tradeoffs demonstrate the need to balance stress responses when optimizing regeneration</cite> <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Ultimately, restoration of meristem function and organ formation validates regenerative competence</cite>.

Practical guidance: combining direct and indirect strategies to estimate and improve “regeneration level”
A common, robust pipeline:
1) Screen indirectly using rapid, non-invasive whole-plant phenotyping to flag superior regenerative vigor. Whole-plant ROS dynamics after standardized wounding and proline-related stress signatures can prioritize genotypes/conditions that resolve injury faster and more broadly. <cite id="b5573fe5-5">System-wide ROS changes accompany injury and can be tracked live across entire plants in soil</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-0">Proline-transporter perturbations alter the balance between immunity and regeneration</cite>. 
2) Confirm and quantify by direct, explant-based regeneration assays. Use two-step shoot regeneration from root explants to compute shoot frequency per explant and average shoot number; incorporate explant manipulations (e.g., apex/cotyledon removal) as quantitative controls to normalize and escalate competence estimates. <cite id="a496e5d9-1">Two-step organogenesis assays provide standardized, quantitative shoot regeneration endpoints across explants</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-6">Specific explant removals can raise maximum regeneration frequency from sub-10% to 50%, offering quantitative levers and controls</cite>. 
3) Overlay genetic-reporter imaging to read pathway-specific mechanisms. Time-series DR5/ER8/GRF-MCS imaging of wounded explants captures competence gradients and validates whether cytokinin or auxin/SA/JA crosstalk is limiting. <cite id="e01d9d06-3">DR5-based reporters delineate competence hotspots for de novo shoot meristem induction and lateral organ formation</cite> <cite id="e01d9d06-6">Reporter activities can distinguish true hormonal competence from non-hormonal injury responses</cite>. 
4) Adjust using mechanistic insights. If ROS bursts are excessive and persistent, increase antioxidant capacity or adjust wounding intensity; if proline accumulation dominates stress over repair, modulate proline transport/signaling; if auxin/cytokinin ratios are suboptimal, tune medium composition and positive feedback loops. <cite id="b5573fe5-3">Proline acts developmentally and stess-respondingly, informing medium and genetic interventions</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-2">Cytokinin’s positive feedback can be engineered or enhanced to lift low regeneration rates</cite>.

Special cases and nuances
Regeneration “level” is highly context-dependent across species and tissues; leaf versus root explants, species sensitivity to wounding, and culture regimes can shift direct and indirect readouts. Thus, establishing assay-specific baselines and controls is essential: standardize explant age/size, medium composition, and injury severity, and tie indirect markers to the same injury/medium regimes to avoid cross-context misinterpretation. <cite id="b9d22b9e-1">Adventitious shoot formation efficiency depends on explant source, basal media, and plant growth regulators</cite> <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Retention of meristem functionality and subsequent organ growth depends on these same conditions, requiring harmonization across direct/indirect measures</cite>.

Summary
Direct methods—histological scoring of meristems, organogenesis counts, survival and elongation, and pathway-reporter imaging—provide organism-level, mechanistic confirmation of regeneration capacity and the most reliable “level of regeneration” metrics. <cite id="b9d22b9e-0">Meristem retention and growth</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-1">Two-step shoot regeneration frequencies</cite> <cite id="e01d9d06-3">DR5/ER8 imaging gradients</cite>. Indirect methods—wound-based ROS and proline flux imaging and hormonal perturbation assays—offer rapid, scalable proxies and causal levers; when combined, they enable discovery, mechanism-grounded optimization, and validation. <cite id="b5573fe5-5">Live whole-plant ROS waves</cite> <cite id="b5573fe5-0">Proline–immunity/repair tradeoffs</cite> <cite id="a496e5d9-2">Cytokinin positive feedbacks</cite>. In practice, use indirect assays for triage and design, and direct assays for quantitative benchmarking and confirmation of regenerative competence. <cite id="e01d9d06-6">Reporter-based controls reveal when indirect signals reflect pathway-specific competence rather than raw auxin mimicry</cite>.

Overview

Residue retention—leaving plant material on the soil surface or incorporating it shallowly—impacts seedling establishment and plant height through physical, nutritional, and chemical mechanisms. Fresh residue layers can block imbibition and emergence, alter soil water/warmer dynamics, and temporarily immobilize nutrients; as residues decompose, microorganisms produce phytotoxins (allelochemicals) from complex molecules that suppress germination and early growth. Over time, leaching and further decomposition reduce phytotoxicity, though crop and weed residues can still depress plant height and shoot growth via released inhibitors and, in some systems, via persistence of bioactive compounds or byproducts <cite id="891547ae-0">The senescent leaves contained an array of allelochemicals that were inhibitory to spruce seed germination and seedling growth</cite><cite id="891547ae-3">Allelochemicals can stimulate or inhibit plant germination and growth, and permit the development of crops with low phytotoxic residue amounts in water and soil</cite><cite id="483faf38-4">The plastic debris had a significant negative effect on plant height and culm diameter during the entire growth stage of soybean</cite>.

Plant residue compounds responsible for growth inhibition (allelochemicals)

- Catechins and polyphenols (tannins): Green tea residues are rich in catechins (e.g., epigallocatechin gallate, EGCG), which strongly suppress germination and early seedling growth of multiple species. The toxicity of tea residues correlates with polyphenol content, while composting and time often reduce inhibition in bioassays <cite id="891547ae-4">Numerous studies have shown that many phenolics are inhibitory to germinating seeds or growing plants</cite><cite id="24c9d85d-6">The most abundant type of catechin in green tea is epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG; 12%)</cite><cite id="24c9d85d-7">We hypothesized that the presence of caffeine released from the tea in the soil is a determinant for weed growth inhibition in tea production</cite><cite id="24c9d85d-0">Incorporation of plant residues into the growth environment of another plant may inhibit the germination and seedling growth</cite>. 

- Phenylpropanoids and phenylcarboxylic acids (ferulic/sinapic): Phenolic profiling studies identify phenolics, including juglone (a quinone), as potent germination and growth inhibitors in black walnut systems and others; these compounds are typical breakdown products of lignin/phenylpropanoid pathways and accumulate during residue processing or microbial conversion <cite id="891547ae-1">Studies have shown that certain phenolic compounds, such as juglone produced by black walnut trees (Juglans nigra), inhibit the germination and growth of nearby</cite><cite id="891547ae-8">A large number of plants produce secondary metabolites known as allelochemicals that are capable of inhibiting the germination of competitive</cite>.
