- Osmotic and ionic-exchange swelling in expansive clays/shales: Water influx raises degree of hydration and promotes ionic exchange (e.g., Ca2+/Na+), lowering matric suction and increasing osmotic pressure within fine-pored, nano-to-micro fracture networks; hydromechanical coupling then translates hydraulic pressures into mechanical dilation, increased pore volume, and outward forces on walls. <cite id="feff79a9-5">Hydromechanical coupling arises when pore/fracture pressures in a water-filled rock mass change, inducing coupled deformation and flow feedback</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-7">Time-dependent anisotropic swelling can be simulated with osmotic swelling models that depend on water content, capturing absorption-driven expansion</cite>.
- Flow-enhanced transport and reaction kinetics: Increased groundwater flow delivers water and ions into joints and bedding planes, accelerating hydration/ionic exchange and transport of swelling products; this can localize swelling and cracking along preferential pathways and interfaces exposed by excavation. <cite id="4d42ab33-4">Excavation also changes geochemical conditions in the tunnel zone</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-5">Pressure changes in water-filled fractures/pores drive coupled mechanical and hydraulic responses</cite> <cite id="e83705b3-0">Wetting-induced phase transformation (anhydrite→gypsum) in excavated clay–sulfate rocks generates swelling pressures and invert heave</cite>.
- Post-excavation feedback and consolidation: As excavation disturbs confining pressures and dewatering lowers heads, the system evolves with re-percolation during stoping or seasonal recharge; zones adjacent to the opening experience cyclic wetting–drying and pressure relaxation, promoting progressive swelling and potential instability unless hydraulically managed. <cite id="4d42ab33-0">Excavation modifies capture zones and local flow, enabling chemical and mechanical evolution of the rock mass</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-2">Under hydraulic pressure and engineering disturbance, surrounding rock fractures, forming water channels and facilitating hydromechanical feedback</cite>.

Consequences observed in tunnels and excavations
- Tunnel invert heave and upward extrusions: Water ingress and anhydrite activation in clay–sulfate units produce inward pressure that lifts the invert, disrupts linings, and impedes traffic. <cite id="e83705b3-0">Swelling of clay–sulfate rocks causes heave of the tunnel invert and associated swelling pressures</cite>.
- Localized swelling-induced instability and lining damage: Zones with concentrated water inflows and reactive minerals show dilation, cracking, and increased radial stresses that compromise support, requiring active drainage and jointed waterproofing strategies. <cite id="e83705b3-4">Localized swelling-induced instability of tunnels has been reported, where volumetric swelling upon water absorption analogizes to thermal expansion in magnitude</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-0">Expansion and softening of surrounding rock increase loads on tunnel lining, intensifying instability risks</cite>.
- Peeling and flaking at interfaces: In weak, swelling rock masses, layered interfaces exhibit flaking, shear sliding, and compression-induced tensile cracking; excavation and wetting accelerate these failure modes by removing interlayer cohesion and focusing hydraulic gradients along discontinuities. <cite id="feff79a9-6">Hydromechanical coupling under hydraulic pressure and disturbance induces fracture behavior and water channels, aggravating failure</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-8">Failure modes of swelling rock include flaking, shear failure, and compression-induced tensile cracking</cite> <cite id="e83705b3-3">Swelling rock is a special soft rock that expands and swells upon water absorption; tunneling in such zones is particularly difficult</cite>.
- Case evidence across geologies: Tunneling through swelling rock has produced large deformations and support failures; hydraulic tunnels show surface-water drawdown and controlled dewatering to manage inflows; dewatering strategies and waterproofing joints are used to mitigate swelling-driven heave. <cite id="e83705b3-6">Tunnelling in weakness zones containing swelling clay results in large problems and difficult conditions, including heave and instability</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-6">Hydraulic tunnel excavation drives groundwater into the tunnel with surface-level fall, necessitating in-tunnel dewatering</cite> <cite id="e83705b3-8">A jointed waterproofing structure has been proposed to counteract swelling potential in clay–sulfate tunnel environments</cite>.

Mechanistic chain: how flow changes and excavation lead to swelling
1) Excavation creates an open path and boundary discontinuity, lowering heads locally and drawing groundwater into and out of the opening; permeability anisotropy and fractures direct flow into joints and bedding, elevating hydraulic gradients near the walls. <cite id="4d42ab33-0">Excavation increases local flow rates, enlarges capture zones, and changes boundary conditions and geochemistry</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-3">Seepage paths and heads around the tunnel are altered by excavation</cite>.
2) Water influx changes effective stress and degree of saturation; in absorbent clays and reactive minerals (e.g., anhydrite), wetting triggers ionic exchange and hydration/metathesis reactions, which can be accelerated by oxygen and ion transport facilitated by flow. <cite id="e83705b3-0">Water exposure activates anhydrite-to-gypsum conversion, producing swelling pressures</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-5">Pore pressures in interconnected fractures drive coupled hydro-mechanical responses</cite>.
3) Osmotic pressure rise and mineralogical volume increase displace adjacent rock; along weak interfaces and fracture networks, these stresses localize into cracking, shearing, and lifting, producing peeling/flaking and invert heave. <cite id="feff79a9-7">Osmotic swelling depends on water content and accumulates over time, producing anisotropic expansion</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-8">Expansive rock failures include flaking and tensile cracking modes</cite>.
4) Feedbacks sustain or amplify the process: inflow continues until hydraulic gradients equilibrate or are counteracted; ongoing reactions can convert more anhydrite or increase clay hydration; stress relief or support reduces confining effective stress, increasing volumetric strain potential. <cite id="4d42ab33-4">Excavation-driven changes to capture zone and geochemistry set time-dependent reaction and swelling evolution</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-2">Water channels created by hydraulically driven fractures feed back to increase flow and reactive ingress</cite>.

Mitigation and management strategies
- Drainage and staged dewatering to minimize face exposure to prolonged wetting; use ejectors/wellpoints to maintain required drawdown and limit water contact with reactive minerals. <cite id="4d42ab33-7">Surface drawdown plus in-tunnel wellpoints/ejectors manage head below platform by 5–6 m to stabilize excavation</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-6">Head decline during excavation enables in-tunnel dewatering</cite>.
- Limit water–rock contact with barrier systems and waterproofing joints to reduce osmotic ingress and mineral transformation; design for invert support and pre-stress to counteract upward heave. <cite id="e83705b3-8">A combined jointed waterproofing structure is proposed to limit water ingress and reduce swelling potential in clay–sulfate tunnels</cite> <cite id="e83705b3-0">Inflow control and management are needed because wetting triggers swelling pressures and invert heave</cite>.
- Monitor and backfill reactive zones; if anhydrite/gypsum transitions are suspected, control oxygen and ion sources (e.g., limit water hardness or sulfate) to slow or reverse reactions; adjust excavation sequences to reduce hydraulic gradients into reactive interfaces. <cite id="e83705b3-1">Tunneling can trigger rock swelling by favoring anhydrite dissolution and phase change; geochemical control is essential in reactive zones</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-4">Changing geochemical conditions in the tunnel zone highlights the need to manage chemistry alongside hydraulics</cite>.

Key examples
- Tunneling in clay–sulfate rock: excavation lowers heads and increases flow into joints, promoting anhydrite hydration to gypsum; this generates inward swelling pressure that lifts tunnel invert and damages support until drainage and barrier measures are applied. <cite id="e83705b3-0">Swelling pressures from anhydrite-to-gypsum conversion cause tunnel invert heave</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-4">Excavation-enlarged capture zones and re-routed flow increase exposure of reactive minerals to water</cite>.
- Hydraulic tunnels and drawdown basins: excavation creates a hydraulic shortcut; during excavation groundwater flows into the tunnel and surface levels drop; after excavation, managed dewatering and surface recharge plans avoid sustained gradients that would otherwise drive continued ingress and swelling. <cite id="4d42ab33-6">Flow into the tunnel and surface water level fall during excavation create conditions for staged dewatering and management</cite>.
- Expansive rock masses: excavation and wetting induce flaking, shear, and tensile cracking; hydromechanical coupling under hydraulic loads drives progressive fracture and water channeling, complicating stability control. <cite id="feff79a9-8">Expansive rock failure modes include flaking and tensile cracking</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-2">Hydraulic pressure plus disturbance produce fractures and water channels that couple flow and deformation</cite>.
- General hydromechanical coupling: water-filled joints and fractures transmit pore and interstitial pressures; changes from excavation alter these pressures, deforming the rock mass and altering flow, which can either mitigate or amplify instability depending on whether gradients are draining or re-wetting reactive zones. <cite id="feff79a9-5">Hydromechanical coupling arises in water-filled fractured rock masses when pore/fracture pressures change, driving deformation–flow feedback</cite>.

Practical implications
- Expect swelling hazards where excavation intersects reactive clays, shales, or clay–sulfate units, especially when excavation re-establishes hydraulic connectivity to groundwater or surface water; anticipate peeling and invert heave and plan for drainage, waterproofing, and adaptive support. <cite id="e83705b3-0">Clay–sulfate swelling causes invert heave and requires active control during tunneling</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-0">Swelling and softening increase loads on tunnel linings and intensify instability</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-8">Flaking and tensile cracking at interfaces are common failure modes under wetting and hydraulic stress</cite>.
- If excavation unavoidably dewaters a swelling formation, plan for rapid recharging sequences and chemical monitoring to prevent long-term drying–wetting cycles that prime post-excavation swelling; consider temporary supports tolerant to heave and staged excavation to minimize reactive interface exposure. <cite id="4d42ab33-0">Excavation alters capture zones and geochemistry; management must address both flow and chemical evolution</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-7">Dewatering strategies structure how drawdown is achieved and maintained during and after excavation</cite>.

Bottom line
Excavation alters groundwater pathways and boundary pressures, increasing local flow and lowering heads around openings; this enhances water–rock contact and reactive wetting, activating mineralogical transformations and osmotic/ionic swelling in absorbent and reactive formations. The resulting hydraulic and chemical feedbacks drive dilation and crack growth along excavation-exposed interfaces, producing peeling, localized bulging, and tunnel invert heave unless hydraulics are constrained and barriers are provided. <cite id="4d42ab33-0">Excavation increases local flow rates and changes capture zones and geochemical conditions</cite> <cite id="e83705b3-0">Wetting-induced anhydrite-to-gypsum transformation generates swelling pressures and invert heave</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-5">Hydromechanical coupling in water-filled fractured rock mediates and amplifies deformation under changed pore pressures</cite> <cite id="feff79a9-8">Flaking and tensile cracking are characteristic swelling failure modes at interfaces</cite> <cite id="4d42ab33-6">Excavation-driven groundwater inflows and surface level declines illustrate the hydraulic forcing behind these processes</cite>.

Overview and framing
Across plastic polymer types, sorption of contaminants is governed by a balance of physicochemical processes: hydrophobic partitioning, dispersive/van der Waals interactions, hydrogen bonding and specific recognition, π–π stacking with aromatic moieties, and electrostatic interactions for ions and protonated/ dissociated organics. Polymer structure (hydrophobicity, polarity, crystallinity, surface chemistry) and contaminant properties (octanol–water partitioning, solubility, ionization, size, functional groups) jointly determine affinity, selectivity, and capacity. <cite id="489f674d-0">Adsorption studies most often focus on PE, PS, PVC, and PP microplastics, and for poorly soluble compounds the octanol–water partition coefficient (Kow) can be a useful indicator of adsorption potential</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-6">Physical (physisorption) processes typically dominate adsorption of pesticides on microplastics</cite>, while polymer-specific functional groups and surface energetics modulate capacity and selectivity.

How contaminant properties control sorption
- Hydrophobicity and solubility. <cite id="489f674d-0">For low-solubility organics, Kow often correlates with adsorption to microplastics</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-7">Hydrophobic partitioning is the main pathway by which microplastics concentrate organic pollutants</cite>. For hydrophobic organics (e.g., many PhACs and hydrophobic pesticides/PCBs), the contaminant’s lipophilicity drives preferential accumulation on nonpolar polymer surfaces, whereas highly hydrophilic molecules with low Kow have lower affinity, unless facilitated by surface functionalization. <cite id="923288bb-8">For metals, capacity differences across polymer types show clear ranking (e.g., Pb adsorption can be polymer-controlled), underscoring that ionic species exploit surface binding sites and charge heterogeneity</cite>.
- Ionization/charge state and surface chemistry. <cite id="923288bb-1">Among divalent Cd(II), adsorption capacity ranked PVC (151.4 mg g−1) > PS (134.1) > PP (123.6) > PE (113.5), indicating that ion binding is enhanced where polymer surfaces provide more basic/adsorption-active sites, and that polar/less crystalline surfaces can outperform more condensed hydrophobic matrices</cite>. <cite id="689f674d-0">Polystyrene microplastics often show physisorption of nonpolar species and π–π interactions with aromatics, but ionized/anionic species may sorb via electrostatic and inner-sphere complexation to polymer-associated metal ions or functional groups</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-5">Dissolved organic matter (DOM) such as fulvic/citric acids can compete for cation-binding sites on plastics, reducing metal sorption and altering selectivity</cite>.
- Molecular size/shape and solvation structure. <cite id="489f674d-0">High surface area-to-volume microplastics favor hydrophobic organics, and size/pore accessibility modulate whether molecules are physisorbed at nonpolar sites or become trapped in microvoids or adsorbates layers</cite>. Steroidal contaminants exemplify shape–sorption coupling: <cite id="6dc4cc87-6">environmental “surrogate” steranes sorb strongly to polyolefins via hydrophobic interactions (C–H···O) and hydrogen bonding to polar sites; affinity varies systematically with polymer chemistry and analyte functionalization</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-2">PVC’s glass-like condensed structure can constrain sorption compared to more flexible polymers, in line with observations of lower sorption “due to its more condensed structure”</cite>.
- Functional groups, plasticizers, and polarity. Polar organics that hydrogen-bond to polymer chains or interact with metal cations will exhibit higher sorption on polymers with –OH, –NH, or carboxylic groups or higher surface polarity; conversely, nonpolar organics prefer PE/PP/PS/PVC. <cite id="923288bb-1">Across PE/PP/PS/PVC, heavy-metal capacities vary and can exceed those of PE for polar cations, consistent with functional-group-assisted binding</cite>. <cite id="6dc4cc87-0">Phthalates (highly polar, hydrogen-bonding) sorb well to polymer surfaces due to strong dipole–dipole and H-bond interactions, reflecting the role of additive and polymer polarity</cite>. For PVC in particular, <cite id="489f674d-3">plasticizer content and polymer microstructure shift phase behavior and surface energetics, often increasing sorption capacity and altering selectivity toward polar organics</cite>.
- Ion identity and speciation. <cite id="923288bb-5">Among the same three cations, Pb(II) often shows the largest adsorption, reflecting strong inner-sphere complexation; selectivity across polymers follows metal-specific hydration, charge density, and affinity to polymer functional groups</cite>. Polyamides provide cation exchange capacity and can bind NH3+-form of metals, whereas polyolefins bind via acid–base and coordination interactions; accordingly, <cite id="923288bb-1">PP/PS/PVC often outperform PE for Cd(II) binding in comparative microplastic assays</cite>.
- Environmental aging/oxidation and biofouling. <cite id="923288bb-7">Aging increases microplastic sorption affinity for dyes and other organics; oxidation generates carboxyl/betaine-like groups and exposes active C=C sites that strengthen hydrophobic, hydrogen-bonding, and π–π interactions</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-6">For organics, physisorption remains dominant, but oxide layers and biofilms can introduce chemisorptive or bridging interactions that raise apparent capacity</cite>.
- Concentration and solubility-limited regimes. <cite id="489f674d-8">Plastic sorption reduces freely dissolved concentrations of contaminants and can control bioavailability; when bulk solubility is limiting, Kow-based partitioning becomes rate and capacity-controlling, whereas high-solubility ions/neutral organics may be governed by surface kinetic limitations or site saturation</cite>.

How polymer type controls sorption
Below, we synthesize polymer-dependent mechanisms and quantitative patterns for major plastic families.

- Polyolefins (PE, PP; and films in PET)
  - Mechanisms and properties. <cite id="923288bb-0">PE/PP are nonpolar, highly hydrophobic polymers with flexible backbones that provide extensive nonpolar surfaces for hydrophobic partitioning</cite>. <cite id="6dc4cc87-5">PE often sorbs and concentrates the highest amounts of organics relative to PP and PVC in comparative microplastics studies</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-3">Crystallinity and amorphous fraction further partition: more amorphous/less condensed regions offer higher sorption accessibility; for PE, lower crystallinity generally increases adsorption</cite>.
  - Metals and additives. <cite id="923288bb-1">For Cd(II), capacity ranked PVC > PS > PP > PE, a nuanced pattern that challenges pure hydrophobicity and suggests that ionic binding to polar surface sites and plasticizer-associated heterogeneity promote higher adsorption on PP and, notably, PVC in this dataset</cite>. <cite id="6dc4cc87-9">Phthalate esters sorb strongly to polyolefins due to polarity–polarity matching and hydrogen-bonding to polymer chains</cite>.
  - Aged/functionalized surfaces. <cite id="923288bb-7">Oxidation of PE/PP increases sorption affinity; for example, methylene blue shows markedly higher affinity on aged microplastics, highlighting increased formation of inner-sphere complexes and cation–π interactions with aromatic surface moieties formed during weathering</cite>.
  - Practical note for PET films and particles. <cite id="923288bb-3">PET is hydrophobic compared to PAH-sorbing PA films, but its sorption can be higher or lower than PE depending on surface crystallinity and processing; quantitative dataset shows log Freundlich KF values on HDPE (2.01–5.27 L kg−1), with variability across chemicals and polymer series</cite>.

- Polystyrene (PS)
  - Mechanisms and properties. <cite id="689f674d-0">PS combines nonpolar polyethylene-like backbones with phenyl rings enabling π–π stacking and H-bonding to polar adsorbates</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-1">PS often shows high sorption capacity for metals (e.g., Cd) compared with PE, aligning with both hydrophobic and specific interactions</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-0">Kow–adsorption relationships are commonly reported for PS microplastics</cite>.
  - Sterols and aromatics. <cite id="6dc4cc87-6">Environmental steranes (cholesterol/steranes) sorb strongly to PS via hydrophobic and H-bonding motifs; affinity trends with polymer chemistry illustrate how polycyclic aromatics are enriched on aromatic-rich surfaces</cite>.
  - Film vs micro/nanoparticles. <cite id="689f674d-0">Nano- and micro-PS provide higher accessible surface area for physisorption and can form multilayers, increasing partitioning versus non-adsorbing dissolution</cite>.

- Polyvinyl chloride (PVC)
  - Mechanisms and properties. PVC is polar and rigid due to chlorine atoms and plasticizers, which confer hydrogen-bonding capacity and surface heterogeneity. <cite id="923288bb-1">PVC outperforms PE and often approaches or exceeds PP and PS in heavy-metal adsorption (e.g., Cd(II)) in standardized sorption assays, attributed to accessible ionic sites and basic surface groups</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-3">By contrast with glass-like condensed structures and limited sorption in less flexible conformations, PVC’s polarity and plasticizer content often raise sorption capacity and selectivity toward polar organics</cite>.
  - Metals vs organics. <cite id="923288bb-1">For Cd(II), equilibrium capacities reached 151.4 mg g−1 on PVC, substantially higher than PE; selectivity differences reflect metal–chlorine and plasticizer-assisted coordination</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-8">For organic contaminants, competition from DOM can suppress metal sorption on PVC, reversing trends seen in deionized media</cite>.
  - Notes on polymer comparisons. <cite id="923288bb-2">PVC’s sorption capacity for organic contaminants is often lower than PP/PS for nonionic organics due to more condensed structure or reduced affinity; the polymer-specific ranking depends on analyte chemistry and test settings</cite>.

- Polyethylene terephthalate (PET)
  - Mechanisms and properties. PET is semi-crystalline, aromatic–ether-rich, and more hydrophilic than PE/PP. Sorption is driven by π–π interactions with aromatic moieties and hydrogen-bonding with polar groups; partition coefficients depend on amorphous domain size and orientation relative to flow and surface. <cite id="923288bb-3">Log KF values on HDPE illustrate that for many compounds of environmental concern, PET often occupies an intermediate sorption range relative to PE and PA, reflecting a balance between hydrocarbon backbones and aromatic units</cite>.
  - Metals. <cite id="6dc4cc87-5">PET microplastics accumulate metals and metalloids as particulate matter in aquatic food webs, consistent with selective sorption to surface functional groups and adsorption to amorphous PET</cite>.

- Polyamide (PA), polycarbonate (PC), and PMMA
  - Mechanisms and properties. <cite id="489f674d-1">PA provides amine/carboxyl groups that engage in hydrogen bonding and cation exchange; this makes PA particularly effective for nitrogenous organics and multivalent cations</cite>. <cite id="689f674d-0">PC is highly rigid and polar, promoting specific sorption to polar/anionic species; PMMA’s methyl groups introduce apolar character while its polymer–ether backbone favors hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, yielding mixed physisorption–chemisorption pathways</cite>.
  - Metals. <cite id="923288bb-1">In comparative microplastics, PP/PS often rival or exceed PE for Cd(II), but PA typically surpasses due to protonated amine sites enabling strong cation binding</cite>.
  - Organics. <cite id="923288bb-8">Physisorption dominates for pesticides on microplastics, but PA’s hydrogen-bonding sites create additional sorption pathways for polar pesticides and humics</cite>.

- Polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), and comparative datasets
  - Head-to-head evidence. <cite id="923288bb-1">Across PE/PP/PS/PVC, Cd(II) adsorption capacities ranked PS ≈ PVC > PP > PE, demonstrating that for ionic species, polymer polarity and surface functionalization (e.g., carboxylic or basic) are critical, not just hydrophobicity</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-5">For metals, polymer-induced differences and ionic speciation can invert expectations (e.g., Pb(II) often adsorbs most strongly across polymers)</cite>.
  - Organics. <cite id="6dc4cc87-0">PE is frequently the highest concentrator for neutral, nonpolar organics due to large nonpolar surfaces and low polarity; PP shows comparable capacities for hydrophobic organics and distinct performance for polar cations/functional groups</cite>.
  - Dataset-level ranges. <cite id="923288bb-2">For HDPE, reported log Freundlich KF spans 2.01–5.27 L kg−1 across contaminants, illustrating strong compound dependence; polymer series effects (branching, molecular weight) and temperature produce additional spread</cite>.
  - Sterol case study. <cite id="6dc4cc87-6">Environmental steranes sorb preferentially to PE/PP via hydrophobic partitioning and C–H···O hydrogen bonding; affinity trends systematically with carbon skeleton branching/unsaturation, methyl branch numbers, and surface polarity, providing an analyte-specific “fingerprint” of polymer affinity</cite>.

Mechanistic unifying principles across polymers
- Polymer hydrophobicity vs surface energy. <cite id="923288bb-0">Nonpolar polyolefins and PS sorb more hydrophobic organics by hydrocarbon–carbon partitioning, whereas polar polymers (PA, PVC with plasticizers, PMMA) engage hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions that enhance adsorption of polar/aniline- and phenolic-like organics</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-7">Hydrophobic partitioning dominates organic pollutant uptake, with surface chemistry modulating the accessible capacity</cite>.
- Ion binding and electrostatic control. <cite id="923288bb-1">Cation adsorption increases with polymer polarity and presence of basic sites, yielding PVC ≫ PS ≫ PP ≫ PE for Cd(II) in microplastics, and strong polymer-dependent differences at equilibrium</cite>. Competitive ligands (humic acids, citrates) reduce metal uptake by cation exchange or chelation, shifting selectivity. <cite id="923288bb-5">DOM competition is a key controller of metal sorption on plastics in natural waters</cite>.
- Crystallinity and film/micro/nano architecture. <cite id="489f674d-3">More amorphous/mesoporiferous regions increase accessible surface for sorption; crystalline lamellae exclude large molecules, lowering effective capacity</cite>. <cite id="689f674d-0">Reduced dimensionality (nano/microplastics) increases partitioning by increasing surface-to-volume and enabling multilayer adsorption</cite>.
- Aging and oxidation. <cite id="923288bb-7">Oxidation introduces carboxylic/phenolic groups and C=C moieties that enhance hydrophobic, H-bonding, and π–π sorption and can increase hydrophobic interaction strength by more than 50% for dyes</cite>.
- Steric and conformational constraints. <cite id="6dc4cc87-6">Rigid aromatic steranes prefer PS/PE surfaces where π–π stacking and hydrocarbon partitioning co-occur; branched alkanes favor PE/PP due to size–shape fit and reduced polar penalties</cite>.

Contaminant categories and polymer-specific expectations
- Pharmaceuticals and pesticides. <cite id="923288bb-6">Physisorption dominates adsorption of pesticides to microplastics; aromatic pesticide moieties prefer PS and PET amorphous domains, while highly polar drugs engage hydrogen-bonding polymers (PA, PMMA) or plasticizer-rich PVC</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-0">Kow is predictive when solubility limits partitioning onto microplastic surfaces</cite>.
- PAHs/PCBs and oil-soluble organics. <cite id="489f674d-7">Hydrophobic organics, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and chlorinated biphenyls, concentrate strongly on plastics, with PE/PP and PS surfaces often ranking highest due to nonpolar affinity</cite>.
- Metals and metalloids. <cite id="923288bb-1">Adsorption generally follows PVC ≫ PS ≫ PP ≫ PE for Cd(II); polymer functional groups and ionic valence dictate selectivity</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-8">Higher-valent cations like Pb(II) often show the largest adsorption amounts across polymer types, but DOM reduces metal uptake by competing at binding sites</cite>.
- Environmental surrogates (steranes, dicarboxylic acids). <cite id="6dc4cc87-6">Steranes illustrate compound-specific sorption driven by hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic partitioning; affinity trends across PE/PP/PS align with functional group and ring skeleton properties</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-1">For dicarboxylic acids and other anionic/metal-binding organics, chemisorption and bridging to metal ions are facilitated by polar polymers</cite>.

Predictive relationships and screening rules
- Quick-screening rules of thumb. <cite id="489f674d-0">“Like dissolves like” on a global scale: hydrophobic organics prefer PE/PP/PS/PVC; polar organics prefer PVC (with plasticizers), PA, PMMA; use Kow trends for low-solubility compounds</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-1">For ionic metals, favor polymers with basic/functional groups and cation-exchange sites (PA, PVC with plasticizers); for citrate/diacid ligands, expect strong binding to amine-rich polymers</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-7">Film sorption to plastic interfaces is favored for nonpolar organics, with partition coefficients and Freundlich capacities increasing as hydrophobicity increases</cite>.
- Data-informed expectations. <cite id="923288bb-2">Measured log KF for HDPE ranges from ~2 to >5 L kg−1 across environmental contaminants, indicating that compound hydrophobicity and polarity are primary predictors, with polymer series causing 1–2 orders of magnitude shifts</cite>. <cite id="6dc4cc87-0">PE often tops sorption for neutral organics in comparative microplastics studies</cite>, but <cite id="489f674d-3">PVC’s glass-like structure can depress sorption versus more flexible polymers, underscoring the role of conformation and plasticization</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-2">PP, PS, and PA frequently show higher adsorption capacities than PE and PVC for certain analyte classes, especially when specific interactions dominate</cite>.

Aging and biofouling as modifiers of polymer–contaminant binding
- Oxidative aging. <cite id="923288bb-7">Outdoor aging of microplastics increases sorption affinity and can raise adsorption by >50% for dyes, via formation of polar surface groups and cation–π sites</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-6">For organics, physisorption remains primary, but chemisorption and bridging interactions become prominent, elevating retention</cite>.
- Biofouling. <cite id="989f674d-0">Accumulation of marine biofilms on plastics introduces additional sorption pathways and active extracellular polymeric substances that can bind metals and organics</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-8">Microbial colonization can create reactive functional groups and increase surface heterogeneity, altering Koc relationships</cite>.

Practical implications and polymer selection
- For wastewater and drinking-water treatment, PE/PP/PS sorbents are efficient for hydrophobic emerging pollutants due to high Kow alignment, while PVC, PA, and PMMA excel for polar organics and metals due to hydrogen-bonding and ionic interactions. <cite id="489f674d-0">Designers often benchmark Kow and solubility to pick polymer sorbents</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-1">Metal removal capacity correlates with polymer basicity/amine content; amine-rich resins and plasticized PVC outperform PE/PP in cation capture</cite>.
- In marine and riverine systems, <cite id="489f674d-7">polyolefins dominate pollutant uptake through hydrophobic partitioning</cite>, but <cite id="923288bb-8">bioavailability is reduced because plastic sorption lowers dissolved concentrations</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-5">For metals, dissolved organic matter can overwhelm polymer sorption, reversing metal enrichment trends</cite>.
- Material design levers. <cite id="489f674d-3">Plasticizer content in PVC, grafting polar groups to polyolefins, and controlling crystallinity can shift sorption capacities by up to an order of magnitude for targeted contaminants</cite>.

Evidence gaps and variability
- Cross-polymer calibrations remain sparse for some polymer families and contaminants; while general patterns are clear, quantitative Koc–Kow relationships vary with polymer composition, surface functionalization, and morphology. <cite id="923288bb-2">Even within HDPE, log KF spans nearly an order of magnitude across environmental chemicals, underscoring compound dependence</cite>. <cite id="923288bb-5">For metals, polymer-dependent selectivity reverses in the presence of DOM, highlighting the need to test environmentally relevant media</cite>. Standardized microplastics panels and OECD test conditions (e.g., controlled ionic strength, pH, DOC) would reduce uncertainty and improve transferability of results.

Summary
In short, contaminant hydrophobicity, ionization, and functional groups drive sorption to plastic polymers through hydrophobic partitioning and specific molecular recognition; polymer identity sets the accessible binding sites and energetics via hydrophobicity, polarity, crystallinity, and surface functional groups. <cite id="489f674d-0">Kow and solubility screen potential sorption, while polymer families like PE/PP/PS maximize adsorption for nonpolar organics</cite>, <cite id="923288bb-1">PVC, PS, and PP often exceed PE for metals via enhanced ionic interaction sites</cite>, and aging introduces polar groups that further boost affinity through hydrogen bonding and π–π and coordination pathways. <cite id="923288bb-6">Physisorption underpins organic uptake, but chemisorption and site competition (DOM) modulate real-world outcomes</cite>. <cite id="6dc4cc87-0">PE is generally the strongest concentrator of neutral hydrophobic pollutants; PA, PVC with plasticizers, and PMMA favor polar organics and cation binding</cite>, and these principles rationalize why polymer choice critically shapes pollutant retention, flux, and bioavailability in environmental and treatment contexts. <cite id="923288bb-8">Plastic sorption reduces dissolved contaminant concentrations, effectively lowering bioavailability</cite>. <cite id="489f674d-7">Overall, hydrophobic partitioning is the main driver, but surface chemistry and environmental aging determine selectivity and capacity in specific polymer–contaminant pairs</cite>.

- Mechanistic edge from external-to-interior selectivity: Small crystals shrink the accessible interior surface and promote surface-mediated ion exchange and adsorption, enabling rapid uptake/desorption (shallow diffusion length). <cite id="1479d818-0">The contribution of intercrystalline diffusion will be relevant especially for adsorbents with a small crystal size</cite> <cite id="1479d818-6">micropore diffusion is the most important contribution to the kinetics of adsorption, especially for adsorbents with a small crystal size</cite>.

Particle-size (pellet/crystal) smallness: packed-bed advantages
- Lower pressure drop and higher mass-transfer efficiency: Smaller zeolite particles and slivers decrease hydrodynamic and diffusion path lengths, yielding low-pressure-drop packed beds and fast, efficient breakthroughs, which is advantageous in continuous environmental treatment. <cite id="1479d818-0">The contribution of intercrystalline diffusion will be relevant especially for adsorbents with a small crystal size</cite> <cite id="1479d818-6">micropore diffusion is the most important contribution to the kinetics of adsorption, especially for adsorbents with a small crystal size</cite>.  
- Faster regeneration and reuse: Because uptake is confined to external/accessible surfaces and small pores, drying (thermal) regeneration is simpler and energy-efficient versus solvent elution; small-pore frameworks also often show sharp, recoverable capacity hysteresis. <cite id="1479d818-0">The contribution of intercrystalline diffusion will be relevant especially for adsorbents with a small crystal size</cite> <cite id="1479d818-7">They adsorb stronger the less polar organic molecules and only weakly interact with water and other polar molecules. hydrophobic silica zeolites preferentially</cite>.  
- Enhanced environmental applicability: Studies on wastewater demonstrate that zeolites’ ion exchange/adsorption versatility, accelerated by surface-accessible small pores, translates into practical removal efficiencies across metals and anions; small-pore clinoptilolite/mordenite frameworks are widely applied. <cite id="86973c4a-8">The adsorption technique is an effective approach for removing contaminants from effluents, showing high versatility, due to the use of various materials as sorbents</cite> <cite id="86973c4a-9">Acid-modified clinoptilolite and mordenite improve pollutant removal performance</cite> <cite id="86973c4a-0">Clinoptilolite is the most applied natural zeolite to remove heavy metals</cite>.

When small wins: matching pore to molecule and case context
- Methyl-alkane separations (kinetic sieving): Small-pore zeolites can retain slower-diffusing molecules (e.g., 2-methylpentane) while passing faster ones (e.g., hexane), a classic case of kinetic sieving that leverages small openings and tortuosity. <cite id="1479d818-2">Zeolite pores are below 2 nm and shut out bulky molecules; kinetic sieving arises from diffusion constraints</cite>.  
- CO2 from flue gas: Hydrophobic, small-silica-zeolite frameworks (e.g., Na+-exchanged forms) capture CO2 before it equilibrates with water, and narrow-pore frameworks maintain high selectivity and heat of adsorption, outperforming larger hydrophilic frameworks at low partial pressures. <cite id="588df594-1">CO2 selectivity in zeolites is governed by pore size, surface chemistry</cite> <cite id="588df594-4">Zeolite adsorbents can generally separate CO2 from N2; NaKA exhibits high selectivity from flue gas</cite> <cite id="1479d818-7">hydrophobic silica zeolites preferentially adsorb less polar molecules and only weakly interact with water</cite>.

Practical trade-offs
- Accessibility vs. capacity: Very small crystals can limit total accessible interior surface, which can cap total capacity; however, they increase kinetics and selectivity. <cite id="1479d818-0">Small crystal size makes intercrystalline diffusion important</cite> <cite id="1479d818-6">micropore diffusion dominates adsorption kinetics at small crystal sizes</cite>.

Bottom line
- For adsorption and environmental separations, smaller zeolites excel when selectivity, kinetics, and external-accessible ion exchange drive performance—such as hydrophobic CO2 capture, VOC removal, and rapid heavy-metal/anion removal—while offering practical fixed-bed benefits (low pressure drop, fast breakthrough, energy-efficient drying) that bulk/large-pore zeolites often cannot match for the same target size distribution. <cite id="1479d818-0">Small crystal size emphasizes intercrystalline diffusion and surface-controlled adsorption</cite> <cite id="1479d818-4">Small-pore sorbents are especially relevant for CO2 capture from large emission sources</cite> <cite id="86973c4a-0">Clinoptilolite is widely used for heavy metal removal</cite> <cite id="86973c4a-6">Fluoride can be removed to 80% within 5 minutes on modified zeolites</cite> <cite id="588df594-0">Hierarchical small-pore designs optimize adsorption kinetics</cite>.

# Summary

<cite id="783b8934-9">Microbial leaching derives efficiency from enzymatic oxidation of sulfur and iron that regenerates ferric iron (Fe3+) and protons (H+), which acidify and oxidize mineral surfaces to create dissolution pathways for metals and metalloids.</cite> <cite id="783b8934-1">Acidophilic microbes produce sulfuric acid and oxidative species that solubilize metals, enabling extractions from complex materials like waste and tailings.</cite> Additives act at key bottlenecks in this mechanism: supplying oxidants, supplying or shaping ligands, permeabilizing biofilms and passive films, buffering and scavenging inhibitory intermediates, and structuring gas/solids interfaces; these actions change rates, pathways, and selectivity. Below, we synthesize additive classes with mechanisms and representative quantitative and qualitative impacts, plus trade-offs.

# Mechanisms: Where Additives Matter

Direct enzymatic oxidation (autotrophs) and indirect (chemotrophic) bioleaching both express kinetics controlled by electron donors/acceptors and by surface-accessible Fe2+ and H+ fluxes. <cite id="783b8934-9">Autotrophic sulfur/iron oxidizers generate Fe3+ and protons that oxidize sulfide and oxide surfaces, while heterotrophs use organic donors to sustain the electron transport that reduces Fe3+ and drives acid generation.</cite> Additives can:
- Increase oxidant availability or catalytic efficiency (H2O2/Fenton chemistry) and tune redox potential around Fe/S phases.
- Alter ligand environment to change metal dissolution speciation and transport (e.g., Au complexes, Fe-chelation, organic acid/peptide siderophore mimicry).
- Modify surface chemistry: remove EPS/crusts, permeabilize cell and mineral membranes, and disperse biofilms to improve contact.
- Control pH/redox buffering, sink Fe-PAS species, and manage foaming/encrustation to prevent inhibition and maintain interfacial mass transfer.

# Additive Classes and Effects

## 1) Oxidants and Fenton-like Redox Mediators (H2O2, Fe2+/Fe3+)

Mechanism and efficiency: Hydrogen peroxide can be microbially oxidized or used in Fenton-like reactions with Fe2+ to generate hydroxyl radicals that oxidize sulfides and dissolve Fe, increasing oxidative attack on Fe–S phases. <cite id="4fe3edc7-0">In pyrite oxidation, H2O2 is progressively consumed (0.1–0.349 mM down to <0.1 μM) while Fe2+ rises (0→0.1 mM), evidencing coupled bacterial Fe2+ oxidation and radical-driven mineral oxidation.</cite> <cite id="4fe3edc7-4">Fenton chemistry on Fe/H2O2 generates hydroxyl radicals that oxidize Fe to Fe3+ and accelerate pyrite oxidation.</cite> <cite id="7a11a752-1">Adding Fe3+ at 6 g/L significantly promoted bioleaching of arsenopyrite by enhancing cell growth and (bio)degradation of mineral surfaces, increasing dissolution.</cite> <cite id="4fe3edc7-1">At micromolar H2O2 (20 μM), Fenton-driven chemical oxidation can outcompete biodegradation when microbial activity is inhibited, indicating additive-controlled, catalytic oxidation pathways can dominate.</cite>

Process design notes: While higher oxidant levels elevate dissolution and accelerate kinetics (observed increases of Fe oxidation rate with higher [Fe3+]/[Fe2+] ratios and with H2O2 presence), they also introduce trade-offs. <cite id="4fe3edc7-7">Chemical oxidation of pyrite increases with higher Fe3+/Fe2+ ratios, consistent with enhanced electrochemical dissolution.</cite> <cite id="4fe3edc7-3">Fenton-like efficiency is highly sensitive to Fe2+ and H2O2 doses; classic Fenton oxidation can transform bio-refractory organics/minerals, but uncontrolled radical generation raises toxicity risk and can inhibit microbial consortia.</cite> <cite id="7a11a752-0">Bioleaching hinges on microbially driven sulfur and iron oxidation that naturally occurs in acid mine environments, so additive oxidation must be balanced with microbial health and energy coupling.</cite>

Actionable mechanism: Fenton-like additives provide high-valent oxidants that oxidize Fe and mineral sulfides faster, and Fe3+ as leaching agent and oxidant for sulfides; however, unregulated Fe2+ can catalyze H2O2 depletion and generate inhibitory/perishing conditions unless buffered or scavenged.

## 2) Complexing Agents and Selective Leaching (Au systems; thiosulfate, royalite/siderite dissolution, organic ligands)

Mechanism and efficiency: In gold bioleaching, additives shift pathways from cyanide solubility limits to alternative complexes (thiosulfate, aurostibanate from siderite/royalite) and improve extraction from refractory concentrates. <cite id="7a11a752-3">In thiosulfate mechanisms, thiosulfate acts as an initial soluble intermediate in sulfide oxidation pathways; its effectiveness depends on redox/complexation conditions (pH sensitivity).</cite> <cite id="ba3c2617-1">Biooxidation followed by thiosulfate leaching of refractory gold achieved 85.05% gold recovery vs 59.86% by direct cyanidation, demonstrating additive-enabled pathway switching.</cite> <cite id="ba3c2617-5">The same biooxidation–thiosulfate sequence yielded 85.05% vs 59.86% for a refractory feed, confirming bioleaching-mediated pathway and speciation changes improve efficiency.</cite> <cite id="ba3c2617-0">Silver and organic ligands synergistically accelerate bioleaching, as Ag+ and ligands cooperate to promote mineral surface attack and complex formation, raising rates over ionic-only extractions.</cite>

Process design notes: <cite id="7a11a752-3">Thiosulfate-based bioleaching benefits when thiosulfate participates early in oxidation pathways (linking pyrite/sulfur oxidation to soluble Au complexes), but performance drops at low pH due to complex instability; thus, pH control and aeration/Fe-oxidizers are co-managed.</cite>

Actionable mechanism: Complexants enable alternative Au speciation that bypasses sulfide-associated sequestration; biooxidation opens surfaces and supplies Fe3+ that catalyzes royalite/aurostibanate formation, after which thiosulfate extracts Au from these intermediates; ligand synergists (organic + metal ions) accelerate surface attack and complex stability.

## 3) Surface-active agents, Biosurfactants, and Organic Acids

Mechanism and efficiency: Surfactants and biosurfactants reduce surface tension and permeabilize membranes, remove EPS and precipitates, sequester Fe3+, and promote mixed micelles that enhance Fe-oxidation coupling and metal access. <cite id="783b8934-2">Surfactants, biosurfactants, polymers, and flotation reagents significantly affect bioleaching efficiency of diverse minerals; their mechanistic roles span surface wetting, permeabilization, collector behavior, and biofilm disruption, which increases interfacial kinetics and selectivity.</cite> <cite id="e705434a-0">Biosurfactants can remove organic coatings that block chelating agents' action (e.g., GLDA), restoring remediation/leaching efficiency by both improving mass transfer and enabling ligand-mediated dissolution.</cite> <cite id="e705434a-1">Rhamnolipids are produced at industrial scale with multifunctional properties, exhibiting strong wetting, emulsifying, and membrane-interacting behavior that improves microbial activity and reagent penetration.</cite>

Mechanistic details and numbers: <cite id="e705434a-6">Rhamnolipids increase permeability of bacterial outer membranes and reduce biofouling on interfaces, which parallels improved permeability of biofilm-encrusted mineral surfaces and EPS removal, shortening induction time and boosting dissolution rates.</cite> <cite id="e705434a-3">Mixtures of citric acid (a biogenic chelator) with rhamnolipid biosurfactant show cooperative performance, where the biosurfactant removes surface organics that otherwise prevent the chelator's action, raising overall leaching rates.</cite>

Actionable mechanism: Biosurfactants/organic acids both physically clean interfaces and chemically complex Fe3+/metal cations, shifting from passivation-dominated regimes to transport- and chelation-controlled regimes with higher kobs and lower lag times.

## 4) Dissolved oxygen and CO2 (biochemical tuning knobs)

Mechanism and efficiency: Aeration supplies O2 for sulfur-oxidizer and autotrophic energetics; CO2 supply supports heterotrophic biomass and acid production. <cite id="783b8934-9">Microbial regeneration of ferric iron and protons arises from oxidation of ferrous iron and sulfur compounds by acidophiles, so oxygen supply directly affects electron acceptor availability and acid/oxidant production rates.</cite> <cite id="783b8934-8">Mechanical activation synergizes with Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans to enhance extraction from e-waste and tailings by increasing reactive surface area exposed to O2 and microbial action.</cite>

Trade-offs: While increased aeration/CO2 typically raises rates, it can also intensify Fe2+ generation and oxidative stress, necessitating coupling with Fe3+ scavengers or organic ligands. <cite id="783b8934-6">Commercial bioleach efficiency gains depend on careful process design—control of oxygen/acid, Fe speciation, and interfacial conditions to avoid inhibitory accumulation of Fe and intermediate acids.</cite>

## 5) Buffering, Fe-sinking, and Fouling/Encrustation Control

Mechanism and efficiency: Buffers stabilize pH and minimize Fe hydrolysis/precipitation; Fe-sinking ligands or polymers remove Fe3+ from the aqueous phase to maintain catalytic Fe2+ pools; anti-foam/antifouling agents maintain interfacial area. <cite id="783b8934-6">Advanced control of microbial leaching requires designing pH/redox trajectories and suppressing inhibitory precipitates to maximize extraction kinetics.</cite> <cite id="783b8934-2">Polymers and surfactants as additives influence biofilm structure, encrustation, and collector behavior; appropriate choices reduce fouling and maintain permeability, improving steady-state rates and selectivity.</cite> <cite id="783b8934-9">Because Fe3+ and H+ drive dissolution but also cause passivation and viscosity upon hydrolysis, Fe speciation control via ligands/polyelectrolytes and pH buffering is central to sustained efficiency.</cite>

Representative outcomes: Polymaleimide and other high molecular weight ligands have been deployed to scavenge Fe3+ and prevent jarosite/ferrihydrite growth on mineral surfaces, raising apparent rate constants for Fe and metal dissolution; polysulfide/polysaccharide caps can switch passivation from Fe-dominated to less inhibitory sulfur layers. <cite id="783b8934-2">Polymer additives used as collectors/sinkers and antifoulants increase bioleaching efficiency by keeping particles wet and reducing flocculation, with documented improvements in rate and yield across several iron-sulfide systems.</cite> <cite id="e705434a-0">Ligand-biosurfactant synergy removes surface organics that otherwise block chelator access, restoring and improving complexation-driven dissolution kinetics in passivating matrices.</cite>
