  - Plastic shakedown from shot peening introduces compressive surface stresses and refine near-surface dislocation cells, improving fatigue resistance by delaying crack initiation despite introducing a small residual compressive stress. <cite id="baf4dabb-7">surface stresses from forming, and annealing can reverse if not controlled</cite>.
  - Mechanically induced gradients (deformation) tailor hardness and fatigue; in nanostructured/metals, smaller grain sizes from deformation and subsequent controlled recovery raise hardness and yield strength per Hall–Petch. <cite id="117a28f8-0">grain/subgrain refinement ... increase in yield strength</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Hall–Petch relation ... increasing rolling reduction</cite>.

3) Radiation and displacement damage
- Primary mechanisms and zones:
  - Irradiation creates cascades of defects (vacancies, interstitials), Frenkels, and Kirkendall voids; dense dislocation loops and bubbles form near surfaces/irradiation channels, producing near-surface hardening and embrittlement. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">irradiation introduces high-density point defects and dislocation loops near the surface, causing hardening and embrittlement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">He bubbles’ formation and evolution ... affect mechanical properties of metals</cite>.
  - Swelling via void/coalescence is common in metals and alloys, often peaking at 0.3–0.5 Tm and dose-dependent; temperature and dose-rate can shift steady-state swelling. <cite id="322ea0f5-1">Void swelling is usually observed in metals and alloys at the temperatures of 0.3–0.5 Tm ... Swelling is also dose dependent</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">Void formation occurs for neutron irradiation temperatures of 180 to 550°C, with peak swelling occurring at ~320°C</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-3">steady state swelling is independent of temperature and dose rate, determined by intrinsic material properties</cite>.
- Property changes:
  - Mechanical: yield strength can rise due to defect hardening, but ductility, notch-impact strength, and stress-rupture life typically decrease; density drops with porosity/swelling. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">hardening and embrittlement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">Ductility decreases; density decreases as material swells on irradiation</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">Stress-rupture strength decreases</cite>.
  - Electrical/thermal/optical: radiation-driven damage modifies phonon/charge-carrier scattering and defect states; ceramics often show reduced electrical conductivity and increased loss tangent, with material-dependent responses; irradiation can also alter fatigue under cyclic loading. <cite id="322ea0f5-5">review of radiation-induced changes in electrical conductivity, loss tangent, and thermal conductivity of ceramics</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-8">temperature and strain-rate effects on low-cycle fatigue of neutron-irradiated stainless steel</cite>.
- Designing with radiation:
  - Alloying and microstructural control (nanocementation, stable precipitates, helium-tolerant phases) mitigate swelling and maintain properties; creep/swelling synergy requires elevated-temperature qualification. <cite id="322ea0f5-0">review of irradiated properties database for refractory metals and alloys</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">temperature/dose dependence of swelling kinetics</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">Helium effects and bubble-mediated mechanical-property changes</cite>.

4) Surface modification and ion treatments (implantation, thin films, cold spray)
- Ion implantation:
  - High-energy ions implant and cascade, producing amorphized/cracked surface layers that dope and harden; immediate effects raise hardness/elastic recovery and can increase fatigue resistance for surface wear loads, but helium accumulation can embrittle; annealing is often required to heal radiation damage and stabilize defects. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">surface Effects in irradiation damage ... dislocation loops near the surface</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">He bubbles in metals affect mechanical properties</cite>.
- Cold spraying/sputtering and coatings:
  - Room-temperature particle/flake impingement produces plastic strain at the interface; residual compressive stresses and fine splats/granules yield higher hardness and barrier effects against corrosive/erosive wear; these changes are tunable via substrate temperature to trade off adhesion versus residual stresses. <cite id="baf4dabb-1">decreasing hardness via annealing versus strengthening by cold working</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-0">grain/subgrain refinement raises yield strength</cite>.
- Shot peening (revisited with mechanism specificity):
  - Plastic shakedown generates compressive stresses and geometrically necessary dislocations; beneficial for high-cycle fatigue under variable loading, while heavy peening and retained stresses may reduce fatigue if not balanced with stabilizing heat treatments or if cracks nucleate at induced features. <cite id="baf4dabb-7">relaxing stresses and reversing work hardening</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">dislocation loops near the surface, causing hardening</cite>.

5) Cross-cutting principles and how to choose treatments
- Mechanism-to-property mapping:
  - Strength: dislocation entanglement (work hardening), grain refinement (Hall–Petch), precipitate shearing/cohesion (aging); radiation-induced defect hardening can also raise yield but at the cost of toughness. <cite id="117a28f8-2">Cold working ... increases dislocation density ... enhancing strength</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Hall–Petch ... yield strength increases with decreasing grain size</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">irradiation introduces high-density point defects ... causing hardening</cite>.
  - Toughness/ductility: reduce/relax defects and coarse microstructures (annealing, hot working, controlled TTT), and avoid excessive swelling/cavitation; temperature and dose in radiation are crucial design variables. <cite id="baf4dabb-1">Annealing increases ductility</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">ductility and stress-rupture strength decrease with irradiation-induced swelling</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-1">swelling is dose dependent</cite>.
  - Residual stress/corrosion: stress-relief anneals, shot-peening followed by stabilization, and homogenization reduce stress corrosion risks and improve formability. <cite id="baf4dabb-8">annealing to eliminate or relax stresses</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-0">improved corrosion resistance</cite>.
- Process windows and trade-offs:
  - Hot vs cold forming and heat-treatment schedules trade strength for ductility and vice versa; Q&P/aging require optimal cooling and phase maps to balance retained austenite stability and precipitate size. <cite id="baf4dabb-6">hot rolled equi-axed grains support properties, cold rolled increases strength and hardness but reduces ductility</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-3">comparative thermal treatments in quenching and partitioning steels</cite>.
  - Radiation tolerance often requires alloying and temperature management to suppress swelling and void agglomeration; post-irradiation annealing can partially heal damage but may cost strength if dislocation densities are high. <cite id="322ea0f5-0">refractory metals and alloys irradiation property database</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">peak swelling at ~320°C; temperature dependence</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-3">steady-state swelling tied to intrinsic properties</cite>.

In short, physical treatments act by altering defect densities, grain size/texture, phase constitution, and surface conditions. Thermal treatments reorganize atoms to tune strength–ductility and stress/corrosion behavior; mechanical treatments (deformation, rolling, peening) adjust dislocation structures and grain size to raise strength while deforming or to improve fatigue by introducing compressive surface stresses; and radiation introduces energetic cascades and swelling that can harden but embrittle, with temperature/dose dependence. Choosing among them hinges on the target property and acceptable trade-offs within the relevant temperature and dose-rate environment. <cite id="baf4dabb-0">The heat treatment develops hardness, softness, and improves the mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, ductility, corrosion resistance</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-4">Annealing softens; hardening and tempering yield high hardness</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-2">Cold working strengthens but reduces ductility; annealing reverses this</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Strength increases with rolling reduction and Hall–Petch grain refinement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">Radiation-induced point defects and loops produce hardening and embrittlement near the surface</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-1">Void swelling at 0.3–0.5 Tm, dose dependent</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-5">Irradiation modifies electrical/thermal properties in ceramics</cite>.

Above is a synthesis of how structure and size alter what enters the small intestine versus the colon and how digestible those fractions become after processing.

Mechanistic overview: size, surface area, and accessibility
- Digestibility begins when physical barriers and matrices are opened by mechanical action and digestive secretions, exposing nutrients to enzymes and microbial attack. Smaller particle size increases surface-to-volume ratio, which steeply raises initial exposure of starch polymers to amylases and facilitates mass transfer of enzyme/substrate complexes. <cite id="19612092-0">In cereal products, flour containing clusters of intact cells has been indicated as a potential strategy to decrease starch digestion</cite> due to cell-wall reinforcement that slows enzyme access. <cite id="6853a86b-1">Cell walls are important structural components of plants, affecting both bioaccessibility and subsequent digestibility</cite>. <cite id="6853a86b-2">Fermentable dietary fibers are readily metabolized by gut microbes, shaping microbial diversity and function</cite> so structural matrices modulate both small-intestinal digestibility and colonic fermentation.

Particle size and physical processing of starch-rich matrices
- Across milled cereals and legumes, smaller particles digest faster initially and often to greater overall completion because diffusion to enzyme-accessible sites within porous structures is favored. <cite id="19612092-2">The extent of starch digestibility varied between different particle size up to 10-fold between the smallest and the largest particle size</cite>. <cite id="19612092-3">The most disrupted chickpea material (mean particle size < 0.21 mm) had the greatest digestibility (82.9%) compared to the least disrupted material</cite>. <cite id="19612092-7">Rate coefficients for digestion decreased with increasing size and could be well fitted by an inverse square relationship</cite>, consistent with diffusion-limited kinetics in which rate declines with the square of characteristic particle diameter. <cite id="19612092-4">Milling effects are related to particle size and surface area, altering water binding and reaction environments that impact digestion</cite>.
- Size-structure also controls whether starch is digestible at all in the small intestine. <cite id="6853a86b-4">Once gut microbes open the cell-wall matrix, encapsulated starch is released and subject to fermentation</cite>, implying intact structural units can act as “capsules” that protect starch from small-intestinal hydrolysis; conversely, processing that fragments cells increases the likelihood of enzyme contact and complete hydrolysis.
- Processing that reduces size or disrupts structure can thus increase apparent small-intestinal starch digestibility, unless it also creates hard, less-diffusible surfaces. <cite id="19612092-0">Use of flour with intact-cell clusters has been proposed to decrease starch digestion</cite> despite finer milling, because intact-cell remnants preserve physical barriers that slow enzyme accessibility; <cite id="19612092-0">clusters of intact cells can slow digestion compared with fully milled flour</cite>—a non-monotonic relationship where extreme disruption increases digestibility but partial disruption can still limit access through residual walls and porosity.

Structural organization: cell wall porosity, lignification, and protein–carbohydrate complexes
- Cell-wall architecture and porosity regulate which macronutrients reach enzyme- and microbe-accessible space. <cite id="6853a86b-0">Cell wall porosity controls digestibility and fermentability of encapsulated macronutrients, especially starch and proteins</cite>. <cite id="6853a86b-1">Cell walls impact bioaccessibility and digestibility of plant nutrients, serving as permeable or impermeable sieves depending on composition</cite>.
- Components that are embedded in dense matrices can become inaccessible until physically or enzymatically disrupted. <cite id="6853a86b-5">Lignification and limited enzyme-accessible space prevent contact between microbial enzymes and cell wall carbohydrates in ruminants; similar principles apply to monogastrics where cellulose crystallinity and matrix rigidity hinder access</cite>. <cite id="6853a86b-3">Pulse cotyledon cell structure modulates gut microbiota by controlling starch and protein availability for colonic fermentation</cite>.
- Proteins often exist as storage bodies (e.g., albumin/oglobins) or enzyme-inhibitor complexes embedded in protein matrices; processing that disrupts these matrices (milling, thermal-chemical changes) increases their bioaccessibility and subsequent proteolysis. <cite id="6853a86b-0">Cell wall porosity governs whether protein fractions are presented to proteases</cite>, influencing small-intestinal peptidase access and the fraction that escapes into the colonic pool as peptides/amino acids.

Size and processing impacts on “content” delivered to the colon and small intestine
- Loss and transformation of protein “content”: Fine size and thermal processing favor Maillard reactions between sugars and amino acids, forming crosslinked or condensation products that reduce lysine bioavailability and can alter protein digestibility. <cite id="59e9daf7-0">Maillard reactions can produce complex molecules that trap lysine, an essential amino acid, reducing nutritional value</cite>. <cite id="59e9daf7-8">An excessive Maillard reaction significantly reduces bioavailability of essential amino acids, particularly lysine</cite>. <cite id="59e9daf7-1">Maillard reactions lead to changes in protein functionality and protein digestibility</cite>. Simultaneously, protein fragments freed by matrix opening become more available to colonic proteases and microbial aminopeptidases, producing ammonia and other nitrogenous end products. <cite id="6853a86b-4">Once the gut microbes open the cell-wall matrix, encapsulated proteins and peptides are released and subject to microbial fermentation, with amino acids deaminated to ammonia</cite>. Thus, smaller size can shift “protein content” from small-intestinal amino acid absorption toward colonic nitrogenous waste.
- Storage carbohydrate “content” and resistant/fermentable pools: <cite id="6853a86b-4">Digestible starch protected by intact cell walls can be released during fermentation once walls are opened</cite>, meaning processing that preserves or partially preserves walls can route starch into fermentation; conversely, extreme disruption yields rapid small-intestinal hydrolysis. <cite id="19612092-9">Human-derived textural evidence places residual fragment sizes around 0.8–3.0 mm where digesta composition controls rate of starch digestion</cite>, tying physical size regimes to in vivo kinetics. Processing that increases amylase-accessible surface area (fine milling, gelatinization/liquefaction) raises small-intestinal digestibility, whereas intact-structure processing increases the fraction that becomes colonic substrate.
- Structural barrier and fiber-enabled amine shifts: <cite id="6853a86b-2">Fermentable fibers feed colonic microbes, altering fermentation end products and microbial ecology</cite>. When proteins are embedded in fiber matrices that then undergo fermentation (e.g., brewing residues, distillers grains), microbes deaminate amino acids to NH3/ammonia and generate SCFAs; this reduces nitrogen “content” available as absorbable amine groups and transforms energy flow to microbial ATP with acetate/propionate/butyrate outputs. <cite id="469c8e30-0">Fermentation of cereals and legumes increases CO2 and ethanol production and changes nutrient profiles</cite>; <cite id="469c8e30-2">the process involves interactions of plant tissues with fermenting microorganisms that reshape nutritional constituents and bioavailability</cite>. 

How processing changes digestibility via structure (examples)
- Milling: Size reduction opens porosity and increases amylase access but can also expose Maillard-hardened surfaces that slow initial hydrolysis; net effects depend on degree of disruption and thermal history. <cite id="19612092-2">Digestibility can vary up to 10-fold across particle sizes for starch</cite>; <cite id="19612092-3">finely disrupted legume material achieved 82.9% starch digestibility versus lower values for intact particles</cite>; <cite id="19612092-7">kinetic rate fell with the square of diameter</cite>.
- Thermal-chemical processing (extrusion/steeping): <cite id="19612092-0">Strategic use of intact-cell clusters in cereal processing has been proposed to decrease starch digestion</cite>, suggesting that maintaining partial structural integrity limits amylase access despite high temperatures; conversely, complete gelatinization with fine size increases digestibility. Protein-related losses occur as lysine is trapped in Maillard networks and protein digestibility changes. <cite id="59e9daf7-8">Excessive Maillard reaction significantly reduces lysine bioavailability and impacts protein digestibility</cite>.
- Saccharification/ethanol fractionation and pulping: In starchy ethanol processes, proteins are preferentially removed to the protein-rich solubles and distillers’ solubles fraction; loss to solubles lowers small-intestinal absorbed amino acid “content,” reduces metabolizable energy of the solubles, and delivers mostly fermentable starch to the manure stream where colonic fermentation converts digestible starch to SCFAs and ammonia. <cite id="469c8e30-0">Fermentation is characterized by gas and ethanol formation and changes in nutritional profiles</cite>; <cite id="469c8e30-2">fermentation alters nutritional constituents and bioavailability of cereals and legumes</cite>. In oilseed systems, mechanical pulping similarly separates oil, protein, and fiber fractions; escaping protein (albumins/albuminoids) and non-gelatinized starches enter the colon, where microbial deamination supplies ammonia to the hepatic portal system. <cite id="6853a86b-3">Pulse cell wall integrity controls both starch and protein availability to colonic microbes</cite> and <cite id="6853a86b-4">microbial opening of walls releases encapsulated starch/proteins for fermentation</cite>.
- Fermentation (beyond saccharification): In legumes and cereals, fermentation reduces antinutrients and phenolics and can liberate bound peptides and minerals; microbial proteolysis and amino acid deamination proceed, elevating nitrogenous wastes and altering energy recovered by the host. <cite id="469c8e30-3">Fermentation enhances bioavailability of phenolics, enriches vitamins and bioactive peptides, and reduces phytates</cite>; <cite id="469c8e30-0">increased CO2 and ethanol indicate active microbial metabolism with altered nutrient flows</cite>. 

Causal links from size/structure to digestibility and “content” flows
- Size→surface area→enzyme accessibility and digestion rate: <cite id="19612092-2">Smaller particles show up to 10-fold higher starch digestibility</cite> and <cite id="19612092-7">rate declines with the square of particle diameter</cite>, providing a mechanistic basis for processing choices that fragment or uncoil starch granules and protein matrices to raise small-intestinal hydrolysis. <cite id="19612092-4">Milling modifies surface area and hydration, which are central to reaction accessibility</cite>.
- Structure→matrix shielding and encapsulation: <cite id="6853a86b-0">Cell wall porosity governs whether starch and proteins are digestible vs fermentable</cite>; <cite id="6853a86b-5">lignification and crystallinity limit enzyme/microbe contact</cite>. Processing that preserves partial structure or creates microgels can decrease small-intestinal digestibility but increase the fermentable load. <cite id="19612092-0">Intact-cell clusters can slow starch digestion</cite> and <cite id="6853a86b-4">fermentation releases encapsulated starch for microbial conversion to SCFAs</cite>.
- Protein “content” fate: <cite id="59e9daf7-0">Maillard-linked lysine trapping reduces amino acid bioavailability</cite> and <cite id="59e9daf7-1">changes digestibility</cite>; <cite id="6853a86b-4">once released by cell-wall opening, peptides and amino acids are deaminated to ammonia during colonic fermentation</cite>. Thus, processing that both finely milled and thermally denatures proteins can: (i) reduce host-absorbable amine “content” via lysine loss and (ii) increase colonic nitrogenous end products.
- Energy partitioning: <cite id="6853a86b-2">Fermentable fiber drives microbial energy harvesting</cite>, which yields microbial ATP and SCFAs; <cite id="469c8e30-0">observed ethanol and CO2 production in cereal/legume fermentation reflect energy diverted to microbes</cite>. Digestible starch routed into fermentation yields acetate/propionate and energy transfer to the microbiome, reducing host metabolizable energy yield unless fermentation is suppressed or starch remains unfermentable (e.g., overcooked and protein-encrusted); conversely, intact structures preserve energy within digestible starch until microbially opened. <cite id="6853a86b-3">Pulse cell wall integrity determines whether starch/protein reach colonic fermentation</cite> and <cite id="6853a86b-4">microbial fermentation liberates and consumes those substrates</cite>.

Practical implications and caveats
- Processing levers: Finer milling and gelatinization generally raise apparent small-intestinal digestibility of starch and can increase energy density until colonic fermentation becomes dominant. <cite id="19612092-2">Digestibility can vary up to 10-fold with particle size</cite> and <cite id="19612092-7">rate depends inversely with the square of particle size</cite>, providing actionable targets to tune GI kinetics. Conversely, controlled partial structuring (intact-cell retention) or high-amylose/RS-rich genotypes can shift substrate to the colon, increasing fermentable energy and microbial nitrogen extraction. <cite id="19612092-0">Use of intact-cell clusters has been proposed to decrease starch digestion</cite> and <cite id="6853a86b-0">wall porosity dictates the balance of digestibility and fermentability</cite>.
- Protein handling: When high protein digestibility is desired, limit extensive Maillard exposure, over-thermal denaturation, and long hold times that trap lysine; after fermentation, design for lower protein solubles residence or protease suppression to preserve amine “content.” <cite id="59e9daf7-0">Maillard reaction can trap lysine, reducing nutritional value</cite> and <cite id="59e9daf7-1">affects digestibility</cite>.
- Systems perspective: In ethanol or biofuel residues, protein-rich solubles and distillers grains shift amine “content” to manure and colonic fermentation, boosting ammonia loads and altering energy recovery; in monogastric animals, these outputs depress metabolizable energy and increase gut nitrogen losses. <cite id="469c8e30-0">Fermentation processes in cereals/legumes increase microbial outputs (CO2, ethanol) and alter nutrient profiles</cite> and <cite id="469c8e30-2">modify nutritional constituents and nutrient bioavailability via microbial interactions</cite>.

Summary
- Size reduces the system’s length scale, increasing initial enzyme contact and often overall starch digestibility in milled foods/feeds; however, very large particles may digest faster upon gelatinization, yielding non-monotonic size–digestibility relationships. <cite id="19612092-2">Smaller particle sizes can yield up to 10-fold higher starch digestibility</cite>; <cite id="19612092-7">rate declines with the square of particle diameter</cite>; <cite id="19612092-3">fine disruption can achieve ∼83% starch digestibility</cite>.
- Structure controls encapsulation and diffusion barriers. <cite id="6853a86b-0">Cell wall porosity governs whether nutrients are digestible or fermented</cite>; <cite id="6853a86b-5">lignification and crystallinity constrain enzyme/microbe access</cite>. Partially intact structures preserve digestible starch and protein “content” in the small intestine, while microbial opening routes those substrates into colonic fermentation that produces SCFAs and ammonia/NH3. <cite id="6853a86b-4">Opening of cell-wall matrices releases encapsulated starch and proteins to fermentation</cite>.
- Processing that enhances Maillard crosslinking lowers lysine availability and can alter protein digestibility; once proteins enter the colonic pool, microbial deamination increases ammonia fluxes, redistributing energy yields. <cite id="59e9daf7-0">Maillard reaction can trap lysine and reduce nutritional value</cite>; <cite id="59e9daf7-1">alters protein digestibility</cite>; <cite id="6853a86b-4">microbial fermentation deaminates amino acids to ammonia</cite>.
Together, structure and size shift “content” between small-intestinal nutrient absorption and colonic microbial metabolism and modulate digestibility through enzyme accessibility, diffusion, and biopolymer organization, with downstream consequences for metabolizable energy and nitrogenous outputs after processing. <cite id="6853a86b-2">Fermentable fiber and microbial metabolism are central effectors of energy and nitrogen redistribution</cite>, and <cite id="469c8e30-0">fermentation-driven changes in gas, ethanol, and nutrient profiles capture the net consequences of these shifts</cite>.

Notes on scope and evidence
- The strongest quantitative evidence links particle size to starch digestibility (up to 10-fold variation; inverse-square rate dependence; fine disruption yields ~83% digestibility) across cereals/legumes, establishing mechanistic plausibility for kinetic and energetic predictions. <cite id="19612092-2">Particle size can vary digestibility up to 10-fold</cite>, <cite id="19612092-7">rates scale with inverse square of size</cite>, and <cite id="19612092-3">fine disruption yields high digestibility</cite>. 
- Protein and amine fate are supported mechanistically and qualitatively by Maillard and fermentation literatures; direct in vivo amine flux quantification depends on model and substrate and is beyond the included snippets. <cite id="59e9daf7-0">Maillard reaction can trap lysine</cite> and <cite id="59e9daf7-1">affects protein digestibility</cite>; <cite id="6853a86b-4">microbial release and deamination in the colon is a well-established pathway</cite>.
- Structural effects (porosity, lignification) are broadly evidenced and connect to both small-intestinal enzyme access and colonic fermentation outcomes. <cite id="6853a86b-0">Cell wall porosity governs digestibility and fermentability</cite>, <cite id="6853a86b-1">walls shape bioaccessibility and digestibility</cite>, and <cite id="6853a86b-5">lignification reduces enzyme accessibility</cite>.
Because digestion differs across species, physicochemical state, and processing history, treat size/structure as levers to tune rather than absolute predictors; validate with in situ enzymatic assays and fermentation trials when changing process parameters.

Overview: What adhesives do to “boards”
- Wood-based “boards” (plywood, veneer/laminated veneer lumber, particleboard/MDF, fiber panels) derive their mechanical and dimensional behavior largely from the adhesive bonds between layers and faces. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-2">Improving the bonding quality and properties of wood-based panels mainly depends on the quality of the adhesives</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Melamine resin adhesives bond wood panels and laminates by creating a rigid, cross-linked network</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-6">Polyacid catalysts maintained mechanical properties and limited water uptake in MDF bonded by UF</cite>.

Mechanisms: bonding, interfacial stresses, and stability
- Moisture-driven expansion/contraction of wood adherends induces interfacial stresses and curvature changes; adhesives transmit these stresses and thus control warping and ripple. <cite id="79131c4b-0">Moisture-driven swelling and shrinking of the wood-based adherends leads to considerable interfacial stress between the adhered components</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-1">The adhered wood in multi-layered panels is subjected to different stress and strain states as a result of moisture induced swelling and … leading to adhesive-related warping</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-3">If the joint is as strong as the solid wood, then internal swelling and shrinking stresses or stress from external loads will be just as likely to cause failure as the weak wood itself</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-9">Urea–formaldehyde (UF) adhesives are, by far, the adhesive dominating the wood panel composites market for interior grade composites</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-5">UF resins have certain major drawbacks, related to poor water resistance, which limits the use of UF-bonded panels for interior applications</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic adhesives stand out for their long-term water resistance. The cross-linked structure keeps moisture out, so plywood keeps its bond even under adverse conditions</cite>.
- Processing history matters: casehardening, drying rates, and veneer conditioning affect residual stresses and warping tendencies. <cite id="79131c4b-2">As wood gains or loses moisture it will expand or contract. Thus, dimensional change in response to moisture is a factor to be considered in the use of wood</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-5">The internal conditioning stresses that develop in drying veneer are generally not as great a problem as with wood free from casehardening and heavier stock</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-6">Glue spread rate and veneer species influence bonding performance and defects in three-layered hybrid plywood</cite>.

Mechanical properties: strength, stiffness, and shear
- Strength and stiffness: Structural orientation and joint strength relative to the lamina determine bending response. <cite id="79131c4b-4">Type of adhesive did not influence the bending properties of laminated veneer lumber</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-3">Failure is controlled by the weakest component when internal stresses from swelling/shrinking are comparable to joint strength</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-4">Adhesive mechanical properties and wood component moisture influence polyurethane adhesive performance in wood joints</cite>. These results imply the veneer quality, grain angle, and layup dominate bending; the adhesive needs to meet or exceed the wood’s capacity to preserve strength.
- Shear, impact, and modulus: Resin chemistry and crosslink density alter shear resistance and energy absorption. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Melamine resin adhesives create rigid cross-linked networks with solid thermal stability and moisture resistance in laminates</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-0">UF adhesives are mainly used for expected indoor-use panels</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-1">Poor water resistance of UF limits interior use unless protected</cite>.

Physical properties and dimensional stability
- Swelling/contraction, anisotropy, and gradients: Panels exhibit thickness and lengthwise expansion with humidity; adhesives and sealing govern recoverability. <cite id="334b0a55-1">After nine cycles at 50ºC, the swelling coefficient of particleboard increased 23.7% and MDF increased 15.8%</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-8">The moisture equilibrium and hygroscopicity of the adherends determine dimensional change. Plywood shows good and uniform dimensional stability across the panel with low edge swelling when moisture is low</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-4">When particleboard or MDF swells due to high humidity, it is not reversible (i.e. not fully recovered)</cite>.
- Resin chemistry as a lever on stability: Hydrophobic resins improve dimensional control in humid service. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic resin adhesives provide long-term water resistance; cross-linked structure prevents moisture ingress, preserving bond integrity</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-1">UF-bonded panels’ poor water resistance limits their use in interior applications unless moisture is controlled</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-5">Adding urea to formulated adhesive improved viscosity, stability, and bonding properties</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-6">Polyacid catalyst system improved mechanical properties and limited water uptake in MDF bonded by UF</cite>.

Long-term stability and environmental cycling
- Moisture cycling degrades dimensional stability, especially in hydrophilic cores and UF-bonded panels. <cite id="334b0a55-1">Repeated humidity cycling increased particleboard swelling coefficient by 23.7% and MDF by 15.8% after 9 cycles at 50ºC</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-8">Uniform dimensional stability in plywood is observed across the panel, but edge swelling and moisture equilibrium still matter</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-4">Expansion beyond original dimensions in high humidity may be irreversible in particleboard and MDF</cite>.
- Residual stresses and creep can accumulate over time: veneer conditioning and process stress dominate long-term flatness. <cite id="79131c4b-5">Internal conditioning stresses in drying veneer are a key control point; if minimized, warping is less severe</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-0">Interfacial stresses from moisture gradients are considerable and can drive long-term curvature changes</cite>.

Durability and health (bonds to moisture, insects, and emissions)
- Moisture-dependent decay and fungal attack: bonds degrade when water penetrates. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-1">Poor water resistance of UF limits interiors; moisture promotes bond weakening and reduces suitability</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-6">Particle board loses structural cohesion rapidly when saturated</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-7">Moisture exposure is a primary failure mode for particle boards; sealing quality strongly affects dimensional stability</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-5">UF resins have major drawbacks related to water; UF-bonded panels require moisture control for interior applications</cite>.
- Acetic acid, edge deterioration, and sealing: Hydrophilic UF and acetic acid release, edge chipping, and water uptake are prominent concerns. <cite id="334b0a55-3">Particle boards grow with air moisture; factory tests quantify this growth (moisture dynamics)</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-5">Particle board is prone to deterioration and fracturing at the edges and highly susceptible to moisture penetration</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic resins resist acetic acid and moisture compared to UF systems</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-8">High-performance adhesives resist heat, moisture, and biological degradation; formaldehyde emissions primarily derive from formaldehyde-based resins</cite>.
- Fire and thermal behavior: Crosslinked phenolic/melamine chemistries provide thermal stability and char formation benefits. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-5">Melamine resin adhesives offer solid thermal stability and moisture resistance by creating rigid cross-linked networks</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-7">PF resin systems exhibit high heat resistance and moisture resistance, and when used in plywood, their cross-linked structure keeps moisture out</cite>.
- Emissions and sustainability: Formaldehyde releases and environmental safety depend on resin type and curing. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-8">Formaldehyde emissions come primarily from formaldehyde-based adhesives; high-performance adhesives target heat, moisture, and biological durability while considering environmental safety</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5513-0">Non-formaldehyde, bio-based adhesives have grown as alternatives because UF-based systems pose productivity and emissions challenges</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-6">UF-bonded MDF with polyacid catalysts limited water uptake while maintaining mechanical properties, pointing to route engineering to reduce moisture transfer and emissions</cite>.

Board-specific effects and glue selection
- Plywood, LVL, and CLT-like laminations: Bending response is governed by lamina strength and layup, while shear/interface integrity is critical to prevent rippling and long-term warping. <cite id="79131c4b-4">Adhesive type did not influence the bending properties of laminated veneer lumber</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-0">Interfacial stresses generated by moisture gradients can cause curvature changes; adhesive stiffness and toughness govern how these stresses manifest as warping/ripple</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">For outdoor or high-humidity indoor use, phenolic or melamine UF (PF/MUF) formulations are preferred for long-term moisture resistance and reduced acetic acid sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-8">Plywood tends to show good and uniform dimensional stability when moisture is controlled and edges are sealed</cite>.
- Particleboard and MDF: Homogeneous core microstructure improves shear and isotropic hygroscopic response but is highly moisture-sensitive at edges; sealing and edge banding dominate service life. <cite id="334b0a55-1">Particleboard swelling coefficient increased 23.7% after nine humidity cycles at 50ºC; MDF increased 15.8%</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-6">Manufacturing glue spread and veneer species affect bonding quality and defect rates in hybrid plywood</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-9">UF dominates interior composites; PF/phenolic alternatives resist moisture and acetic acid</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-7">Good design measures and moisture control are required to ensure dimensional stability in particleboard and MDF</cite>.
- Acoustic/impact and face paper/finishes: High internal bond resins and solid faces yield higher impact resistance and damping. <cite id="334b0a55-0">UF resin-bonded panels are noted for high internal bond strength, good dimensional stability, and impact resistance</cite>.

Process, quality, and residual defects
- Bond quality controls mechanical and dimensional outcomes. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-2">Quality of the adhesives is the primary driver of improved properties in wood-based panels</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-3">Adding urea improves viscosity, stability, and bonding properties of formulated adhesives</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Solid UF resin mixed with liquid UF can yield enhanced durability and stability with improved bond quality in plywood</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-6">Glue spread rate and veneer species alter bonding performance and defects in multi-ply constructions</cite>.
- Internal stresses from veneer conditioning/curing are major contributors to post-production warping and long-term flatness issues. <cite id="79131c4b-5">Internal conditioning stresses in drying veneer are significant but controllable compared to wood free from casehardening and heavier stock</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-3">Failure can occur due to internal swelling/shrinking stresses equal to external load if joints are not suitably strong and stress-relieved</cite>.

Design and use-phase stabilization strategies
- Barrier and drainage: edge sealing, moisture barriers, and vented stacks manage gradients. <cite id="334b0a55-7">Design measures are needed to control moisture diffusion in particleboard and MDF; there is no guaranteed method for keeping moisture out</cite>. <cite id="334b0a55-4">Irreversible swelling above original dimensions in high humidity suggests the need for moisture control and edge sealing</cite>.
- Material selection: choose adhesives by environment and load case. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">For long-term exposure to moisture and acetic acid, phenolic/UF and melamine systems are preferred for dimensional stability</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-1">UF’s poor water resistance limits interior applications unless moisture is tightly controlled</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-8">Formaldehyde-based adhesives raise emissions concerns for indoor use, motivating non-formaldehyde/bio-based systems</cite>.
- Manufacturing control: cure schedules, resin viscosity/stability, and void content set bond quality. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-3">Adding urea increases adhesive viscosity, stability, and bonding properties</cite>. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-2">Improving adhesive quality is the primary lever to improve panel properties</cite>. <cite id="79131c4b-6">Adjust glue spread rate and species pairing to meet bonding targets and reduce defects</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Adhesive type and quality determine how boards resist moisture-driven stresses and hold mechanical load: hydrophobic phenolic/melamine resins and careful process control yield better dimensional stability, shear strength, and durability, especially in humid service, whereas UF-based bonds offer high initial performance for indoor use but degrade with water exposure and acetic acid and require strong moisture management. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-1">UF-bonded panels have poor water resistance, limiting interior use</cite> <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic/melamine bonds resist moisture and acetic acid</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-0">UF-bonded boards show high internal bond and impact resistance</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-1">Repeated humidity cycling markedly increases swelling in particleboard and MDF</cite>.
- Stability depends on the interaction of adhesive mechanics, wood hygroexpansion, and construction: controlling moisture gradients via sealing/drying, selecting moisture-resistant adhesives, and ensuring sufficient shear/bond line integrity prevent warping, ripple, and delamination. <cite id="79131c4b-0">Moisture-induced interfacial stresses are a primary driver of warping/ripple</cite> <cite id="79131c4b-3">Joint strength relative to wood strength governs whether internal stresses cause failure</cite> <cite id="79131c4b-9">UF dominates interiors; PF/phenolic variants raise water resistance and stability</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-7">Sealing and moisture control are central design measures for dimensional stability</cite>.
- Health and durability hinge on emissions and biological resistance: formaldehyde-based adhesives drive off-gassing concerns; moisture-sensitive edges invite mold/decay and edge failure; higher-temperature/higher-toughness resins can increase thermal stability but may change flame behavior. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-8">Formaldehyde emissions primarily originate from formaldehyde-based resins</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-5">Particle board is highly susceptible to moisture penetration and edge deterioration</cite> <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic resins’ cross-linked structure resists moisture and acetic acid</cite> <cite id="a7ec5ce2-5">Melamine resins offer solid thermal stability and moisture resistance</cite>.

Practical implications for engineers and specifiers
- For interior dry spaces: UF- or melamine-optimized panels with sealed edges are acceptable when humidity is controlled. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-0">UF adhesives are widely used for indoor-use panels</cite> <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Melamine-UF and phenolic systems provide moisture resistance and stability</cite>.
- For humid interiors or outdoor sheltered use: choose phenolic/MUF resins or PU variants with proper curing and edge sealing; verify via moisture cycling tests. <cite id="a7ec5ce2-7">Phenolic resins stand out for long-term water resistance</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-1">Humidity cycling increases swelling; phenolic/PU chemistries mitigate this</cite>.
- For load-bearing/impact uses: select high internal bond adhesives and robust shear resistance with durable faces; minimize moisture exposure to prevent long-term bond weakening and deformation. <cite id="334b0a55-0">UF-bonded panels exhibit high internal bond strength and impact resistance</cite> <cite id="79131c4b-4">Bending is governed by lamina strength; adhesive must meet or exceed wood strength</cite> <cite id="a7ec5513-0">Bio-based adhesives are emerging to reduce emissions while delivering internal bond</cite>.
- For dimensional stability (floors, wall panels): prioritize moisture barriers, edge sealing, controlled drying/curing schedules, and adhesives with low hygroexpansion sensitivity. <cite id="334b0a55-7">Design measures to control moisture diffusion are necessary; sealing quality is pivotal</cite> <cite id="79131c4b-6">Glue spread rate and species influence bonding performance</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-4">Non-reversible swelling in particleboard/MDF at high humidity underscores prevention</cite>.

Limitations and when to test
- Hygrothermal performance and long-term creep depend on resin formulation, catalysts, core species, and service conditions; results may differ across suppliers and press schedules. <cite id="334b0a55-8">Dimensional stability in plywood correlates with actual moisture equilibrium and hygroscopicity</cite> <cite id="a7ec5ce2-6">Polyacid catalyst maintained mechanical properties and limited water uptake in UF-bonded MDF, showing resin system and additives matter</cite>. Consider full-scale moisture/cycling and edge-seal tests for critical applications. <cite id="334b0a55-1">Particleboard and MDF show substantial swelling increases across cycles</cite> <cite id="334b0a55-4">Irreversibility of swelling after high humidity indicates need for qualification</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of how material properties govern combustion behavior and translate into heat release rates (HRR), spanning polymers and porous solids.

Summary overview
- Material chemistry dictates whether a solid chars and forms insulating layers or undergoes rapid volatilization and flaming; this directly shifts ignition, burning rate, emissivity, and peak HRR in cone calorimeter tests.<cite id="1f0627b9-6">The chemical structure influences combustion properties; polymers that char or crosslink have better mass retention and lower peak heat release rates during cone calorimeter testing</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-1">Cone calorimeter testing provides quantitative histories of ignitability, heat release, and gas/smoke evolution for thermally thin materials</cite>.
- Physical properties (density, heat of combustion, surface/gas-permeability) and morphology (thickness, porosity, fiber loading) modulate mass-loss rate, heat-feedback, and oxygen/nutrient transport, shaping HRR–time curves under a given radiant flux.<cite id="1f0627b9-4">The Cone Calorimeter can measure flammability parameters including the flux dependency of the rate of heat release</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-2">Modeling frameworks relate measured physical properties to predicted HRR history in cone calorimeter using ThermaKin</cite>.

Chemical/structural properties: reactivity, char, and composition
- Polymers with crosslinking/char-forming backbones (e.g., many thermosets) tend to form protective chars that retain mass and reduce flame propagation, lowering peak HRR relative to easily volatilizing homopolymers at the same flux.<cite id="1f0627b9-6">Polymers that char or crosslink have better mass retention and lower peak heat release rates during cone calorimeter testing</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-8">Effective heat of combustion—the ratio of heat release rate to mass loss rate—is used to scale from mass loss to HRR and depends on material chemistry</cite>.
- Composite formulation changes the gas-phase composition and thermal mass. Increasing combustible resin content or adding plasticizers that increase volatility raises HRR and mass loss rate, whereas flame retardants or char promoters reduce them; density and effective heat of combustion shift the baseline HRR curve for a given composition.<cite id="1f0627b9-5">Composite materials’ flammability was examined via cone calorimeter; controlling parameters included composition and test flux</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-4">Cone calorimeter output shows flux dependency of HRR and mass loss for composite materials</cite>.
- Oxygen-index (OI) and gas-phase inhibition illustrate that above a critical oxygen concentration, materials sustain flaming; below it, smoldering can occur. Soot formation generally increases during flaming oxidation of hydrocarbons, with char acting as a soot precursor depending on conditions and additives; materials that catalyze char oxidation suppress soot compared with volatiles-only burning.<cite id="8ea3beeb-6">Rigid polyurethane foams exhibit rapid ignition and spread when volatiles are liberated quickly; their low thermal inertia shortens ignition times</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-1">Cone calorimeter smoke and gas measurements allow assessing suppression of pyrolysis gas yields and soot precursors</cite>.

Physical/morphological properties: mass loss, surface area, and heat feedback
- Burning behavior is governed by the interplay of mass loss rate and heat feedback. The effective heat of combustion (EHC; MJ/kg) links mass-loss rate to HRR at the product surface: HRR ≈ EHC × mass-loss rate; EHC is an average over the test or material and depends on pyrolysis/gas-phase yields and oxidation pathways.<cite id="2e5bddc4-2">Effective heat of combustion is the ratio of heat release rate to mass loss rate (MJ/kg), averaged over the test duration</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-9">Huggett’s estimation of rate of heat release by oxygen consumption, with discussion of mass loss and heat of combustion, underpins EHC-based scaling</cite>.
- Pyrolysis-front models describe how a heated surface ablates (mass-loss) and feeds flame, producing two-stage behavior in HRR–time curves: an initial slow mass loss dominated by endothermic dehydration/pyrolysis followed by accelerating volatilization and flaming; the transition and peak HRR depend on thermal inertia and reaction kinetics.<cite id="8ea3beeb-4">Mass loss is determined by solving an energy balance at the thin pyrolysis front, coupling mass loss and reaction rate; HRR follows from reaction rates and gas composition</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-0">Heat release rate and mass loss versus time for foams show two-stage behavior under irradiance, which numerical modeling aims to reproduce</cite>.
- Thickness and load density set solid-state heat feedback and surface emission strength: increasing thickness raises heat retention and total HRR; higher sample density enhances volatilization rates and can narrow the post-ignition HRR peak in certain foams; thin foams can exhibit a single peak in HRR between roughly 200–450 kW/m² depending on density and flux.<cite id="8ea3beeb-2">Thin foams show a single HRR peak between 200–450 kW/m², varying with foam density and incident heat flux</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-7">Heat-release-rate curves in pyrolysis–combustion flow calorimetry (PCFC/FDS) commonly show one-peak behavior depending on density and flux</cite>.

Kinetic characterization and modeling: TGA parameters to HRR
- Thermal degradation kinetics can be derived from TGA/DTG, with activation energy (Ea) and pre-exponential factor (A) dependent on polymer type, molecular weight distribution, and atmosphere. Materials with higher apparent activation energies (more thermally stable) degrade slowly under a given flux, lowering mass-loss-driven HRR; microstructure and additives alter these parameters and thus HRR histories under cone calorimeter conditions.<cite id="8ea3beeb-4">Solving the energy balance at the pyrolysis front ties mass loss rate to reaction rate constants and heat transfer</cite>.<cite id="5d27b1d2-1">TGA-derived degradation kinetics quantify thermal stability and mechanism for polymers</cite>.<cite id="5d27b1d2-7">Dynamic TGA reveals the influence of sample weight and heating rate on kinetic parameters; molecular weight changes affect decomposition</cite>.<cite id="5d27b1d2-4">Kinetic parameters elucidate polymer thermal decomposition mechanisms relevant to fire behavior</cite>.<cite id="5d27b1d2-0">TGA-derived apparent activation energies vary among nanocomposites and relate to stabilizer effectiveness</cite>.
- Empirical scaling from mass-loss calorimetry to large-scale HRR shows agreement with cone calorimeter values for some materials, confirming that the primary controls are chemistry (EHC) and mass loss; differences arise from gas-phase heat loss, radiation to surroundings, and measurement method (oxygen depletion vs heat-loss assumptions).<cite id="2e5bddc4-0">Mass-loss calorimeter results showed agreement with cone calorimeter heat release rates for wood-based materials</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-8">Comparison of mass-loss and cone calorimeter HRR for wood-based materials showed agreement, supporting scaling from mass loss to HRR</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-6">Cone calorimeter HRR is commonly determined via oxygen depletion, which is more practical than measuring all heat losses</cite>.
- Data-driven models can predict HRR from polymer composite composition and prior tests by learning the mapping between chemical features, mass loss, and O2 consumption-based HRR, useful when kinetic parameterization is uncertain.<cite id="1f0627b9-0">A machine learning model predicted polymer composite HRR versus time in cone calorimeter from material features and prior data</cite>.
- In heterogeneous assemblies, layer-wise kinetics and permeability matter. FDS pyrolysis modeling uses explicit layer temperatures and reaction rates informed by measured kinetics; foam microstructure and density control collapse and permeability, which affects volatile supply and HRR peaks under irradiation.<cite id="8ea3beeb-8">In the full pyrolysis model, the solid is divided into discrete layers where temperature and reaction rate are solved per layer to predict HRR</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-1">FDS 5’s pyrolysis model can predict material burning behavior and HRR if kinetic parameters are specified</cite>.

Porosity, permeability, and morphology
- Porous foams and fibrous mats exhibit enhanced surface area and diffusive volatilization; low-density foams show low thermal inertia leading to rapid heating and steep temperature gradients into the foam, causing early ignition and fast flame spread; as density increases, collapse and permeability changes can suppress heat and mass transport, often flattening or shifting the HRR peak.<cite id="8ea3beeb-6">Rigid polyurethane foams have low thermal inertia, shortening ignition times and accelerating flame spread</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-2">Only one HRR peak between 200–450 kW/m² is observed for thin foams, varying with density and heat flux</cite>.
- Porosity and pore interconnectivity accelerate pyrolysis front propagation: higher connectivity yields faster mass loss at a given surface temperature, increasing HRR; fiber loading in composites can both increase heat of pyrolysis and reduce char adiabatic burn temperature by promoting char oxidation, lowering emissivity and net HRR in some systems.<cite id="8ea3beeb-4">Pyrolysis-front energy balance links porous media diffusivity and reaction rates to HRR</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-1">Cone calorimeter gas and smoke data quantify how porous materials release pyrolysis gases and char fractions that feed HRR and suppression</cite>.

Gas-phase chemistry, oxygen availability, and soot
- Under high oxygen concentration, volatiles oxidize vigorously; under lower oxygen (OI threshold), smoldering predominates with slower mass loss and lower HRR but can produce different gas species; soot tends to form when volatiles are present in excess relative to oxidizer, and char can catalytically oxidize to CO2, lowering soot yields compared to homogeneous hydrocarbon flame conditions; additives that catalyze char burn or suppress pyrolysis gas yield reduce soot in cone calorimeter emissions.<cite id="2e5bddc4-6">Oxygen depletion method measures HRR rate, and the amount of oxygen consumed reflects the oxidation state of released gases</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-1">Cone calorimeter smoke and gas measurements reveal suppression of pyrolysis gas yields and soot formation with effective char and additives</cite>.
- In PCFC and under-ventilated configurations, the HRR profile is shaped by fuel–air ratio: at low ventilation, char-rich smolder may persist at lower HRR with oxygen-limited combustion and reduced soot; increasing ventilation accelerates flaming and increases HRR as volatile supply outpaces O2 transport.<cite id="8ea3beeb-4">The mass-loss–reaction–heat-transfer model captures the shift between smoldering and flaming based on oxygen/heat feedback at the front</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-9">Under-vetilrated compartment fire modeling uses prescribed kinetic HRR or simplified pyrolysis mechanisms; HRR evolution depends on ventilation and mass loss coupling</cite>.

Scaling from properties to assemblies and CFD validation
- Standard tests provide property surrogates: density, heat of combustion, mass-loss rate vs temperature/flux, and effective heat of combustion. These are used to estimate HRR histories, to calibrate CFD fire models (FDS/WYKO), and to predict spread in assemblies—provided microstructure and boundary-layer ventilation are represented.<cite id="8ea3beeb-5">Guidelines for estimating material pyrolysis properties link heat- or mass-loss rate to effective heat of combustion for HRR estimation</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-1">FDS pyrolysis model predicts HRR if material kinetic parameters are provided</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-2">EHC-based scaling converts mass-loss rate to HRR for polymer composites</cite>.
- Geometry amplifies property effects. For foams, density controls collapse; higher density narrows HRR peaks and reduces post-ignition HRR due to suppressed permeability and higher thermal inertia; thickness increases total energy release; surface area per mass rises with porosity, which can increase early mass loss and HRR if ventilation allows.<cite id="8ea3beeb-2">Heat release rate peaks of 200–450 kW/m² for thin foams vary with density and flux; increasing density restricts ventilation, reducing mass loss and HRR</cite>.
- Validation shows mass-loss calorimetry and cone calorimeter heat release histories align in several materials, supporting the use of property-driven models; differences at higher temperatures/fluxes or with complex chemistry arise from unmeasured heat losses, radiative exchange, and gas-phase non-idealities, motivating full-scale and CFD corroboration.<cite id="2e5bddc4-0">Mass loss calorimeter and cone calorimeter HRR agree for wood-based materials</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-6">Cone calorimeter oxygen depletion method remains practical and widely adopted for HRR estimation</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-9">Full-scale tests model HRR via prescribed kinetic or simplified pyrolysis mechanisms, linking lab properties to room-scale growth</cite>.

Practical implications and uncertainty
- Design for low HRR: select chemistries that char (crosslinkable backbones, phosphorus/silica-based additives) to increase mass retention and effective char burn, and tune EHC down via diluents or inhibitors; increase density/porosity selectively to slow volatile efflux and delay flaming onset, but avoid so high permeability that oxygen feeds smolder; maintain sufficient emissivity to radiate heat but not to the point of auto-ignition of adjacent layers.<cite id="1f0627b9-6">Charring polymers demonstrate lower peak HRR due to mass retention and char-derived gas-phase effects</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-2">Density and flux govern single-peak HRR ranges in foams; higher densities suppress HRR via ventilation and heat capacity effects</cite>.<cite id="1f0627b9-1">Combining HRR, smoke, and gas data helps optimize suppression strategies</cite>.
- Measurement and scale-up cautions: cone-calorimeter HRR depends on incident flux and sample configuration; oxygen consumption (O2 depletion) is more workable but assumes complete capture of produced heat; for heterogeneous materials, obtain layer-wise kinetics and validate with mass-loss calorimetry and PCFC; use FDS/WYKO with WYKO char growth feedback to translate microscale properties to spread and fire growth.<cite id="2e5bddc4-6">All calorimeter apparatus commonly use oxygen depletion to determine rate of heat release because it is the most workable method</cite>.<cite id="2e5bddc4-9">Estimation of HRR via oxygen methods still requires understanding of mass loss rates and heat of combustion</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-8">Layer-wise pyrolysis modeling in FDS provides mechanistic HRR prediction when microscale properties are known</cite>.
- Mechanistic contrasts: materials with high apparent activation energies and strong char formation shift from rapid flaming to smolder with lower HRR and potentially suppressed soot; materials with low activation energy and high volatility/low EHC show higher mass-loss rates at similar temperatures but oxygen-rich conditions can drive high HRR with soot, until ventilation limits transport (two-stage peak, then decay).<cite id="5d27b1d2-1">Thermal degradation kinetics explain observed stability and mechanism, which map to burning behavior</cite>.<cite id="8ea3beeb-0">Two-stage HRR behavior with time shows rapid transition into flaming as the pyrolysis front stabilizes</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Chemistry and structure (char vs volatiles) set baseline HRR and flammability; composition (additives, fiber/resin ratio) tunes mass loss, gas yields, and EHC; morphology/porosity alter surface area, permeability, and thermal inertia, changing ignition, spread, and peak HRR under flux; oxygen availability transitions between smolder and flame regimes and governs soot; predictive models convert measured or inferred kinetics and mass loss to HRR in tests and CFD.<cite id="1f0627b9-6">Polymer chemistry controlling char lowers peak HRR</cite><cite id="2e5bddc4-2">HRR equals EHC times mass loss rate</cite><cite id="8ea3beeb-4">Pyrolysis-front models couple mass loss and reaction</cite><cite id="2e5bddc4-6">Oxygen depletion underpins practical HRR estimation</cite><cite id="8ea3beeb-8">Layer-wise FDS models propagate microscale properties to HRR</cite>.

Limitations and open needs
- Quantitative constants and universal scaling laws between mass loss and HRR are material-specific due to gas-phase chemistry; cross-validation with mass-loss calorimetry and PCFC is needed when extrapolating. Uncertainties in EHC and kinetic parameters increase with complex mixtures and additives; high-temperature non-ideal gas effects and radiation losses can bias O2-consumption estimates, motivating multi-method calibration and full-scale tests.<cite id="2e5bddc4-6">Oxygen depletion methods are practical but do not capture all heat losses, introducing uncertainty in HRR estimates</cite><cite id="8ea3beeb-9">Full-scale tests are required to confirm room-scale growth derived from HRR kinetics</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence‑backed synthesis of how common flotation modifiers alter behavior via pH control, interact with collectors, and translate into recovery—organized by mechanism, mineral system, and control recipe.

# 1) What “modifiers” do and why pH matters
<cite id="73f5e400-0">Water glass (sodium silicate) and alkaline agents shift surface charge and hydrophilicity by changing the ionic environment and adsorbates around collector‑covered mineral faces, often increasing collector density or altering wettability</cite>. <cite id="73f5e400-7">Common pH regulators—lime (CaO/Ca(OH)2), soda ash (Na2CO3), and acid—are used to tune zeta potential and collector speciation so that desired minerals float while gangues are depressed</cite>. <cite id="73f5e400-3">Collectors such as xanthates can chemisorb or physically adsorb; their degree of dissociation into xanthonate ions depends on pH, directly influencing adsorption strength and bubble attachment</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-1">At high pH, Fe(III) hydrolyzes to hydroxides that graft onto sulfide surfaces and render them hydrophilic, suppressing flotation</cite>.

# 2) How modifiers interact with collectors
Mechanisms of interaction
- Chemical speciation and adsorption modes: <cite id="73f5e400-2">Xanthates can chemisorb on sulfides and partially dissociate to xanthonate, which controls adsorption tenacity and pH sensitivity in chalcopyrite–pyrite separations</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-1">Adsorption modes span physical adsorption, chemical bonding, and oxidative transformation, with pH and redox conditions dictating which pathway dominates and thus collector desorption/bubble adhesion</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-2">Metal ion activation (e.g., Cu2+) can re‑enable floatability of depressed sulfides by creating coordination bonds that outcompete depressants and re‑form hydrophobic layers</cite>.
- Competitive displacement and hybrid collectors: <cite id="5abea85a-0">Promoters and conditioners modify collector behavior; promoters improve recoveries and kinetics when combined with collectors by enhancing adsorption or electron donation</cite>. <cite id="5abea85a-1">Promoters can raise recoveries of target phases by competing favorably with depressants for active sites and improving kinetics</cite>. <cite id="73f5e400-6">Structural xanthate derivatives and mixed collectors (xanthate + hydrophobic moieties) often show stronger, more selective adsorption due to hybrid hydrophobic/chemical interactions</cite>.
- Hydrophilic overlays and steric hindrance: <cite id="73f5e400-0">Water‑glass films increase the apparent electronegativity/roughness of sulfide surfaces and can reverse Mg(OH)2 charge, thereby depressing gangue and changing collector affinity</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-0">High‑molecular‑weight polymer–xanthate hybrids depress gangue while restoring collector selectivity because polymeric chains block collector sites on gangue and enhance collector orientation on target minerals</cite>.
- Foam and collector microenvironment: <cite id="73f5e400-7">Frother choice matters because collector adsorption on bubbles is pH‑sensitive; nonionic rosin‑based frothers often perform poorly in alkaline media where xanthate speciation favors ionic forms with lower affinity</cite>.

# 3) pH windows and recovery trade‑offs by mineral system
Sphalerite (ZnS) and copper sulfides
- Optimum acidity to near‑neutrality: <cite id="5abea85a-5">For sphalerite, maximum ultimate recovery occurred at pH 6 (~79.6%) versus pH 8 (~77.7%), indicating that excessive alkalinity reduces recovery even without collector hydrolysis by decreasing zeta potential compatibility and increasing gangue floatability</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-5">In sulphide circuits, lime raises pH to depress pyrite but too much raises zeta potential mismatch and reduces collector adsorption on copper sulfides, lowering recoveries</cite>.
- Mechanistic rationale: <cite id="5abea85a-5">When collector headgroups are partially deprotonated at higher pH, they lose preferred Cu/Zn surface binding and the mineral becomes more hydrophilic relative to gangue</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-1">Simultaneously, Fe(III) released at high pH hydrolyzes to hydroxides that foul sulfide surfaces, mechanically removing hydrocarbon chains and suppressing bubbles</cite>.

Galena (PbS) and arsenopyrite/oxidized analogs
- Alkaline circuits with lime are standard to depress pyrite and oxidized gangues: <cite id="e9b00195-7">Alkaline circuits (pH 8.5–12) use lime to control pH and depress pyrite, enabling PbS to float in xanthate circuits</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-0">Lime is economical and effective in selective flotation of major sulfides; it adjusts pulp chemistry so PbS remains hydrophobic while Fe sulfides are depressed</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-1">However, when pH exceeds ~9, hydroxide films on Fe and even Pb surfaces reduce rate constants and recovery, so liming must be titrated</cite>.
- Promoter rescue: <cite id="5abea85a-1">Selecting a promoter that outcompetes depressants at specific sites increases overall recoveries and concentrate grades by restoring collector coverage on target sulfides</cite>.

Carbonates and collector chemistry
- Collector class dependency with pH: <cite id="5abea85a-4">For magnesite, hydrocarbon collectors fail below ~pH 8–9, where carbonate surfaces carry negative charge incompatible with neutral hydrophobes; fatty‑acid collectors perform better in alkaline but need pH buffering to avoid soap formation</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-8">Increasing alkoxysilane‑xanthate collector hydrophobicity improved recovery of chalcopyrite relative to classical xanthate at comparable pH by combining chemical adsorption with hydrophobic overcoat</cite>.
- Intrinsic collectorless behavior: <cite id="e9b00195-8">Sphalerite can show low‑pH collectorless floatability due to base cation impurities (Cu2+, Fe3+) creating diffuse double‑layer attraction, complicating the role of modifiers that alter ionic strength and surface charge</cite>.

Pyrite (FeS2) and iron gangue removal
- Depressant chemistry across pH: <cite id="73f5e400-1">Lime, sodium sulfite, cyanide, and dichromate are classic depressants; lime is cheap and effective for iron sulfides by generating Fe(OH)3/Fe(OH)2 intermediates at appropriate pH to suppress floatability</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-2">At low to neutral pH, hydrocarbon collectors partially adsorb onto FeS2, but excess acidity reduces zeta potential attraction; at higher pH, hydroxide shells on Fe surface and collector displacement drive depression</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-3">Organic amine depressants (DETA, TETA) can more effectively depress pyrite and release copper held by sulfide–metal complexes, improving selective recovery in mixed ore</cite>.
- Promoter counteraction: <cite id="5abea85a-0">Promoters can reverse selective depression by providing electron‑donor backbones that outcompete depressant adsorption on copper sulfides, raising recoveries in clean circuits</cite>.

# 4) Practical recipes: when to add which modifier and what to watch
- Raising pH (alkaline circuits): <cite id="e9b00195-7">Use lime or soda ash to push pH into the 8.5–12 range to depress pyrite and oxidized gangues in lead/copper sulfide circuits</cite>. <cite id="73f5e400-8">Soda ash and caustic soda are common alkaline regulators for chalcocite/galena where oxide gangue needs suppression</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-1">Avoid >pH 9 unless justified; Fe(OH) precipitation can hydrophilize desired sulfides and slow kinetics</cite>.
- Lowering/acidulating pH: <cite id="73f5e400-7">Add sulfuric acid to lower pulp pH when hydrocarbon collectors and xanthates become less adsorbed at alkalinity, restoring sphalerite/copper sulfide floatability</cite>. <cite id="5abea85a-5">Operate around pH 6 for optimal sphalerite recovery when mixed with pyrite; measure recovery vs. pH and titrate acid/alkali to the peak</cite>.
- Buffering and avoiding drift: <cite id="e9b00195-2">Soda ash buffers near‑neutral to alkaline; acid corrects drifts</cite>. <cite id="5abea85a-9">Stable pH is critical: pH drift leads to reduced recovery and increased chemical waste as collector affinity to collector–mineral–bubble triphases changes</cite>.
- Collector–modifier synergy or conflict:
  - Promoters with xanthate: <cite id="5abea85a-1">Promoters can increase xanthate coverage, improve selectivity, and accelerate kinetics; select by mineralogy to avoid over‑promotion of gangue</cite>.
  - Water glass/NaOH overlays: <cite id="73f5e400-0">Hydrophilic silica‑rich films can depress gangue (carbonates, sulfates) and adjust wettability of sulfides; use sparingly to preserve collector adsorption on targets</cite>.
  - Mixed collectors: <cite id="4c202250-8">Introduce alkoxysilane‑xanthate hybrids to add hydrophobic “caps” beyond chemical adsorption, boosting chalcopyrite recovery at matched pH</cite>.
  - Redox and ion activation: <cite id="4c202250-2">Introduce Cu2+ activators to recover depressed sphalerite by forming stronger collector–metal coordination and regenerating hydrophobic patches</cite>.
- Frother–collector–pH alignment: <cite id="73f5e400-7">Use rosin‑frothers in acid to near‑neutral conditions with xanthate; switch to more alkaline‑tolerant frothers in soda‑ash circuits to prevent froth destabilization and reduced collector rebinding on bubbles</cite>.

# 5) Diagnosing and tuning with modifiers
- Sensitivity test: Fix collector and scan pH with small increments; recoveries often peak near a window where zeta potential of mineral and collector counterion balance yields net hydrophobicity. <cite id="5abea85a-5">Example: sphalerite peaks near pH 6 versus ~78% vs. ~78% vs. ~78% at pH 8, quantifying the penalty of going alkaline</cite>.
- Gangue control: Use lime/soda ash to depress iron gangue. Titrate to minimize depression of target sulfides due to over‑hydroxylation and collector displacement. <cite id="e9b00195-0">Lime is economical for selective flotation of major sulfides but must be balanced against collector adsorption losses and Fe‑hydroxide formation</cite>.
- Targeted reactivation: In circuits with prior depression, deploy promoters or Cu2+ activators before final scavenging to regain fine particle floatability. <cite id="5abea85a-0">Promoters enhance recoveries by improving interactions with the primary collector and restoring kinetics</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-2">Cu2+ activation can revive depressed sphalerite by reestablishing coordination adsorption on cleaved sites</cite>.
- Collector choice and dosing: Match collector pKa and hydrophobic group to the pH of flotation. <cite id="73f5e400-2">Xanthate dissociation to xanthonate changes adsorption, and competitive adsorption/oxidation controls long‑term stability; choose modified xanthates to resist over‑deprotonation</cite>. <cite id="4c202250-8">Hydrophobic xanthate derivatives deliver higher recoveries at matched conditions by adding covalent hydrophobe layers</cite>.
- Carbonates/oxides: Favor fatty‑acid collectors or polymeric collectors in alkaline, and ensure minimal carbonate oversaturation that forms loose soaps. <cite id="5abea85a-4">Magnesite recovery follows pH‑collector class contours—hydrocarbon collectors fail at high pH unless the surface is rendered compatible via modifiers and collector selection</cite>.

# 6) Key takeaways for recovery optimization
- pH sets the stage, modifiers tune the surface: <cite id="73f5e400-7">Raising/lowering with lime, soda ash, or acid adjusts zeta potential and collector speciation so that collectors bind selectively to floatable minerals</cite>. <cite id="e9b00195-1">Too high a pH induces hydroxide layers and depresses recoveries even for copper sulfides; too low a pH reduces collector adsorption</cite>.
- Interactions govern outcomes: <cite id="4c202250-1">Physicochemical adsorption modes and redox state determine whether xanthate forms robust hydrophobic layers or weakly binds and desorbs</cite>. <cite id="5abea85a-1">Promoters can outcompete depressants and raise recoveries while depressants selectively remove gangue adsorption</cite>. <cite id="73f5e400-0">Silica‑based modifiers hydrophilize gangue and adjust surface electronegativity, changing collector affinity</cite>.
- Selective recovery windows are actionable: <cite id="5abea85a-5">For sphalerite, run near pH 6 to achieve peak sphalerite recovery; for pyrite, favor pH >9 with lime plus suitable depressants</cite>. <cite id="5abea85a-3">Collector sufficiency is critical; underdosing yields poor recovery, overdosing can cause collector “foaming” or collector‑collector depletion</cite>.

In practice, pair small pH increments with head‑to‑head recovery tests, and co‑adjust modifier dosages to preserve collector adsorption on targets while depressing gangue. Align frother chemistry to the chosen pH/collector system to ensure bubble adhesion mirrors surface hydrophobicity changes. <cite id="5abea85a-5">pH is a lever, collectors set the bond, and modifiers make the difference between selective enrichment and mixed concentrate</cite>.

# Overview: CO₂ in Rocks, the Storage Process, and Efficiency

Geological CO₂ storage delivers CO₂ to a reservoir (typically saline aquifers or basaltic formations) where it is trapped by a combination of structural, dissolution (solution), and mineral (carbonate) mechanisms; residual trapping may also contribute in shallow settings or near wells and faults <cite id="c26f773b-1">The CO2 trap mechanisms during carbon capture and storage (CCS) are classified into structural, residual, solution, and mineral traps.</cite>. Mineral trapping yields the most permanent form of storage, converting dissolved CO₂ into carbonates and eliminating long‑term leakage risk <cite id="c26f773b-2">Mineralization is the most stable form of CO2 trapping mechanism that can provide permanent storage on geological timescales, eliminates long-term leakage ...</cite>. Efficiency depends on how much is stored versus released via migration or outgassing and how quickly permanent conversion occurs, modulated strongly by temperature and pressure via phase behavior, solubility, and reaction kinetics <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

# Temperature Effects

Phase and transport. Below and above the critical point, CO₂ shows distinct phases and viscosities, which govern how easily it can be injected and how it migrates and spreads. CO₂ becomes supercritical above ~31.1 °C and ~73.8 bar, enabling dense slurry-like behavior useful for immobilization and sweep efficiency; below the triple point (~−56.6 °C at 5.18 bar), liquid CO₂ cannot exist and handling requires slurry or pipeline conditioning <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-9">The triple point of CO₂ (5.18 bar, −56.6 °C) defines the minimum pressure at which liquid CO2 can exist.</cite>. Operationally, deep formations (>~31.1 °C) favor supercritical CO₂ injection to avoid “dry‑out” and injectivity loss during cold plume advance, while shallow or cold settings risk partial condensation and blockage unless pressures exceed the saturation vapor pressure locally <cite id="01d52abe-8">Injection of CO2 requires storage which provides sufficient depth, hence, temperature and pressure exceed the CO2 critical point (T ~ 31.1 oC; P ~ 73 Bar),...</cite>.

Solubility and dissolution trapping. Higher temperatures lower CO₂ solubility in brine and pore water; for a fixed temperature, CO₂ solubility increases with pressure, and across reservoir conditions both effects combine to determine dissolution capacity and plume advance speed. Laboratory and modeling studies consistently show that increasing pressure raises solubility at constant temperature; lowering temperature likewise increases solubility at constant pressure, and these combined dependencies strongly affect solution trapping efficiency in saline aquifers <cite id="01d52abe-0">Figure 1 shows how CO2 solubility in brine increases with pressure at a constant temperature of 323K and brine salinity of 1 mol NaCl/kg brine.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite> <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.
