Warm reservoirs store less CO₂ as dissolved species per unit volume than cold reservoirs at equal pressures, tending to accelerate migration and favor structural or mineral capture as the dominant long‑term sink <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

Kinetics of mineral trapping (carbonation). Temperature controls reaction rates and product phase assemblages. Elevated temperatures generally accelerate basalt carbonation rates, but high pressure boosts CO₂ solubility and mass transfer, together enhancing carbonate formation; basaltic systems rich in Ca, Mg, and Fe yield rapid and permanent fixation, and field results show pressure increases accelerate in situ mineralization <cite id="18cc0e2f-6">Elevated temperatures accelerate reaction kinetics, while higher pressures increase CO2 solubility in water. # Pressure Effects

Phase and injectivity. Pressures above the critical pressure and above the CO₂ saturation vapor pressure of brine favor supercritical injection and dense CO₂ slugs, improving sweep efficiency and reducing phase change issues; deep, high‑pressure formations are preferred for direct supercritical injection. # Integrated Pressure–Temperature Pathways and Operational Efficiency

Energy to move CO₂. Moving CO₂ into storage requires work equal to compressing it to and above the storage conditions; above the critical point, density allows high volumetric capacity per bar‑hour at modest power but higher compression stages are needed. Cold CO₂ plumes reduce formation damage and viscosity at fixed pressure head, but warm supercritical CO₂ reduces solubility and may spread faster; energy efficiency trade‑offs require site‑specific compression curves and well‑head temperature management. In deep basaltic formations and ocean basins, direct carbonation pathways are effective precisely because pressure and temperature windows promote rapid dissolution and mineral lock‑up, decreasing net energy per ton stored for the same capture rate <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-5">SC-CO2 treatments are typically performed at moderate temperatures (35–55 °C) critical point (31.1 °C, 7.38 MPa) CO2 solubility increases with pressure and ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-0">Basalt rich in alkaline earth elements facilitates rapid and permanent CO2 fixation as carbonates. elevating the CO2 pressure can increase the carbon ...</cite>.

Pumping, phase control, and monitoring. Controlling temperature and pressure at the wellhead (e.g., via heat exchangers or by choosing cold sources like ambient air or cold ocean water) can improve injectivity by reducing viscosity and preventing hydrates in the surface network, enabling higher volumetric rates. Conversely, in shallow or cold reservoirs, maintaining sufficiently high downhole pressure and temperature (e.g., via steam injection or by depth selection) prevents partial condensation and non‑darcy flow restrictions. Integrated reservoir–chemistry models and field tests (e.g., EGS‑like stimulation, basalt carbonation pilots) use P–T pathways to maximize pressure diffusion coupling and carbonate growth while bounding migration risk by timely pressure buildup behind the plume <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite>.

Seal performance and safety windows. Increasing injection pressure tightens pressure diffusion coupling and enhances retention near injectors, but it narrows the safety margin against induced seismicity; increasing reservoir temperature increases gas mobility and can accelerate CO₂ breakthrough. Best practice uses a balanced P–T program that achieves rapid pressure buildup behind the front to promote dissolution/mineralization while keeping the footprint below caprock failure thresholds. Carbon mineralization prior to structural trapping is favored in hot, high‑pressure fields (e.g., Iceland) to pre‑consume alkalinity and convert CO₂ to solid carbonates before it reaches the caprock interface, improving permanent storage efficiency versus delaying strategies <cite id="01d52abe-8">Injection of CO2 requires storage which provides sufficient depth, hence, temperature and pressure exceed the CO2 critical point (T ~ 31.1 oC; P ~ 73 Bar),...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-7">In this paper we describe the thermodynamic and kinetic basis for mineral storage of carbon dioxide in basaltic rock, and how this storage can be optimized.</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-5">Investigation of carbon sequestration through coupled basalt mineralization and CO2 hydrate formation in low-temperature marine settings.</cite>.

How reactivity varies among trace elements in soils, sediments, and waters: environmental controls, speciation, and rates
Summary of controlling conditions
Across environments, trace element reactivity is set by pH and redox potential (Eh), mineral and organic surfaces, aqueous ligands, temperature, and biological activity. <cite id="bb36abb1-2">Mobility and bioavailability generally decline with increasing pH, organic matter, cation exchange capacity, and redox potential</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-3">Sorption/desorption on Fe/Mn/Al oxides, carbonates, phyllosilicates, and organics; ligand exchange; cation exchange; and precipitation/dissolution dominate metal fate</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-8">Partitioning with Fe–Mn–S minerals is central in contaminated sediments, with redox-driven transformations controlling dissolution and reprecipitation</cite>.

Redox-sensitive transition metals: Fe and Mn
Iron and manganese constitute redox hot-spans in many systems. <cite id="0ee1481a-0">Reduction of Fe(III) or Mn(IV) coupled to organic matter oxidation is a major biogeochemical reaction in aquatic sediments and soils</cite>. <cite id="0ee1481a-3">Under circumneutral, suboxic conditions, microbial reduction of poorly soluble Fe(III) to Fe(II) is rapid, redistributing Fe between aqueous/adsorbed and precipitated phases</cite>. <cite id="0ee1481a-7">Because Fe(II) oxidizes quickly to Fe(III) with O2 and Fe(III) oxyhydroxides have low water solubility, Fe accumulates in upper sediments and reduces diffusive Fe(II) transport</cite>. <cite id="0ee1481a-4">Fe(II) can serve as an electron donor to iron-oxidizing microbes, while Fe(III) can accept electrons from anaerobes, reinforcing two-way redox coupling</cite>. <cite id="0ee1481a-5">In Fe–Mn coupled systems, Fe/Mn oxides can oxidize reduced sulfur intermediates; conversely, reduced sulfur compounds can drive Fe(III) reduction, linking Fe/Mn and S cycles</cite>. <cite id="0ee1481a-2">New insights place Mn(III) as a key intermediate in Mn redox cycling, with Fe(II) abiotically oxidized by Mn(oxides) and Mn(III) mediating interconversion</cite>. These dynamics translate to mobility and bioavailability shifts: Eh oscillations mobilize or immobilize Mn and Fe, and associated metal oxyhydroxides control sorption and precipitation kinetics <cite id="bb36abb1-0">Nickel mobility is directly tied to Eh, with redox changes altering dissolution/precipitation and release dynamics across soils</cite>.

Halogenophile/anoxophile contrast: Hg and As
Environmental pH and Eh strongly partition Hg among halides, thiols, hydroxides, and scavenged sulfide phases, with large biological implications. <cite id="ddbe7759-4">Mercury methylation in anaerobic microhabitats (often by sulfate-reducing bacteria) is central to producing neurotoxic methylmercury, and methylation rates depend on organic matter, temperature, pH, salinity, and sulfide conditions</cite>. <cite id="ddbe7759-9">Sulfide controls Hg speciation and bioavailability to methylating bacteria in sediment pore waters</cite>; consistent modeling shows that sulfide titration governs aqueous Hg–halide speciation and MeHg precursor availability. <cite id="ddbe7759-1">Organic matter, sulfide, halide concentrations, and grain size shape Hg species distributions in bottom sediments</cite>. For arsenic, redox state is the primary classifier of bioreactivity and mobility. <cite id="bb36abb1-0">Under oxidizing conditions, As(V) predominates and sorbs to Fe/Mn oxides as arsenate; under reducing conditions, As(III) predominates and diffuses more readily, often interacting with Fe/Mn solids through surface complexes</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-6">Fluctuating redox conditions mobilize trace metals by changing Fe and sulfur speciation, thereby switching As(III) release pathways vs. resequestration</cite>.

Oxidation–reduction of Cr and bioavailability trade-offs
Chromium behavior contrasts redox-immobile 3+ and highly mobile 6+ forms. <cite id="bb36abb1-1">Redox reactions of Cr are key to risk; Cr(VI) is oxyanion-mobilized and bioavailable, while Cr(III) forms hydroxides that strongly sorb and precipitate, lowering mobility and toxicity</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-2">Higher Eh favors Cr(VI) speciation and increased mobility; elevated pH/organic matter and oxidized solids tend to promote reduction to Cr(III) or surface precipitation, lowering bioavailability</cite>.

Sorption/complexation with organic matter, oxides, and carbonates
Organic matter and secondary minerals create diverse sorption edges and complexation that reshape aqueous geochemistry. <cite id="8da3a7f3-0">Potassium availability is governed by sorption to Al/Si oxides and ion-exchange, with adsorption magnitudes and kinetics modulated by competing ions and surface chemistry</cite>. <cite id="8da3a7f3-2">Carbonate in calcareous soils weakens K–surface interactions and accelerates desorption/desorption kinetics, indicating pH-dependent carbonate competition and mineralogy effects</cite>. For transition metals:
- Lead often partitions between carbonates, Fe/Al/organic complexes, and clays. <cite id="bb36abb1-5">Chemical speciation frameworks in mining-impacted soils show Pb co-precipitating with Fe/Mn/S phases and organically complexed; speciation dictates mobility differences among sites</cite>.
- Mercury, while weakly binding OM, shows strong halide/sulfide control in anoxic sediments (see above); thiocyanate/iodide can keep Hg in solution in reducing zones until sulfide appears to remove Hg as HgS or Hg–thiolates.
- Zinc, cadmium, and copper react differently with natural organic ligands and sulfides. <cite id="bb36abb1-8">Under reducing conditions, Zn/Cd partition into sulfide-bearing minerals and Fe/Mn sulfates, often associated with Hg scavenging; oxidative conditions promote desorption into aqueous solutions</cite>. Natural organic matter also promotes Cu/Zn/Cd complexation that elevates aqueous lability under circumneutral pH compared with Fe-hydroxide binding, increasing transport risk.

Base cations (K, Ca) vs transition metals: exchange, carbonate, and phyllosilicate control
Alkali and alkaline earth cations are typically sorbed to phyllosilicate edges, Al/Si oxide surfaces, and organic domains via cation exchange and adsorption. <cite id="8da3a7f3-0">Potassium exhibits strong surface sorption and exchange control, with bioavailability tightly coupled to its sorption behavior and competition on reactive sites</cite>. <cite id="8da3a7f3-5">Calcium dynamics in soils are dominated by cation exchange reactions that alter δ44/40Ca and Ca distribution among minerals and organic matter</cite>. Carbonate and secondary mineral precipitation create additional control points. <cite id="8da3a7f3-2">In calcareous soils, carbonate weakens K adsorption and accelerates desorption kinetics, reflecting buffering by CaCO3 and competitive ion effects</cite>. <cite id="8da3a7f3-6">Secondary mineral precipitation can regulate dissolution of primary minerals, with Fe oxyhydroxides and Ca-oxalate/carbonates precipitating at interfaces to immobilize trace metals</cite>. In contrast, transition metals commonly form inner-sphere complexes with Fe/Mn oxides, or outer-sphere associates with humic substances, producing strong site-specific retention and pH/redox sensitivity <cite id="bb36abb1-3">Sorption/desorption patterns reflect surface chemistry and lability of binding moieties, so reactive trace elements often show pronounced hysteresis under redox/pH swings</cite>.

Sulfide minerals and partitioning hotspots
Reduced zones in soils and sediments develop sulfides that scavenge metals, compressing aqueous concentrations and forming authigenic precipitates. <cite id="bb36abb1-8">Partitioning of trace metals with Fe–Mn–S minerals is a dominant control under mining contamination; metal mobility co-varies with dissolution of these solids as redox conditions evolve</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-6">Fluctuating redox can thus alternately mobilize and resequester metals by altering Fe/S speciation and metal sulfide formation/dissolution</cite>.

Microbial mediation: sulfate-reducing, Fe/Mn-cycling, As-metabolizing communities
Biological processes reorganize electron transfer, ligand pools, and mineral formation, thereby switching metal reactivity. <cite id="0ee1481a-0">Organic matter oxidation coupled to Fe(III)/Mn(IV) reduction underpins anaerobic zones, transforming sorption-active Fe/Mn oxides into soluble Fe(II)/Mn(II) pools and increasing metal lability</cite>. <cite id="ddbe7759-3">Anaerobic enrichment shows SRB drive mercury methylation, with bioavailability to methylating consortia controlled by sulfide speciation and Hg–halide complex equilibrium</cite>. Iron-oxidizing and -reducing guilds similarly toggle between oxidized precipitates that immobilize contaminants and soluble ferrous iron that enhances transport of co-contaminants and reduces uranium <cite id="0ee1481a-7">Soluble Fe(II) produced by microbial reduction can be re-oxidized to ferric phases at oxic interfaces, modulating contaminant fate</cite><cite id="0ee1481a-4">Fe can act as electron donor or acceptor depending on microbial guild and redox couple</cite><cite id="0ee1481a-5">Mn oxides can oxidize reduced sulfur intermediates, coupling Fe–Mn redox with sulfur oxidation and impacting metal mobility</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-6">Redox oscillations tied to Fe and sulfur speciation therefore control metal mobilization or sequestration</cite>.

Comparative patterns among representative trace elements
• Oxidizable vs. inert behavior: Fe, Mn, Cr, As are redox- and speciation-sensitive; mobility increases under reducing conditions for Fe(II), Mn(II), As(III), and Cr(VI), while Cr(III) and Fe/Mn oxyhydroxides precipitate or strongly sorb, lowering mobility and bioavailability as Eh and pH rise. <cite id="0ee1481a-0">Biochemical Fe/Mn reduction increases lability in anaerobic sediments</cite><cite id="0ee1481a-3">Rapid Fe(II)–Fe(III) cycling under suboxic zones modulates transport</cite><cite id="0ee1481a-2">Mn(III) as an intermediate couples Mn redox and Fe(II) oxidation</cite><cite id="bb36abb1-0">Nickel mobility and release dynamics covary with environmental Eh</cite><cite id="bb36abb1-1">Cr(VI) is oxyanion-mobilized, Cr(III) precipitates to hydroxides reducing bioavailability</cite>. 
• Halogenophilic/anoxophilic enrichment: Hg preferentially partitions into halides and thiols under anoxia; methylation to methylmercury by SRB increases neurotoxic bioviability. Sulfide and halide chemistries control Hg’s environmental lability and bioaccumulation potential. <cite id="ddbe7759-4">Mercury methylation under anaerobic conditions and dependence on environmental factors</cite><cite id="ddbe7759-9">Sulfide control on Hg speciation and bioavailability to methylating bacteria</cite>. 
• Carbonate, phyllosilicate, and oxide controls: Aluminosilicates and Fe/Mn oxides create strong sorption edges for transition metals; carbonates titrate protons and compete for exchange/adsorption sites, shaping metal availability in alkaline, calcareous settings. <cite id="8da3a7f3-0">Potassium sorption/CEC coupling exemplifies oxide–cation interactions</cite><cite id="8da3a7f3-2">Carbonate weakens K–surface bonding and modulates kinetic exchange</cite><cite id="bb36abb1-3">Sorption/desorption and precipitation/dissolution pathways determine metal bioavailability</cite>. 
• Organic matter interactions: OM can increase lability and mobility of transition metals via outer-sphere association and inner-sphere complexation, yet also immobilize metals through coprecipitation and SOM-metal bonding. Bioavailability of alkali/alkaline earth cations often reflects sorption and exchange rather than strong chemical reduction/oxidation. <cite id="bb36abb1-2">Organic matter generally reduces metal mobility and bioavailability</cite><cite id="bb36abb1-5">Speciation of Pb, Zn, Cu, Cr, As in contaminated soils reflects interactions with organic matter and Fe/Mn/S minerals</cite>. 
• Base cations (K, Ca) show strong cation-exchange control and calcite/oxide buffering; their aqueous fluxes respond to pH/Eh via mineral dissolution/precipitation and competitive ion effects, contrasting with transition-metal redox-transformations. <cite id="8da3a7f3-0">K behavior tied to oxide and exchange sites</cite><cite id="8da3a7f3-5">Ca redistribution by cation exchange alters isotopic composition and distribution</cite><cite id="8da3a7f3-2">Carbonate modulates K exchange kinetics</cite><cite id="8da3a7f3-6">Secondary mineral precipitation constrains primary mineral solubility and metal fluxes</cite>.

Environmental drivers and timescales
Reactivity shifts occur over multiple timescales. <cite id="0ee1481a-0">Microbial Fe/Mn reduction can transform solids within days to months in sediments</cite>, while <cite id="bb36abb1-8">precipitation–dissolution kinetics of Fe/Mn/S solids govern long-term metal partitioning</cite>. <cite id="ddbe7759-4">Hg methylation rates depend on temperature and available organic matter and sulfide</cite>, linking reactivity to seasonal and biological pulses. Redox oscillations in wetlands and riparian zones drive metal resuspension–reprecipitation cycles; <cite id="bb36abb1-6">bioaccessibility can swing with Eh fluctuations via Fe/S speciation changes</cite>.

Implications for risk and management
Predicting chemical reactivity requires matching element chemistry to environmental controls: oxidizing, high-pH settings favor Fe/Mn oxide formation and Cr(VI)/As(V) mobility, while reducing, sulfate-rich conditions promote Hg methylation and sulfide scavenging of metals including Zn/Cd and often Hg. <cite id="bb36abb1-6">Management can leverage redox manipulation and Fe/S mineral dynamics to immobilize metals, but fluctuating conditions can reverse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="bb36abb1-8">In contaminated sediments, promoting Fe/Mn/S mineral precipitation or anoxic zones can immobilize metals, yet remobilization accompanies redox recovery</cite>. <cite id="8da3a7f3-2">In calcareous soils, maintaining carbonate buffering and understanding K/Ca exchange kinetics informs nutrient and contaminant allocation</cite>. <cite id="ddbe7759-9">For Hg, controlling sulfide and halide chemistry and methylating-community activity reduces MeHg production</cite>. Collectively, these principles explain why reactivity varies across trace elements: base cations are exchange- and mineral-controlled, transition metals are redox- and ligand-controlled, and metalloid/redox couples like As and Hg are highly responsive to microbial and aqueous speciation shifts. <cite id="bb36abb1-2">Higher pH, organic matter, and Eh generally decrease mobility/bioavailability</cite><cite id="0ee1481a-0">Microbial reduction of Fe/Mn oxides increases metal lability</cite><cite id="ddbe7759-9">Sulfide-rich conditions govern Hg bioavailability and methylation</cite>.

- In comparative, multi‑plant leachability studies, many elements remain largely immobile under TCLP‑like acidic extraction, while those that do leach seldom reach levels in simulated exposure solutions that exceed acute or chronic toxicity screening thresholds—supporting low hazard quotients when normalized to realistic ingestion/dermal exposure doses; such studies show element‑specific solubilization differences and note conservatism built into laboratory tests (e.g., acetic acid) compared with in situ geochemistry <cite id="de8bdb0f-5">Heavy metal concentrations were higher in TCLP eluates, TCLP method showed some interference owing to acetic acid toxicity</cite>. 
- Bioaccessibility/gut/lung solubility tests on fly ash provide additional evidence that most metals are relatively insoluble in biological fluids; for example, experiments dissolving fly ash in simulated gut and lung fluids quantify low solubility and bioaccessible fractions for many metals, a line of evidence often used to argue that TCLP’s acidic extraction overestimates human bioaccessibility relative to more realistic exposure media, and thus the “failure” mode in some leach tests is overly conservative for exposure endpoints while still protecting against unreasonable risk <cite id="1d34c064-7">we have approximated the latter exposure pathways to determine the solubility of various metals from fly ashes in simulated gut and lung fluids</cite>. 

3) Examples “from different places”

In this study, 41 soil samples and 32 cabbage samples were collected from the area surrounding the ...</cite><cite id="3ac523aa-4">Results showed that the average concentrations of Cd, Cr, Co, and Ni were all below the risk screening values reported for environmental pollutants (pH > 7.5)</cite>.

Acute Toxicity to Aquatic Invertebrates. 8. No Hazard. 22. No Hazard. Toxicity to Aquatic Algae. 16. No Hazard. 12. No Hazard (11)</cite>. 
- China and other regions: multi‑site, multi‑method leaching and risk coding across coal power plants report that, after controlling disposal conditions (e.g., landfilling with liners, caps, leachate treatment), most metal concentrations and risk indices fall into lower risk classes; national literature compiles case evidence that CFA is the third‑largest industrial waste yet can be managed without undue hazard when engineered controls and monitoring are applied, aligning with test programs that screen for leaching and toxicity endpoints <cite id="3ac523aa-9">In China, coal fly ash (CFA) is the third-largest industrial waste and causes significant economic and environmental problems</cite><cite id="3ac523aa-1">by T Takao · Cited by 5 — Fly ash is set in the bottom of a plastic pipe, and water penetrates by gravity … a dissolution of harmful element</cite>.
