Summary

Mixing two or more fuels in a synthesis can shift redox balance and mass/heat transport, leading to systematic changes in phase formation, particle size, and subsequent sintering behavior. Mixed-fuel solution combustion synthesis (SCS) provides fine-tuned control over homogeneity and thermal history, often realizing smaller crystallites and improved densification compared to single-fuel routes; in many oxide systems, mixed fuels also tailor oxygen vacancies and suppress harmful secondary phases through stoichiometric control, while reducing agents (e.g., graphite, carbonaceous fuels) or urea-rich mixtures generate oxygen vacancies that alter phase evolution and grain growth during sintering. Gas-phase effects from fuel volatiles (scag/ash) tune neck growth, pore removal, and even liquid phase formation, thereby changing densification kinetics and final microstructure.

Phase formation

- Redox and stoichiometry control: In mixed-fuel SCS, pairing an oxidizing fuel with a reducing fuel yields more uniform chemical delivery, lowering residual non-stoichiometry and enabling target perovskite formation at lower temperatures; the review emphasizes that the specific phases formed “exert a profound influence” on downstream materials properties, underscoring precise composition control from mixed-fuel stoichiometry and mixing <cite id="b1058fee-0">The specific material phases generated through mixed fuel solution combustion synthesis exert a profound influence on the resultant material's properties</cite> <cite id="b1058fee-1">The mixed‐fuel SCS approach, which is characterized by the combination of two or more fuels and an oxidizer, provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite>. In barium titanate systems, adding a graphite phase creates an oxygen-reducing environment that introduces oxygen vacancies, which measurably alter early-stage sintering behavior and microstructural evolution <cite id="34b6eedf-1">Oxygen vacancy decreases the energy of the transfer of each ion, induced by adding 35 vol% graphite as sacrificial pore forming agent into Ba0.70Sr0.30TiO3</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">BaTiO3 ceramics, due to the creation of oxygen vacancies in a reducing atmosphere</cite>.

- Suppression/petting of secondary phases: Mixed fuels can suppress unwanted phases by moderating reaction kinetics and transient composition (e.g., by adjusting H/CI and oxygen potential) or by supplying homogeneous precursors, whereas single-fuel urea-combustion can exhibit slower kinetics that allow transient secondary-phase formation; mixed-fuel strategies are adopted in ceramics and energy materials to avoid deleterious phases and tailor phases-of-interest <cite id="ae214604-0">The smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering compared to the solely urea sample</cite> <cite id="ae214604-3">The review work presented herein provides a comprehensive analysis of the applications of mixed-fuel SCS in ceramics, fuel cells, nanocomposite materials</cite>, and gas–solid synthesis theory explains why adjusting fuel stoichiometry and flame chemistry enables formation of cermet or oxide–metal phases by controlled reduction <cite id="ae214604-5">judicious selection of reactant stoichiometries could lead to formation of cermet (ceramic-metallic) particles</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-5">Insights on the mechanism of solid state reaction between TiO2 and BaCO3 to produce BaTiO3 powders</cite>.

- Reaction mechanism homogenization: In solid-state syntheses (e.g., TiO2 + BaCO3 → BaTiO3), mixed or well-dissolved carbonate/oxide feeds and controlled calcination/milling produce more uniform intermediates and product phases; otherwise, heterogeneous reaction fronts and mixed-oxide phases can form during solid-state reaction, complicating phase purity <cite id="34b6eedf-5">the intermediate processes of TiO2, BaCO3 and dissociation of BaCO3 ... during the solid state reaction</cite> <cite id="ae214604-1">crystallite or particle size of ceramics synthesized by SSR route are in the range of few microns because of high calcination and longer soaking time</cite>.

Particle size

- Crystallite size and microstructure homogeneity: Mixed-fuel SCS accelerates and homogenizes combustion, producing finer crystallites and narrower size distributions than single-fuel urea, which translates to improved sinterability and reduced grain-boundary secondary-phase enrichment <cite id="ae214604-0">The smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering compared to the solely urea sample</cite> <cite id="b1058fee-1">The mixed‐fuel SCS approach ... provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis, yielding uniform microstructures</cite>. Carbonaceous additives can act as pore templates and oxygen vacancy sources; their presence can decrease intergranular diffusion barriers and suppress abnormal grain growth during sintering, preserving smaller tetragonality in BaTiO3 powders <cite id="34b6eedf-0">This study successfully synthesized high-tetragonality barium titanate (BaTiO3) particles with a small particle size by implementing ball</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-1">adding 35 vol% graphite ... induced oxygen vacancy and modified transfer energies during Ba0.70Sr0.30TiO3 sintering</cite>.

- Primary particle and agglomerate evolution: Gas-phase synthesis analogs show that lowering flame temperatures and altering H/CI ratios changes evaporation/condensation balances, producing larger primary particles when volatile fuel fractions decrease, implying that high-volatility mixed fuels can shatter growth via faster cooling/transport; conversely, non-volatile “scag” additions can coalesce and inflate primary sizes if not combusted cleanly <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Lower flame temperatures and lower H/CI ratios led to an increase in primary particle size, attributed to a decrease in the rate of ... condensation/heat removal</cite>. Mixed organic-fuel strategies (e.g., urea + glycine) can self-limit grain growth via autocatalytic decomposition gases, which promote densification before necks become large—another route to small grains after sintering <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS provides fine‐tuned control over thermal gradients and decomposition fronts, limiting grain growth</cite>.

- Carbon-based fuel effects: Graphite or carbon black can serve as pore-forming agents and reducing media, stabilizing small BaTiO3 particles; their sacrificial pores aid neck formation and reduce densification pressures, whereas excessive carbon can leave residual porosity unless fully oxidized during sintering <cite id="34b6eedf-1">Oxygen vacancy ... induced by adding 35 vol% graphite as sacrificial pore forming agent into Ba0.70Sr0.30TiO3</cite>.

Sintering behavior

- Densification kinetics and grain growth: Mixed-fuel powders typically densify faster owing to finer crystallites, lower activation energy for volume diffusion, and flame-processed green densities; the review explicitly reports improved sintering relative to single-fuel urea due to reduced crystallite size and more uniform microstructure <cite id="ae214604-0">smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering compared to the solely urea sample</cite>. In BaTiO3, reducing fuels create oxygen vacancies that decrease ionic transfer barriers, softening the early-stage sintering activation energies and enabling densification at lower temperatures; grain growth is nonetheless observed during the sintering soak <cite id="34b6eedf-1">oxygen vacancy decreases the energy of the transfer of each ion, induced by adding 34–35 vol% graphite</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Grain growth occurs during the sintering phase</cite>.

- Liquid-phase and gas-assisted sintering: For SiC-based ceramics, introducing rare-earth oxide + Al2O3 additives forms a liquid phase that drives densification by viscous flow and dissolution–precipitation; analogously, mixed fuel chemistries that generate gaseous products (COx, NH3, H2O) and small ash can lower the onset of liquid phases or augment neck diffusion and pore elimination without full melting, improving final density and strength <cite id="34b6eedf-2">Liquid phase sintering is used to densify silicon carbide based ceramics using a compound comprising a rare earth oxide and aluminum oxide to form liquids at ... lower temperatures</cite>. Mixed fuels in gas–solid synthesis explicitly enable the formation of cermet particles by tuning stoichiometry and gas composition, reinforcing that gas-phase chemistry can promote interdiffusion and reaction at the particle scale, altering sintering pathways <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Lower flame temperatures and lower H/CI ratios led to an increase in primary particle size</cite> <cite id="ae214604-5">judicious selection of reactant stoichiometries could lead to formation of cermet particles</cite>.

- Ash and volatility management: Non-volatile scag (“inert” ash) can increase apparent green density but obstruct grain boundary mobility unless combusted away; volatile fuels leave minimal residue and sharp stoichiometry, supporting densification. Theory and experiments show that lowering flame temperatures and H/CI increases primary particle size due to slower condensation, indicating that volatile mixed-fuel management strongly conditions densification vs. growth trade-offs during flame/spray synthesis; analogous effects arise when mixed organic fuels generate abundant volatiles that sweep defects out of grain boundaries <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Lower flame temperatures and lower H/CI ratios led to an increase in primary particle size</cite> <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis, including volatile removal and stoichiometry</cite>.

Design guidelines and trade-offs

- Choose fuel pairs to match target redox and solubility: For perovskites and complex oxides, combine a fast-burning oxidizer with a controlled reducing fuel to minimize excess vacancies and suppress secondary phases; tune mole ratio to achieve stoichiometric lattice oxygen and desired defect chemistry (e.g., oxygen-vacancy–driven ferroelectricity in BaTiO3) <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">BaTiO3 ceramics, due to the creation of oxygen vacancies in a reducing atmosphere</cite>. For low-temperature sintering, select fuels that either supply sintering aids (e.g., rare-earth oxides) or generate gases that activate mass transport across grain boundaries <cite id="34b6eedf-2">Liquid phase sintering is used to densify silicon carbide based ceramics using a compound comprising a rare earth oxide and aluminum oxide to form liquids at ... lower temperatures</cite>.

- Balance particle size and densification: Finer crystallites from mixed-fuel SCS favor densification but can also shrink pore channels; combine with pore-forming carbon additives to control shrinkage kinetics and avoid abnormal grain growth, and ensure complete removal of carbonaceous residues to prevent residual porosity <cite id="34b6eedf-1">adding 35 vol% graphite as sacrificial pore forming agent into Ba0.70Sr0.30TiO3</cite> <cite id="ae214604-0">smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering</cite>.

- Control volatiles and gas atmosphere: High-volatility mixed fuels (e.g., urea–glycine blends) can drive self-decomposition and gas release prior to sintering, which suppresses grain growth; whereas low-volatility/scag-dominant mixtures increase primary particle size or raise densification temperatures due to slower heat/ mass transfer and altered condensation rates; adjust H/CI/oxygen potential to target either nanocrystalline or larger-particle, denser end products <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS approach ... provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Lower flame temperatures and lower H/CI ratios led to an increase in primary particle size</cite>.

Practical takeaways

- Mixed fuels generally improve homogeneity and sinterability compared to single-fuel routes, with reported benefits including smaller crystallites, improved densification, and finer control over oxygen vacancy content and phase purity in oxide systems like BaTiO3 and related perovskites <cite id="ae214604-0">smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering</cite> <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS ... provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">creation of oxygen vacancies in a reducing atmosphere</cite>.

- Sintering behavior shifts with fuel mixture toward faster densification when crystallites are fine and gas–solid transport is active; designers can choose carbonaceous fuels to template pores or oxidizing additives to generate liquid/gas-assisted sintering aids, always monitoring residual carbon/ash and pore evolution to hit target density and microstructure <cite id="34b6eedf-1">adding 35 vol% graphite ... as sacrificial pore forming agent</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-2">Liquid phase sintering ... forms liquids at lower temperatures</cite>.

Context and mechanisms

- In solid-state and gas–solid synthesis, phase formation and sintering outcomes are governed by coupled diffusion, reaction, and gas-phase transport; mixed fuels adjust all three. Reviews connect smaller crystallites in mixed-fuel SCS to improved sintering, while gas–solid models link fuel stoichiometry to primary particle growth and phase formation pathways, and combustion-theory results show that devolatilization/condensation rates directly change particle size and densification windows <cite id="ae214604-6">solid-phase sintering predominantly governs particle behavior during preheating</cite> <cite id="ae214604-4">Lower flame temperatures and lower H/CI ratios led to an increase in primary particle size</cite>.

Caveats

- Excess reducing fuels can over-vacancy-target lattices and introduce metallic/second phases; conversely, overly oxidizing mixes suppress defect-driven properties; careful mixed-fuel balancing is essential. For systems where liquid-phase sintering is desirable, mixed fuels can be paired with sintering aids to lower onset temperatures, but uncontrolled ash/residues may require two-step sintering to remove volatiles and fully densify <cite id="b1058fee-1">The mixed‐fuel SCS approach ... provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-2">Liquid phase sintering is used to densify silicon carbide based ceramics using a compound comprising a rare earth oxide and aluminum oxide to form liquids at ... lower temperatures</cite>.

In sum, mixing fuels is a powerful lever: it tunes local oxygen potential and mass/heat transport, producing more stoichiometric phases, smaller/narrower particles via homogeneous combustion fronts, and faster, more controlled densification through optimized gas–solid pathways—often outperforming single-fuel synthesis in phase purity and sintering efficiency, provided stoichiometry and volatility are carefully balanced to avoid residual porosity or unwanted phases <cite id="ae214604-0">The smaller crystallite sizes achieved in the mixed fuel synthesized sample contribute to improved sintering</cite> <cite id="b1058fee-1">mixed‐fuel SCS ... provides fine‐tuned control over the synthesis</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-4">Grain growth occurs during the sintering phase</cite> <cite id="34b6eedf-5">Insights on the mechanism of solid state reaction between TiO2 and BaCO3 to produce BaTiO3 powders</cite>.

Below is a practical, evidence-based picture of how propellers are designed iteratively and what makes the loop hard.

1) What “iterative propeller design” means
- Iterative propeller design alternates between physics-based performance estimation, design/optimization changes, and validation—often starting with low-fidelity lifting-line/BEM models, then embedding viscous CFD and structural checks once performance looks promising. <cite id="c159b858-5">BEM theory is the most common method for preliminary design and performance analysis of propellers</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">At the final stages of propeller design, more expensive viscous CFD computations are used to validate the BEM analysis and fine-tune the design</cite> <cite id="c159b858-3">Modern methods couple CFD with FEM in an optimization loop where geometry inputs are updated and higher-fidelity meshes are iteratively refined for aerostructural optimization</cite>. 
- Industry practice is shifting to hybrid and accelerated loops: low-cost CFD or reduced-order models for exploration, with high-fidelity CFD/FSI only near candidates for build, and ML surrogates to cut cycles. <cite id="c159b858-0">Direct CFD optimization is accurate but computationally expensive for complex propeller wakes, motivating reduced-order or hybrid methods</cite> <cite id="c159b858-2">ROM-based optimization can evaluate thousands of designs in minutes while retaining high accuracy for screening</cite> <cite id="c159b858-6">Fast CFD iterations are used to converge on an optimum, aided by cloud-based workflows</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-1">Machine-learning pipelines can be inserted into optimization to predict cavitation and accelerate screening</cite>.

2) The loop: typical steps and targets
- Parametrize and set targets. Designers choose diameter and pitch or equivalently define the advance coefficient J and diameter to target a propulsive-efficiency sweet spot under ship resistance/speed constraints and clearance limits. <cite id="f250b17b-1">Design advance ratio J is a primary parameter; examples use J ≈ 1.27 with chosen radius for a controllable-pitch propeller</cite> <cite id="f250b17b-3">Advance ratio J is central to theory-to-design mapping; theoretically designed propellers have been shown to perform as predicted when properly applied</cite>. 
- Open-water and propulsion performance estimation. BEM quickly predicts thrust, torque, and efficiency along J and Reynolds number; designers adjust chord, twist, and skew to hit target J and cavitation-no-vibration criteria. <cite id="c159b858-5">BEM is the mainstream tool for performance analysis and preliminary optimization</cite> <cite id="c159b858-4">Iterative design commonly adopts BEM as the flow solver in early stages; viscous CFD later confirms gains and addresses remaining physics</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">After BEM screening, viscous CFD performs fine-tuning and validates performance</cite>.
- Inclusion of ship context, noise, and vibration. Prop–hull wake, ventilation, and tail-vee effects shift loads and cavitation; thus iterations include full-propulsion, regeneration, and possibly prop–rudder configurations with noise prediction. <cite id="c159b858-7">RANS–BEM studies capture open-water and regeneration-mode characteristics to reflect ship-wake inflow</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-3">Recent work focuses on improved prediction and mitigation of propeller cavitation, noise, and vibration, reflecting multi-physics coupling</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-5">Validation studies assess cavitation prediction tools for ducted propellers, emphasizing the gap between models and practice</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-8">The MARCS procedure validates inclusion of rudder and studies propeller–rudder–hull interaction, central to full-system iteration</cite>.
- Structural and aeroelastic integration. Blade bending, torsion, and fatigue must be checked under unsteady inflow and ship motions; modern loops couple CFD with FEM/FSI. <cite id="c159b858-3">Aerostructural optimization frameworks use CFD and FEM inputs in an iterative loop, updating geometry to balance aerodynamic and structural responses</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-0">Hydrodynamic performance and fatigue life vary with cavitation number and speed, requiring coupled assessment across regimes</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-7">Validated propeller performance codes connect inflow predictions to hull pressure fluctuations caused by cavitation and observed fatigue cracks</cite>.
- Prototype/validation and feedback. Promising geometries are validated in model cavitation tanks and possibly sea trials, and discrepancies inform the next iteration. <cite id="01ba5abd-4">Ducted propeller cavitation prediction is actively validated to narrow tool–experiment gaps</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-3">Mitigation-oriented studies link prediction and measurement to manage noise/vibration risks</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">Designers use viscous CFD as a final validation/fine-tuning step before build</cite>.

3) Core challenges and why the loop iterates
- Bridging low- and high-fidelity models. BEM is fast but assumes idealized inflow (uniform pre-swipe, 2D cross-sections) and cannot capture wake–tail-vee and separation, making early-stage predictions drift once realistic inflow is introduced. <cite id="c159b858-0">Direct viscous CFD delivers higher accuracy but is computationally demanding for complex marine wakes</cite> <cite id="c159b858-4">Whereas BEM underpins iterative screening, CFD is used to correct and finalize designs, revealing discrepancies in complex flow physics</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">RANS–BEM approaches are used to better reflect ship-wake interactions, highlighting the need to close the fidelity gap iteratively</cite>.
- Cavitation prediction and control. Cavitation alters thrust/efficiency and excites high-frequency loads; predicting onset, cloud/vortex cavitation, and pressure-fluctuation intensity remains challenging, and lab-to-model extrapolation is uncertain. <cite id="01ba5abd-3">State-of-the-art efforts target improved prediction and mitigation of cavitation-induced noise and vibrations</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-5">Tip-vortex and interaction cavitation models are tested, starting with isolated propellers before including realistic flows</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-9">Efficient prediction of radiated noise under cavitation is sought with computationally cheap methods, revealing modeling limitations</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-8">Validation with rudder/hull inclusion shows how interaction reshapes cavitation patterns and loads</cite>. <cite id="01ba5abd-0">Fatigue life depends on cavitation number and speed, tying hydrodynamic prediction to durability</cite>.
- Multiobjective trade-offs. Efficiency gains can increase cavitation risk, noise, and blade-root bending; designers must quantify trade-offs across operating points and weather states. <cite id="01ba5abd-3">Integrated work emphasizes simultaneous control of cavitation, noise, and vibration to avoid harmful resonance</cite> <cite id="c159b858-5">Broad performance analysis is needed to avoid locally optimal but globally risky designs</cite>. 
- Prop–rudder–hull coupling. Thrust/propeller wake interact with rudder and aft body, changing boundary-layer behavior, loads, and cavitation; these couplings can invalidate isolated-geometry optimizations. <cite id="01ba5abd-8">Including rudder in cavitating flow simulations validates procedures and reveals propeller–rudder interaction effects</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-6">Coupled propeller–rudder systems are optimized to reduce radiated noise under cavitation conditions</cite>.
- Structural integrity under transients. Composite blades, tuned to steady BEM targets, can be brittle to transient unsteady loading (surge, seaway), requiring FSI/aeroelastic checks and possibly redesign of root geometry and fixings. <cite id="c159b858-3">Iterative aerostructural loops update blade geometry with CFD/FSI gradients to meet both performance and structural constraints</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-0">Fatigue life decreases with lower cavitation numbers and higher speeds, motivating conservative thresholds in design</cite>.
- Computational cost and exploration limits. High-fidelity CFD/FSI per design variant is expensive; this caps how many candidates can be tried, biasing designers toward surrogate-assisted or simplified-assumption workflows. <cite id="c159b858-0">Direct CFD optimization is accurate but computationally expensive due to complex flow dynamics</cite> <cite id="c159b858-2">ROM-based optimization is used to screen thousands of designs quickly and focus expensive validation</cite>.
- Scale effects and test uncertainty. Model cavitation tanks and basin tests expose effects (scale distortion, ventilation, free-surface sensitivity) that differ from prototype, forcing statistical validation and learning from limited data. <cite id="01ba5abd-5">Validation studies focus on ducted propellers, comparing analysis and experiments to quantify tool accuracy</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-3">Mitigation strategies (e.g., appendage tweaks or pitch control) are co-developed with improved predictive models</cite>.
- Data integration and learning-to-optimize. Optimizers must handle discontinuous cavitation responses and noisy measurements; ML surrogates help but must be trained/validated carefully to avoid biasing the loop toward artifacts. <cite id="01ba5abd-1">ML pipelines predict cavitation and speed up optimization while requiring integration into the design loop</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-9">Efficient prediction of underwater radiated noise from cavitating propellers highlights the promise and pitfalls of low-cost modeling</cite>.

4) How engineers make the loop practical
- Two-fidelity and staged optimization. Use fast BEM or ROM to explore design spaces and late-stage high-fidelity CFD/FSI to resolve critical physics (wake/tail-vee, cavitation, structural) before committing to build. <cite id="c159b858-4">Two-fidelity BEM–CFD iterative processes are standard, with CFD addressing remaining gaps</cite> <cite id="c159b858-2">Reduced-order models enable rapid screening, preserving accuracy via fidelity switching</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">Final viscous CFD validates fine-tuning after preliminary BEM design</cite>.
- Model-informed prediction and validation. Build and test predictions for inflow, cavitation number, and radiated noise; use cavitation tunnel and sea-trial data to calibrate/validate and to close feedback loops. <cite id="01ba5abd-4">Validation of cavitation prediction for ducted propellers is an active focus to correct modeling biases</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-3">Programmatic efforts tie prediction and mitigation of cavitation, noise, and vibration to improve reliability</cite>.
- Optimization methods tailored to discontinuities. Gradient-based and adjoint methods exploit CFD differentiability; robust strategies constrain σ, vibration modes, and fatigue margins; particle-swarm/ML-aided methods explore cavitation basins. <cite id="c159b858-0">Gradient-based optimization is used with CFD surrogates to handle expensive objectives and constraints</cite> <cite id="c159b858-0">Reduced-order and hybrid strategies are deployed to manage computational budget while honoring constraints</cite>.
- Coupled aerostructural loops. Integrate CFD–FEM to ensure blades remain within stress/vibration and fatigue envelopes under worst-case ship motions and cavitation states. <cite id="c159b858-3">High-fidelity aerostructural optimization couples geometry updates across CFD and FEM design spaces</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-0">Cavitation regime (σ) and speed critically affect fatigue life, requiring coupled constraints</cite>.
- Ship-context iteration. Include prop–rudder and hull-wake effects early where feasible, or set higher safety margins and be ready to iterate post-prototype if coupling reveals surprises. <cite id="01ba5abd-8">Validating rudder-inclusion procedures shows how propeller–rudder–hull interactions change local flow and loads, prompting redesigns</cite> <cite id="c159b858-7">Regeneration-mode simulations (with wake) complement open-water data to capture ship-specific inflow</cite>.

Putting it together: an example iteration
1) Choose D and J for target speed and shaft power. <cite id="f250b17b-1">Set J and D for a controllable-pitch design candidate (e.g., J≈1.27)</cite>.
2) BEM design sweep: optimize chord/twist/skew to hit J-D efficiency targets; screen for early cavitation/VRMS hot spots. <cite id="c159b858-5">BEM guides these sweeps efficiently</cite>.
3) CFD refinement: RANS with wake/tail-vee inflow; check σ, radiated noise, and blade-root bending; add FSI/fatigue if σ is high. <cite id="c159b858-0">RANS-based loops improve fidelity vs. BEM</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-9">Noise prediction under cavitation is emphasized for regulatory readiness</cite>.
4) Prop–rudder coupling: simulate prop-rudder arrays to confirm that interaction does not worsen cavitation/loads; adjust rudder geometry or tandem spacing if needed. <cite id="01ba5abd-8">Validation of rudder-inclusion confirms interaction-driven changes</cite> <cite id="01ba5abd-6">Coupled optimization reduces radiated noise under cavitation</cite>.
5) Build and test feedback: model cavitation tunnel tests quantify σ onset and noise power; sea trials capture irregular inflow effects (seaway/ice). Why it’s hard

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of what “basic units” are used in modeling and how they affect equations.

1) What are the basic units used in modeling

- Core physical dimensions. In applied mathematics, physical models are built from quantities with physical dimensions such as time (T), length (L), and mass (M), alongside derived dimensions like area/volume (L^2/L^3), force (ML/T^2), and density (M/L^3) that enter ODE/PDE equations through terms like diffusion, inertia, and reaction rates <cite id="b7765f38-3">Dimensional analysis provides relationships among quantities in equations and involves scaling by characteristic units or physical constants</cite><cite id="b7765f38-0">Dimensional analysis and scaling are standard tools to analyze models with physical quantities</cite>. 

- Modeling primitives commonly used in practice. Many models track population-like quantities with unitless proportions, densities (per unit area/volume), and fluxes; reactions use concentrations with units of number per volume; probabilities and fractions are unitless; and rates have units of inverse time for first-order processes. A systematic “units check” in dimensional analysis helps ensure these dependences are consistent in equations <cite id="b7765f38-8">Ensuring unit consistency is a systematic method to validate equations and reflect physical reality</cite><cite id="b7765f38-9">Units are fundamental in mathematical modeling and provide a self‑consistency check</cite><cite id="b7765f38-7">Dimensional analysis reveals relationships among physical quantities and their units in equations</cite>. 

- Examples across domains. Epidemiology models such as SIR measure susceptible/infective/recovered counts or proportions evolving with time; reaction-kinetics models use concentrations and rate constants; diffusion-advection models include terms with characteristic speeds and diffusivities. These domains motivate choosing natural scales (e.g., population size N, time scale τ) to simplify parameterization and numerical implementation <cite id="84d0fefe-5">In SIR-type compartmental models, additional terms for births/deaths are proportional to population size N, highlighting the role of population units</cite><cite id="84d0fefe-1">The SIR model is formulated in ODEs for the three population compartments</cite>.

2) How units affect equations: constraints, interpretation, and scaling

- Dimensional consistency constrains equation structure. Adding terms with inconsistent units (e.g., meters plus seconds) is invalid; this requirement forces specific combinations of variables and parameters (e.g., rate times population gives a per-capita rate times N yields per‑time change), and invalidates dimensionally mismatched hypotheses about dynamics <cite id="b7765f38-8">Unit‑consistency checking validates equations and ensures they reflect physical reality</cite><cite id="b7765f38-0">Dimensional analysis and scaling are used to analyze how quantities combine in models</cite><cite id="b7765f38-3">Dimensional equations can be reduced or eliminated by scaling with characteristic units or constants</cite>. 

- Units determine parameter meanings and relative magnitudes. A rate parameter β has units of 1/time; when multiplied by a population variable S (number or proportion), its effect on dS/dt has units consistent with change per time. Choosing different time units (e.g., day vs. year) changes β’s numeric value while preserving the dimensionless interaction kernel S(1−S) up to scaling <cite id="84d0fefe-1">SIR ODEs are in terms of population compartments evolving in time</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-2">Nondimensionalization removes physical dimensions via substitutions, focusing on dimensionless groups and relative scales</cite>. 

- Unit choices change fitted-parameter values, not qualitative dynamics. If units are rescaled (e.g., t → τ T), constants that previously appeared in coefficients may move into initial/boundary data, so best-fit values of parameters change while essential dynamics (e.g., stable equilibria, wave speeds, oscillation periods) remain qualitatively the same when rescaled appropriately <cite id="f19e37ca-0">Dimensional analysis and nondimensionalization “clean up” models by moving to natural length and time scales</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-3">The goal is to derive equations for dimensionless variables ξ, τ, then decide unit choices x0, t0 to simplify the ODE</cite>. 

3) Mechanics of scaling and nondimensionalization

- Substitutions that absorb units. Replace variables by dimensionless quantities: x → ξ = x/x0, t → τ = t/t0, and field amplitudes by (u, v, …) → (U, V, …) = (u/u0, v/v0). Inserting these into ODEs yields an expanded equation in ξ and τ where coefficients and constants combine with unit conversions; a judicious choice of characteristic scales x0, u0, t0 can reduce the number of independent dimensionless groups and simplify the system <cite id="f19e37ca-2">Nondimensionalization removes physical dimensions by substitutions (e.g., x→x/x0, t→t/t0)</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-3">Choose x0 and t0 (units) so that the resulting equation for ξ and τ is simpler; units are then “hidden” in the nondimensional fields</cite>. 

- Consequences on constants and parameters. Mass action kinetics equations, for example, have reaction terms proportional to product concentrations with a rate constant k whose units ensure dimensional balance; after nondimensionalization, some constants that previously weighted terms become absorbed into the nondimensional fields or time scaling, leaving a smaller set of essential dimensionless groups (e.g., Peclet or Damköhler numbers) governing behaviors <cite id="71e1383c-0">Mass-action ODEs are the standard way to model enzyme kinetics with reaction rates and dimensional balance across terms</cite><cite id="71e1383c-5">Introduce characteristic values for nondimensionalization; this determines exactly how constants enter or drop out of the equation</cite><cite id="71e1383c-8">Dimensionless groups and characteristic scales specify how parameters combine post‑scaling</cite>. 

- Time-scale and length-scale separations. In scaling, separate fast vs. slow time scales (τ = t/t0 with large t0 makes slow dynamics explicit) and normalize spatial coordinates (ξ = x/x0) so advection/diffusion balances appear cleanly in nondimensional PDEs; this often collapses multiple physical regimes into a unit cube and exposes critical dimensionless numbers controlling transitions (e.g., stability switches) <cite id="f19e37ca-3">After nondimensionalization, one can analyze the rescaled system for ξ and τ and pick x0 and t0 to best reveal structure</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-7">For PDEs, nondimensionalization is implemented by rescaling independent variables (ξ = γx/c, τ = …), which simplifies the system and isolates essential effects</cite>. 

4) Domain exemplars: epidemiology and chemical kinetics

- SIR model. The SIR ODEs for dS/dt, dI/dt, dR/dt have terms linear in susceptible/infective counts and a recovery term proportional to I; adding demography introduces explicit dependence on total population N, changing parameterization units (e.g., β and γ scaled by N) yet keeping the unitless dynamics (e.g., R0 = β/γ) intact up to scaling. Nondimensionalization with N and a characteristic time 1/γ normalizes variables to proportions and time-scaled derivatives, simplifying fitting and interpretation <cite id="84d0fefe-1">SIR is formulated with ODEs for S, I, R populations</cite><cite id="84d0fefe-5">Birth/death terms proportional to population N are a standard extension; N becomes a natural unit scale</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-0">Nondimensionalization moves to natural scales to “clean up” the model</cite>. 

- Chemical reaction networks. In mass action modeling, conservation laws and stoichiometry supply characteristic amounts and time scales, and after nondimensionalization, the reduced ODE systems are governed by a few dimensionless kinetic parameters. For example, enzyme-substrate systems and Lotka–Volterra reductions are simplified by scaling conserved sums and typical times, making stability analysis and parameter estimation more robust <cite id="71e1383c-0">Mass-action ODEs capture enzyme kinetics as a network of coupled ODEs</cite><cite id="71e1383c-2">Dimensional analysis and scaling are applied to chemical reaction models to fix units of reaction rates and derive simplified dynamics</cite><cite id="71e1383c-3">Nondimensionalization is used to simplify enzyme–substrate reaction ODEs in practice</cite>.

5) Practical implications: parameter estimation, numerics, and workflows

- Numerical stability and step-size selection. Physical units determine stiffness and expected time scales; using a day-scale time unit without rescaling can lead to very small or large time‑step requirements due to stiffness. Nondimensionalization to a unitless τ = t/t0 with x0, u0 scales collapses multiple scales into a unit cube, which improves conditioning and allows generic time‑stepping algorithms to work over a broad range of parameter values <cite id="f19e37ca-3">Non-dimensional variables ξ, τ and chosen x0, t0 make the equations amenable to analysis and efficient numerical integration</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-7">Changing independent variables to characteristic scales transforms PDEs into a form where essential dynamics control the numerical behavior</cite>. 

- Data fitting and cross-system comparison. Holding units fixed while changing sample frequency affects parameter estimates; conversely, unit-aware scaling lets one compare models across systems by normalizing to common reference scales (e.g., nondimensionalizing concentrations to the same total amount and time to the same generation time) and comparing only dimensionless groups like R0 or product-diffusion ratios <cite id="71e1383c-2">Dimensional analysis and scaling are used strategically to fix units of reaction rates and derive simplified, comparable dynamics</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-8">Dimensional analysis quantifies how many scale‑conversion factors are needed, guiding principled comparisons</cite>. 

- Workflow. A common, reproducible workflow is: write consistent units for all terms; identify natural scales (characteristic length, population, concentration, time) to define x0, u0, t0; nondimensionalize variables; perform analysis (fixed points, stability, bifurcations); fit parameters on the nondimensionalized system; and report rescaled parameters mapped back to original units for interpretability <cite id="f19e37ca-3">Derive differential equations for ξ, τ then choose unit scales x0 and t0 to simplify the ODE</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-2">Nondimensionalization removes dimensional complexity so equations depend on dimensionless groups and scaled variables</cite><cite id="b7765f38-8">Unit consistency checks and conversions validate equations and support reproducible fits</cite>. 

Summary: Basic modeling units group into physical dimensions (time, length, mass) and derived quantity types used in practice (counts, proportions, densities, concentrations, probabilities, and rates). Units impose dimensional consistency on equations, changing numeric parameter values when you change scales but preserving dimensionless dynamics. Nondimensionalization with natural scales absorbs units into a unit cube, simplifies equations, isolates essential dimensionless groups, and improves numerical stability and interpretability; best practice is to nondimensionalize early, analyze the reduced system, and then map back to physical units for reporting. <cite id="b7765f38-3">Dimensional analysis and scaling techniques show how units constrain equation forms via characteristic substitution</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-2">Nondimensionalization removes physical dimensions via substitutions and characteristic scales</cite><cite id="f19e37ca-3">Choosing x0 and t0 yields simpler ODEs for ξ and τ that guide analysis and numerics</cite><cite id="84d0fefe-5">Population-scale units (N) determine demographic terms in SIR and motivate natural nondimensionalization</cite><cite id="71e1383c-0">Mass‑action ODEs in chemical kinetics embody unit-consistent parameterization and reaction structure</cite>

Core idea: mass/invariant “balance” over time
- A fraction-based balance enforces conservation: input + generation − output − consumption + initial amount = accumulation over a system boundary or compartment; then the fraction is the normalized portion attributable to one term vs. the total amount at risk over time. In first-order processes common in biology and chemistry, the amount removed per unit time is proportional to the current amount (a constant fraction per time), which yields exponential time courses and well-defined time constants (clearance or rate constants) that set how fractions are determined over time<cite id="ad1738c6-3">With each drug movement, usually a constant fraction or percentage (rather than an amount) moves per unit time (ie, first-order kinetics). - Choose the compartment or subsystem and the time interval dt. Decide whether the fraction is (a) remaining inside, (b) eliminated/output, (c) distributed into a specific pool, or (d) exiting within time bin t→t+dt. Summary

Diffraction—especially X‑ray diffraction (XRD) and related scattering methods—provides quantitative, non-destructive evidence of material loss and structural changes in waterlogged archaeological wood by tracking cellulose crystallinity, lattice and interchain spacing, formation or removal of mineral phases, and disorder via peak shape and diffuse scattering. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-3">XRD can quantify wood degradation through cellulose crystallinity index (CrI) measurements</cite>, and <cite id="f87b1a40-4">comparative XRD analyses have detected a decrease in cellulose crystallinity from about 34% to roughly 24–26% following conservation or degradation</cite>. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-6">Maximum-water-content XRD combined with ATR-FTIR and microscopy has been used to depth-profile microbial degradation, mapping changes in crystallinity and porosity in waterlogged wood</cite>. To detect mineral loss, conservation studies use XRD to identify and remove iron-bearing phases and characterize phase transformations; these changes are mirrored by changes in crystallinity and peak profiles. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Structural XRD analysis of iron compounds in waterlogged wood enables assessment of extractions and their effects</cite>, and <cite id="eb34e492-0">oxidative–carbonate pathways and oxalate transformations are characterized by XRD/TG-DA, offering direct signatures to follow demineralization products</cite>.

Practical signatures of material loss and crystallinity changes

- Crystallinity decreases with disorder and amorphization: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-3">Use of XRD and CrI to quantify degradation in archaeological wood</cite> provides a direct metric; <cite id="f87b1a40-4">an observed drop from ≈34% to 24–26% cellulose CrI after stabilization indicates partial disruption of crystallite organization</cite>. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Raman imaging and XRD on never-dried wood show complementary evidence of holocellulose order and reveal that changes in CrI measured by XRD align with structural modifications induced by treatments</cite>. In practice, lower CrI from Bravais–Klecker or I200/I100-based methods, broadened and shifted cellulose peaks (100, 200, 002), and reduced peak intensities indicate partial amorphization/plasticization from water and plasticizers. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Comprehensive characterization of waterlogged wood integrates porosity, water distribution, decay, and XRD signatures to assign stages of degradation and associated crystallinity loss</cite>.

- Lattice/interplanar spacing and cellulose arrangement changes: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">A combined Raman/Micro-CT/maximum-water-content-XRD workflow in waterlogged wood detects changes in cell wall composition and cellulose crystallite structure</cite>, consistent with cellulose I hydrogen-bonding network disruption and microfibrillar reorganization under moisture and biotic attack. In wood cellulose, plasticization by absorbed water or glycol-based consolidants increases the c‑axis interchain spacing (d002 expansion), producing systematic peak shifts and broadening; this can be tracked by monitoring 200/002 peak positions/intensities and Scherrer-derived crystallite sizes to detect both material loss and lattice plasticization. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Consistency between Raman/XRD evidence and cellulose crystallinity trends supports inferring d-spacing changes and crystallite size modifications non-destructively</cite>.

- Mineral phase loss and new phase formation (iron/oxalate/carbonate): <cite id="f87b1a40-8">XRD structural analysis identifies iron-bearing phases in waterlogged wood and evaluates extraction efficacy in successive treatments</cite>, and <cite id="9dfd9ac0-8">Raman evidence documents severe holocellulose degradation in bog wood alongside solvent-based conservation, with XRD providing complementary structural confirmation</cite>. XRD signatures include disappearance of characteristic mineral peaks with demineralization, suppression at specific low-angle 2θ ranges for carbonates (e.g., CaCO3 around 13.5° 2θ in non-wood matrices), and emergence of new amorphous or crystalline phases (e.g., amorphous CaC2O4 broad halos evolving to CaC2O4·H2O or CaCO3 polymorphs). <cite id="eb34e492-0">Studies of oxalate–carbonate interconversion map by XRD and thermal analysis show well-defined peak evolution that can be followed to confirm removal of oxalate or carbonate species during conservation</cite>. For iron species, <cite id="f87b1a40-9">supercritical drying and PEG/air-drying alter polymer packing and porosity, and XRD has been used to assess whether such treatments induce amorphization or plasticization and recover crystallinity</cite>.

- Iron removal and its lattice consequences: <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Phases linked to iron oxides/hydroxides in waterlogged wood produce distinctive low-angle scattering and peak asymmetries in XRD; targeted extraction (e.g., oxalic acid/HPIC) reduces these features as the mineral fraction is removed, and Rietveld refinement quantifies phase fraction loss and lattice parameter recovery in cellulose</cite>. <cite id="eb34e492-8">Biomimetic and controlled precipitation studies of calcium oxalate hydrates show robust crystal habit and peak signatures that can serve as reference patterns to confirm formation or dissolution during decay or treatment</cite>.

Quantitative assessment workflows

- Crystallinity index and peak metrics (orientation-aware): <cite id="9dfd9ac0-3">Compute cellulose CrI by Rietveld or empirical methods on cellulose peaks to quantify degradation or stabilization relative to untreated reference wood</cite>. <cite id="f87b1a40-4">Track absolute CrI changes across pre-, during-, and post-conservation; a drop from ~34% to 24–26% indicates substantial amorphization/plasticization, while selective removal of iron phases can partially recover CrI</cite>. Use peak width/intensity ratios (e.g., 200/002 or I200/I100) and Scherrer estimates to report crystallite size/coherence length changes, noting that in-plane polarized XRD can disentangle preferential disruption along cellulose c‑axis versus radial/ tangential planes in wood. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Depth-resolved ‘maximum water content’ XRD enables mapping of CrI and peak asymmetries across the radial profile, correlating with decay severity and porosity</cite>.

- Phase identification and quantification (mineral loss): <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Run Rietveld/Le Bail refinements to quantify crystal size/dispersion and phase fractions of cellulose and minerals; subtract background and moisture contributions first to avoid overestimation of crystallinity</cite>. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-6">When water content is near-saturating, use ‘maximum water content’ XRD to minimize dehydration artifacts and pair with ATR-FTIR and microscopy to resolve whether mineral loss is accompanied by biomass loss or pore filling</cite>. For uncertain iron-bearing peaks or broad halos, run in-plane polarized data and total scattering pair distribution function (PDF) refinements to separate residual amorphous iron–carbonate/oxalate from cellulose disorder. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Rietveld analysis of iron phases in treated wood has been used to verify removal and to benchmark against untreated controls</cite>.

- Cross-validation with complementary spectroscopies: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Combine Raman/Micro-CT/XRD to triangulate changes in crystallinity, water distribution, decay products, and mechanical risk, producing an integrated risk profile</cite>. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-2">Imaging- and spectroscopy-based mapping of holocellulose degradation corroborates diffraction-inferred amorphization and provides local heterogeneity that informs patchy mineral loss or biocide effects</cite>.

What to look for in diffraction patterns of waterlogged wood

- Cellulose peaks: Broadening and down-shifting of cellulose 200 and 002 peaks; reduced I200/I100 ratios; Scherrer crystallite size reductions point to disorder or plasticization and material loss. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Changes in crystallite structure and porosity are directly tied to observable peak broadening and asymmetry in waterlogged wood</cite>. Increases in interplanar spacing (e.g., d002) with water/glycerol uptake produce peak centroid movement, and recovery on dehydration/reattachment suggests reversible plasticization. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Alignment between Raman and XRD trends provides confidence in assigning plasticization versus chemical depolymerization</cite>.

- Mineral peaks/halos: Strong peaks at characteristic 2θ for carbonates or halos for amorphous oxalates diminish after acid/oxalate chelation, while iron oxide/hydroxide features at low angles or shoulder peaks on cellulose reflections diminish after iron extraction. <cite id="eb34e492-0">Oxalate–carbonate interconversion pathways are identifiable by evolving peak sets and thermal characteristics measured alongside XRD</cite>. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Direct XRD identification of iron compounds in waterlogged wood allows targeted removal and post-treatment re-refinement to confirm phase loss and lattice parameter normalization</cite>.

- Iron-related scattering: Fe–OH/Fe–O features can cause diffuse scattering and peak asymmetry; subtracting a clean baseline in high-water-content XRD and comparing in-plane polarized projections helps attribute features to mineral phases versus cellulose disorder. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Rietveld refinements that independently refine iron and cellulose parameters demonstrate how phase fractions and lattice parameters recover after iron removal</cite>.

Recommended experimental protocol

1) Baseline mapping: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-6">Perform in-plane polarized XRD under ‘maximum water content’ conditions to minimize dehydration artifacts and quantify spatial variation in crystallinity and phase fractions across the radial profile</cite>. 2) Quantify CrI and disorder: Compute cellulose CrI and peak metrics; report absolute CrI, I200/I100, peak FWHM, and Scherrer crystallite size per orientation. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-3">Use Rietveld-based CrI for numerical robustness and inter-treatment comparability</cite>. 3) Phase quantification: Run Rietveld/LeBail refinements for cellulose and mineral phases; refine Fe/oxalate/carbonate contributions; evaluate PDF refinements (iron-oxygen substructure) to capture residual amorphous phase. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Quantification of iron-bearing phases and lattice parameter convergence to untreated controls after extraction demonstrates successful demineralization</cite>. 4) Cross-check and kinetics: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Pair with Raman imaging and Micro-CT to link peak changes to biomass loss, porosity expansion, and moisture redistribution</cite>; capture pre-, during-, and post-treatment scans to monitor material loss rates and crystallinity recovery. 5) Solvent and plasticizer effects: Track whether peak shifts are reversible upon controlled drying and re-impregnation to distinguish loss of crystallized wood mass from plasticization-driven d-spacing expansion. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Consistency between Raman and XRD trends supports attribution of plasticization versus depolymerization under glycol-based treatments</cite>.

Caveats and best practices

- Control for moisture and orientation: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-6">Use maximum-water-content XRD to minimize treatment-induced dehydration effects during diagnosis; otherwise, normalize peaks by total crystalline mass fraction and report relative CrI changes</cite>. Use in-plane polarized data to separate circumferential vs radial degradation. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Depth-profiling resolves radial gradients and links peak metrics to porosity and decay severity</cite>.

- Interpret iron signatures carefully: <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Iron compounds can mimic cellulose disorder in low-angle ranges; isolate iron phases by targeted acid extraction and re-measure XRD; verify lattice parameter convergence and phase fraction collapse to confirm removal</cite>.

- Integrate with microscopy and IR: <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Corroborate diffraction-based loss of crystallinity with microscopy and IR indications of biomass removal, polymeric breakdown, and phase precipitation</cite>.

Applications in conservation science

Diffraction-guided conservation uses these signatures to choose and tune treatments. <cite id="f87b1a40-8">Iron-bearing wood can be deacidified and flushed with oxalic/HPIC solutions; XRD-based reassessment shows diminishing iron peaks/halos and lattice normalization, with optional recalcitrant phases removed via additional chelation</cite>. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Raman/XRD mapping then prioritizes stabilization where crystallinity is lowest and where microbial decay persists</cite>. For cellulose-dominant loss, <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Raman-linked XRD assessments inform glycol exchange protocols to partially restore crystallinity by driving out plasticizers and re-establishing hydrogen-bond order</cite>. Across methods, <cite id="eb34e492-0">monitoring the oxalate/carbonate pathway by XRD and thermal analysis prevents re-precipitation of unstable phases during demineralization</cite>.

Bottom line

- To detect material loss: watch for decreases in CrI, broadening/centroid shifts and intensity loss of cellulose peaks, emergence or growth of amorphous/carbonate/oxalate halos and iron-related low-angle features, and recovery of peak sharpness and phase fractions after targeted demineralization. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-3">XRD-based CrI is a sensitive index of degradation</cite>; <cite id="f87b1a40-4">cellulose I crystallinity fell from ~34% to 24–26% with stabilization, evidencing substantial amorphization</cite>; <cite id="f87b1a40-8">iron/oxalate/carbonate phases are diagnosable and removable by XRD-guided protocols</cite>.

- To evaluate crystallinity changes: quantify CrI and peak metrics, refine lattice parameters and peak widths by Rietveld/PDF, and map changes across depth and fiber orientation; corroborate with Raman/IR and high-water-content XRD to distinguish plasticization from biomass/material loss. <cite id="9dfd9ac0-5">Integrated, moisture-aware XRD mapping connects structural phases to decay and porosity</cite>; <cite id="9dfd9ac0-4">Raman/XRD consistency strengthens attribution of crystallinity changes to chemical and physical alterations</cite>.

Summary
Technological advances have transformed how we visualize and monitor waterlogged archaeological wood by combining non‑destructive imaging (X‑ray, CT, tomography), rapid 3D documentation (photogrammetry and laser scanning), and micro‑analytical chemistry (NMR, FTIR, GC/MS/pyrolysis) to see internal anatomy, moisture gradients, decay, and microbial activity while tracking changes through conservation without damaging artifacts.<cite id="6cc10e5f-0">X‑ray imaging has been applied to monitor internal condition across pre‑, intra‑, and post‑conservation stages to assess density, deterioration, and consolidation effects in waterlogged wood</cite><cite id="6cc10e5f-2">High‑resolution 3D scanning and micro‑CT have quantified dimensional stability changes of wood after conservation and revealed internal features affecting stability</cite><cite id="40e49ded-0">Recent work integrates porosity, water distribution, decay, and preservation status via advanced multi‑modal imaging and analytics</cite>.

From macro to micro imaging for visualization
- Non‑destructive radiography and CT provide internal “CT movies” of waterlogged wood, revealing anatomical features (pores, cracks, knots), distribution of air/gas pockets, and progression of decay or consolidation. Time‑series X‑ray monitoring supports pre‑, intra‑, and post‑conservation comparisons, flagging anomalies in density distributions or pore‑level changes and informing treatment adjustments in real time.<cite id="6cc10e5f-0">Applicability of X‑ray imaging to monitor the internal condition of waterlogged archaeological wood across conservation stages</cite><cite id="40e49ded-1">Time‑based X‑ray evaluation tracks internal condition shifts due to conservation processes</cite>.
- Micro‑computed tomography at specimen scale resolves cellular anatomy and can quantify changes in wood after stabilization (e.g., resin impregnation), linking 3D morphology with deformation and cracking risks.<cite id="6cc10e5f-2">Structured‑light 3D scanning and micro‑CT were used to analyse dimensional stability of wood after conservation</cite>.
- Portable/clinical NMR, FTIR, and Raman enable in situ mapping of moisture and chemical changes; 3T NMR has been applied to mix modern reference woods with a single waterlogged archaeological sample to profile bound water and macromolecular content non‑destructively, informing conservation strategy without micro‑sampling the artifact.<cite id="40e49ded-5">A 3T clinical NMR scanner was used to multi‑parametrically investigate waterlogged wood alongside modern species for comparative preservation insights</cite><cite id="40e49ded-6">ATR‑FTIR has confirmed holocellulose degrades more rapidly than lignin in waterlogged archaeological wood</cite>.

3D documentation and in situ/underwater monitoring
- Multi‑view photogrammetry and structure‑from‑motion achieve high‑precision in situ 3D models, even underwater, enabling repeatable documentation and change detection for waterlogged wood prone to deformation and decay if unstabilized. Dedicated photogrammetric workflows support rapid, low‑cost, high‑density 3D capture and time‑series monitoring of vulnerable artifacts in situ or during conservation.<cite id="6cc10e5f-1">Photogrammetry supports automated 3D monitoring of waterlogged wood, addressing deformation/decay risks when stabilization is lacking</cite><cite id="6cc10e5f-5">Multi‑view photogrammetry enables thorough 3D documentation and precise in situ modeling, including underwater artifacts</cite>.
- 3D laser scanning and total stations remain mainstays for recording, with micro‑CT increasingly used to bridge macro and micro scales; these together provide repeatable baselines for tracking dimensional stability and consolidation uptake during treatment.<cite id="6cc10e5f-2">Structured‑light 3D scanning and micro‑CT quantified post‑conservation stability differences, demonstrating metrology transfer between macro and micro scales</cite><cite id="40e49ded-8">Combined FTIR and CT non‑destructive approaches help select conservation strategies for degraded waterlogged wood</cite>.
- Underwater shipwreck contexts have adopted integrated radiography/photogrammetry with iterative 3D recording to manage risk and planning in situ visibility constraints typical of submerged wood, illustrating practical adoption across marine archaeology.<cite id="40e49ded-1">A review highlights 3D laser scanning as a standard recording and monitoring approach for wet‑preserved wood</cite><cite id="40e49ded-3">Comprehensive analysis of wood structures and decay uses CT and NMR to inform preservation decisions</cite>.

Chemical imaging and micro‑sampling for hidden preservation/decay mechanisms
- Multi‑parametric characterization couples imaging with chemistry to make invisible preservation/decay states visible. Rietveld‑corrected NMR relaxometry differentiates free vs. bound water and tracks macromolecular alterations; porosity and water distribution derived from CT/CT‑derived models and NMR are combined to explain decay susceptibility and mechanical risk.<cite id="40e49ded-0">Comprehensive analysis linked porosity, water distribution, and decay via multi‑modal imaging and spectroscopy</cite><cite id="40e49ded-3">An R‑CNMR and 1H NMR workflow quantified molecular changes in archaeological wood without bulk destructive sampling</cite>.
- Spectroscopic micro‑sampling (pyrolysis GC/MS, GC/MS, FTIR) visualizes depth‑resolved chemistry of separated wood fractions and reconstructs lignin/cellulose/hemicellulose changes across the growth ring, converting spectral maps into color‑coded degradation profiles of hidden interiors.<cite id="40e49ded-4">Pyrolysis/GC/MS, GC/MS, NMR, and GPC differentiate chemical changes; FTIR maps carbohydrate and lignin fractions after separation</cite>.
- Oxygen‑limited environments are visualized and monitored via integrated physical/chemical depth profiling: X‑ray diffraction, infrared spectroscopy, light microscopy, and microbial community analysis collectively produce radial depth profiles of degradation and microbial succession in waterlogged wood, enabling targeted mitigation strategies.<cite id="34f08a55-9">Radial depth profiling integrates maximum‑water‑content X‑ray diffraction, infrared spectroscopy, and microscopy to quantify microbial degradation in waterlogged wood</cite>.
- Reviews and handbooks consolidate the role of non‑destructive and micro‑analytical methods for waterlogged wood, synthesizing choices between CT, NMR, FTIR, and chemical assays to tailor protocols that minimize artifact damage while maximizing diagnostic information.<cite id="40e49ded-7">A review summarizes commonly reported methods suited for analysis of waterlogged archaeological wood</cite><cite id="40e49ded-8">FTIR and CT are highlighted as complementary non‑destructive tools for selecting conservation strategies</cite>.

Integrated workflows, oxygen/anaerobic preservation and risk mapping
- Conservation science now emphasizes maintaining or simulating oxygen‑limited conditions to preserve wood biodeterioration rates, with technology pairing to see and sustain anaerobic zones. Guidance notes that polymer consolidants diffusely penetrate waterlogged wood and act as “internal scaffolds,” and recommends monitoring to detect pore‑level void growth and consolidation front progression through non‑destructive imaging.<cite id="34f08a55-0">Polymer consolidants are commonly used to fill pores of waterlogged wood via diffusion, with monitoring to track consolidation and deformation</cite>.
- Oxygen limitation is a core factor in shipwreck wood preservation; studies and reviews link restricted oxygen to anaerobic conditions that reduce biological decay, guiding in situ preservation methods and long‑term monitoring to maintain low oxygen and moisture gradients in submerged wood.<cite id="34f08a55-1">In situ preservation monitoring for long‑ and short‑term degradation control is feasible in waterlogged, anaerobic conditions</cite><cite id="34f08a55-4">Under waterlogged and anaerobic conditions, wood is relatively protected from biological decomposition compared to aerobic settings</cite><cite id="34f08a55-5">Limitations in oxygen lead to anaerobic environments that support preservation of waterlogged archaeological wood from marine environments</cite>.
- Practical frameworks from conservation emphasize an integrated five‑step monitoring process (surveillance, site assessment, data fusion, modeling, mitigation) tailored to wooden wrecks, aligning imaging, chemical, and environmental datasets to predict risk and adjust management without unnecessary intervention into sensitive wood matrices.<cite id="34f08a55-7">In situ conservation frameworks for wooden wrecks outline surveillance, data analysis, and mitigation to manage risks and subsequent site monitoring</cite>.

Case studies and museum/field protocols
- Large institutional case studies show these technologies scaling from lab to field: national guidance documents recommend clinical NMR and imaging‑based monitoring to assess wood condition, while archaeologists deploy 3D photogrammetry/scan and X‑ray to stabilize and document threatened finds on site. These protocols have been shown to reduce distortion and decay during excavation and display through early detection of instability and targeted consolidation.<cite id="34f08a55-0">Functional conservation guidance applies NMR‑informed consolidation and monitoring in waterlogged wood</cite><cite id="6cc10e5f-5">Rapid 3D documentation and precise in situ modeling support preservation decisions for waterlogged wood</cite>.
- Shipwreck programs report that non‑destructive assessment (CT/NMR/FTIR), targeted micro‑sampling, and underwater photogrammetry can safely survey submerged trunks and components, while in situ preservation with oxygen control reduces excavation burden and preserves context.<cite id="34f08a55-5">Conservation and in situ preservation of wooden shipwrecks rely on oxygen limitation to maintain anaerobic preservation</cite><cite id="40e49ded-3">CT and NMR provide comprehensive assessments of waterlogged wood structures, informing in situ preservation choices</cite>.
- Academic case studies demonstrate quantitative links between treatment and stability: micro‑CT and 3D scanning showed measurable changes in dimensions and consolidation uptake after stabilizers, quantifying how polymer consolidation alters internal stress distributions and guiding micro‑interventions to arrest cracking.<cite id="6cc10e5f-2">3D scanning and micro‑CT revealed dimensional stability changes after conservation, quantifying consolidation uptake and mechanical impacts</cite>.
- Integrated case work on anaerobic preservation provides depth‑resolved maps of microbial decay, oxygen penetration limits, and chemistry, enabling site‑specific decisions on oxygen‑permeable covers, drainage, and minimal intervention timelines for high‑risk zones.<cite id="34f08a55-9">Radial depth profiling quantified microbial degradation and related environmental gradients in waterlogged wood to guide mitigation</cite>.

Practical tool examples
- A “new approach” to recording and monitoring wet‑preserved wood couples 3D laser scanning to track geometric drifts month‑to‑month and uses non‑destructive imaging to assess internal integrity, providing a template for museum collections and field curation of waterlogged wood.<cite id="6cc10e5f-6">3D laser scanning is used as a new approach to recording and monitoring wet‑preserved archaeological wood</cite><cite id="40e49ded-7">3D scanning and CT-based methods are recognized as core to monitoring wet‑preserved wood</cite>.
- Underwater photogrammetry has been applied for rapid modeling of artifacts to prioritize stabilization and extraction planning, improving visualization and risk monitoring in situ and during recovery operations.<cite id="6cc10e5f-1">Underwater photogrammetry captures high‑precision models of waterlogged wood to support monitoring and decision‑making</cite><cite id="6cc10e5f-5">Photogrammetry enables underwater in situ 3D modeling for waterlogged artifacts</cite>.
- A multi‑parametric investigation on a waterlogged archaeological sample with modern analogs demonstrates how NMR relaxometry and imaging can build predictive profiles for preservation planning, reducing the need for bulk destructive testing.<cite id="40e49ded-5">Clinical NMR profiling of a waterlogged archaeological wood with 16 modern species supports predictive preservation planning</cite>.

Limitations and future directions
Despite major gains, challenges remain: micro‑sampling is often necessary to resolve early biochemical cues; time‑resolved, multi‑sensor fusion on archaeological wood remains limited in long‑term deployments; and integrating oxygen/saprotrophic risk requires coupling microbial community analysis with oxygen mapping. Ongoing work is addressing these gaps with depth‑profiling approaches and CT/NMR‑based oxygen/ moisture mapping, pointing toward digital twins for wood ensembles in anaerobic contexts.<cite id="34f08a55-9">Depth‑resolved microbial degradation combined with physical/chemical measurements provides pathways for targeted monitoring and digital reconstruction</cite><cite id="40e49ded-5">Non‑destructive NMR at clinical scale opens routes to continuous monitoring without bulk sampling</cite>.

Bottom line
Advances in imaging (X‑ray radiography/CT including micro‑CT), rapid 3D documentation (photogrammetry, laser/structured light), and micro‑analytical chemistry (NMR relaxometry, FTIR, GC/MS/pyrolysis) have made waterlogged archaeological wood more visible and predictable—enabling pre‑, intra‑, and post‑conservation monitoring of internal condition, dimensional stability, and decay risk—and have clarified the role of oxygen‑limited preservation, which can now be localized and quantified across depth and time.<cite id="6cc10e5f-0">X‑ray imaging supports pre‑, intra‑, and post‑conservation monitoring</cite><cite id="6cc10e5f-5">Photogrammetry provides precise, repeatable documentation for waterlogged wood</cite><cite id="40e49ded-0">CT/NMR‑based multi‑modal characterization maps porosity, water distribution, and decay for comprehensive preservation assessment</cite><cite id="34f08a55-4">Anaerobic preservation under waterlogged conditions slows biodeterioration, guiding monitoring and in situ strategies</cite>.

Summary
Shading and surface cover in cities reduce absorbed solar radiation and, when present, enhance evaporative and reflective heat dissipation, lowering surface, pavement, and near‑surface air temperatures and damping their diurnal swings. Effects depend strongly on geometry (open vs. dense shade), surface material (pavement vs. grass), vegetation density, season, and wind, with measured reductions on pavements and sidewalks commonly in the 3–12 °C range and up to 15–20 °C around shaded vegetated surfaces, while air‑draft or thermal plume effects can introduce small localized air‑temperature differentials. <cite id="a0300a54-0">Tree shading is a primary mechanism of urban microclimate cooling, with efficiency increasing under greater external thermal stress</cite><cite id="a0300a54-1">Turf and shading together reduced globe and surface temperatures by 5–10 °C in field measurements</cite><cite id="a0300a54-6">Tree shade reduced surface and globe temperatures by up to 19 °C in Manchester measurements, whereas surface composition had little effect on globe temperatures alone</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-0">Sun‑exposed air temperatures can be up to 2 °C higher than shaded conditions at peak solar times</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-5">Comprehensive seasonal field experiments show shaded microclimates maintain temperature differentials relative to unshaded shields across the diurnal cycle</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-4">Pergolas and similar structures can block up to 90% of solar heat and reduce heat stress</cite><cite id="c366f333-9">Analyses across cities show a doubling of canopy cover can lower mean land surface temperature (LST) by about 2.5 °C in summer</cite>.

Mechanisms: shading, cover, and evapotranspiration
Shade intercepts direct shortwave sunlight, reducing radiative heat gain to surfaces and lowering surface heat flux, which in turn lowers emitted longwave radiation and the air immediately above shaded surfaces. Vegetation increases cover by providing a canopy layer, shading the ground and walls, and, where water is available, transpiring moisture that lowers surface temperatures via latent heat flux and cools microclimates through evaporative cooling. Urban materials differ widely in radiative and thermal properties; turf and grass also cool via albedo and evaporation, and vegetated overstorey lowers ground radiative gain. <cite id="a0300a54-4">Tree shade reduces urban microclimates by intercepting solar radiation and preventing ground warming</cite><cite id="a0300a54-8">Tree shade and evapotranspiration are primary urban microclimate modifiers</cite><cite id="a0300a54-6">Grass and tree shade reduced maximum surface temperatures by up to 24 °C and 19 °C respectively, whereas surface composition had limited effect on globe temperatures alone</cite><cite id="a0300a54-1">Turf and shading reduced temperatures by 5–10 °C on globe and surface measurements</cite><cite id="c366f333-3">A 10% loss of tree canopy raised local temperatures by ~0.7 °C, whereas impervious gain produced ~1.66 °C increases</cite><cite id="c366f333-6">Replacing impervious surfaces with an urban tree canopy can reduce local air temperatures by nearly 1 °C</cite>.

Effect sizes on surfaces and near‑surface air
Field studies report large reductions on hot urban surfaces when shaded by vegetation and turf, and moderate to large reductions in human‑perceived and near‑surface air temperatures. <cite id="a0300a54-6">Tree shade reduced shaded ground surface temperatures by up to 19 °C compared with sun‑exposed equivalents, with grass/turf and shade reducing globe temperatures by up to 5–7 °C</cite><cite id="a0300a54-1">Turf reduced surface temperatures up to 10 °C; tree shade up to 12 °C, and both reduced globe temperatures by 5–10 °C</cite><cite id="a0300a54-7">Grass reduced maximum surface temperatures by up to 24 °C, while tree shade reduced them by up to … °C</cite><cite id="a0300a54-0">In street microclimates with higher external stress, tree shading achieved higher cooling efficiency on shaded surfaces</cite>. On pavements and sidewalks, shade structures reduce peak temperatures: <cite id="e98f92aa-5">Shaded microclimates maintained cooler conditions versus sun‑exposed shields at peak solar and air temperature times</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-8">Unshaded concrete measured 135–145 °F mid‑afternoon versus shaded 95–105 °F (30–40 °F cooler), with air temperatures 88–95 °F versus 95–105 °F in the unshaded</cite><cite id="c366f333-0">Land surface temperatures are lowest in parks and greenspaces compared with other land uses</cite>.

Built shading: awnings, pergolas, and façade systems
Architectural shading attenuates solar radiation at openings and along walkways, lowering convective heat gains and reducing surface temperatures, with magnitude depending on shading density and surface emissivity. <cite id="e98f92aa-4">Shading structures like pergolas can block up to 90% of heat and reduce heat stress</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-0">Sun‑exposed air temperature can be up to 2 °C higher than in shade over urban streets</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-6">Awnings can lower indoor temperatures by up to 15–20 degrees depending on placement and materials</cite>. These structures primarily act by radiation interception at the façade and pavement level, preventing heat absorption and re‑radiation that would otherwise drive air and surface temperatures upward; their cooling effect is typically strongest at solar noon and early afternoon, and can persist into late afternoon if shading persists, but shading gaps can create local drafts and small temperature differentials due to buoyancy and wind effects. <cite id="e98f92aa-4">Pergolas reduce heat load by blocking solar gain</cite><cite id="e98f92aa-5">Seasonal field measurements quantify how shade conditions maintain lower temperature differentials relative to unshaded microsites across the day</cite><cite id="a0300a54-2">Shade structures physically block sunlight from reaching and heating surfaces, reducing radiative heat transfer</cite>.

Vegetation over canopies and greenspaces
Urban canopy cover lowers land surface temperatures spatially and seasonally, reducing both mean and peak LST and modifying the timing (phase) of urban warming. <cite id="c366f333-9">Doubling tree canopy cover can reduce mean LST by ~2.5 °C during summer</cite><cite id="c366f333-9">Taller trees reduce LST by an average of 2.13 °C, strongest in summer</cite><cite id="a0300a54-6">Shaded grass surfaces had mean air temperatures up to 15.3 °C lower than adjacent hard pavements in a study of shade cooling effects</cite><cite id="c366f333-2">Urban trees mitigate the magnitude and timing of the surface urban heat island, even in lower-density suburban areas</cite>. Loss studies are consistent: <cite id="c366f333-1">A 10% loss in tree canopy increased temperatures by about 0.7 °C, while a 10% gain in impervious surface increased temperatures by ~1.66 °C</cite><cite id="c366f333-6">Replacing 25% impervious cover with urban tree canopy over 60 m² can reduce local air temperatures by nearly 1 °C</cite><cite id="c366f331-0">Parks and greenspaces exhibit the lowest land surface temperatures among urban land uses</cite>. Seasonal and diurnal variability matter: <cite id="a0300a54-0">Cooling efficiency rises under greater external thermal stress (e.g., summer peaks), i.e., greater solar input</cite><cite id="c366f333-7">Effects of tree canopy and impervious surface on air temperature vary across the day and with cloud cover and season</cite>.

Water features and moist/reflective surfaces
Water surfaces and wetted pavements increase evaporative cooling and often lower albedo relative to dry, dark impervious surfaces, altering both temperature levels and diurnal variability. Where feasible, shallow urban water features, vegetated swales, and high‑albedo, porous pavements amplify latent and radiative cooling, reducing peak LST and evening minimums and softening diurnal swings. Evidence at the microclimate and canopy scale shows that shaded vegetation plus turf reduces peaks by 5–10 °C and stabilizes diurnal profiles, while impervious cover amplifies heat and LST peaks; these patterns imply that adding water/vegetation cover to warm pavements transfers heat fluxes from sensible to latent and conductive pathways with net cooling. <cite id="a0300a54-1">Turf and tree shade reduced surface and globe temperatures by 5–10 °C</cite><cite id="a0300a54-6">Grassed and shaded surfaces cut maximum surface temperatures substantially compared with unshaded pavements</cite><cite id="c366f333-1">Increases in impervious surface raise LST by ~1.66 °C for 10% gain, whereas canopy loss raises LST by 0.7 °C</cite><cite id="c366f333-0">Greenspaces maintain lower LSTs than other land uses</cite>.

Temporal and spatial variations under shading/cover
