Carbon-fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) uses matrix (polymer resin) to bind and transfer load to reinforcement (carbon fibers) through an interphase that suppresses micro-slip; designers tune fiber orientation and volume fraction to target stiffness and fatigue resistance, with performance emerging from the synergy and interface quality between components rather than any single material’s intrinsic properties alone.<cite id="230d0ca8-5">Methodological sections guide decomposition and focus, akin to defining constituent roles in composite design</cite><cite id="eaaffaaf-0">Confounding illustrates the need to control hidden components; analogously, interphase/ interface properties in composites control load transfer and property emergence</cite>.

How to define and categorize components in your study
- Start from purpose and unit of analysis. Identify your research question, outcomes, and units (people, cells, events); then decide whether components will be:
  • Conceptual/constructual: definitions of constructs and their operationalization into IVs/DVs, mediators, moderators, and confounds.<cite id="eaaffaaf-4">Mediators and moderators should be explicitly integrated in design to explain and qualify effects</cite><cite id="eaaffaaf-5">IV/DV designation specifies causal or predictive focus</cite>.
  • Procedural/analytical: design choices for sampling, measurement protocols, statistical models, and sensitivity analyses to detect or mitigate confounding and model misspecification.<cite id="230d0ca8-7">Elements like sampling and analysis are core design components</cite><cite id="eaaffaaf-0">Confounding threats require targeted controls</cite>.
  • Representational/data: variables/features, dimensionality reduction components (e.g., PCA), and derived indicators that preserve information while improving tractability and interpretability.<cite id="0d3473b2-0">PCA formalizes dimensionality reduction with information minimization</cite>.
- Organize them with explicit interfaces and documentation. For complex systems, define component interfaces and contracts (inputs/outputs, assumptions/guarantees), including data schemas and model evaluation protocols, so components can be validated, substituted, or scaled independently.<cite id="85fd164d-2">Encapsulation behind interfaces supports modular integration</cite><cite id="85fd164d-0">Interfaces enumerate method calls provided and used</cite>.
- Align categories with functions and evidence needs. Map each component to a function (measurement clarity, mechanism explanation, prediction or causal effect, system modularity, information retention, performance tailoring) and provide examples demonstrating how the component is constructed and evaluated within the study or product lifecycle.<cite id="eaaffaaf-6">Mediators clarify causal pathways</cite><cite id="0d3473b2-1">PCA components retain most original information for efficient modeling</cite><cite id="85fd164d-6">Each component contains well-scoped functionality for reuse</cite>.
- Anticipate confounds and boundary conditions. Identify potential confounding components early and plan controls (covariate adjustment, randomization, matching) and diagnostics (sensitivity analyses), and explicitly model boundary conditions with moderators and heterogeneous effects analyses.<cite id="eaaffaaf-4">Moderators affect relationship strength/direction</cite><cite id="eaaffaaf-0">Integrating mediators/moderators strengthens outcome studies</cite>.

Summary
- Components unify research practice as modular units with clear roles: they define constructs and measurements (variables, mediators, confounds), operationalize design and analysis (sampling, data collection/analysis), provide explicit interfaces and contracts for systems, and compress or tailor information in data and materials to achieve goals such as interpretability, performance, and maintainability.<cite id="230d0ca8-3">Research design binds data collection and analysis to questions</cite><cite id="eaaffaaf-4">Mediator/moderator roles refine causal inference</cite><cite id="85fd164d-2">Component interfaces enable black-box composition</cite><cite id="0d3473b2-0">PCA components deliver loss-minimizing dimensionality reduction</cite>.

Below are evidence-based methods to design and construct glued‑in rod (GIR) connections so they remain ductile and avoid brittle failure. The guidance integrates lessons from timber/GLT joints and bonded FRP anchorage practice.

Summary of brittle failure modes to prevent
- Adhesive/FRP debonding at glue interfaces (wood–adhesive or adhesive–FRP/steel) under tensile stress concentration, often at interfaces or near end anchorage, can be sudden and low-displacement (<cite id="ce0d026b-3">Debonding of externally bonded FRP from concrete is prevented via code-prescribed anchorage and detailing</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-5">Intermediate crack debonding can be eliminated by proper anchorage such as integrated composite anchors or FRP U‑jackets</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-6">FRP anchors and compatible adhesives prevent premature debonding and improve load transfer in practice</cite>).
- Wood splitting and edge failure when rod-to-edge distance is small, eccentric loading, or inadequate transfer across grain; adhesive/wood interface failure if overlap/anchorage is too short (<cite id="chalmers68932">Splitting generally occurs if rod-to-edge distance is too small, especially with angled loading, and can be accompanied by glue line failure</cite>; <cite id="b53fc2ee-502b-4c95-8e98-4bb99748a8ce">Designs with adequate anchorage length were used to avoid wood splitting and glue-line failure in full‑size GIR tests</cite>).
- Pull‑out or insufficient bond length in shear/axial, particularly for FRP/CFRP where bond is critical; overlap deficits lead to local debonding of overlapped laminates (<cite id="ce0d026b-1">Insufficient overlap causes overlapping FRP laminates to debond; overlap must be sufficient to make laminate failure precede debonding</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-0">FRP reinforcement provides sufficient bonding strength to prevent debonding, but requires compatible anchors and detailing</cite>).
- Sudden rupture of steel rods (portland steel) or brittle response of FRP/epoxy systems if stress concentrators are not controlled; ductility is promoted when steel yields plastically or FRP is arranged to see slip/anchorage yielding rather than immediate rupture (<cite id="ce0d026b-4">ACI guide emphasizes controlling debonding and ensuring ductile response in externally bonded FRP systems</cite>; <cite id="44814bb4-4">In timber moment connections with glued‑in steel rods, a ductile failure mode can result from rod yielding and plasticizing under shear</cite>).

Design principles to target ductility
- Provide a yielding steel mechanism: Use steel rods with adequate cross‑section so rod yielding occurs before adhesive/wood rupture, and design moment/shear regions to develop local yielding and plastic rotation. <cite id="44814bb4-4">Timber moment connections have shown ductile behavior due to rod yielding and plasticizing when shear was induced</cite>. 
- Ensure adhesive ductility by bond length: For shear connectors, select overlap/anchorage such that adhesive shear capacity governs, with a margin to allow inelastic slip and distribution of cracking; avoid very short laps that force FRP/wood interface failure. <cite id="44814bb4-8">Average adhesive shear strength near 7 MPa was found from push-out and modeling, with variability that argues for conservatively designed shear overlap</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-1">Overlap should be provided to make FRP laminate failure occur before debonding of overlapped laminates</cite>. 
- Control failure mode sequencing: Favor “steel yield then adhesive/slip redistribution” over “abrupt interface fracture or pull‑out.” This is achieved by adequate bonding depth, spacing, and edge distance and by using end anchorage that permits controlled slip and frictional retention. <cite id="ce0d026b-3">Code practice prevents debonding by anchorage and detailing criteria</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-5">U-jackets and anchors eliminate PE (progressive) debonding failure</cite>.
- Use FRP anchorages where needed: In concrete or timber with FRP rods/strands, install CFRP anchors, U‑jackets, or similar devices at supports/cracks to arrest and reverse progressive debonding. <cite id="ce0d026b-5">Proper anchorage prevents intermediate crack debonding</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-2">FRP anchors can delay or prevent debonding failures</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-6">ASCE practice guides to ensure FRP anchors bond effectively and prevent premature debonding</cite>.

Adhesive and bond-layer details that improve ductility
- Choose system and depth for shear vs. axial action: In timber (GLT), bond depth of 40–80 mm has been studied; select depth so tensile stresses in adhesive stay below cohesive/adhesive rupture. <cite id="26c541c7-9">Experimental tests determined optimal bonding depth into solid timber, behavior of different adhesives, and tensile stresses along the bond line</cite>. 
- Provide adequate overlap length for shear or axial capacity: Increase bond overlap at least one rod diameter beyond pure lap splice to ensure stress relief along the bond, and use overlapping regions at supports or over internal/external cracks. <cite id="ce0d026b-1">Overlap must be sufficient so the overlapped FRP laminates do not debond, and FRP laminate failure precedes debonding</cite>. 
- Avoid thin adhesive films and local voids: Bonded anchors/GIR literature notes adhesion failures occur when concrete–adhesive or adhesive–FRP interfaces have insufficient surface preparation or bond (voids). <cite id="ce0d026b-7">Bond failures occur at concrete–adhesive or adhesive–FRP interfaces if there is insufficient surface preparation and adhesion; adequate adhesion depends on surface condition; anchorage systems reduce premature debonding</cite>. 
- Use temperature/moisture compatible systems: Excessive thermal cycling and elevated service temperatures degrade adhesive performance. Provide curing and operation envelopes within manufacturer limits, and, where possible, pre‑stress after temperature equilibration. <cite id="26c541c7-5">Timber with glued‑in rods can be vulnerable at temperatures above 40 °C; adhesive performance depends on temperature</cite>. 
- Provide stepped/adapted bond profiles (optional): To reduce stress concentration at the substrate edge, reduce adhesive film thickness near edges, provide bevels/chamfers, or use two-sided bonding to sandwich the wood where bond depth is large.

Structural and anchorage details
- Minimize edge effects: Keep rod-to-edge distance at least several rod diameters and greater than the overlap reduction at edges; avoid eccentric loading and large interface slopes to limit splitting/debonding stress peaks (<cite id="44814bb4-8">Design with minimum edge/spacing requirements consistent with avoiding wood splitting and glue line failure</cite>; <cite id="26c541c7-4">Splitting generally occurs if rod-to-edge distance is too small or load is applied at an angle</cite>). 
- Use distributed anchorage over cracks and reentrant corners: Install bonded FRP anchors, U‑wraps, or two‑row anchorage so progressive cracking does not create local bond‑slip that culminates in sudden detachment. <cite id="ce0d026b-5">Integrated FRP composite anchors and FRP U‑jackets eliminate progressive intermediate debonding</cite>. 
- Provide two‑sided bonding (where geometry allows): Bury the same reinforcement into wood on both sides separated by a bonded timber plate; this reduces direct adhesive overlap demand and spreads load into axial wood resistance. <cite id="26c541c7-3">Nonlinear analysis and parameter studies show that interaction and load path routing materially affect interface stresses and failure mode</cite>. 
- Control rod stress concentration via stress-relief and pre‑tensioning: Stress-relieve steel before final tightening to avoid residual stresses; pre‑tension after adhesive cure so that service loads occur within the elastic shakedown of the bond, increasing tolerance to localized damage. <cite id="44814bb4-4">Plasticizing via shear development allows local yielding and redistribution, increasing ductility</cite>. 
- Select rod type and modulus to match ductility target: Use threaded steel rods with good fatigue/creep performance; for FRP/GFRP rods, select matrices and fiber volumes that allow controlled creep and fracture energy release. <cite id="44814bb4-9">In axial pulling, load transfer is governed by adhesive shear; adhesive strength and surface condition govern interfacial behavior</cite>.

Construction and maintenance measures
- Prepare and clean the substrate and interface and follow the adhesive’s service window: Use SCF sanders, vacuum combs, and dust extraction for wood; control moisture and temperature to avoid voids and early debonding under sustained load. <cite id="ce0d026b-7">Insufficient surface preparation leads to adhesion failures; good bonding depends on proper surface condition and adhesion properties of the system</cite>. 
- Detail and execute installation per ACI FRP anchorage practice: Ensure overlap and anchorage conformance to prescriptive/experimental criteria, use compatible anchors/wraps, and verify quality assurance at layups and repairs. <cite id="ce0d026b-3">ACI criteria revised to include prescriptive detailing for externally bonded FRP anchorage</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-0">FRP reinforcement can provide sufficient bonding if anchorage and detailing are appropriate</cite>. 
- Provide construction staging to check bond integrity: Cure adhesive fully before live‑load installation; apply jacking/relieving devices during installation and monitor for slip, creep loss, and temperature effects. <cite id="ce0d026b-5">Using anchors/wraps allows controlled slip and prevents PE debonding under service</cite>. 
- Control service environments: Avoid long-term elevated temperatures and unmitigated moisture cycles; provide thermal breaks or pre‑condition before stressing. <cite id="26c541c7-5">Elevated temperatures above 40 °C can compromise bonded performance in glued‑in rod timber joints</cite>.

Verification and test-based validation
- Full‑size and subassembly tests to confirm mode and slip: Test joint specimens to failure, capturing load–slip and crack opening; confirm ductile yielding/slip before interface fracture or pull‑out. <cite id="b53fc2ee-502b-4c95-8e98-4bb99748a8ce">Full‑size tests designed with minimum anchorage length to avoid wood splitting and glue‑line failure</cite>; <cite id="44814bb4-0">Experimental investigation of glued‑in rod joints in timber beams shows high strength/stiffness, motivating careful mode control</cite>. 
- Parametric studies for spacing, edge distance, and bond depth: Use 3D FE or parameter studies to map stress concentrations and failure initiation, guiding minimum edge distances and overlap at supports. <cite id="26c541c7-0">Nonlinear 3D FE model and parameter study reveal sensitivity of interfacial stresses and failure to bond length, geometry, and material properties</cite>; <cite id="26c541c7-7">Worked projects include tests varying distance between rods and to timber edge, quantifying axial capacity sensitivity</cite>. 
- Pull‑out and push‑out capacity checks with ductility factors: Ensure bond capacity margins with respect to steel/FRP yield, and assess slip compatibility in cracked sections. <cite id="26c541c7-2">Experimental assessment of axial strength of glued‑in rods in CLT informs pull‑out/axial design and interface behavior</cite>. 
- Robustness to defects and serviceability: Account for knots, cross‑grain, and moisture defects that lower effective bond and raise splitting risk; use generous safety factors and QA/QC per EOTA TR 070. <cite id="26c541c7-6">Defects reduce capacity in glued‑in rod timber joints, motivating robust performance testing and conservative detailing</cite>; <cite id="44814bb4-1">EOTA TR 070 establishes test‑based design envelopes for epoxy/polyurethane glued‑in rods across adhesive types</cite>.

Putting it together: Recommended practice
1) Select a compatible system (epoxy or polyurethane) with proven performance for the substrate and environment and follow EOTA TR 070 or equivalent agency testing, then verify adhesive shear in overlap against target slip/ductility (cite id="44814bb4-1"). 
2) Detail GIRs for yielding: provide sufficient overlap to force steel yield and bond slip before interface fracture, with overlap at least one rod diameter past midspan/crack for shear and at least nominal anchorage development for axial, and design for a ductile rotation capacity (cite id="44814bb4-8"); avoid short laps that cause glue-line and wood splitting (cite id="26c541c7-4") with edge distances and spacings mapped via FE/parameter studies or tested subassemblies (cite id="26c541c7-0"); add CFRP anchors and U‑jackets on concrete/timber sides to arrest progressive debonding (cite id="ce0d026b-5"). 
3) Construct with adhesive-friendly preparation, controlled cure, and room‑temperature installation; pre‑tension after cure to move operating point into linear/low‑slip region (cite id="ce0d026b-7"); install two‑sided rods or FRP anchorage at concentrated crack interfaces to spread bond demand and confine the joint (cite id="26c541c7-3"); maintain service conditions within adhesive performance envelopes (cite id="26c541c7-5"). 
4) Verify via tests or simulations that the connection exhibits a pronounced post‑yield softening that does not include step‑like brittle failures: accept a design slip compatibility and reserve a bond/steel yield margin validated on full‑size specimens (cite id="b53fc2ee-502b-4c95-8e98-4bb99748a8ce"). 
5) For FRP additions to timber/concrete, apply ACI 440.2R/557 anchorage methods and design overlaps per FRP laminate overlap rules, using prescriptive anchors/wraps to prevent intermediate crack debonding; ensure adhesion on both sides of the joint and use FRP-U or composite anchors to lock slip (cite id="ce0d026b-4"), (cite id="ce0d026b-1"), (cite id="ce0d026b-2"), (cite id="ce0d026b-6"). 
6) If brittle behavior is mandated by code path (e.g., FRP anchorage in concrete), still improve ductility by adding bonded steel rod trussing and timber wraps to create a composite yielding zone over cracked ranges (cite id="ce0d026b-3") and by keeping rod-wood-adhesive interface stresses below cohesive failure via larger bond depth/overlap and smaller interface slopes (cite id="26c541c7-9").

Notes on materials and form
- For wood, polyurethane adhesives often accommodate greater humidity and temperature swings than epoxy if within tested envelopes; either can be ductile if properly overlapped and anchored. <cite id="44814bb4-1">Epoxy or polyurethane adhesive types are covered in EOTA TR 070 design</cite>; <cite id="26c541c7-5">Elevated temperatures can reduce adhesion performance; service envelopes matter</cite>. 
- Steel rods can show ductile behavior in wood if edge distances and overlap are adequate and interface stresses are kept from causing cohesive/adhesive rupture. <cite id="44814bb4-4">Steel yielding and plasticizing in shear produces ductile joint behavior</cite>. 
- FRP rods/plates on concrete or timber require dedicated anchorage: increase overlap and add anchors/wraps to prevent “edge‑effect” debonding or progressive crack‑driven separation. <cite id="ce0d026b-1">Overlap sizing should make the laminates fail in shear before debonding at overlaps</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-5">U‑jackets and integrated anchors prevent progressive debonding</cite>. 

In short, ductile, brittle‑resistant glued‑in rod connections are obtained by pairing robust steel/FRP yielding mechanisms with sufficient adhesive overlap and edge distances, compliant surface prep, thermally/moisture‑compatible adhesives, and end/edge anchorage (anchors, U‑jackets, two‑sided bonding) verified through test and analysis to deliver controlled slip and post‑yield rotation rather than sudden interface fracture or wood splitting. <cite id="44814bb4-8">Adequate anchorage length avoids wood splitting and glue-line failure</cite>; <cite id="26c541c7-4">Sufficient edge distance prevents splitting</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-7">Good surface adhesion prevents debonding at interfaces</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-5">U-jackets and anchors eliminate progressive debonding</cite>; <cite id="ce0d026b-4">ACI guidance prevents sudden debonding via proper anchorage and detailing</cite>; <cite id="44814bb4-4">Controlled yielding/plasticizing confers ductile behavior</cite>.

# Summary

Wind affects particle deposition and stain formation by coupling aerodynamic transport (advection, shear, turbulence), hydrodynamic settling, and surface–particle interactions that govern capture, resuspension, and adhesion. Higher wind speeds generally increase collision frequencies and flux toward surfaces and also enhance resuspension via drag and boundary-layer mixing, with net effects depending on particle size, surface roughness, humidity, and flow structures such as separation and recirculation zones. These processes accumulate as visible soiling (discoloration, haze, or film stains) through physical occlusion, chemical adsorption, and, on exposed materials, mechanical abrasion that exposes deeper, more stain-prone layers. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-5">Wind tunnel studies quantify deposition to material surfaces via “deposition velocities” that depend strongly on particle diameter and flow speed</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-1">Experimental deposition velocities increase with wind speed for given particle diameters</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-3">Wind deposits sediment when it slows over obstacles or boundaries</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-3">In urban canopies, resuspension can begin when winds exceed roughly 7 m/s at canopy top</cite>.

# Mechanisms: How Wind Alters Deposition and Resuspension

Wind supplies three concurrent mechanisms: advective flux of suspended particles, shear-driven wall collisions and film transfer, and episodic turbulence that both drops particles and lifts adhered ones. On flat or aerodynamically smooth surfaces, faster winds increase the number of impacts per unit time and reduce residence time, often favoring net deposition for fine particles (in suspension or saltation creep), whereas on rough or porous surfaces, shear and separation may promote rebound and entrainment, shifting the balance toward resuspension and airborne recirculation. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-5">Deposition velocities quantify the combined effect of interception, sedimentation, and diffusion and depend on flow speed and particle size</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-3">Wind carries and deposits sediment; deposition occurs as the flow decelerates, e.g., over obstacles or roughness elements</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-4">Wind sorts and deposits particles as size–settling and turbulence balance</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-3">Wind-driven urban resuspension is triggered when mean winds exceed threshold shear aloft the urban canopy</cite>.

Wind also couples to moisture and chemistry. For hygroscopic or moisture-sensitive coatings, advection of humid air or wind-driven rain/spray alters adhesion strength and film growth; pollutants in air react at the surface, and mechanical abrasion from particle bombardment exposes fresh reactive layers that stain more readily. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">On stone façades, interactions among atmospheric pollutants, surface layers, and wind-driven rain erode or abrade surfaces, enabling soiling and staining</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-2">Wind-driven particle impacts increase surface roughness and can induce chemical changes and fragmentation under high stress, altering stain kinetics</cite>.

# Quantitative Patterns: Wind Speed vs. Deposition/Resuspension

Multiple lines of evidence show non-linear, sometimes non-monotonic responses of deposition to wind. For fixed particles, deposition velocity generally increases with wind speed or friction velocity, but can saturate as collisional capture is offset by enhanced turbulence and rebound. <cite id="e3248f9a-2">Deposition velocity generally increases monotonically with wind speed or friction velocity up to saturation</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-2">Resuspension may be either negligible or significant as winds increase, depending on balance of advection, shear, and recirculation</cite>. Size and surface properties shape outcomes: fine particles (<0.1 mm) are most mobilized and rapidly deposited by low-speed winds; coarser grains require higher shear to saltate but deposit farther downstream. <cite id="e3248f9a-8">Fine particles (<0.1 mm) are lifted and transported parallel to surfaces by strong winds and then settle</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-0">Over oceans, aerosol deposition rates correlate with surface wind speed and insolation fields</cite>.

Measured thresholds give concrete anchors for urban and building contexts. Within street canopies, resuspension often begins when winds at canopy top exceed about 7 m/s, with the most intense recirculation and near-surface fluxes feeding façades and pedestrians. <cite id="e3248f9a-3">Simulation in an urban system shows resuspension when inlet wind speed beyond the canopy at 40 m exceeds 7 m/s</cite>. Experiments in ducted flows show that deposition rates to walls decrease with increasing air speed in smooth geometries due to reduced residence time, highlighting that higher wind can suppress capture on certain surfaces even as it increases flux. <cite id="e3248f9a-4">In horizontal ventilation ducts, differences in deposition rates to floor, wall, and ceiling decrease with increasing air speed</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-4">Across duct cross sections, deposition diminishes with air speed as particles spend less time in boundary layers</cite>.

On exterior ocean/land surfaces, dry deposition models and observations explicitly use wind speed to parameterize the transfer of aerosols to surfaces, including complex interactions with roughness, stability, and wet deposition. <cite id="e3248f9a-1">Experiments quantify deposition velocity increases with wind speed for monodisperse particles</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-4">Dry deposition models for oceans and water surfaces encode wind-speed dependence and wind-specific processes</cite>.

# From Deposition to Stain: Pathways and Timescales

Particle deposition can form stains in two complementary ways. First, captured particles occlude light and accumulate into films that alter color and gloss; organic carbon and transition metals catalyze browning, while sulfates and nitrates appear as whitish films. Second, wind also accelerates surface abrasion and roughening, which increases light scattering and exposes reactive subsurface layers that stain more deeply and resist removal. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">Wind-driven rain and pollutant interactions erode stone surfaces, promoting soiling and stain formation by exposing fresh, reactive layers</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-2">Wind-driven impacts can chemically alter surface layers and increase roughness, leading to fragmentation and stain development under high-stress exposure</cite>.

Moisture and time mediate the transition from “spot” to persistent film stains. Winds that periodically wet surfaces (rain or spray) reduce adhesion energy, increase diffusion and chemical reactivity, and then dry to set adhered networks; conversely, dry winds favor rebound and resuspension. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">Interactions with wind-driven rain and pollutants erode surface layers and facilitate staining</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-3">Deposition events occur when wind decelerates (obstacles/boundaries), then films accumulate; subsequent winds redistribute or resuspend material</cite>.

# Case Studies on Surfaces

- Façades and stone: Wind-driven mechanisms combine abrasion, saltation near edges/cornices, and rain-enhanced chemistry; the net is loss of gloss, color change, and staining as iron/transition-metal catalysis and organic aerosols polymerize in microcracks and pores. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">Wind-driven rain interacting with pollutant-bearing atmospheres erodes limestone façades, creating conditions for erosion–soiling–stain feedbacks</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-8">Edge deposition and cornice formation modify local winds; airborne snow/ice fragments can stick and later stain when melted</cite>.

- Photovoltaic and glazing surfaces: Wind speed is a dominant predictor of soiling accumulation with strong seasonal cycles; higher winds accelerate both incoming dust flux and cleaning via wash-off and resuspension, producing episodic discoloration and performance loss. <cite id="16c5b499-5">Studies consistently report wind speed influences dust accumulation on PV panels, matching expectations for advection-driven soiling and wind-enhanced wash-off/resuspension</cite>.

- Indoor ventilation systems and built environments: Fans and wind tunnels show dust sticks in low-velocity “trapping” zones (bends, stagnation) and is resuspended under higher flows; this manifests as dust films on grilles, ductwork, and room surfaces and can discolor painted or laminated finishes. <cite id="16c5b499-0">Particles carried by ventilation airflow degrade indoor air quality and deposit on surfaces within ducts and rooms</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-1">Turbulence and flow structures strongly modulate particle resuspension from indoor materials</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-6">Resuspension increases when inlet wind speeds exceed thresholds in street canyons</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Design Controls

- Exposure and geometry: Obstacles, parapets, and rooflines create separation and eddies that concentrate particle flux and prolong residence, favoring deposition and staining; wind tunnels and CFD map hotspots for targeted cleaning/maintenance. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-3">Deposition concentrates where wind must move over or around obstacles</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-3">Resuspension onset and canyon-scale circulation depend on height-relative wind speeds</cite>.

- Materials and hydrophobic modification: Surfaces prone to staining benefit from roughness/optics tuned to reduce adhesion and increase wash-off under prevailing winds; hydrophobic and sacrificial coatings can curb initial adhesion and delay film formation, but wind-driven abrasion can breach coatings and expose stain-prone substrates. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">Erosion of stone by wind-driven rain plus pollutants exposes reactive layers that stain</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-2">Surface roughening and fragmentation under wind stress change how dust adheres and stains</cite>.

- Operation of ventilation: In buildings, lowering peak air speeds in critical zones (window perimeters, ceiling jets, duct bends) and using laminar screens can reduce deposition in stagnant pockets while avoiding turbulence-driven resuspension; maintenance protocols should target high-wind periods. <cite id="16c5b499-0">Indoor ventilation carries dust that deposits on surfaces</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-1">Resuspension rises with turbulence and flow separation on indoor materials</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-4">Deposition to walls/ceilings decreases with increasing air speed in smooth ducts</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Finer particles deposit more readily under moderate winds; coarser grains require higher shear and deposit farther downstream. <cite id="e3248f9a-1">Deposition velocity increases with wind speed for fixed particle sizes</cite> <cite id="e3248f9a-8">Fine soil particles are lifted and transported by winds and then settle</cite>.

- Net deposition vs. resuspension shifts with flow speed and geometry; thresholds of around 7 m/s at canopy top often trigger urban resuspension cycles, while stagnation zones favor accumulation. <cite id="e3248f9a-3">Resuspension begins when winds exceed roughly 7 m/s above urban canopies</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-4">Higher air speed reduces deposition on duct walls, illustrating wind–residence-time trade-offs</cite>.

- Stain arises from occlusion, chemical aging, and abrasion-driven roughening; wind-driven rain and pollutants accelerate erosion and film setting, particularly on masonry and stone. <cite id="c0ffb3e1-0">Erosion by wind-driven rain and pollutants on stone promotes soiling and staining</cite> <cite id="c0ffb3e1-2">Wind impacts chemical change and fragment surfaces, altering staining behavior</cite>.

- In buildings, managing airflow, turbulence, and access points reduces indoor deposition and visible dust films; on exteriors, wind-aware cleaning and protective treatments mitigate soiling and discoloration. <cite id="16c5b499-1">Turbulence enhances resuspension from indoor surfaces</cite> <cite id="16c5b499-5">Wind speed is a dominant control on dust accumulation and wash-off on PV surfaces</cite>.

Below is a concise synthesis of how “conditions” alter the properties and performance of concrete admixtures.

Concept and scope
- Admixtures are sensitive to conditions because their molecules interact with cement hydration products, aggregates, water, and each other; environmental and process variables shift reaction rates, dispersion, and surface interactions, changing dosage effectiveness, rheology, durability, and stability across life-cycle states. <cite id="5366ad11-9">In hot weather, superplasticizers and retarders maintain concrete workability by decreasing water demand and slowing the setting time, preventing rapid slump loss</cite>.

Environmental exposure (service conditions)
- Temperature and humidity during curing/early-ageing change hydration kinetics; superplasticizers show high temperature sensitivity, with heat-accelerated hydration reducing workability windows and increasing early strength demands. <cite id="5366ad11-2">The initial hydration heat release of rapidly hydrating systems is highly temperature sensitive and can impact the high temperature sensitivity of superplasticizers</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-4">Temperature affects admixture performance by changing hydration speed, workability retention, air stability, and early strength development</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-5">At different temperatures, the effect of retarder on initial setting time decreases as temperature increases, requiring dosage adjustment</cite>.
- Freeze–thaw (FT), UV/radiation, and climate aging modify concrete surfaces and interfaces. Air-entraining/adhesion admixtures show strengthened role in mitigating damage pathways opened by FT cracking, while exposure can also degrade polymer-rich surfaces. <cite id="461089af-2">Freeze–thaw damage creates cracks that allow water and harmful ions to penetrate</cite>. <cite id="461089af-5">Freeze–thaw temperature, curing conditions, and rate are key factors affecting FT durability</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-4">Air-entraining agents and water reducers can enhance FT resistance via different mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-0">Freeze–thaw performance of air-entrained mixes is a recognized design concern; comparisons have been made with resin-based systems</cite>. <cite id="461089af-8">Long-term exposure to elevated temperatures causes water loss and decreased compressive strength, with associated property changes in hardened states</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-7">Temperature and humidity affect drying rate and plastic shrinkage, altering cracking risk in early ages</cite>. 
- UV/radiation and chemical weathering further accelerate binder aging and can modify polymer-based admixture films, affecting air stability and adhesion; protective admixtures (e.g., styrene–butadiene lattices) are selected for improved freeze–thaw and chemical attack resistance. <cite id="461089af-0">Systematic exposure to UV followed by freeze–thaw cycles degrades surface layers, affecting durability evolution</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-9">Styrene–butadiene latex admixtures provide excellent chemical attack and freeze–thaw resistance due to polymer modification</cite>.

Mixing, placement, and curing conditions
- Ambient and pour-time conditions govern early hydration and slump stability. Warmer mixes hydrate faster, reducing workability retention windows and increasing the need for heat-tolerant superplasticizers and/or higher doses of retarders. <cite id="5366ad11-1">Dosage and ambient temperature are key factors affecting superplasticizer performance; high range water reducers are sensitive to these effects</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-6">Higher temperatures accelerate cement hydration; to achieve the same retarding time, more retarders are required</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-9">Hot weather requires superplasticizers and retarders to maintain workability and prevent rapid slump loss</cite>.
- Air-entraining admixtures deliver freeze–thaw durability through air-void system quality, but performance depends on correct dosage, w-c ratio, and mixing energy; marginal mixes entrain fewer/fewer-dispersed air voids and show weaker FT resistance. <cite id="6001fee2-2">Tiny and well-dispersed entrained air voids promote FT durability by accommodating ice pressure</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-0">Synthetic air-entraining admixtures can yield marginal air mixes; entrained air content and freeze–thaw performance are critical</cite>.
- Cold-weather admixtures depress the freezing point and manage early strength when ambient temperatures fall; set-controlling systems are tailored to prevent freeze damage during curing. <cite id="461089af-3">Cold-weather admixture systems lower the initial freezing point and promote early strength gain as concrete cures, improving in-place performance</cite>.

Chemical and material environment (composition and aggregates)
- Alkalinity and cement dissolution products (e.g., Ca(OH)2, PO4^3−) determine complexation and dispersion of polyelectrolytic admixtures; high-alkali cements/pozzolans can change required dosages and compatibility. High range water reducers (HRWRs) often rely on sulfonated compounds whose interactions with cement and SCMs govern slump and retention. <cite id="5366ad11-8">In cement-based self-leveling mortars, excessive water causes bleeding/segregation; chemical admixtures balance fluidity and stability</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-2">High temperature sensitivity and early heat release drive interactions between HRWR chemistry and hydration kinetics</cite>.
- SCMs (fly ash, slag) change pore solution chemistry and viscosity, altering HRWR action and FT behavior; some admixtures are selected specifically to work with SCMs to achieve stable workability and durability. <cite id="6001fee2-1">Reviews of additives, including SCMs and chemical admixtures, discuss how supplementary materials interact with admixtures to influence performance</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-4">Chemical admixtures such as air-entraining agents and water reducers enhance FT resistance in mixes containing SCMs</cite>.
- Aggregate–polymer interactions and sorption affect admixture distribution and film formation; entrained air and internal curing paths via SAPs can stabilize drying and reduce plastic shrinkage. <cite id="6001fee2-5">Internally cured concrete using SAPs performs satisfactorily in freeze–thaw when an air-entraining admixture is used, indicating coupled effects of internal curing and air-entrainment</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-8">High fluidity mixes risk segregation; polymer-based viscosity modifiers and internal curing strategies stabilize workability and reduce bleeding</cite>.

Specific admixture classes and condition sensitivities
- Superplasticizers/HRWRs: sensitivity to temperature and w/c, with dosages needing adjustment in hot weather or high-heat systems; polymer surfactancy and counterion binding change in alkaline cement liquor, affecting dispersion and retention. <cite id="5366ad11-5">The effect of retarder on initial setting time decreases as temperature rises, requiring higher dosages to maintain set delay</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-2">High temperature accelerates hydration heat release and makes HRWR performance highly temperature sensitive</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-0">Comparative tests at 25 and 40 °C showed both reference admixtures exhibited dispersing effects and reduced water demand</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-9">HRWRs are used to decrease water demand and maintain workability under hot weather</cite>.
- Retarders: performance scales with temperature and humidity-driven drying; they are deployed to extend setting times in hot, windy, or rapidly drying conditions. <cite id="5366ad11-5">As temperature increases, the effect of a retarder on initial setting time decreases and dosage must increase to maintain performance</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-6">High-temperature environments demand higher retarder dosages to achieve the same retarding effect</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-1">Factors affecting use include ambient temperature and dosage rate</cite>.
- Air-entraining agents: create microvoid networks for FT resistance, but their air-void system, dosage, mixing time, and cement type determine durability outcomes. <cite id="6001fee2-2">Well-dispersed entrained air improves frost durability</cite>. <cite id="461089af-2">Freeze–thaw cracking worsens with poor air-void structure</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-4">Air-entraining agents enhance FT resistance by specific mechanisms</cite>.
- Shrinkage/compaction and internal curing: conditions like temperature swings and low compaction pressure lead to plastic shrinkage; polymer-based shrinkage-control admixtures and internal curing (SAPs with air-entrainment) stabilize laterability/porosity. <cite id="5366ad11-7">Temperature and humidity increases drying rate and shrinkage, leading to cracking before final setting</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-5">SAP-based internal curing, with an air-entraining admixture, yields acceptable FT resistance</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-9">Latex-based admixtures improve freeze–thaw and chemical resistance via polymer-modified interfacial zones</cite>.
- Surface/repair/adhesion: UV and radiation exposure degrade polymer films and adhesive surfaces; freeze–thaw opens microcracks that reduce bond; specialized adhesion and crystalline/latex admixtures are selected to restore durability and bonding under such conditions. <cite id="461089af-0">UV followed by freeze–thaw exposure drives progressive surface degradation</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-8">Polymer-modified systems improve resistance to damage mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="461089af-8">Extensive freeze–thaw cycles and chemical exposure worsen fatigue resistance of strengthened concrete</cite>.

Practical implications across conditions
- Cold environment: use freezing-point-depressing/corrosion-controlling admixtures, adjust dosage for slower hydration, and ensure early strength gain before freeze; protect against moisture loss. <cite id="461089af-3">Cold-weather admixture systems depress the freezing point and promote early strength</cite>. 
- Hot, dry/windy conditions: increase superplasticizer dosage or select heat-resistant formulations, add more retarder per temperature-rise, control evaporation, and monitor early losses; consider internal curing to reduce plastic shrinkage. <cite id="5366ad11-5">Higher temperatures require higher retarder dosages to maintain set times</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-4">Admixtures affect workability retention and air stability under temperature effects</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-7">High temperature and humidity accelerate drying and shrinkage</cite>. 
- Freeze–thaw/chemical exposure: specify air-entraining admixtures that produce stable air-void systems and use polymer-modified waterproofing/adhesion or crystalline admixtures; validate compatibility with SCMs and dosages for long-term FT resistance. <cite id="6001fee2-2">Entrained air void quality governs FT durability</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-4">Air-entrainers and water reducers enhance FT resistance</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-9">Polymer admixtures improve chemical and FT resistance</cite>. 
- Aging/UV/thermal cycling: anticipate loss of polymer film integrity and bond strength; select UV-stable chemistries, use latex-based or crosslinked polymers, and re-profile curing/adhesion practices for exposed surfaces. <cite id="461089af-0">UV exposure precedes FT cycles and degrades performance evolution</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-9">Latex emulsions provide superior resistance to chemical attack and freeze–thaw</cite>.

Action checklist
- For a given climate and schedule, pre-test admixtures at target temperatures and humidity to adjust dosing; verify air-void content and slump-time curves; pair air entrainers with internal curing when using SCMs. <cite id="6001fee2-2">Well-dispersed entrained air improves FT durability</cite>. <cite id="6001fee2-5">SAPs with air entrainment sustain FT resistance</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-5">Adjust retarder dosage upward as temperature increases</cite>. 
- For hot/dry placements, use high-molecular-weight viscosity modifiers and water-reducing/retaining polymers; for cold, use glycol-based and accelerating/early-strength admixtures compatible with the specific air-entraining system. <cite id="5366ad11-4">Temperature affects workability retention and early strength</cite>. <cite id="461089af-3">Cold-weather admixtures promote early strength and prevent freezing</cite>. 
- In aggressive service (chlorides, sulfates, UV), verify polymer and calcium-release compatibility, and confirm bond durability and sealing efficacy via accelerated exposure and bond testing. <cite id="461089af-0">Surface degradation under UV and FT accelerates with exposure sequences</cite>. <cite id="461089af-2">Freeze–thaw opens pathways to harmful ions</cite>. <cite id="461089af-8">Fatigue resistance degrades without adequate protection</cite>. 
- In mix design, calibrate HRWR/retarder with w/c and SCM type; avoid excessive water to prevent bleeding/segregation, and avoid over-entraining air that harms strength. <cite id="5366ad11-8">Excess water harms stability in self-leveling mortars</cite>. <cite id="5366ad11-0">Admixtures reduce water demand and improve dispersion at standard temperatures</cite>.

# Summary

Composites commonly use high‑strength reinforcement fibers such as carbon, glass (E‑ and S‑glass), aramid (e.g., Kevlar), and historically boron; natural and bio‑based fibers (flax, jute, hemp, kenaf, etc.) are also used, as are hybrid combinations of these types. Fibers are supplied as continuous tows/rovings, chopped strands or mats, woven and non‑woven fabrics, prepregs (pre‑impregnated with resin), and thermoset sheet/bulk molding compounds (SMC/BMC). Manufacturing typically follows one of several primary routes—hand/wet lay‑up and vacuum bag/bladder, compression molding (including autoclave/autovacuum), injection molding (esp. long‑glass), resin transfer molding (RTM), pultrusion, and filament winding—selected to match fiber form and product requirements. <cite id="286e590d-3">Several types of fibers are used for polymeric composites, with glass, aramid (for example, Kevlar), and carbon being the most common; boron fiber was also widely discussed historically.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-5">Glass fiber is the most common and least expensive reinforcement used in molding compounds, aramid provides wear resistance, and carbon fiber offers high specific strength/ stiffness.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-2">Hybrid composites and core methods like hand lay‑up, compression molding are emphasized in recent reviews.</cite>

# Materials used for reinforcement fibers

- Carbon fiber: High specific strength and stiffness; used in UD (unidirectional) or woven forms for aerospace, automotive, and sports equipment. <cite id="286e590d-3">Carbon is among the most common reinforcement fibers for polymeric composites.</cite>
- Glass fiber: Widely used (E‑glass for electrical insulation, S‑glass for higher mechanical load), available as chopped strand, woven roving, fabrics, and mats; economical and versatile. <cite id="286e590d-3">Glass is one of the most common reinforcement fibers.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-5">Glass fiber is the most common and least expensive reinforcement used in molding compounds.</cite>
- Aramid fiber: High toughness and impact resistance (e.g., Kevlar), often used as chopped strand or fabric for wear/impact‑prone parts. <cite id="286e590d-3">Aramid (e.g., Kevlar) is a common fiber reinforcement.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-5">Aramid fiber provides wear resistance in molded composites.</cite>
- Boron: Historically important for high specific modulus; supplanted by carbon in many applications. <cite id="286e590d-3">Boron fiber was widely used before competitive materials like carbon fiber gained prominence.</cite>
- Natural/silk/bio‑fibers: Increasingly used for sustainability; stiffness and properties are fiber‑ and process‑dependent. <cite id="286e590d-0">Natural fiber composites are reviewed with processing methods such as decortication, retting, and enzymatic extraction.</cite>

# Forms in which fibers are available

- Continuous fibers:
  - Tow/strand/yarn: very fine fibers bundled as continuous strands; used for weaving fabrics, pultrusion, winding, and as UD prepregs. <cite id="0cf004db-1">Tow is the thread used to weave carbon fiber fabrics; as a standalone it can be used to make wound parts, pultrusions, or chopped for molding compounds.</cite>
  - Roving/strands: thick bundles of continuous filaments/strands; commonly supplied for pultrusion, filament winding, and as reinforcement in structural laminates. <cite id="0cf004db-0">Roving is a simple and common form of glass fiber; it can be chopped, woven, or otherwise processed into secondary forms.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-2">Fibre rovings are directly utilised in pultrusion or filament winding processes.</cite>
- Chopped/short fibers:
  - Chopped strands/bales: short fiber cuttings used in compression, injection, and SMC/BMC; available as free‑chop or chopped‑preg. <cite id="0cf004db-8">Common fiber sale formats include strands (rovings/tow/yarn), chopped/preg options available for molding.</cite> <cite id="0cf004db-4">Reinforcements include chopped strands used in composites manufacturing.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-2">BMC uses chopped glass fibers in its formulation, while SMC is compounded and molded as sheets for large parts.</cite>
- Sheets and fabrics:
  - Woven roving/UD fabrics: continuous fibers woven into dense sheets for layup in bagging, compression, and vacuum molding. <cite id="0cf004db-6">Woven roving mats and stitched fabrics combine strength and stiffness for high‑performance laminates.</cite>
  - Nonwoven/mats: randomly oriented chopped fibers in a binder for hand lay‑up; used in marine/automotive parts with moderate loads. <cite id="0cf004db-0">Roving can be chopped, woven, or processed into secondary fiber forms; mats are derived from roving.</cite> <cite id="0cf004db-4">Mats and chopped strands are standard reinforcement formats.</cite>
- Prepregs and bulk/sheet molding compounds:
  - Prepreg (PF, LM, LF): B‑stage resin‑impregnated fabrics/tows stored at ambient or refrigerated, then autoclave‑pressed into laminates. <cite id="8d74c766-7">Hybrid layups using UD prepreg and SMC combinations were investigated, with forming constraints due to interply shear stresses.</cite>
  - SMC/BMC: sheet and bulk molding compounds using chopped glass/long fibers and catalyzed resins; injection/compression molded into complex shapes. <cite id="8d74c766-2">SMC excels in strength and surface finish for large parts, whereas BMC is optimized for small, complex, and electrically demanding components.</cite>

# Typical manufacturing methods for composite parts

- Hand/wet lay‑up and spray‑up:
  - Dry reinforcement (fibers, roving, mats, fabrics) hand‑laid over resin; optional chop‑bar chopping; cured by room‑temperature or heated bagging/bladder. Used for prototyping/low‑volume parts. <cite id="286e590d-4">Hand lay‑up is a foundational process, often followed by vacuum bagging and bladder molding for improved consolidation.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-2">Hybrid laminates are commonly fabricated with hand lay‑up and compression molding processes.</cite> <cite id="0cf004db-8">Strand-based formats are practical for wet lay-up as tows, rovings, and chopped products.</cite>
- Vacuum bagging and bladder/vacuum‑inflated molding:
  - Parts built from fabrics/mats/rovings are sealed and vacuum‑drawn to remove air and consolidate; optional heaters. Improves quality over open wet lay‑up; used widely for aircraft and premium composites. <cite id="8d74c766-4">Vacuum bag molding is a primary composite process and an improvement over wet lay‑up by applying pressure via vacuum to enhance consolidation and quality.</cite>
- Compression molding:
  - Prepreg or sheet/part feeding into heated tool; closed‑die; fast cycle; used for SMC/BMC and sheet molding; autoclave optional for higher quality/heat resistance. <cite id="8d74c766-8">Compression molding places a feeding material into an open heated mold, closes the tool, and cures under pressure and heat.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-4">Compression molding is a core route, often combined with lay‑up methods.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-3">SMC and BMC specifically employ compression molds for high‑rate production.</cite>
- Injection molding:
  - Bulk or chopped fiber feedstock (long‑glass compounds or free‑chop) melts and is forced into molds; rapid cycle; used for automotive interior parts and mass‑producible components with glass fibers. <cite id="8d74c766-2">SMC and BMC are sheet and bulk molding systems; BMC compounding addresses small, complex geometries, while SMC is optimized for large parts.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-5">Injection molding compounding mixes and injects resin and fibers into the mold cavity for curing.</cite>
- Resin Transfer Molding (RTM) and closed‑mold processes:
  - Dry or chopped fiber preforms placed in molds, then resin injected under vacuum/pressure; variants include closed‑RTM, Vacuum Assisted Resin Transfer Molding (VARTM), and autoclaveable systems; widely used for production parts. <cite id="286e590d-4">Vacuum bagging advances over wet lay‑up are part of closed‑mold families used to achieve pressure consolidation and better quality.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-4">Vacuum bag molding is widely applied across closed‑mold composite production to improve fiber wetting and consolidation relative to open lay‑up.</cite>
- Pultrusion:
  - Continuous fibers (tow/rovings) impregnated, heated, and drawn through a die to form constant‑cross‑section profiles; commonly glass or carbon roving; high throughput for beams, rods, channels. <cite id="0cf004db-0">Roving is simple and common; processing into secondary forms supports pultrusion.</cite> <cite id="0cf004db-2">Fibre rovings may be directly utilised in pultrusion, offering a primary route for continuous reinforcement into profiles.</cite>
- Filament winding:
  - Continuous tow/rovings wound under tension onto a rotating mandrel with resin, followed by curing; used for pressure vessels, tubes; fiber orientation tailored by winding pattern. <cite id="0cf004db-2">Continuous sheet products are preferred; rovings are directly applicable to pultrusion and also used in filament winding processes.</cite>
- Long‑glass and hybrid molding:
  - Injection and compression molding of long‑glass (LG) compounds for automotive parts; hybrid laminates combine carbon UD with glass mats/prepregs to balance stiffness, impact, and cost. <cite id="286e590d-2">Hybrid composites combining different fiber types are built via hand lay‑up and compression molding routes.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-7">Hybrid layups combining carbon UD prepreg with SMC showed poor forming characteristics due to interply shear stresses, highlighting design/manufacturing trade‑offs in hybrid stacking.</cite>

# Fiber–process matchings (rules of thumb)

- Continuous tows/rovings: weave into fabrics or use as UD prepregs for autoclave lamination; wind (filament winding) or pull through dies (pultrusion); produce structural beams, pipes, laminates. <cite id="0cf004db-1">Tow weaves into fabrics and is used in winding and pultrusion depending on form.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-3">Carbon and glass continuous fibers are core to advanced polymer matrix composites.</cite>
- Chopped mats/strands: hand lay‑up/vacuum bag or compression mold into sandwich cores and structural parts; use in SMC/BMC for low‑density, complex parts, and injection molding for mass production. <cite id="0cf004db-0">Chopping and mat formation converts roving into a secondary form suitable for molding.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-2">SMC/BMC rely on chopped fiber formats for molding into parts of varied complexity.</cite>
- Prepreg UD/fabrics: autoclave lamination (prepreg) or compression bag molding (wet fabric/mat), producing high‑quality aerospace/automotive laminates. <cite id="8d74c766-7">Forming of hybrid (UD prepreg with SMC) shows interply stresses can limit layup combinations; careful process design is needed.</cite>
- Sheet molding: SMC/BMC compression molding for automotive exteriors, dashboards, truck beds; rapid cycle time. <cite id="8d74c766-2">SMC excels for large parts with surface quality, while BMC suits small, complex, electrically demanding parts.</cite> <cite id="8d74c766-3">Compression molds for SMC and BMC are common tooling platforms.</cite>

# Notes on performance and trends

- Hybridization (e.g., carbon UD for stiffness with glass mat/prepreg for toughness/cost) is prevalent; forming behavior depends on fiber orientation compatibility and interfacial shear, which can limit hybrid layup options without tailored cure schedules. <cite id="8d74c766-7">Hybrid layup combinations exhibited poor forming characteristics due to high interply shear stresses, underscoring the need to manage orientation transitions and bonding at cure.</cite>
- Vacuum bag/bladder and compression processes improve fiber‑to‑resin ratios and surface quality versus open wet lay‑up, enabling higher performance at moderate volumes. <cite id="8d74c766-4">Vacuum bag molding improves over wet lay‑up by applying pressure through vacuum to consolidate laminates, producing better quality.</cite>
- Natural and bio‑fibers are growing due to sustainability; properties and durability are fiber‑specific and process‑dependent, often traded against carbon/glass for wet heat and mechanical extremes. <cite id="286e590d-0">Recent reviews cover extraction/processing for natural fibers and their integration into composite matrices.</cite> <cite id="286e590d-5">Glass, aramid, and carbon dominate for structural strength, whereas natural and silk fibers are used where stiffness tolerances are moderate and sustainability is prioritized.</cite>

# Summary

Board games with social negotiation and hidden information act as "micro-labs" for social decision-making. They scale down real-world uncertainties—hidden roles, conflicting agendas, imperfect communication, and small-group debate—so teams can be studied, iterated, and measured at low cost. These mechanics mirror core social-cognitive processes: asymmetric information and deception (The Resistance), strategic persuasion and misinformation resistance (Codenames/Secret Hitler), advisor reliance under concealed actions (Spymasters-like hidden-movement), and deliberative voting with memory/history effects (Werewolf-style eliminations). Multiple studies show that behavior in such games relates to real-world decision tendencies and that targeted game designs can train resistance to bias and disinformation. <cite id="1a296671-0">Reviews of social decision-making situate these behaviors in established frameworks spanning behavioral experiments and neural mechanisms. <cite id="1a296671-2">Work linking in‑game and real‑world choices demonstrates external validity for behavior readouts.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-6">Design programs (e.g., Tiltfactor) explicitly target biases like stereotype threat and prejudice through game mechanics.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-3">The Resistance exemplifies social deduction mechanics where hidden roles and debate drive outcomes.</cite>

# Mechanisms mirrored in games

## Asymmetric information, deception, and deduction

Social deduction games center on asymmetric information: players know partial data, have incentives to lie or mislead, and must infer others' knowledge and intentions. <cite id="1a296671-3">The Resistance presents opposing teams (Resistance vs. Spies), secret roles, and mission success criteria where communication, bluffing, accusation, and vote dynamics determine outcomes.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-5">Social deduction games formalize the problem of uncovering hidden role or allegiance via socially produced evidence and voting.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-8">Algorithmic analyses of Werewolf-like mechanics emphasize deliberation quality and the study of voting strategies under uncertainty.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-9">Empirical studies in social deduction show players rely on historically observed evidence, trust signals from peers, and strategic considerations about whether interlocutors intend to deceive.</cite> These designs operationalize classic questions in game theory and social psychology: how do teams coordinate under hidden payoff-relevant information; when do false accusations outperform information sharing; and under what conditions can majorities infer the correct culprit?

## Persuasive communication, leadership framing, and misinformation resistance

Games like Codenames and Secret Hitler embody leader‑mediated agendas and strategic communication. A designated leader sets the interpretive frame ("red" might hint at "attack," "ambush," or "agent"), teammates must infer intentions and filter competing cues, while opponents attempt to sow discord. <cite id="7ed7d8d6-3">Interventions developed in misinformation research demonstrate that training improves resistance to deceptive narratives, aligning with Codenames-like tasks where players must critically evaluate cues, identify bias, and avoid cascades to falsehoods.</cite> <cite id="7ed7d8d6-0">Psychological reviews of misinformation show how familiarity, emotion, and motivation bias acceptance, explaining why repeated or emotionally charged leader cues can dominate.</cite> <cite id="7ed7d8d6-2">Integrative models emphasize cognitive and social risk factors that facilitate misinformation uptake, matching the conditions under which a leader's misframed agenda can steer teams toward suboptimal missions.</cite> <cite id="7ed7d8d6-4">Active interventions to build metacognitive checks and verification habits in group discussion align with game mechanics that force players to justify interpretations and justify why others' interpretations are wrong.</cite> Together, these mechanics mirror real-world crisis decision-making, where initial frames set cascades in intelligence briefings, crisis talks, or political negotiations. <cite id="7ed7d8d6-6">Disinformation research highlights how narratives are crafted to exploit psychological susceptibilities on a large scale, reinforcing the relevance of leader‑influenced small-group communication in games.</cite>

## Hidden movement, cascades, and advisor influence

Hidden-movement games (e.g., Spymasters) keep agents' actions concealed while decisions depend on partial, strategically interpreted telemetry. This mirrors organizational settings where leaders enact policies behind a fog of ambiguity and subordinates must infer goals from sparse signals. <cite id="c1fb0435-1">Hidden-movement mechanics appear across a genre defined by persistent concealment of unit/action knowledge.</cite> <cite id="c1fb0435-5">Information cascades occur when agents ignore private signals and follow predecessors' actions—a mechanism directly relevant to how teams read misleading or noisy leader cues over time.</cite> <cite id="c1fb0435-0">Formal models show that capturing dynamic decision processes is essential to explain how cascades emerge, which maps to players who over‑weight early accusations or alliance signals.</cite> <cite id="c1fb0435-3">Active-inference models of repeated interactions highlight how uncertainty, confidence, and priors shape sequential choices, paralleling players' updating after each intercepted mission or disputed clue.</cite> Advisor-dependent hidden-movement games encode classic "multi-advisor" problems: aggregating heterogeneous interpretations, resisting groupthink, and weighing confidence in sources—precisely the challenges faced in intelligence analysis, policy review, and crisis response. <cite id="c1fb0435-9">Foundational definitions of "hidden/disclosed information" clarify when evidence becomes public and how timing affects reliance, a core design lever in these games.</cite>

## Deliberation, voting, and decision trees

In deliberative social deduction, teams debate, pool evidence, and vote. Over rounds, this creates memory and path dependence: early debates change what later voters consider credible. <cite id="6cc41192-8">Werewolf-like settings formalize voting as a decision procedure under uncertainty, enabling study of coalition formation, strategic abstention, and "moving the goalposts" dynamics.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-2">Pragmatic analyses describe how players internalize simple decision trees—resistance plans propose assignments that optimize mission success against possible spy countervalue, while spies choose worst-branch responses.</cite> This encodes classic coordination/commitment problems: can majorities commit to independent evaluation of evidence, or will they drift toward "in-group" signals and polarized outcomes? <cite id="1a296671-0">Behavioral and neural models show how social preferences and recursive reasoning affect cooperation in interactive settings.</cite>

# Why games matter as research platforms

Games make social decision experiments scalable, fast, and transparent. They allow orthogonal manipulation of uncertainty (hidden roles vs. revealed), agenda quality (leader priors), communication style (direct/indirect), and network structure (who talks to whom), with immediate payoff structures (mission pass/fail) that make outcomes measurable. <cite id="1a296671-0">Reviews highlight how human social decision-making is studied with interactive paradigms spanning behavioral economics and neuroscience.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-2">Experimental work demonstrates in‑game behaviors correspond to real-world behavioral tendencies, strengthening external validity.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-6">Applied programs (e.g., Tiltfactor) show how game design can explicitly target bias and social-cognitive skills, offering templates for intervention studies.</cite>

Quantitatively, hidden-role studies examine how teams update on evidence and when accusations become informative versus destructive. <cite id="6cc41192-7">Closed-environment studies manipulate opponents/conditions to measure reliance data, trust calibration, and deception detection, yielding testable hypotheses about deliberation quality.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-9">Players' reliance on different data types (earlier votes, facial cues, consistency) and assessments of likely intentions mirror real-world diagnostic heuristics, useful for debiasing.</cite>

On communication quality, AI analyses of social deduction dialogues provide controlled datasets to benchmark persuasion and deception detection, which can be mapped to human teams learning verification routines. <cite id="6cc41192-6">Diplomacy-derived deception datasets and models of persuasion strategies operationalize linguistic cues and strategic intent, offering a bridge from boardroom to lab to AI evaluation.</cite>

# Designing for insight (and rigor)

Researchers can adapt social games to study specific mechanisms and translate findings to policy. <cite id="c1fb0435-5">Information-cascade experiments can test whether randomized "early dissent" moves or evidence diversification breaks harmful cascades.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-6">Games can be engineered to train metacognitive checks, implicit bias mitigation, or misinformation resilience; Tiltfactor shows how mechanics are matched to target skills.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-8">Board games improve critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and decision-making—skills central to social negotiation—providing a plausible pathway from play to measurable competence gains.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-2">Cross-validation against real-world behavior metrics is essential to avoid playground-validity traps.</cite>

When building a study:
- Map mechanics to mechanisms explicitly: hidden-movement to information cascades; leader-wording to agenda-setting; voting patterns to coalition stability. <cite id="c1fb0435-5">Use cascade theory to define manipulation levers (e.g., early verifiable signals).</cite> <cite id="7ed7d8d6-2">Incorporate misinformation risk factors (motivation, emotion) into leader-cue designs.</cite>
- Instrument both content and process: log votes, time stamps, confidence ratings, and eye/voice data to separate inference quality from influence dynamics. <cite id="c1fb0435-3">Active inference models motivate measuring uncertainty and confidence states.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-7">Eye-tracking and movement data capture reliance on surface vs. substantive cues.</cite>
- Control the social graph and role mix; randomize leader quality and initial frames to isolate effects. <cite id="1a296671-6">Mechanics should be engineered to train targeted biases while maintaining ecological plausibility.</cite>

# Practical takeaways for The Resistance and friends

- In The Resistance, mission outcomes hinge on teams solving a decision-theoretic puzzle: aggregate noisy, potentially adversarial signals under time pressure. <cite id="6cc41192-2">Resistance plans embed decision trees, with spies adversarially pruning branches—ideal for studying robust inference under hidden sabotage.</cite>
- In Codenames/Secret Hitler, the leader's mapping of words/emotions to actions tests persuasion and disinformation resistance. <cite id="7ed7d8d6-0">Familiarity and emotional "hot cues" increase acceptance risk, so interventions that force verification or dissent increase decision quality.</cite> <cite id="7ed7d8d6-3">Bad News–style interventions can be embedded into leader-cue rounds to build resistance to misleading frames.</cite>
- In hidden-movement spycomms, research can test whether decentralized querying or centralized synthesis reduces cascades and advisor dominance. <cite id="c1fb0435-5">Theoretically, cascades arise when early signals outweigh private evidence—so experiments can test whether protocols flip that balance.</cite> <cite id="c1fb0435-0">Models emphasize dynamic updating rules, aligning with round-by-round mission debriefs and revised accusations.</cite>

# Caveats and opportunities

Games compress reality; results must be interpreted with face-validity checks and, where possible, linked to consequential skills and behaviors. <cite id="1a296671-2">Evidence that in‑game choices predict real‑world choices supports external validity when studies measure decision quality and bias changes.</cite> <cite id="6cc41192-6">AI deception datasets show how lab-designed communication tasks can be double‑bladed—useful for benchmarking, yet easily gamed without process rigor.</cite> <cite id="1a296671-6">Conversely, carefully designed games can train and transfer bias-resistance skills, illustrating the design‑science potential of social decision-making research.</cite>

Below is how object‑recognition–specific brain activations have been characterized across complementary methods and brain regions, emphasizing hallmark signatures and dissociations.

Overview: distributed, hierarchical “what” pathway
- Core evidence converges on a distributed ventral–lateral–parietal network that supports object recognition, with strong involvement of inferotemporal cortex and lateral/retrosplenial parietal areas, and lesser but specific contributions from parietal “place/trajectory” systems that become engaged when object position or affordances are encoded or used for navigation or action planning. <cite id="e68a01d3-0">Object-recall effects were evident in regions inferior and posterior to primary somatosensory cortex, around the ventral/retrosplenial/angular cortex, implicating posterior/ventral parieto‑temporal systems for object representations and recall</cite> <cite id="e68a01d3-2">Parietal inactivation influences inferotemporal cortex activations, and distal parietal damage can drive changes in object processing in inferotemporal cortex</cite> <cite id="e68a01d3-3">Posterior parietal cortex supports spatial representation of objects for action planning and control</cite> <cite id="b5842150-3">Inferior temporal neurons encode positions of different objects in scenes, linking “what” and “where/how” systems</cite> <cite id="b5842150-8">Primate hippocampal “view” representations are intertwined with inferotemporal object input and orbitofrontal value, consistent with a hierarchy that integrates object identity with scene and action contexts</cite>.

1) Lesion and neuropsychological dissociations: category‑specific effects and parietal–temporal substrates
- Human category‑specific deficits dissociate object agnosia from face or place recognition when lesions target parietal lobe and its connections to inferotemporal cortex; such cases show preserved basic vision yet impaired object recognition while scene/face systems remain intact or relatively spared, with lesion overlap at posterior parietal cortex. <cite id="e68a01d3-4">According to object agnosia (e.g., DF), posterior parietal lesions overlap the left parietal region and produce selective deficits in object recognition despite intact basic vision</cite> <cite id="e68a01d3-8">Parietal cortex is the brain region most consistently implicated in visual agnosia by functional neuroimaging in these patients</cite> <cite id="dbd1381b-1">The lateral occipital complex has a central role in human object recognition; reviews of lesions and neuropsychology converge on posterior occipital/parietal contributions to object agnosia</cite> <cite id="dbd1381b-4">Object selectivity and category representations are argued not to be fully captured by the object-recognition framework alone, pointing to additional category systems (face, place) with distinct neural substrates and dissociable profiles</cite>.
- Converging anatomy links inferotemporal cortex to parietal object memory/affordance systems. <cite id="b5842150-5">Neurons coding spatial position relative to body parts and affordances are found in posterior parietal cortex and its connected networks, providing a substrate for object use and recognition</cite> <cite id="b5842150-2">Hypotheses on posterior parietal specializations propose subregions tuned to object use and affordances, bridging visual form and action</cite>.

2) Single‑unit recordings and place/object concepts in inferotemporal and parietal cortex
- Inferior temporal neurons represent objects with some positional components (“view” and “place”) and integrate object identity with location/affordance signals; macaque studies show object neurons whose firing depends on object position within a scene, and mixed “object‑place” concept responses whose tuning can be driven by either object or location features. <cite id="b5842150-3">Inferior temporal neurons encode positions of different objects in the scene</cite> <cite id="b5842150-5">Posterior parietal representations of spatial positions relative to body parts connect to object-related processing</cite> <cite id="b5842150-7">Object‑place cells in macaques can be activated by object or by place, showing concept‑like properties with dual selectivity</cite> <cite id="b5842150-9">Primate posterior parietal cortex maps position within trajectories, suggesting broader spatial‑coding substrates relevant to object use within environments</cite>.
- Hippocampal “view” and “concept” cells receive object “what” inputs from inferotemporal cortex and spatial inputs from parietal cortex, organizing object identity by scene view and context—functional characterization of object representations in terms of multi‑feature selectivity and contextual coupling. <cite id="b5842150-0">Inferior temporal object inputs and orbitofrontal reward inputs connect to hippocampal spatial view systems; in macaques these associations have been demonstrated</cite> <cite id="b5842150-8">Spatial view neurons provide representations of locations in viewed space and integrate information from inferotemporal cortex</cite>.

3) fMRI signatures of object selectivity, adaptation, and category dissociations
- fMRI adaptation measures dissociate object categories from faces/scenes across ventral temporal–parietal cortex: category‑general object regions (e.g., lateral/retrosplenial parietal and inferotemporal) show robust repetition suppression, whereas category‑specific regions (PPA/LOPP) and specialized streams (OFC for faces; medial/lateral parietal for scenes) exhibit distinct adaptation profiles; quantitative analyses link category tuning to the strength of adaptation and show distributed repetition effects during object viewing. <cite id="dbd1381b-0">fMRI‑adaptation studies quantitatively relate category selectivity to repetition‑related BOLD suppression, demonstrating category‑general and category‑specific object effects across ventral cortex</cite> <cite id="dbd1381b-2">Extensive characterization shows concurrent category‑selective activity across ventral occipito‑temporal regions, supporting a hierarchical and context‑dependent organization of object recognition</cite> <cite id="e68a01d3-0">Object‑recall-related BOLD increases localize to posterior/ventral parietal regions inferior and posterior to somatosensory cortex, indicating category‑general object memory effects distinct from sensory cortex</cite>.
- Functional dissociations by task: TMS to category‑selective areas shows that disrupting occipital face area selectively impairs recognition relative to categorization, consistent with the idea that posterior streams support perceptual recognition of exemplars and specialized categories, whereas ventral/temporal systems support abstract categorization; similar causal manipulations in lateral occipital regions alter detection/categorization with reaction‑time dissociations. <cite id="dbd1381b-6">TMS to occipital face area affects recognition but not categorization of faces, indicating a dissociation between exemplar‑level recognition and category‑level processing in extrastriate cortex</cite> <cite id="dbd1381b-9">State‑dependent TMS of right lateral occipital complex revealed a dissociation between object detection and categorization and established a direct causal link between rLOC and object recognition performance</cite>.
- Invariance and tuning: object‑selective regions show strong invariance to view and perspective in multivoxel/decoding analyses and population tuning; posterior parietal and inferotemporal sites in particular support decoding of object identity across transforms, with posterior parietal sites also providing access to inferred spatial context. <cite id="e68a01d3-0">Decoding/invariance analyses over posterior parietal and adjacent cortex show object‑related activity that supports category‑general object memory and view‑tolerant representations</cite> <cite id="b5842150-8">Inferior temporal “what” inputs drive hippocampal spatial view representations, consistent with invariant object identity signals modulated by scene view</cite>.
